Problem Solved: Eliminates miscommunication, functional gaps, unnecessary rework, and outdated documentation by establishing precise, testable, and collaboratively defined specifications.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Discovery / elicitation / analysis / specification / prioritisation / validation / change management
Input Artifacts: Business goals, stakeholder requests, existing documentation, user stories, use cases, legacy software data, customer feedback/emails
Output Artifacts: Scope statement, specifications with examples, executable specifications, living documentation system, acceptance criteria
Participants & Roles: Sponsor, business owner, SME, end user, BA, product manager, architect, developer, tester, compliance/legal
Prerequisites: Access to business stakeholders or proxy SMEs, shared agreement on business goals, and willingness to collaborate across disciplines.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Derive implementation scope collaboratively from high-level business goals. 2. Engage business stakeholders, BAs, developers, and testers in collaborative specification sessions (e.g., workshops or 'Three Amigos'). 3. Illustrate specifications with concrete, realistic examples to clarify edge cases and business logic. 4. Refine raw examples into concise, self-explanatory specifications with examples using domain language. 5. Automate validation of the specifications without modifying the specification text. 6. Run automated executable specifications continuously via continuous integration environments. 7. Evolve executable specifications continuously into a structured, searchable living documentation system.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: • What business goal are we trying to achieve with this feature? • How would this proposed feature/requirement be useful to the user? • Can you provide a concrete example of this rule in action? • What is an alternative way to check or verify this functionality? • What happens in edge cases (e.g., zero values, negative amounts, or missing dependencies)? • Is there anything else that would happen when this action occurs?
Minimal Realistic Example: A business rule for 'Free Delivery' defined with examples: 'Free delivery is offered to VIP customers purchasing at least 5 books.' Examples Table: | Customer type | Cart contents | Delivery | | VIP | 5 books | Free, Standard | | VIP | 4 books | Standard | | Regular | 10 books | Standard |
Quality Criteria & Verification: Quality is verified when all executable specifications pass automatically during continuous validation runs; specifications must be concise, testable, written in ubiquitous domain language, and self-explanatory without needing technical execution details.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: • Scripting instead of specifying (writing low-level UI steps like 'click button' rather than business rules). • Treating test automation code as second-class, unmaintained code. • Overspecifying examples by attempting to cover every single combinatorial permutation in one document. • Coupling specifications tightly with software design or UI mechanics. • Automating existing manual test scripts directly without refining them.
When NOT to Use: Not recommended when stakeholder access is completely absent with no proxy, on one-off throwaway prototypes, or for purely non-deterministic subjective requirements (such as game playability or visual aesthetics) that cannot be validated programmatically.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Test-Driven Development (TDD), Product Backlog Refinement (PBR) workshops, Continuous Integration, User Story Mapping, Effect Mapping, Feature Injection.
Supported Decisions: Scope selection, feature prioritization, release readiness/acceptance, architectural refactoring safety, regulatory compliance, release sign-off.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: For agentic and automated BA workflows: Inferred: AI agents can serve as automated facilitators to generate initial concrete examples from high-level user stories, cross-examine domain rules for missing boundary cases, generate test fixtures/glue code from business-language specifications, and perform automated checks against living documentation to detect shotgun surgery risks before code commits. Human-in-the-loop guardrails are strictly required for approving business goals, validating domain terminology, and signing off on living documentation boundaries.

Problem Solved: Uncovers underlying root causes rather than symptoms of business problems, clarifies ambiguous problem statements, and resolves conflicting stakeholder perspectives.
Input Artifacts: Initial problem requests, background documents, company reports, organisation charts, current process documentation.
Output Artifacts: Problem statement, Rich picture, Mind map, Fishbone diagram, Context diagram, project scope/ToR.
Participants & Roles: Sponsor, Business Owner, BA, SME, Business Staff.
Prerequisites: Initial business problem statement or change request, access to stakeholders and documentation.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Investigate the current situation and problem/opportunity. 2. Understand the strategic context. 3. Identify and articulate business needs. 4. Define the root problem using diagnostic techniques. 5. Define the scope of the business change project. 6. Formulate terms of reference (OSCAR) or rationale for rejection.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Why do you do this? What value does it add? What is the root cause? What is happening in practice versus what is documented? What is the real problem to be solved?
Minimal Realistic Example: Investigating declining juice sales and rising complaints at Simply Juices to reveal that aggressive telesales targets and a poorly designed website (not product quality) were the root causes.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Verification that root causes rather than symptoms are identified, alignment with strategic context, stakeholder consensus on problem statement.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Leaping to premature software solutions without investigating the problem, confusing symptoms with root causes, accepting verbal statements without quantitative validation.
When NOT to Use: When the issue is purely technical with zero business impact, or the root cause is completely known and verified.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: PESTLE, Five Forces, CATWOE, Activity Sampling, Surveys, Interviews, Workshops.
Supported Decisions: Scope, project initiation, project rejection.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI tools can perform automated document analysis, sentiment analysis, and initial data clustering to highlight potential anomalies or recurring complaint topics.

Method Name: Feasibility Assessment and Business Case Development
Problem Solved: Reduces financial, technical, and business uncertainty before committing resources to a change initiative.
Input Artifacts: Problem statements, option descriptions, cost and benefit estimates, risk logs, strategic context.
Output Artifacts: Business Case, Feasibility Report, CARDI/RAID log, Investment Appraisal (NPV, IRR, Payback), Benefits Plan.
Participants & Roles: Sponsor, Business Owner, BA, Finance SME, Solution Architect, Project Manager.
Prerequisites: Clear definition of the business problem, identified options for solution, initial cost and benefit data.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Generate and describe options to resolve the problem. 2. Remove unviable options. 3. Identify and analyse impacts and risks for each option. 4. Identify and quantify costs and benefits. 5. Evaluate financial, technical, and business feasibility. 6. Evaluate strategic alignment (e.g., VMOST, POPIT). 7. Produce the business case and present recommendations.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Is this solution technically feasible? Can we afford it? What is the ROI/NPV? Does it fit our culture and strategy? What are the risks of doing nothing?
Minimal Realistic Example: Evaluating three options for an event registration system (basic manual upgrade, COTS package, bespoke build), proving through NPV that the COTS package offers the best risk-adjusted return.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Passes 'decision gates', demonstrates positive NPV/IRR, satisfies Force-Field analysis, clear alignment with corporate strategy.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Over-promising intangible benefits, underestimating transition costs, presenting a single preferred solution without evaluating alternatives (including 'do nothing').
When NOT to Use: When changes are minor, low-risk, or strictly mandated by legal/compliance requirements with no alternative implementation routes.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Financial models (NPV, Payback, IRR), PESTLE, Force-Field Analysis, POPIT, CARDI/RAID logs.
Supported Decisions: Scope, financial commitment, project go/no-go, option selection.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can run probabilistic financial simulations (e.g., Monte Carlo) on costs/benefits and perform real-time market/vendor analysis for COTS feasibility.

Problem Solved: Reduces operational inefficiencies, bottlenecks, hand-off errors, waste, and poor customer experiences.
Input Artifacts: Enterprise value streams, 'as is' process models, customer journey maps, performance metrics.
Output Artifacts: 'To be' business process models, task definitions, gap analysis report, revised job roles, process measurement targets.
Participants & Roles: Process Owner, BA, SME, End User/Actor, Solution Architect.
Prerequisites: Documented 'as is' business processes, clear understanding of customer value expectations and organisational targets.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Model existing ('as is') processes. 2. Analyse hand-offs, bottlenecks, and wastes (TIMWOODS). 3. Define required ('to be') processes. 4. Perform gap analysis between 'as is' and 'to be'. 5. Define process measures (time, quality, cost). 6. Identify implementation actions (e.g., POPIT changes, automation). 7. Ensure alignment with supporting IT systems.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Why is this step necessary? Where are the hand-offs? Where do queues or bottlenecks form? Does this task add value to the customer? How can we eliminate waste?
Minimal Realistic Example: Redesigning an order-fulfillment process by combining stock-checking and reservation steps, reducing processing time from 2.5 days to 4 hours.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Process efficiency gains, reduction in TIMWOODS wastes, alignment with value propositions, verification via simulation or walkthroughs.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Optimising an individual task at the expense of the end-to-end process (sub-optimisation), ignoring hand-off delays, paving over bad processes with IT automation.
When NOT to Use: When the business domain is entirely new and requires greenfield process engineering rather than incremental improvement.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: SIPOC, Value Stream Mapping, Value Chain Analysis, Six Sigma (DMAIC), Customer Journey Mapping, Lean.
Supported Decisions: Process architecture, job role design, resource allocation, automation scope.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic AI can monitor live process execution data to automatically map 'as is' variants, detect bottlenecks, and propose optimal task routing.

Problem Solved: Reduces ambiguity, miscommunication, scope creep, conflicting requirements, and solution delivery failure.
Input Artifacts: Project charter/ToR, business case, 'to be' process models, stakeholder interviews, user roles/personas.
Output Artifacts: Requirements catalogue, User stories/product backlog, Use case diagrams/descriptions, Data models (ERD/Class model), BRD.
Participants & Roles: Sponsor, Product Owner, BA, SME, Developer, Tester, Solution Architect.
Prerequisites: Agreed project scope, identified stakeholders, defined business objectives.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Elicit requirements using qualitative and quantitative techniques. 2. Uncover tacit knowledge and resolve assumptions. 3. Analyse and filter requirements (check for clarity, completeness, feasibility, correctness). 4. Structure and model requirements (use cases, data models, process models). 5. Document requirements (catalogue or user stories with acceptance criteria). 6. Prioritise requirements (MoSCoW/INVEST). 7. Validate requirements with stakeholders for baseline or backlog readiness. 8. Manage changes and maintain traceability.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: As a role, why do you want feature? What is the acceptance criterion? Is this requirement atomic, testable, and unambiguous? What happens in exception scenarios?
Minimal Realistic Example: Defining, modelling, and validating functional and non-functional requirements for an online retail portal, categorising them using MoSCoW, and creating an ERD to capture data rules.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Requirements meet quality criteria (Clear, Concise, Consistent, Relevant, Unambiguous, Correct, Testable, Traceable), validated via formal walkthroughs or INVEST checks.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Treating elicitation as passive 'requirement gathering', confusing solutions with requirements, ignoring non-functional requirements, neglecting tacit knowledge.
When NOT to Use: When using a pure COTS package with zero customization allowed, though user needs still drive selection.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: User Stories, Use Case Modelling, Prototyping, Class Modelling, ERD, MoSCoW, INVEST.
Supported Decisions: Scope, release planning, acceptance criteria, architecture, compliance.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can evaluate requirements sets for ambiguity, testability, and conflict, generate draft user stories, and automatically maintain traceability matrices.

Method Name: Stakeholder Analysis and Management (CATWOE & Power/Interest Grid)
Problem Solved: Reduces political resistance, conflicting perspectives, poor buy-in, and communication breakdowns during change initiatives.
Input Artifacts: Stakeholder list/wheel, project objectives, interview findings, organisational charts.
Output Artifacts: Power/Interest Grid, Stakeholder Management Plan, CATWOE definitions, Business Activity Models (BAM), RACI/RASCI matrix.
Participants & Roles: Sponsor, BA, Project Manager, Key Stakeholders.
Prerequisites: Identification of project stakeholders across internal and external categories.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify stakeholders using the Stakeholder Wheel. 2. Analyse stakeholders' power and interest. 3. Map stakeholders onto the Power/Interest Grid. 4. Formulate stakeholder management strategies (e.g., Key Player, Keep Satisfied). 5. Elicit individual stakeholder perspectives using CATWOE. 6. Build Business Activity Models (BAM) for contrasting perspectives. 7. Resolve conflicts to build a consensus BAM. 8. Define stakeholder responsibilities using RACI/RASCI.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Who is impacted by this change? Who holds the power to block or support it? What is the stakeholder's World View (Weltanschauung)? Who is responsible, accountable, consulted, or informed?
Minimal Realistic Example: Resolving a clash between a Sales Manager (wanting aggressive telesales) and a Customer Services Manager (wanting relationship management) by mapping their CATWOEs and building a consensus BAM.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Consensus or owner-approved BAM, clear RACI matrix, implemented stakeholder engagement plan, reduction in resistance.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Treating stakeholder groups as homogeneous, placing stakeholders on the grid where they 'should' be rather than where they 'are', ignoring low-power groups who can aggregate power.
When NOT to Use: When a change is strictly mechanical, non-contentious, and affects no human roles or responsibilities.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Soft Systems Methodology (SSM), Persona Analysis, RACI/RASCI, Mind Mapping, Rich Pictures.
Supported Decisions: Scope, priority, change management, governance structure.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI can perform social network analysis and sentiment analysis on stakeholder communications to dynamically update the Power/Interest grid and flag emerging conflicts.

Problem Solved: Reduces operational disruption, user rejection, solution defects, and failure to realize planned business benefits.
Input Artifacts: Validated requirements, acceptance criteria, 'to be' process designs, business case, solution architecture.
Output Artifacts: Test scenarios/scripts, User acceptance sign-off, Business readiness assessment, Training materials, Benefits Realisation Report.
Participants & Roles: Sponsor, Business Owner, BA, Tester, End User, Change Manager.
Prerequisites: Developed software/solution, defined acceptance criteria, readiness assessment tools (POPIT/CPPOLDAT).
Step-by-Step Procedure: Agree testing scope and accept criteria. 2. Define test scenarios, test cases, and decision tables. 3. Support business staff during user acceptance testing (UAT). 4. Conduct business readiness assessment (using POPIT/CPPOLDAT). 5. Plan transition and deployment strategy (e.g., direct, parallel, pilot, phased). 6. Address human responses to change (managing the SARAH curve). 7. Deliver training and documentation. 8. Execute deployment and transition to operational support. 9. Conduct post-implementation and benefits realisation reviews.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Does the solution satisfy the acceptance criteria? Is the business ready across People, Process, Organisation, and Technology? How will we support users through the SARAH emotional curve? Have the business benefits been realised?
Minimal Realistic Example: Assisting customer service staff in executing UAT scripts derived from use case descriptions, evaluating business readiness via CPPOLDAT, and managing a phased rollout of a new CRM system.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Formal UAT sign-off, successful business readiness evaluation, realization of benefits tracked in the Benefits Realisation Report.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Treating UAT as a late, rushed phase; neglecting the emotional/human side of change; failing to track post-implementation benefit realization.
When NOT to Use: When no business or human processes are changing (e.g., pure backend technical infrastructure upgrades requiring only automated technical testing).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: CPPOLDAT, POPIT, Decision Tables, State Charts, SARAH Curve, Benefits Dependency Network.
Supported Decisions: Release, acceptance, rollout strategy, benefits sign-off.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can automatically generate UAT test scenarios directly from user stories and acceptance criteria, as well as predict user adoption risks based on system telemetry.

Problem Solved: Prevents projects from rushing into presumed solutions, starting on vague foundations, or solving the wrong business problem.
Input Artifacts: Initial stakeholder request, business problem statement, or market opportunity.
Output Artifacts: Goal Statement (Purpose-Advantage-Measurement), Work Context Diagram, Stakeholder Map/Matrix, Business Event List, Risk List, Business Case.
Participants & Roles: Sponsor, Product Owner, Business Analyst, Product/Program Manager, Subject Matter Experts (SMEs), Architect, Key Stakeholders.
Prerequisites: Access to key decision-makers and high-level business objectives/mandates.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define the real business problem/opportunity. 2. Establish project goals using Purpose-Advantage-Measurement (PAM). 3. Draft a Work Context Diagram to define the problem space boundary. 4. Identify and map all relevant stakeholders. 5. Discover initial business events triggering the scope. 6. Evaluate project risks, constraints, and initial cost/effort. 7. Develop the Business Case. 8. Conduct Go / No-Go decision checkpoint.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What is the real business problem we are trying to solve?", "What measurable advantage does solving this bring?", "Who are the key stakeholders affected by or influencing this work?", "What external events trigger a response from this business space?", "Why is the current situation non-compliant or inefficient?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Defining the Blastoff scope for Carmen's Taperia to reduce food order errors and delivery delays by mapping customer-waiter-kitchen interactions.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Measurable goals established (e.g., quantifiable time/cost reduction); clean context boundary; agreed stakeholder list; positive Go/No-Go business case evaluation.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Presuming a specific software solution upfront; skipping Blastoff; ignoring key negative or external stakeholders; vague/unmeasurable goal statements ("make it better").
When NOT to Use: Trivial low-risk bug fixes, routine operational maintenance, or simple predefined feature tweaks with fully known domain constraints.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Agile Mini-Blastoff (iterative approach), Lean Inception, Chartering, Business Model Canvas.
Supported Decisions: Scope boundary, project Go/No-Go, budget allocation, initial release priority, stakeholder involvement strategy.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic prompts can automatically draft initial context diagrams, analyze historic project data for risk factors, and synthesize stakeholder interview transcripts into goal candidates; Human-in-the-Loop validates scope boundaries and makes the final Go/No-Go call.

Problem Solved: Reduces uncertainty when stakeholders do not know or cannot articulate what they need until they see a concrete representation.
Input Artifacts: Problem statements, goals, user personas, business event use cases.
Output Artifacts: Sketches, Low-Fidelity Wireframes, Storyboards, Mind Maps, Interactive Prototypes, Feedback Logs, Discovered Requirements.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, UX Designer, End User, SME, Product Owner.
Prerequisites: Basic understanding of the problem boundary and candidate business event use cases.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select a business use case or user scenario. 2. Generate multiple candidate solutions (avoiding a single assumed solution). 3. Create low-cost, quick sacrificial prototypes (sketches, storyboards, wireframes). 4. Walk stakeholders through the candidate prototypes. 5. Probe the prototypes to question the problem space (double-loop learning). 6. Extract essential requirements and throw away (sacrifice) the prototype.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Tell me why this candidate would solve your problem?", "How would this affect the rest of your business?", "Is this addressing all of the problem or just a symptom?", "What would you do if you had this solution?", "Does this candidate suggest another better idea?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Sketching 5 alternative ways for college students to acquire textbooks (store purchase, second-hand search, print-on-demand, tablet download, Espresso printer) to explore their actual needs.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Safe-to-fail execution; stakeholder engagement and discovery of previously hidden requirements; double-loop learning achieved (confirming or correcting the real problem).
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Pygmalion effect (falling in love with a prototype); building high-fidelity or non-sacrificial prototypes too early; treating the prototype as the final specification prematurely.
When NOT to Use: Well-understood, highly standardized technical domains with zero UI/workflow uncertainty.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Traditional Interviewing, Trawling, Scenario Walkthroughs, Contextual Inquiry.
Supported Decisions: Solution approach selection, scope refinement, user experience flow approval, requirement validation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can rapidly generate UI wireframe code, mockups, or scenario diagrams based on prompt definitions; BAs evaluate candidate variants with human users to validate underlying intent.

Method Name: Business Event and Business Use Case (BUC) Analysis
Problem Solved: Reduces complexity and organizational bias by partitioning the problem space based on external events rather than internal department structures.
Input Artifacts: Work Context Diagram, Data Dictionary, External Communication Specs.
Output Artifacts: Business Event List, Business Use Case (BUC) Descriptions/Scenarios, BUC Process Models, Event-to-Data Matrix (CRUD).
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, SME, Business Owner, System Architect, Product Owner.
Prerequisites: Defined work scope boundary and identified adjacent systems.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify adjacent systems on the Work Context Diagram. 2. List incoming data flows (triggers) and outgoing data flows. 3. Determine the business event outside the system that caused each flow. 4. Define the Business Use Case (BUC) response for each event. 5. Specify BUC start triggers, internal activities, stored data references, and exit conditions. 6. Prioritize BUCs for detailed analysis and release planning.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What happening in the outside world forces this business to respond?", "What data arrives to inform the work that an event occurred?", "What is the desired business outcome when this event is processed?", "What time-based or conditional rules trigger a response?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Analyzing the event "Customer orders coffee" in an online store, mapping its triggering data flow "Capsule Order" to its BUC response ending with order confirmation and fulfillment dispatch.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Data conservation check (all incoming data is accounted for and outgoing data is generated from inputs/stored data); clear event boundaries (independent processing units).
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Partitioning work by internal departments instead of external events; confusing UI mouse-clicks with business events; missing time-triggered or conditional events.
When NOT to Use: Pure computational algorithms or batch processing modules devoid of external interactions.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Functional Decomposition, Domain-Driven Design (Bounded Contexts), User Story Mapping.
Supported Decisions: Scope boundaries, iteration planning, subsystem architecture partitioning, requirement ownership.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic event monitors can automatically classify log inputs and external system messages into discrete business event categories; LLMs can draft baseline BUC responses based on event inputs.

Problem Solved: Eliminates confusion during requirements discovery between current physical implementations and future essential requirements.
Input Artifacts: Existing documentation, user interviews, process observations, target goals.
Output Artifacts: How-Now Model (Current Physical), What-Now Model (Current Essential), Future-What Model (Future Essential), Future-How Model (Future Physical).
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Business Owner, SME, Architect, UX Designer.
Prerequisites: Understanding of the business scope and objectives.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Model the current physical implementation ("How-Now") if needed to baseline. 2. Abstract away current technology, people, and organizational structures to uncover the current essential business policy ("What-Now"). 3. Add new business goals, innovations, and policy changes to define the desired future essential state ("Future-What"). 4. Apply modern technology, human roles, and ready-made components to design the future physical solution ("Future-How").
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "How do you do this job today?" (How-Now), "Why do you do this activity? What is the underlying business policy?" (What-Now), "What should the business policy be in the future, independent of technology?" (Future-What), "What technology/people will implement this future policy?" (Future-How)
Minimal Realistic Example: Analyzing a luggage check-in process: moving from paper boarding passes and counter staff (How-Now) to verifying reservation and passenger identity (What-Now), adding self-service identity matching (Future-What), and implementing facial recognition kiosks (Future-How).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Clear separation between 'above-the-line' (essential) and 'below-the-line' (physical) models; elimination of technological fossils from the future essential model.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Jumping directly from How-Now to Future-How (rushing from one technology implementation to another without finding the essential business policy); getting stuck indefinitely in How-Now modeling.
When NOT to Use: Pure greenfield initiatives with zero existing legacy processes or completely novel product domains where no current baseline exists.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Essential Systems Analysis, As-Is / To-Be Process Mapping, Value Stream Mapping.
Supported Decisions: Business process re-engineering, technology selection, legacy system replacement strategy, core business rule definition.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can analyze legacy code or process logs to extract essential business rules ("What-Now") automatically, freeing human analysts to focus on innovative "Future-What" design.

Problem Solved: Eliminates ambiguity and subjectivity in requirements, making soft, vague, or complex functional/non-functional requirements testable and verifiable.
Input Artifacts: Requirement Descriptions, Rationales, User Stories, Business Rules, Quality Standards.
Output Artifacts: Atomic Requirements with Fit Criteria (Volere Snow Cards), User Stories with Given/When/Then Acceptance Criteria, Test Cases.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Product Owner, Tester/QA Lead, SME, Developer.
Prerequisites: Draft requirement descriptions or user stories with clear business rationales.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Take a requirement description or story. 2. Analyze its rationale ("So that...") to understand the core justification. 3. Determine the appropriate scale of measurement (time, accuracy, %, compliance standard). 4. Define a precise, unambiguous threshold or condition (Fit Criterion / Acceptance Criterion). 5. Review with testers and stakeholders to ensure objectivity and feasibility. 6. Formulate test cases based on the criteria.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "How will we know if the delivered solution successfully satisfies this requirement?", "What is the scale of measurement for this quality attribute?", "What result would be considered a failure?", "Given context, when action, what is the expected then outcome?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Converting the requirement "The product shall be user friendly" with rationale "To ensure rapid adoption" into the Fit Criterion: "80% of a test panel of casual users shall successfully complete order placement within 3 minutes on their first attempt without training."
Quality Criteria & Verification: Criteria are binary (pass/fail); quantifiable or objectively verifiable against a clear standard or test; agreed upon by both customer and QA.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Using unmeasurable adjectives ("fast", "intuitive", "secure", "flexible") without fit criteria; setting unrealistic or uncoordinated tolerance levels.
When NOT to Use: None; all valid requirements and stories require fit or acceptance criteria to be testable.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Behavior-Driven Development (BDD), Test-Driven Development (TDD), Planguage (Tom Gilb's method).
Supported Decisions: Requirement sign-off, QA test pass/fail determination, product release readiness, vendor compliance validation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLMs can suggest precise Given/When/Then acceptance criteria and test cases from user story descriptions; human testers and BAs review and adjust thresholds for domain realism.

Problem Solved: Prevents bad, ambiguous, incomplete, or out-of-scope requirements from passing into development, reducing costly downstream rework.
Input Artifacts: Snow Cards, User Stories, Requirements Specification, Work Context Diagram, Project Goals.
Output Artifacts: Validated Requirements Repository, Quality Review Feedback/Defect Log, Approved Requirements/Backlog.
Participants & Roles: Requirements Guardian / Senior BA, Product Owner, System Architect, QA/Tester.
Prerequisites: Formulated requirements or stories containing descriptions, rationales, and fit/acceptance criteria.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Submit candidate requirements to the Quality Gateway before adding them to the official repository/backlog. 2. Check for Scope Alignment using the Context Diagram. 3. Check for Relevancy against Project Goals. 4. Check for Completeness (all snow card fields or story attributes present). 5. Verify testability of Fit/Acceptance Criteria. 6. Check for consistency of terminology against the Data Dictionary. 7. Check for viability, gold plating, and potential conflicts. 8. Approve, reject, or request rework for the requirement.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Is this requirement inside our context boundary?", "Does it directly contribute to our project goals?", "Is the fit criterion testable?", "Is this requirement gold-plating?", "Are the terms used defined consistently in the data dictionary?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Rejecting a proposed requirement "The system shall play a greeting sound when the user logs in" because its customer dissatisfaction score is 1 (nobody cares if missing), identifying it as gold plating that adds cost without business value.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Requirement passes 100% of gateway checklist tests (In Scope, Relevant, Complete, Testable, Consistent, Viable, Non-Gold-plated).
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Bypassing the gateway due to schedule pressure; treating reviews as rubber-stamping; lacking clear objective criteria for requirement acceptance.
When NOT to Use: Informal exploratory prototyping phases where ideas are explicitly disposable.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Formal Fagan Inspections, Walkthroughs, BDD Specification by Example.
Supported Decisions: Backlog approval, baseline specification sign-off, developer task assignment readiness.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can act as automated Quality Gateway auditors to instantly scan requirements for vagueness, missing rationales, or terminology inconsistencies against the data dictionary, flagging defects for human BA resolution.

Method Name: CRUD Analysis (Create, Read, Update, Delete Check)
Problem Solved: Identifies missing business events, missing requirements, and orphan data entities across the system.
Input Artifacts: Business Data Model / Class Diagram, Business Event List, Work Context Diagram.
Output Artifacts: CRUD Matrix (Table linking Data Classes/Entities with Business Events), Updated Event List, Updated Context Diagram.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Data Architect, SME, System Analyst.
Prerequisites: Draft Business Data Model (or entity list) and Business Event List.
Step-by-Step Procedure: List all business data classes/entities along the vertical axis of a matrix. 2. List all business events along the horizontal axis. 3. For each entity, map which events Create (C), Read (R), Update (U), or Delete (D) instances of that entity. 4. Analyze empty rows and columns. 5. If an entity is never Created, find the missing creation business event. 6. If an entity is Created but never Read, determine if it is unneeded or if a reading event is missing. 7. Update the event list, context diagram, and data model to resolve gaps.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What business event creates instances of this data class?", "Which events read or reference this data?", "When and why is this data updated?", "What business rule or event permits deletion or archiving of this data?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Building a CRUD matrix for a Road Deicing System and discovering that the 'Invoice' entity is created by 'Time for invoices to be sent' but never read by any event, revealing a missing event or interface with an external accounting system.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Every data class has at least one Create and at least one Read event mapped in the matrix; no orphaned data or dangling references remain.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Performing CRUD analysis on physical database tables instead of essential business data classes; omitting housekeeping/lifecycle events (archiving, deletion).
When NOT to Use: Small stateless applications that do not store or persist business data.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Information Engineering Data Flow Analysis, Domain-Driven Design Event Storming.
Supported Decisions: Data model completeness approval, system integration boundary verification, missing functional requirement identification.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI data analysis agents can automatically construct and cross-check CRUD matrices from draft event specs and data models, immediately highlighting missing C, R, U, or D operations.

Problem Solved: Prevents requirements from being lost, unimplemented, or un-tested, and manages scope changes and implementation progress visuality.
Input Artifacts: Requirements Repository, Test Cases, Implementation Units/Code Modules, Story Map, Kanban Board.
Output Artifacts: Traceability Matrix, Kanban Status Board, Requirements Status Reports, Change Impact Logs.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Project Manager / Product Owner, QA Lead, Developers.
Prerequisites: Uniquely identified atomic requirements or stories, established test cases, and code modules.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Assign a unique ID to every requirement or story. 2. Map links forward from Business Events -> BUCs/Stories -> Atomic Requirements -> Implementation Units -> Test Cases. 3. Maintain a Traceability Matrix or tool-based link repository. 4. Set up a visual Kanban board with workflow columns (Proposed, Analyzing, Design, Backlog, Implementing, Validating, Deployed). 5. Establish pull limits for each column. 6. Track requirements movement and update statuses continuously. 7. Evaluate all requested changes via a formal change supremo triage process.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Which implementation unit satisfies requirement #75?", "Which test cases prove that this requirement is met?", "What is the current status of the requirements for Business Event #3?", "If we change this requirement, which other requirements, designs, and tests are impacted?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Tracing Requirement #75 ("Record treated roads") to BUC #9, to code module 'TrkLog.cs', and to Test Case TC01, verifying its status as 'Validating' on the project Kanban board.
Quality Criteria & Verification: 100% forward and backward traceability for all baseline requirements; zero orphan code modules or untested requirements; clear visual status visibility.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Allowing requirements to be changed directly by developers without change supremo approval; failing to update the matrix when code or tests change; excessive manual overhead in tracking without appropriate tool support.
When NOT to Use: Disposable prototypes or ultra-short exploratory spikes.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Impact Analysis, Automated Traceability in ALM Tools (e.g., Jira, Azure DevOps), Value Stream Mapping.
Supported Decisions: Release readiness, scope change approval/rejection, defect root-cause analysis, project progress reporting.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic ALM integrations automatically link code commits and automated test results to requirement IDs, dynamically updating traceability matrices and moving Kanban cards through pipeline stages.

Problem Solved: Prevents poor user adoption and customer dissatisfaction by mapping emotional pain points and needs across end-to-end customer interactions.
Input Artifacts: User Personas, Stakeholder Interviews, User Observation Logs, Support Tickets.
Output Artifacts: Customer Journey Map, Touchpoint Identification Chart, Experiential Non-Functional Requirements, Service Blueprints.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, UX Designer, Customer/End User, Marketing Lead, Service/Support Lead.
Prerequisites: Defined customer personas and identified core customer goals/transactions.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select a target customer persona and goal. 2. Map the end-to-end timeline of touchpoints across three phases: Before, During, and After. 3. Identify customer actions, feelings, and pain points at each touchpoint. 4. Highlight emotional highs/lows and information needs. 5. Brainstorm requirements to eliminate friction and enhance convenience/delight. 6. Derive functional and non-functional requirements to support the improved journey.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What is the customer experiencing before touching our product?", "What information does the customer need at this specific touchpoint?", "What causes frustration or anxiety here?", "How can we make this step effortless or delightful?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Mapping a refrigerator repair journey across 'Before' (fridge breaks, finding repair service), 'During' (waiting for engineer, getting quote, fixing), and 'After' (restocking, follow-up), deriving requirements for automated SMS arrival windows and digital quotes.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Journey map reflects genuine end-user perspective rather than internal organizational view; pain points directly mapped to newly defined requirements.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Mapping internal business processes instead of the customer's actual journey; assuming the customer's emotional state without observation or research.
When NOT to Use: Internal backend system components with no direct or indirect human user touchpoints.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Empathy Mapping, Storyboarding, Contextual Inquiry / Apprenticing, Service Blueprinting.
Supported Decisions: UX design priority, customer-facing feature scope, service improvement investments.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLMs trained on customer feedback and sentiment data can draft initial customer journey maps, highlighting common emotional friction points across touchpoints for BA review.

Problem Solved: Uncovers hidden, implicit, or forgotten business rules, data attributes, and requirements buried in existing documentation, legacy screens, and paper forms.
Input Artifacts: Legacy system specifications, user manuals, paper forms, reports, screenshots, support ticket logs, existing policy documents.
Output Artifacts: Extracted Data Dictionary Entries, Legacy Business Rules, Functional Requirements, Candidate Entities and Attributes.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, SME, Legacy System Maintainer, Compliance/Legal Lead.
Prerequisites: Access to existing system documentation, forms, or legacy artifacts.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Collect samples of all relevant forms, reports, manuals, files, and screens. 2. Inspect documents to extract nouns (potential data entities and attributes). 3. Question each extracted element (Who uses it? Why? Where does it come from?). 4. Identify repeating groups, business rules, and hidden constraints. 5. Cross-check extracted elements against business use cases and data models. 6. Distinguish essential business data/rules from outdated technological fossils.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What is the business purpose of this field/report column?", "Who uses this document and what decision does it support?", "Which business event creates or updates this information?", "Is this field still needed, or is it a technological fossil?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Analyzing legacy paper invoice forms and user manuals for a shoe manufacturer, extracting data attributes (material codes, sizes, order dates) and discovering an unrecorded business rule regarding bulk discounts.
Quality Criteria & Verification: All extracted data elements defined in the data dictionary; essential business rules verified with current SMEs; technological fossils identified and removed.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Blindly copying outdated legacy forms into the new system without questioning their current validity; mistaking legacy technology constraints for essential requirements.
When NOT to Use: Completely novel greenfield projects in brand-new domains with no prior artifacts.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Apprenticing / Job Shadowing, Reverse Engineering, Interface Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Legacy migration scope, data dictionary definitions, business rule baselining.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: OCR and LLM document processing agents can automatically parse thousands of legacy PDFs, forms, and manuals, extracting draft data dictionaries and business rule catalogs for human BA validation.

Problem Solved: Uncovers tacit knowledge and operational details that users cannot articulate in conference rooms or formal interviews.
Input Artifacts: Observer notes, current process sketches, task logs.
Output Artifacts: Detailed Task Models, Current-State Scenarios (How-Now), Exception Logs, Discovered Business Rules.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst (Apprentice), User/SME (Master Craftsman).
Prerequisites: Access to the operational workplace and permission to observe live work.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Sit with the user at their actual workplace during normal operations. 2. Observe the user performing real daily tasks. 3. Listen to the user's running commentary on what they are doing and why. 4. Ask clarifying questions on the fly ("Why did you do that?", "What happens if this data is missing?"). 5. Sketch process models or scenarios while observing. 6. Validate the models with the user and abstract essential needs from physical workarounds.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Why did you perform that specific action?", "What does this code/value mean?", "How often does this exception happen and how do you handle it?", "Where do you get the information needed for this step?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA sits alongside a customer service agent handling insurance claims, observing how the agent manually cross-references three different legacy screens to verify policy details.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Discovered workflow reflects real-world operational reality (including informal workarounds) rather than idealized management procedures; models validated by the operator.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Interrupting high-risk/high-stress operations inappropriately; taking management's idealized process description as truth without observing actual workers.
When NOT to Use: High-security classified environments, hazardous locations, or emergency ultra-high-pressure tasks (e.g., active surgery, air traffic control during crisis).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Contextual Inquiry, Video Analysis, Interactive Workshops, Document Archaeology.
Supported Decisions: Usability requirements, current-state baseline verification, exception handling workflow design.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Screen-recording and process-mining AI agents can record user desktop actions to draft initial task workflows; BAs use these AI-generated logs during shadowing to focus on asking 'why' rather than manually charting steps.

Problem Solved: Converts complex, abstract business use case flows into easily understood, visual, or narrative step-by-step stories for stakeholders.
Input Artifacts: Business Use Case summaries, user interviews, process observations.
Output Artifacts: Normal Case Scenarios, Exception Scenarios, Alternative Scenarios, Storyboards, Misuse/Negative Scenarios.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, SME, End User, UX Designer, Facilitator.
Prerequisites: Identified Business Use Case and target user roles.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify the BUC, trigger, actors, and preconditions. 2. Draft a 3–10 step narrative/visual (storyboard) sequence for the Normal Case (happy path). 3. Review the Normal Case with stakeholders to reach consensus. 4. Abstract away current technology to reveal the essential scenario. 5. Systematically examine each step to identify Alternatives (wanted business choices). 6. Systematically examine each step to identify Exceptions (unwanted errors/failures) and write recovery steps. 7. Identify Misuse Cases (antagonist abuse/fraud) and specify protective steps.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What is the first step when this event occurs?", "What happens next?", "What could go wrong at this step?", "What choices does the user have here?", "How could a hostile actor abuse this step?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Writing a 8-step scenario for airport international flight check-in, identifying alternatives (checking in online vs counter) and exceptions (invalid passport, dead phone battery).
Quality Criteria & Verification: 3–10 steps per scenario level; clear trigger and outcome; full coverage of normal path, key alternatives, and critical exceptions; validated by end users.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Writing scenario steps with excessive low-level technical detail; chasing rare exceptions before agreeing on the normal path.
When NOT to Use: Pure mathematical algorithms or background system jobs with no sequential step structure.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: BPMN Activity Diagrams, User Story Mapping, Use Case Specifications, Wireframe Walkthroughs.
Supported Decisions: Workflow approval, exception handling design, user interface structure, test case generation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLMs can generate comprehensive list of potential exception and misuse scenarios for any given normal path scenario; human analysts validate relevance with domain SMEs.

Problem Solved: Prevents teams from settling for pedestrian, incremental, or presumed solutions by systematically generating innovative, high-value candidate ideas.
Input Artifacts: Problem Statement, Project Goals, User Personas, Constraints.
Output Artifacts: Innovative Candidate Solutions, Brainstorming Logs, Value Propositions, Slogans/Elevator Pitches.
Participants & Roles: Facilitator (BA), Innovation Team (SMEs, Designers, Developers, Product Owner).
Prerequisites: Safe, non-judgmental environment; clearly defined business problem statement.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Assemble a diverse, 4–8 person cross-functional team. 2. Establish ground rules: no criticism, no idea killers, suspend constraints. 3. Apply Creative Triggers (Participation, Convenience, Connections, Information, Feeling, Speed, Grandchildren). 4. Apply Lateral Thinking (challenge assumptions, remove constraints, combine existing concepts). 5. Generate a large volume of candidate ideas. 6. Group, combine, and refine candidate ideas into sacrificial candidate prototypes. 7. Evaluate and select promising ideas for further probing.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What would make this service 10x more convenient?", "How can we involve the customer in doing this work?", "What if we had zero budget / no time limit?", "What solution would your grandchildren use?", "What if we removed specific constraint?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Applying the 'Convenience' trigger to metro ticketing, asking 'What if commuters didn't need to buy tickets?', leading to the idea of contactless credit card/phone entry at turnstiles.
Quality Criteria & Verification: High volume and diversity of generated ideas; team feels safe to propose radical ideas; at least 3 distinct candidate solutions created for probing.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Allowing immediate criticism or 'idea killers' during generation; focusing on the first obvious idea; settling for minor incremental tweaks.
When NOT to Use: Strict regulatory compliance tasks where solutions are 100% legally prescribed with zero room for variation.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Design Sprints, TRIZ, SCAMPER, Lateral Thinking Puzzles, Brainstorming.
Supported Decisions: Product strategy, innovative feature selection, breakthrough solution architecture.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI ideation tools (e.g., Design Sparks) can be prompted with business problem statements and creative triggers to generate hundreds of unexpected candidate solution concepts for workshop evaluation.

Problem Solved: Replaces flat, disorganized product backlogs with a structured, visual map that conveys product scope, user flow, and incremental release priorities.
Input Artifacts: Business Events, User Personas, Functional Stories, Detailed Tasks, Non-Functional Requirements.
Output Artifacts: Visual Story Map (Backlog), Release Slices (MVP, Release 1, Release 2), Prioritized Task Lists.
Participants & Roles: Product Owner, Business Analyst, Agile Development Team, UX Designer, Key Stakeholders.
Prerequisites: Identified customer personas, work scope, and high-level business events.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Lay out the top row of the map: Business Event Stories across the horizontal axis (representing the end-to-end user flow). 2. Under each Business Event Story, add Functional Stories representing key functional steps. 3. Under each Functional Story, add columns of Detailed Tasks in descending order of priority/sophistication. 4. Annotate cards with user profiles, wireframes, and Non-Functional Requirements. 5. Draw horizontal slice lines across the map to define releases (MVP, Release 1, etc.). 6. Pull stories iteratively from the map for sprint development.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What is the end-to-end flow of events a user experiences?", "What functional steps make up this event response?", "Which tasks are absolute 'Must Haves' for a minimal viable release?", "What non-functional requirements apply to this task?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Mapping a flight booking system with top-level events ('Find flights', 'Model & compare', 'Make reservation', 'Pay'), with vertical columns of detailed tasks sliced horizontally into MVP and Release 1.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Map provides a complete, understandable horizontal narrative of the product; vertical columns are strictly prioritized; releases represent viable, deliverable slices of business value.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Building a story map without top-level business event backbone (creating a flat, unorganized list); neglecting non-functional requirements on the map.
When NOT to Use: Single, isolated bug-fix tasks or small standalone script developments.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Flat Product Backlog, Impact Mapping, Feature Breakdown Structure, Event Storming.
Supported Decisions: Release planning, MVP definition, sprint backlog selection, incremental delivery scheduling.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agile management tools with AI can automatically structure flat story lists into visual story maps based on event dependencies, suggesting optimal release slices based on velocity estimates.

Problem Solved: Prevents organizations from buying ready-made software that fails to fit their business processes, or incurring unexpected, massive customization costs.
Input Artifacts: Work Context Diagram, Business Event List, Data Dictionary, Non-Functional Requirements, Constraints.
Output Artifacts: Request for Proposal (RFP) / Request for Information (RFI), Vendor Evaluation Matrix/Scoring Sheet, Fit-Gap Analysis, Purpose-Based Alignment Quadrant.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Product Owner, System Architect, Procurement/Legal Lead, Vendor Representatives.
Prerequisites: Defined work context, clear data definitions, and prioritized business events.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define the work scope context diagram and data dictionary for the problem space. 2. Compile an RFP containing context models, business event list, expected outcomes, and key non-functional constraints. 3. Issue RFP / RFI to candidate vendors or download open-source candidates. 4. Evaluate responses by mapping ready-made capabilities against business event outcomes. 5. Score fit (4=out-of-the-box, 3=configured, 2=minor customization, 1=major customization, 0=no fit). 6. Apply Purpose-Based Alignment Model to decide whether to Configure, Customize, or adapt the Organization. 7. Select the optimal ready-made solution.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Does this ready-made produce the required outcome for this business event out-of-the-box?", "How much configuration vs customization is required?", "Is this business event a market differentiator (warranting customization) or parity (warranting configuration)?", "Will this ready-made take us out of the vendor's upgrade path?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Evaluating a ready-made Warehouse Management System against 11 business events, scoring each event's outcome fit, and using Purpose-Based Alignment to decide to configure standard picking flows while customizing unique packaging rules.
Quality Criteria & Verification: RFP based on essential outcomes rather than rigid technical solution specs; vendor scoring incorporates full lifecycle integration and disruption costs; clear decision on configure vs customize.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Buying an off-the-shelf system before understanding the business scope; over-customizing ready-made code until future upgrades become impossible; ignoring organizational change/disruption costs.
When NOT to Use: Building 100% custom, highly proprietary core IP algorithms with zero commercial software equivalents.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Custom Build vs Buy Analysis, Proof of Concept Spikes, Purpose-Based Alignment Modeling.
Supported Decisions: Software procurement, Build vs Buy vs Borrow decisions, vendor selection, customization budget approval.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI procurement agents can ingest vendor RFP responses and automatically cross-reference them against requirements specifications, generating initial fit-gap scores and highlighting compliance risks for human BA review.

Method Name: The PEGS Standard Plan for Requirements
Problem Solved: Replaces outdated requirements document structures (like IEEE 830) with a modern, comprehensive 4-book structure addressing missing domain context, unstated assumptions, poor project planning, and fragmented system scope.
Input Artifacts: Stakeholder requests, existing process documentation, regulatory texts, interviews, workshops, meeting minutes.
Output Artifacts: Requirements Repository organized into four core books: Goals Book (G), Environment Book (E), System Book (S), and Project Book (P).
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst / Requirements Engineer (Lead), Subject-Matter Experts (SMEs), Project Manager, Sponsor/Product Owner, System Architects, Testers, Compliance/Legal.
Prerequisites: Access to key stakeholders, initial project charter or business mandate, identified domain constraints.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Set up the Requirements Repository with templates for books P, E, G, S. 2. Draft Goals Book (G.1-G.7) capturing business context, current state, expected benefits, and high-level usage scenarios. 3. Draft Environment Book (E.1-E.6) establishing the domain glossary, environment components, constraints, assumptions, effects, and invariants. 4. Draft System Book (S.1-S.6) defining system architecture/clusters, detailed functionality, external interfaces, usage scenarios, priorities, and acceptance criteria. 5. Draft Project Book (P.1-P.7) detailing roles, technical choices, schedule, tasks, deliverables, technology dependencies, risks, and process logs. 6. Establish cross-references across books adhering to valid reference rules. 7. Review, verify quality criteria, and obtain formal stakeholder endorsements.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Why is this project needed? What business problem are we solving? What external laws, domain rules, or engineering constraints limit us? What assumptions facilitate development? What must the system do, and what is explicitly out of scope?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Structuring an e-commerce refund system into Goals (reducing manual processing by 20%), Environment (payment gateway APIs, GDPR privacy rules), System (automated refund calculation, refund UI), and Project (milestones, technical stack choices).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Verification against 14 quality criteria (Correct, Justified, Complete, Consistent, Unambiguous, Feasible, Abstract, Traceable, Delimited, Readable, Modifiable, Verifiable, Prioritized, Endorsed); formal sign-offs in front/back matter.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Creating a rigid linear document rather than a living repository; confusing environment constraints with system decisions; omitting out-of-scope limits; skipping justification for technical choices.
When NOT to Use: Trivial micro-projects where formal specifications incur unnecessary overhead and full 4-book structure is excessive.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: IEEE 830 / ISO 29148 templates, Planguage, Goal-oriented RE (KAOS/i*), User Story Mapping.
Supported Decisions: Scope determination, release architecture, compliance verification, milestone planning, acceptance testing.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Prompt AI agents to parse raw stakeholder transcripts into specific PEGS books/chapters, using automated consistency-checking guardrails across constraints and requirements.

Problem Solved: Reduces the risk of missing critical requirements, unstated expectations, or project failure caused by neglecting key influencers or over-focusing on vocal but low-impact individuals.
Input Artifacts: Organizational charts, project charter, stakeholder lists, preliminary meeting notes.
Output Artifacts: Stakeholder Map (classified into Key Stakeholders, Shadow Influencers, Fellow Travelers, Observers), Stakeholder List (Chapter G.7).
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst / Requirements Engineer (Lead), Project Manager, Sponsor, SMEs, End Users, Legal/Compliance officers.
Prerequisites: Project mandate and initial list of potential stakeholder groups on both target (customer) and production (development) sides.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify all potential stakeholder categories on both target and production sides. 2. Evaluate each group's influence (ability to affect or be affected by the project/system) and availability. 3. Plot stakeholders onto the 2x2 grid (Key Stakeholders, Shadow Influencers, Fellow Travelers, Observers). 4. Formulate engagement strategies: prioritize Key Stakeholders and actively seek out Shadow Influencers. 5. Document category definitions and key representatives in Chapter G.7 of the Goals Book. 6. Re-evaluate stakeholder map periodically during requirements evolution.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Who will use the system? Who will be affected by its deployment? Who makes acceptance decisions? Whose non-involvement could derail the project?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Mapping a university course management system: Instructors & Students = Key Stakeholders; Sysadmins = Shadow Influencers (high impact, busy); Enthusiastic student rep = Fellow Traveler; Legal = Observer.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Coverage completeness check: ensuring no critical category (e.g. testers, legal, client programmers) is omitted; verification against Chapter G.7.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confounding individual persons with stakeholder categories; neglecting Shadow Influencers (e.g. sysadmins); over-catering to 'vocal' Fellow Travelers; treating the map as static.
When NOT to Use: Small single-user applications with trivial stakeholder landscapes.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: RACI Matrix, Power/Interest Grid, Persona Development.
Supported Decisions: Resource allocation for elicitation, interview/workshop scheduling, acceptance sign-off hierarchy.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can analyze organizational charts and communications to automatically suggest potential stakeholder maps and flag under-represented high-influence groups.

Problem Solved: Reduces semantic ambiguity, misunderstandings, and defects caused by 'kidnapped words' (ordinary words used in a specialized domain sense), acronym confusion, or conflicting terminology among stakeholders.
Input Artifacts: Domain documents, stakeholder interview transcripts, legacy documentation, regulatory texts.
Output Artifacts: Glossary (Chapter E.1 of the Environment Book), establishing standardized terminology, definitions, and acronym expansions.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst / Requirements Engineer (Compiler), Subject-Matter Experts (Domain Authorities/Endorsers).
Prerequisites: Initial elicitation discussions or domain documentation containing domain-specific jargon or repurposed terms.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify technical terms, acronyms, and everyday words used in a specialized sense during elicitation. 2. Question SMEs persistently to uncover exact meanings of 'obvious' or 'kidnapped' words. 3. Draft concise, unambiguous definitions for each term. 4. For acronyms, include both the official expansion and an explanatory description of the underlying concept. 5. Document entries in Chapter E.1 (Glossary) of the Environment Book. 6. Obtain formal endorsement from qualified SMEs. 7. Hyperlink all occurrences of defined terms across all requirements specifications.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What exactly do you mean by term X? Is 'vat' the same as 'tank'? Does 'student' mean undergraduate or PhD researcher? What does this acronym stand for and what concept does it represent?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Defining 'PhD Student' in a university system as 'a junior scientific collaborator/employee' rather than a standard student, preventing incorrect system permissions.
Quality Criteria & Verification: No-Synonym Principle (one concept = one name); full coverage of all domain-specific terms; SME endorsement of definitions.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Defining acronyms by expansion alone without concept explanation; using synonyms interchangeably in requirements texts; assuming ordinary meanings for 'kidnapped' domain terms.
When NOT to Use: Never omit; a glossary is mandatory for all non-trivial domains.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Data Dictionary, Domain Model, Conceptual Class Diagram.
Supported Decisions: Data modeling, API field naming, user interface terminology, domain-specific logic specifications.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can scan requirements text to identify undefined acronyms or inconsistent synonym usage, automatically proposing glossary entries grounded in domain corpora.

Problem Solved: Reduces single-source bias, availability bias, and cross-departmental conflicts by bringing diverse stakeholder groups together to establish shared understanding and resolve contradictory needs efficiently.
Input Artifacts: Draft Goals book, preliminary issue list, stakeholder map, Doodle/calendar schedules.
Output Artifacts: Workshop Report (contributing to Chapter P.7), updated requirements repository entries, list of action items and open issues.
Participants & Roles: Workshop Facilitator / Business Analyst (Lead), Scribe/Recorder, Cross-functional Stakeholders (SMEs, End Users, Managers, Developers).
Prerequisites: Clear agenda and issue list circulated 2-3 weeks in advance; suitable room/virtual meeting setup; representation from key contrasting stakeholder groups.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define a list of specific issues to resolve and set a strict time-boxed agenda including an 'other items' buffer. 2. Select participants ensuring balanced representation across stakeholder categories. 3. Circulate agenda and prep materials with sufficient lead time. 4. Set up room (U-shape/circular) or virtual tools (cameras required, quality audio). 5. Facilitate the workshop: enforce schedule, ensure quiet voices are heard, cut off long side-discussions. 6. Focus on discovering unsaid assumptions and resolving conflicting perspectives. 7. Draft an egoless, summary-focused Workshop Report highlighting decisions made and open action items. 8. Distribute report for participant review and integrate findings into the requirements repository (P.7).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What happens next? What factors are involved? How do you currently handle this? Are there any other reasons? Did we miss anything important?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Conducting a 2-hour workshop with Claims Adjusters and Sales Managers to reconcile conflicting refund authorization thresholds, resulting in an agreed dual-signature policy.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Peer review of workshop report by participants; inclusion of key decisions in Chapter P.7; resolution or explicit tracking of identified conflicts.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Allowing vocal personalities to dominate; producing verbatim meeting minutes instead of structured decision summaries; poor hybrid/audio setup; failing to circulate agendas in advance.
When NOT to Use: Deep-dive technical discussions involving only a single expert; highly sensitive one-on-one confidential evaluations.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Individual Stakeholder Interviews, Focus Groups, Joint Application Design (JAD).
Supported Decisions: Cross-departmental workflow rules, feature prioritization, scope boundaries, policy trade-offs.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can act as real-time scribes during workshops, transcribing conversations, extracting candidate requirements, detecting contradictions, and generating action-item reports.

Problem Solved: Reduces ambiguity and silence regarding individual role-specific domain knowledge, user workflows, and hidden operational constraints.
Input Artifacts: Interview gaide / prep form, background information on interviewee's role, draft Glossary.
Output Artifacts: Interview Report (summarizing key lessons and requirements input for P.7), candidate requirements statements.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst / Requirements Engineer (Interviewer), Individual Stakeholder / SME (Interviewee).
Prerequisites: Identified stakeholder role, established objectives for the interview, prepared set of structured and open-ended questions.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define interview objectives, specific role context, and target duration (1-2 hours). 2. Prepare structured question guide containing both specific closed questions and context-free open questions. 3. Schedule meeting and confirm attendance. 4. Conduct interview: stick to time box, maintain an egoless attitude, ask basic/probing questions, and explore the 'unsaid'. 5. Save time for meta-questions ('What else should I be asking you?'). 6. Produce an egoless Interview Report focusing on key domain lessons rather than verbatim transcript. 7. Validate findings with interviewee and integrate into repository (P.7).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What is the goal of this task? What happens when an error occurs? How do you know when you are done? Is there anything else I should be asking?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Interviewing a Senior Payroll Specialist for 1 hour to uncover edge cases in monthly tax deductions for remote employees, discovering an unstated regional tax constraint.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Review of report by interviewee for correctness; extraction of verified requirements into Book E or S.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Timidity (fearing to ask basic questions); selection and availability bias; conducting rigid, non-adaptable interviews; writing verbatim minutes rather than abstracting key requirements.
When NOT to Use: Resolving cross-departmental policy disputes (use Workshops instead).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Workshops, Questionnaires/Surveys, Contextual Inquiry / Observation.
Supported Decisions: Detailed functional behavior, specific UI requirements, domain constraint definitions.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can generate customized interview guides based on current gaps in the PEGS repository and analyze audio transcripts to auto-populate interview reports.

Problem Solved: Reduces 'criticality inflation' (where stakeholders mark all requested features as critical) and resolves priority conflicts by forcing realistic economic trade-offs.
Input Artifacts: Candidate features list (Chapter S.2), estimated development effort, theoretical budget allocation rules.
Output Artifacts: Prioritized Feature List in Chapter S.5 (categorized into Critical/Show-stopper, Important, Nice-to-have, with numerical weightings).
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst (Facilitator), Stakeholders / Product Owner / Client Representatives (Participants).
Prerequisites: Delimited list of proposed system features extracted from elicitation.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Compile the list of candidate system features (S.2). 2. Provide participants with a virtual budget (e.g., $100) and set minimum/maximum investment rules per feature. 3. Instruct stakeholders to distribute their budget across features based on true business value. 4. Aggregate results across participants to compute relative importance scores. 5. Categorize features into Critical (show-stoppers), Important, and Nice-to-have. 6. Document priorities in Chapter S.5 of the System Book. 7. Validate prioritization against project feasibility and development effort with developers.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "If you only had $100 to buy features for the first release, how much would you spend on feature X versus feature Y? Which feature can you live without if budget gets cut by 20%?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Stakeholders allocating $100 across 5 proposed features: 'Export to PDF' gets $45, 'Email Alerts' gets $35, while 'Dark Mode UI' gets $5, clearly marking Dark Mode as 'nice-to-have'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Categorization completeness (every S.2 feature has an S.5 entry); alignment between business value and development cost estimates; Product Owner endorsement.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Allowing stakeholders to declare everything 'Critical'; ignoring developer effort estimates; failing to document priorities before project crises occur.
When NOT to Use: Safety-critical mandatory features where regulatory compliance makes prioritization non-negotiable.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: MoSCoW Method (Must/Should/Could/Won't), Kano Model Analysis, 100-Point Method, Pairwise Comparison.
Supported Decisions: Scope slicing for sprints/releases, deferred functionality choices during schedule cuts, resource allocation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic systems can automatically run interactive virtual budgeting web tools, aggregate stakeholder votes, perform multi-criteria trade-off optimization, and draft S.5 priority chapters.

Problem Solved: Reduces technical uncertainty, uncovers dependency risks ('dependency hell'), and verifies whether external technology components or unproven algorithms can actually deliver expected performance.
Input Artifacts: Required Technology Elements list (Chapter P.5), Risk Analysis (Chapter P.6), interface specifications.
Output Artifacts: Feasibility Prototype Code, Feasibility Report integrated into Chapter P.6, updated technology choices in P.2/P.5.
Participants & Roles: Requirements Engineer / System Architect / Lead Programmer (Developer), Business Analyst (Evaluator).
Prerequisites: Identification of critical external software dependencies, hardware integrations, or novel algorithms with unverified capabilities.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify critical, unproven external technologies or dependencies in Chapter P.5. 2. Formulate explicit risk hypotheses in Chapter P.6. 3. Design a targeted, small-scale mini-project (prototype) solely to test the specific capability or integration point. 4. Implement and run the prototype ('tracer code' or benchmark). 5. Measure performance, compatibility, stability, and dependency constraints. 6. Evaluate results against requirements criteria. 7. Update Risk Analysis (P.6) with mitigation strategies or select alternative technology choices (P.2/P.5).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Can Library X really process 10,000 transactions per second? Does API Y support mobile platforms? Will upgrading to Version Z break existing dependencies?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Building a 2-day prototype to test if a third-party PDF rendering library can process 500-page invoice files within 2 seconds before committing it to Chapter P.5.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Explicit risk reduction in P.6; objective benchmark metrics demonstrating technical feasibility.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confusing feasibility prototypes with shippable code; skipping feasibility checks and discovering technical roadblocks late in construction.
When NOT to Use: Standard, well-understood technologies with proven track records in the organization.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Tracer Code, Architectural Spikes, Benchmarking, Literature/Vendor Review.
Supported Decisions: Architecture selection, third-party library adoption, risk mitigation strategies, project schedule estimation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can automatically generate synthetic test spikes, execute micro-benchmarks against external APIs, and summarize performance risks into Chapter P.6.

Method Name: Scenario-Based Requirements Analysis (Use Cases and User Stories)
Problem Solved: Reduces abstractness and communication gaps between non-technical stakeholders and developers by illustrating concrete, step-by-step usage paths through the system.
Input Artifacts: Stakeholder requests, workflow observations, draft Glossary, Goals Book.
Output Artifacts: High-level usage scenarios in Goals Book (G.5), Detailed Usage Scenarios in System Book (S.4), User Stories, Epics, Use Case Slices.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst / Requirements Engineer (Author), Subject-Matter Experts / End Users (Inputs & Reviewers), Developers/Testers (Consumers).
Prerequisites: Identified system scope and target user roles.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify primary user roles and their operational objectives. 2. For high-level business paths, draft Use Cases in Chapter G.5 specifying primary actor, preconditions, triggers, main success scenario, success guarantees, and extensions. 3. For fine-grained development work items, draft User Stories in the standard template: 'As a role, I want feature, so that benefit'. 4. Verify User Stories against INVEST criteria (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable). 5. Group stories into Epics or decompose complex Use Cases into Use Case Slices. 6. Detail special/error handling paths as Use Case Extensions. 7. Use scenarios to derive test cases (S.6) and to extract abstract system behaviors (S.2).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Who performs this action? What triggers it? What is the main success path? What can go wrong? What is the expected outcome?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Writing a Use Case 'Process_loss_claim' (Primary Actor: Claims Adjuster, Trigger: Claim reported, Main Scenario: Register loss -> Assign agent -> Investigate -> Evaluate -> Set reserve -> Negotiate -> Close).
Quality Criteria & Verification: INVEST criteria compliance for stories; scenario completeness (S.2 functionality covers all scenario steps); validation by SMEs.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Treating scenarios as full requirements specifications rather than illustrations/tests; operational overspecification; scenario explosion (trying to write an extension for every conceivable combination).
When NOT to Use: As a substitute for abstract behavioral specifications or formal logic constraints.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Object-Oriented Requirements with Contracts, Abstract Data Types, Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN), Statechart Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Sprint backlog construction, acceptance test design, UI workflow validation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic LLMs excel at generating initial use cases and user stories from interview transcripts, checking them against INVEST criteria, and auto-generating corresponding test scripts.

Problem Solved: Prevents premature time-ordering overspecification, handles combinatorial case explosions, and provides stable, modifiable, and reusable requirements architectures.
Input Artifacts: Elicited scenarios (use cases/user stories), domain glossary (E.1), environment component list (E.2).
Output Artifacts: Object-Oriented Requirements Specification consisting of Class Definitions, Feature Signatures (Queries, Commands, Creators), and Contracts (Preconditions, Postconditions, Class Invariants).
