Participants & Roles: Business Analyst / Requirements Engineer (Architect), Subject-Matter Experts (Reviewers).
Prerequisites: Domain vocabulary defined in Glossary; fundamental understanding of object-oriented modeling principles.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify object types (classes) from the environment and system domain (e.g., Concrete Environment, Abstract Environment). 2. For each class, identify applicable Queries (information retrieval) and Commands (state modifications). 3. Define class interfaces without implementation details, marking features as deferred. 4. Attach Contracts to features: Preconditions (require) for commands, Postconditions (ensure) for state changes, and Class Invariants for persistent properties. 5. Establish inter-class relations: Client-Supplier and Inheritance. 6. Categorize classes into the 7 Kinds of Class. 7. Use scenario classes (specification drivers) to validate that valid execution sequences satisfy feature preconditions.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What types of objects exist in this domain? What questions can we ask about an object (queries)? What operations modify it (commands)? What must be true before an operation can run (precondition)? What is guaranteed afterward (postcondition)?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Defining class INSURANCE_CLAIM with query is_investigated, command evaluate (require is_investigated; ensure is_evaluated), and invariant (is_evaluated implies is_investigated).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Command-Query completeness; contract consistency; abstractness (no implementation leakage); seamless reversibility.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confusing classes with implementation code; omitting preconditions; forcing rigid sequential ordering instead of logical constraints; premature optimization.
When NOT to Use: Simple procedural batch scripts with no complex domain object lifecycle.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Abstract Data Types (ADTs), Formal Specification Languages (Z, B), Entity-Relationship Modeling.
Supported Decisions: System architecture decomposition, class API design, modular work assignment, seamless transition to design and code.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can parse natural language use cases into formal OO class definitions with Eiffel-style contracts, automatically verifying contract consistency and query completeness.

Problem Solved: Eliminates subtle ambiguities, internal contradictions, falsehoods, and edge-case oversights in critical requirements by deriving precise mathematical models and converting them back into crystal-clear natural language.
Input Artifacts: Informal natural-language requirements, domain assumptions, mathematical notation conventions.
Output Artifacts: Formal Mathematical Specification (Sets, Predicates, Functions, Relations, Axioms) and 'Back-from-the-Picnic' Natural-Language Specification.
Participants & Roles: Requirements Engineer / Formal Methods Specialist (Author), Stakeholders / SMEs / Programmers (Reviewers).
Prerequisites: High-school/undergraduate discrete mathematics (logic, sets, functions, relations, sequences).
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify critical requirements parts where ambiguities or high risks exist. 2. Define mathematical types/sets for domain entities. 3. Formulate operations as mathematical relations or functions (signatures, domains, ranges). 4. Express behavioral constraints and business logic as formal predicate expressions or minimization/optimization formulas. 5. Formulate and formally prove key requirements theorems (e.g., Feasibility Theorem). 6. Translate the formal specification back into plain, highly structured, unambiguous natural language ('Formal Picnic'). 7. Include both the formal model and picnic text in the specification, explicitly designating which is binding.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What is the exact set of elements? Is this function total or partial? Under what precise mathematical conditions does a solution exist? How do we formalize 'as many as possible'?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Formalizing text reformatting as a minimization formula over the set of 'recast' strings (S1: min newlines among recasts with line length <= M), proving the Feasibility Theorem, and deriving a 9-clause picnic specification.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Mathematical proof of correctness/feasibility theorems; Non-ambiguity; Command-Query / Sufficient Completeness.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Failing to translate formal models back for non-math stakeholders; overcomplicating math models with operational algorithm details; confusing mathematical specs with program code.
When NOT to Use: Non-critical, rapidly changing UI prototype ideas where mathematical rigor offers little ROI.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Z, B Method, TLA+, Alloy, Abstract Data Types.
Supported Decisions: Verification of safety-critical logic, algorithm feasibility proofs, unambiguous contract definitions for sub-contractors.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic LLMs can formalize natural-language statements into first-order logic/set theory, run automated theorem provers/model checkers (e.g., Alloy/Z3), and generate picnic-style natural language summaries.

Problem Solved: Provides a purely external, mathematical specification of data types based strictly on available operations and axioms, eliminating overspecification and providing a formal definition of completeness.
Input Artifacts: Domain concept definitions, identified queries, commands, and creators.
Output Artifacts: Formal ADT Specification comprising Functions & Signatures, Preconditions, and Axioms.
Participants & Roles: Requirements Engineer / Systems Analyst (Author).
Prerequisites: Basic set theory and discrete math concepts (functions, signatures, boolean logic).
Step-by-Step Procedure: Name the new ADT (T) and identify required previous types (e.g., INTEGER, BOOLEAN). 2. Define function signatures for Creators (-> T), Queries (T -> PreviousType), and Commands (T -> T). 3. Identify partial functions and state their exact preconditions in the Preconditions section using total query functions. 4. Write algebraic Axioms defining the effect of every creator and command on every query. 5. Verify that preconditions are correct expressions. 6. Prove Sufficient Completeness: demonstrate that axioms allow reducing any correct query expression to a value of a previous type.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What information can we ask about this object (queries)? What operations modify it (commands)? What creates it (creators)? What is the value of query Q after applying command C? Under what conditions is command C valid?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Specifying ADT COUNTER: Creators: new -> COUNTER; Queries: item -> INTEGER; Commands: up, down -> COUNTER (partial); Preconditions: up(c) require item(c) < 10; Axioms: item(new) = 0, item(up(c)) = item(c) + 1.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Proof of Sufficient Completeness (ability to reduce any correct query expression); ADT Precondition Rule compliance.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Specifying internal data representations (e.g., array vs linked list) instead of external operations; writing circular axioms; omitting preconditions for partial functions.
When NOT to Use: Simple static configuration files or unstructured data blobs.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Object-Oriented Classes with Contracts, Z Specification, Model-Based Formalisms.
Supported Decisions: API contract specification, abstract domain modeling, proof of specification completeness.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can check ADT specifications for sufficient completeness by running term-rewriting reductions on sample query expressions and flagging un-axiomatized command-query pairs.

Problem Solved: Prevents costly downstream software defects, project failures, and legal disputes by systematically evaluating requirements against 14 objective quality criteria.
Input Artifacts: Draft Requirements Repository (Books P, E, G, S), stakeholder interview/workshop reports, regulatory constraints.
Output Artifacts: Requirements Quality Verification Report, issue logs, signed endorsement pages.
Participants & Roles: Requirements Engineer / Quality Auditor (Lead), Subject-Matter Experts, Lead Developers, Testers, Sponsor / Product Owner.
Prerequisites: Completed initial draft of requirements books conforming to the Standard Plan.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Evaluate Environment and System requirements against domain reality and stakeholder intent (Correctness). 2. Verify that every project/system requirement traces to a goal or constraint (Justification, Traceability). 3. Perform the 6 completeness checks (Document, Goal, Scenario, Environment, Interface, Command-Query Completeness). 4. Inspect text for internal contradictions and terminology mismatches against the glossary (Consistency, Non-ambiguity). 5. Review technical feasibility with developers and assess schedule realism (Feasibility). 6. Verify that requirements specify 'what' not 'how', converting operational overspecifications into implementation hints (Abstractness). 7. Verify scope limits in G.6 (Delimitedness) and check readability rules (Readability). 8. Check auto-numbering/indexing for Modifiability and falsifiability/testability for Verifiability. 9. Verify that all system behaviors in S.2 have priority ratings in S.5 (Prioritization). 10. Obtain formal written sign-offs from key decision-makers (Endorsement).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Is this requirement correct and justified? Can it be tested or falsified? Does it prescribe an implementation choice? Is it consistent with the glossary? Have all decision-makers endorsed it?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Auditing a requirement 'The system shall display messages instantaneously' -> flagging it for ambiguity/unverifiability -> rewriting to 'display messages within 0.1s' -> verifying feasibility with developers.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Compliance with all 14 Quality Criteria: Correct, Justified, Complete, Consistent, Unambiguous, Feasible, Abstract, Traceable, Delimited, Readable, Modifiable, Verifiable, Prioritized, Endorsed.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Aiming for 'perfection' at the expense of system delivery (violating the Requirements Effort Principle); treating verification as a one-time Waterfall phase rather than an ongoing process.
When NOT to Use: Quality verification principles apply to all projects, though the level of rigor scales with project risk.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: SMART Criteria inspection, Fagan Inspection, Peer Review, Prototype Validation.
Supported Decisions: Project phase-gate approvals, user acceptance test readiness, sign-off on legal/development contracts.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can continuously audit requirements repositories against the 14 quality criteria, detecting ambiguous words ('user-friendly', 'fast'), cross-reference errors, missing priorities, or orphan requirements.

Method Name: The Unified PEGS Lifecycle Model Management
Problem Solved: Eliminates the rigid, late-code risks of the Waterfall and the 'no-upfront-planning' chaos of extreme Agile by providing a flexible, iterative, sprint-based lifecycle model with balanced, evolving requirements.
Input Artifacts: Project Plan (Book P), Goals Book (Book G), Sprint Backlogs, Cluster Architecture.
Output Artifacts: Iterative Sprint Deliverables, continuously updated Requirements Repository (Books P, E, G, S), User Acceptance Test Plans.
Participants & Roles: Project Manager, Business Analyst / Requirements Engineer, System Architect, Lead Developers, Testers, Product Owner.
Prerequisites: Minimum upfront requirements outcome (G.1, G.3, G.7, S.1, S.2, E.3, P.4, P.5) and cluster division.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Produce initial upfront version of the requirements repository (Minimum Requirements Outcome) during early sprints. 2. Divide system into logical Clusters (e.g., Model, View, Controller). 3. Structure development into fixed-duration time-boxed Sprints. 4. Apply the NASACE Principle: ensure early sprints focus on definition/architecture + UI/feasibility prototypes; middle sprints focus on cluster implementation; final sprints focus on system verification. 5. Each sprint executes a definition phase (goals, environment, project planning, cluster definition) followed by an implementation phase (cluster construction and verification). 6. Apply reversibility: update requirements and design repository elements whenever implementation reveals new domain insights. 7. Execute final acceptance verification based on updated requirements.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What are the minimum upfront requirements needed to start coding? Which clusters are most critical/risky? How do we update requirements based on lessons from the latest sprint?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Sprint 1: Draft overall PEGS requirements + build UI prototype; Sprint 2: Refine requirements, define architecture, start core Model cluster; Sprints 3-N: Continue cluster builds + update specs; Final Sprint: System verification & bug fixes.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Adherence to Requirements Elaboration Principle; continuous alignment between code and requirements repository; successful UAT execution.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Freezing requirements upfront (Waterfall trap); doing zero upfront requirements and writing user stories on the fly (Agile trap); shipping throwaway prototypes; ignoring reversibility.
When NOT to Use: Replaced by lightweight DevOps continuous delivery for ultra-rapid cloud web maintenance, though underlying elaboration principles still apply.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Rational Unified Process (RUP), Agile Scrum, Spiral Model, Cluster Model.
Supported Decisions: Sprint planning, release scheduling, change request management, resource re-allocation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI systems can manage repository updates across sprints, automatically re-tracing requirements changes to impacted test suites and code modules after each iteration.

Problem Solved: Reduces domain uncertainty, lack of foundational business context, and improper use of domain terminology before interacting with busy stakeholders.
Input Artifacts: Organizational charts, business plans, policy manuals, financial reports, minutes of meetings, job descriptions, business forms, industry books, regulations, past system defect reports, complaints, change requests, user manuals.
Output Artifacts: Initial background sections of a preliminary draft proposal, domain glossary of terms.
Participants & Roles: BA (Analyst).
Prerequisites: Access to existing organizational, regulatory, and system documentations.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Acquire meta-knowledge to identify required vs unnecessary information. 2. Prune the documentation space. 3. Collect relevant documents (business, domain, system-as-is). 4. Read, analyze, and synthesize document contents. 5. Extract core concepts, regulations, policies, and reported weaknesses. 6. Draft initial proposal sections and establish a glossary of domain terms.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What do I need to know vs not need to know? What is the structure, business objectives, and policies of the organization? What terminology is standard in this domain? What defects and complaints were reported for the system-as-is?
Minimal Realistic Example: A business analyst reviews a university's library policy manuals and past patron complaints to understand loan periods, fine rules, and missing book issues prior to interviewing library staff.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Document currency and accuracy verification; meta-knowledge filtering to ensure pruning of irrelevant documentation; consensus on extracted glossary definitions.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Getting overwhelmed by massive volumes of documentation (data-mining problem); relying on outdated or inaccurate documentation without verification.
When NOT to Use: Rarely skipped entirely, but restricted when documentation is completely absent, untrustworthy, or obsolete.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Data collection, questionnaires, interviews, observation, model-driven meta-knowledge filtering.
Supported Decisions: Scope delimitation, baseline terminology definition, interview targeting.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLMs can ingest large document corpora to automatically draft domain glossaries, summarize system defect reports, and highlight regulatory constraints; human-in-the-loop validates accuracy and resolves document contradictions.

Problem Solved: Reduces uncertainty regarding system performance metrics, costs, usage trends, and non-functional baseline numbers that are not documented.
Input Artifacts: System logs, transaction databases, operational statistics, performance metrics.
Output Artifacts: Statistical datasets, usage metrics, benchmark reports, performance constraints.
Participants & Roles: BA, SME, System Administrator.
Prerequisites: Availability of quantitative data sources or access to operational metrics.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify missing quantitative facts (e.g., peak throughput, operational costs). 2. Select representative data sets or design statistical sampling methods. 3. Gather quantitative operational metrics or execute experimental data collection. 4. Analyze and interpret statistical results. 5. Derive non-functional requirements (performance, cost, usability targets).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What are the peak transaction volumes? What is the current average response time? What are the operational costs per transaction?
Minimal Realistic Example: Measuring the peak number of parallel meeting requests per hour during corporate planning cycles to set scalability requirements.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Statistical sampling representativeness, statistical significance, correct mathematical interpretation.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Drawing conclusions from non-representative or un-sampled data sets; misinterpreting operational metrics into incorrect non-functional targets.
When NOT to Use: When accurate operational metrics are already documented or when time constraints prevent deploying statistical sampling.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Background study, performance benchmarking, questionnaires.
Supported Decisions: Non-functional scope, performance criteria, capacity planning.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic data pipelines can continuously extract and aggregate operational log data to predict capacity thresholds; human review ensures realistic constraint setting.

Problem Solved: Reduces uncertainty regarding stakeholder perceptions, subjective preferences, and priority distributions across a large or geographically distributed user base.
Input Artifacts: Stakeholder list, specific elicitation topics (multiple-choice options, weighting criteria).
Output Artifacts: Completed survey responses, aggregated statistical summaries of preferences/risks.
Participants & Roles: BA, End Users, Stakeholders.
Prerequisites: Representative target sample identified; well-defined topics requiring quantitative or weighted subjective input.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify the target group and required information. 2. Design closed-ended, weight-based, or multiple-choice questions. 3. Include redundant/control questions to detect inconsistencies. 4. Pre-validate and pilot the questionnaire for clarity and non-ambiguity. 5. Distribute to target sample. 6. Collect responses, filter out inconsistent answers, and analyze statistical findings.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Which features do you rank as highest priority? On a scale of 1 to 5, how critical is feature X? How frequently do you encounter issue Y?
Minimal Realistic Example: Distributing a online survey to 500 university students to rate their preference for borrowing physical books versus accessing digital libraries.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Pre-validation for non-ambiguity; representativeness and statistical significance of target respondents; coverage of options; absence of bias.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Biased or opinionated formulations; overly open-ended prompts causing low response rate; sample selection bias; misinterpretation of prompts by respondents.
When NOT to Use: When deep qualitative exploration, complex process discovery, or domain learning is required.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Interviews, group sessions/workshops, card sorting.
Supported Decisions: Prioritization, selection between high-level alternative options, feature trade-offs.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can generate unbiased survey questions based on preliminary topic goals, auto-analyze free-text survey responses, and flag statistical anomalies.

Problem Solved: Reduces ambiguity and uncertainty surrounding domain concepts, implicit categorization criteria, and tacit domain knowledge held by experts.
Input Artifacts: Pre-elicited domain concepts, cards representing domain concepts (textual or graphical).
Output Artifacts: Concept-attribute matrices (Repertory Grids), categorized concept trees/taxonomies, candidate domain properties and requirements.
Participants & Roles: BA, SME, Domain Experts.
Prerequisites: A set of core domain concepts has already been identified.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Prepare concept list or set of concept cards. 2. Ask stakeholders to characterize concepts with attributes and value ranges (Repertory Grid) OR partition concept cards into subsets based on their own criteria (Card Sort). 3. Elicit the rationale/properties explaining the groupings. 4. Classify extracted properties as descriptive (domain properties) or prescriptive (requirements). 5. Repeat sorting with new criteria if necessary.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Why do these concepts belong together while those do not? What attribute characterizes this group? Is this property a natural law (descriptive) or a desired rule (prescriptive)?
Minimal Realistic Example: A librarian sorts cards representing 'Books', 'Journals', and 'Proceedings' into 'Borrowable Items' vs 'Reference Only', uncovering the rule that reference items cannot leave the building.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Consistency of classification criteria across iterations; expert validation of elicited domain properties.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Generating overly subjective taxonomies that do not reflect operational reality; complexity explosion when managing excessively large concept sets.
When NOT to Use: When dealing with large, highly complex concept spaces without tool support, or when domain concepts are already standardized.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Conceptual laddering, background study, class diagrams (object modeling).
Supported Decisions: Domain concept structuring, taxonomy definition, initial rule classification.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLMs can propose candidate concept groupings and attributes from domain glossaries for expert refinement during sorting sessions.

Problem Solved: Reduces ambiguity, misunderstandings, and disconnects between abstract textual descriptions and real-world operational interactions across stakeholders.
Input Artifacts: Initial problem world descriptions, stakeholder interaction goals, user roles.
Output Artifacts: Storyboards (snapshots, sketches), sequence diagrams, event trace diagrams, normal/abnormal interaction scenarios, acceptance test cases.
Participants & Roles: BA, End User, SME, Developer, Tester.
Prerequisites: Key system components and user roles are identified.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify the interaction goal and participating components/players. 2. Outline the normal sequence of interaction steps (who does what, how, and why). 3. Identify potential deviations and exceptional situations (abnormal scenarios). 4. Document concrete examples using text, sequence diagrams, or visual storyboards. 5. Review scenarios with stakeholders in passive (explanation) or active (exploration) mode. 6. Extract underlying implicit goals, requirements, and domain properties.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Who are the players? What happens to them? How does it happen? Why does this happen? What if such and such an event occurs? What could go wrong?
Minimal Realistic Example: A 6-step interaction scenario showing a meeting initiator submitting a request, the scheduler asking participants for constraints, participants responding, and the scheduler issuing a date notification.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Coverage of normal and exceptional courses; validation by stakeholders; consistency across scenario granularity levels; explicitly extracting underlying implicit requirements.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Combinatorial explosion due to enumerating every interaction combination; premature commitment to interaction sequencing (overspecification); leaving underlying requirements implicit.
When NOT to Use: Should never be skipped entirely, but caution is needed to avoid over-relying on scenarios for capturing complete system-wide declarative rules.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Use cases, state machines, prototyping, goal modeling.
Supported Decisions: User interaction design, exception handling design, acceptance test criteria.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can automatically generate sequence diagrams from textual meeting transcripts, hypothesize abnormal exception scenarios, and trace scenario steps to formal goals.

Problem Solved: Reduces uncertainty, cognitive distance, and misinterpretation regarding dynamic user interface interactions and complex system functionalities.
Input Artifacts: Unclear, complex, or usability-critical requirements, interaction models.
Output Artifacts: Throwaway prototypes (mock-ups), evolutionary prototypes, validated/revised requirements.
Participants & Roles: BA, End User, Developer, UI/UX Designer.
Prerequisites: Specific requirements are identified as ambiguous, complex, or heavily dependent on user interface dialogues.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select unclear or usability-critical requirements. 2. Rapidly build a low-fidelity mock-up or executable prototype (functional or UI). 3. Demonstrate prototype executions to stakeholders. 4. Collect user feedback and observe interaction difficulties. 5. Revise and refine requirements or prototypes. 6. Repeat until stakeholder agreement is achieved.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Does this interface layout fit your expectations? What happens when you click here? Is this workflow sequence intuitive?
Minimal Realistic Example: Building an interactive Web screen allowing meeting initiators to select date ranges and drag-and-drop invited participants to evaluate usability.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Stakeholder agreement on usability and workflow; alignment between updated requirements documentation and prototype behavior.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Setting unrealistically high stakeholder expectations regarding non-functional qualities (performance, security); converting 'quick and dirty' throwaway code into production systems; code-requirements mismatch.
When NOT to Use: For highly stable, well-understood requirements or purely backend/non-visual computational algorithms where visual feedback adds no value.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Storyboards, scenarios, user interface specifications.
Supported Decisions: UI/UX design, workflow acceptance, functional scope confirmation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Generative AI tools can instantly convert user story descriptions into interactive UI mock-ups, auto-generating front-end code for immediate user validation.

Problem Solved: Reduces elicitation time, incomplete requirements discovery, and reinventing the wheel by leveraging pre-existing domain structures, taxonomies, and patterns.
Input Artifacts: Requirements taxonomies, domain-independent meta-models, abstract domain patterns (e.g., resource management), past project specifications.
Output Artifacts: Transposed requirements, domain properties, candidate goals, structured system models.
Participants & Roles: BA, Domain Architect, SME.
Prerequisites: Availability of reusable catalogues, meta-models, or abstract domain frameworks.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Retrieve relevant knowledge fragments (taxonomies, meta-models, or abstract domains like 'resource management'). 2. Match target problem world concepts with abstract concepts. 3. Transpose abstract knowledge fragments by specialization and domain-specific renaming. 4. Validate transposed specifications with stakeholders. 5. Adapt, complete, and integrate the transposed fragments into the system model.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Is there any requirement of Taxonomy Class X in my system? How does target concept Y specialize abstract concept Z? What non-functional constraints usually apply to this pattern?
Minimal Realistic Example: Transposing the abstract domain 'Resource Management' (resource unit, user, checkout) to the 'Library System' (book copy, patron, borrow) to automatically inherit loan limitation rules.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Adequacy and accuracy of transposed specifications in the target context; domain expert validation of instantiated rules.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Forcing inappropriate abstract features onto a mismatched domain; spending excessive effort in tricky adaptations rather than fresh elicitation; lack of tool support for analogical matching.
When NOT to Use: For radical design projects or highly novel domains where no past experience, patterns, or abstractions exist.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Background study, analogical model reuse, domain modeling.
Supported Decisions: Architecture selection, domain rule adoption, comprehensive feature identification.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic systems can automatically search pattern libraries using semantic matching to retrieve relevant abstract models and auto-rename variables to fit the target glossary.

Problem Solved: Reduces uncertainty, unstated expectations, and lack of clarity by gathering deep qualitative insights, real-life practices, personal complaints, and improvement ideas directly from key people.
Input Artifacts: Stakeholder map, background study findings, interview guide (structured/unstructured prompts).
Output Artifacts: Interview transcripts, interview summary reports, validated requirements and goals.
Participants & Roles: BA (Interviewer), Stakeholder (Interviewee: SME, Manager, User, Operator).
Prerequisites: Target stakeholders identified; interviewer has acquired preliminary domain context via background study.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select the right stakeholder based on role, expertise, and exposure. 2. Prepare structured questions targeting specific goals/problems while planning open-ended prompts. 3. Conduct the interview: establish rapport, introduce context, ask easy questions first, explore 'why' behind decisions, avoid biased/opinionated questions. 4. Record and transcribe answers. 5. Synthesize input into structured reports. 6. Submit report to interviewee for review, validation, and refinement.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Why is this step performed? What problems do you encounter daily? How would you like this issue to be addressed? What if this exception occurs?
Minimal Realistic Example: An analyst interviews a chief librarian to discover why duplicate journal subscriptions occur and extracts the goal of centralized subscription management.
Quality Criteria & Verification: High utility and coverage of acquired knowledge relative to time spent; post-interview transcript validation by interviewee; absence of interviewer bias.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Asking biased, opinionated, or affirmative questions; appearing unprepared or asking 'stupid' domain questions; failing to transcribe promptly; rambling without structured control.
When NOT to Use: When target stakeholders are unavailable, or when quantitative statistical trends across thousands of users are needed (use questionnaires instead).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Questionnaires, group sessions/workshops, observation.
Supported Decisions: Problem root-cause confirmation, stakeholder preference alignment, goal elicitation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI audio-transcribers can record and summarize interviews in real time, extract key requirements/goals using natural language processing, and flag inconsistencies against existing documents.

Problem Solved: Reduces tacit knowledge gaps, unstated routine habits, and discrepancies between official documentation and actual operational practice.
Input Artifacts: Observation protocols, task lists, workplace context.
Output Artifacts: Observation notes, video recordings, workflow logs, tacit operational requirements, human mental models.
Participants & Roles: BA (Observer), End User/Operator (Observed subject).
Prerequisites: Observer granted access to actual working environment; trust established with workers.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select target operational tasks and establish trust with subjects. 2. Perform passive observation (watching/recording without interference, protocol analysis, or long-term ethnography) OR active observation (participating in tasks). 3. Record activities, gestures, informal workarounds, and social interactions. 4. Analyze logs to infer implicit mental models and unstated constraints. 5. Organize debriefing meetings with observed personnel to validate findings.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Why did you perform that manual workaround? What information on that paper slip was critical for your decision?
Minimal Realistic Example: Observing air traffic controllers handling physical paper flight strips to uncover an implicit mental model of flight progress before automating the strip display.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Validation of debriefing reports with observed workers; observation across varied workload conditions (peak vs off-peak).
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Hawthorne effect (people changing behavior when observed); misinterpreting observed actions; getting lost in massive irrelevant details; high cost/time overheads.
When NOT to Use: When quick results are required under tight deadlines, or for brand new futuristic systems where no current operational task exists.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Interviews, storyboards/scenarios, task analysis.
Supported Decisions: Usability requirements, workflow automation boundaries, tacit constraint validation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Computer vision and screen-recording AI agents can analyze user desktop workflows to automatically generate task-flow diagrams and highlight repetitive manual workarounds.

Problem Solved: Reduces conflicting stakeholder viewpoints, slow consensus building, and lack of cross-functional synergy regarding high-level system requirements.
Input Artifacts: Session agenda, wall charts, preliminary proposal drafts, presentation aids.
Output Artifacts: Brainstormed idea lists, prioritized feature lists, agreed high-level requirement proposals, workshop decision logs.
Participants & Roles: Session Leader/Facilitator, Moderator, Scribe/Reporter, BA, Sponsor, SME, End User, Developer.
Prerequisites: Key decision makers and cross-functional representatives are committed to attend structured workshops.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define session objectives, roles (leader, scribe, participants), and structured templates. 2. For Brainstorming: (a) Spontaneously generate ideas without criticism/prejudice; (b) Jointly evaluate, filter, and prioritize ideas against cost/feasibility. For Structured JAD/Workshops: Execute structured agenda to draft/refine requirements collaboratively. 3. Resolve conflicting viewpoints through real-time negotiation. 4. Record decisions on wall charts/visual tools. 5. Document results in a consolidated session report.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What creative ideas can solve this bottleneck? Do all parties agree with this trade-off? How do we rank these candidate features?
Minimal Realistic Example: A 2-day JAD workshop bringing together library directors, IT consultants, and student union reps to agree on electronic reservation features and fine policies.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Active participation across all key roles; formal sign-off on workshop decision logs; consensus achievement on conflicting items.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Dominance by vocal individuals; lack of executive facilitator control; absence of key decision makers; superficial coverage of complex technical details due to time pressure.
When NOT to Use: When key stakeholders cannot commit dedicated multi-day blocks, or when detailed low-level technical specification is required.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Interviews, questionnaires, negotiation/multicriteria analysis.
Supported Decisions: High-level feature selection, conflict resolution, project scope commitment.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI workshop assistants can transcribe multi-speaker audio, categorize brainstormed ideas in real time, and highlight emerging goal conflicts on a digital whiteboard.

Problem Solved: Reduces contradiction, divergence, and misalignment among multi-stakeholder requirements and non-functional concerns.
Input Artifacts: Overlapping requirements, stakeholder win conditions, interaction matrices, goal models.
Output Artifacts: Conflict interaction matrix, boundary conditions, agreed conflict resolutions, weakened/revised requirements.
Participants & Roles: BA, Stakeholders (with conflicting views), Business Owner, Sponsor.
Prerequisites: Requirements or goals have been elicited from multiple sources and checked for overlaps.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify overlapping statements referring to common/interrelated concepts. 2. Detect conflicts/divergences (formally, heuristically, or informally) and identify boundary conditions making them inconsistent. 3. Document conflicts using interaction matrices or requirements database links. 4. Generate alternative resolutions using resolution tactics (Avoid boundary condition, Restore, Weaken, Drop lower priority, Specialize source/target). 5. Evaluate alternative resolutions against soft goals. 6. Negotiate with stakeholders to select the mutually agreed 'best' resolution.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Under what boundary condition do these two statements become incompatible? Can we weaken statement A without violating its core objective? Which stakeholder win condition has higher priority?
Minimal Realistic Example: Detecting a divergence between 'Return books within 2 weeks' and 'Keep books as long as needed' under the boundary condition 'Needing book > 2 weeks', and resolving it by allowing online loan renewals.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Complete elimination of strong logical contradictions; stakeholder consensus on win-win trade-offs; formal consistency verification.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Resolving conflicts too prematurely before understanding root goals; ignoring weak conflicts (divergences) that only manifest under rare boundary conditions; overriding user concerns without authority.
When NOT to Use: When statements do not overlap or when inconsistencies represent trivial terminology clashes (which should be solved via glossaries).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Goal refinement, risk analysis, multicriteria decision analysis.
Supported Decisions: Scope trade-offs, priority setting, policy harmonization.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Logic-based AI agents can automatically detect divergences using boundary condition generators, propose tactic-based resolutions, and simulate the trade-off impact on soft goals.

Method Name: Risk Analysis and Management (DDP / Obstacle Analysis)
Problem Solved: Reduces over-idealism, unhandled exceptions, safety hazards, security threats, and operational failure risks in system requirements and environmental assumptions.
Input Artifacts: Goal model, environmental assumptions, domain properties, risk checklists, fault/threat trees.
Output Artifacts: Risk assessment tables, impact/effectiveness matrices (DDP), obstacle diagrams, countermeasure requirements.
Participants & Roles: BA, Risk Analyst, SME, System Architect, Safety/Security Specialist.
Prerequisites: System goals, requirements, and environment assumptions have been initially formulated.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify product/process risks and obstacles (via checklists, component inspection, fault/threat trees, or regressing goal negations). 2. Assess risk likelihood and severity of consequences to calculate risk exposure or criticality. 3. Populate DDP impact and effectiveness matrices. 4. Explore alternative countermeasures using risk-reduction tactics (Reduce likelihood, Avoid risk, Mitigate consequence, Restore). 5. Calculate Risk Reduction Leverage (RRL) or DDP effectiveness vs cost. 6. Select cost-effective countermeasures and integrate them as new/revised goals in the goal model.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What could go wrong with this assumption? What is the likelihood and severity of this hazard? Which countermeasure provides the highest risk-reduction leverage for its cost?
Minimal Realistic Example: Identifying the obstacle 'Train driver unresponsive' to the safety goal 'Stop at red signal', evaluating its catastrophic severity, and introducing the countermeasure requirement 'Send periodic driver responsiveness prompts'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Domain completeness of identified obstacles; cost-effectiveness of selected countermeasures (RRL); elimination or mitigation of catastrophic risk exposures.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Assuming an over-ideal world where environment components never fail; subjective/inconsistent risk scoring without domain expert grounding; ignoring unstated environmental assumptions.
When NOT to Use: When the system is trivial, non-critical, and carries negligible financial, safety, or operational risk.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: FMEA, Fault Tree Analysis (FTA), Threat Modeling (Anti-goals), Goal-oriented obstacle analysis.
Supported Decisions: Countermeasure selection, architecture robustness choices, release readiness.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Risk-reasoning AI agents can regress goal negations through domain properties to auto-generate obstacle trees, quantify risk exposures using historical data, and run simulated annealing algorithms to select optimal countermeasure packages under budget constraints.

Method Name: Evaluating Alternative Options (Decision Making / NFR Framework)
Problem Solved: Reduces arbitrary or sub-optimal decision making when choosing among competing system proposals, goal refinements, responsibility assignments, or architecture styles.
Input Artifacts: Alternative options (refinements, assignments, resolutions), soft goals (quality requirements), fit criteria, evaluation criteria.
Output Artifacts: NFR contribution graphs, qualitative satisficing labels (++, +, -, --, S, D, C, U), weighted decision matrices, selected 'best' option proposal.
Participants & Roles: BA, System Architect, Business Owner, Sponsor, Stakeholders.
Prerequisites: Alternative system options and non-functional soft goals have been identified.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify evaluation criteria from non-functional soft goals. 2. For Qualitative Reasoning (NFR Framework): (a) Assess individual positive/negative contributions (+, ++, -, --) of options to leaf soft goals; (b) Propagate labels (S, D, C, U) upwards along goal contribution paths to evaluate top-level goal satisficing; (c) Select the option best satisficing top goals. 3. For Quantitative Reasoning (Weighted Matrices): (a) Assign relative weights to criteria; (b) Score each option (% satisfaction or gauge variables); (c) Compute total weighted score; (d) Select the highest-scoring option.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How does alternative X contribute to soft goal Y? Which option maximizes overall weighted satisficing of our quality requirements? What is the cumulative cost vs benefit of this assignment?
Minimal Realistic Example: Comparing 'e-mail request' vs 'e-agenda access' options against soft goals 'Fast Response', 'Reliable Response', and 'Minimal Inconvenience', leading to selecting 'e-agenda' due to higher convenience and speed.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Consistently assigned scores/weights grounded in expert judgment; clear traceability from selected options to non-functional goals.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Selecting technical options without mapping them to non-functional quality criteria; subjective score assignment without consistency checks; ignoring cross-cutting impacts of choices.
When NOT to Use: When there is only one feasible way to satisfy a requirement, or when options carry identical risk and quality profiles.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), Cost-Benefit Analysis, Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA).
Supported Decisions: Architecture style selection, automation boundary decisions, goal refinement path selection.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic systems can evaluate option trade-offs by executing qualitative label propagation rules across complex goal models and running multi-criteria scoring algorithms based on telemetry data.

Problem Solved: Reduces budget overruns, missed deadlines, and unmanaged scope creep by ordering requirements for phased/incremental release under limited resources.
Input Artifacts: Elicited independent requirements/goals at comparable granularity, project cost estimates, business value criteria.
Output Artifacts: Pairwise comparison matrices, normalized value/cost distribution percentages, Value-Cost priority diagrams (High, Medium, Low priority tiers).
Participants & Roles: BA, Product Manager, Sponsor, Customer, Lead Developer/Architect.
Prerequisites: Requirements are well-defined, comparable in granularity, and mutually independent.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select comparable and independent requirements. 2. Apply Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) for Value: (a) Perform pairwise comparisons of requirements on a 1-9 scale of relative value; (b) Construct n x n matrix and compute reciprocals; (c) Normalize columns and average across rows to get relative value % for each requirement. 3. Repeat AHP for Cost (using developer estimates) to get relative cost % for each requirement. 4. Plot requirements on a Value-Cost diagram (x=Cost %, y=Value %). 5. Partition diagram into priority tiers (High, Medium, Low) in consultation with stakeholders.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Does Requirement A contribute slightly, strongly, or extremely more value than Requirement B? What is the relative implementation cost of Requirement A vs B?
Minimal Realistic Example: Prioritizing 5 scheduler features using AHP, revealing 'Produce Optimal Dates' (49% value, 18% cost -> High Priority) vs 'Multi-lingual Support' (5% value, 22% cost -> Low Priority).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Transitivity and consistency ratio check on pairwise comparison matrices; stakeholder agreement on priority tiers.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Comparing items at different granularity levels; prioritizing dependent requirements independently; subjective ad-hoc ranking without cost vs value balancing.
When NOT to Use: When all requirements are strictly mandatory legally, or when the total project scope is extremely small and fully funded.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: MoSCoW method, Group brainstorming/voting, Goal-model-based prioritization.
Supported Decisions: Release planning, budget allocation, scope pruning during change management.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AHP prioritization algorithms can be embedded in BA tools to calculate consistency ratios automatically, flag intransitive stakeholder ratings, and auto-plot Value-Cost matrices.

Problem Solved: Reduces natural language ambiguities, noises, misplaced remorse, missing cases, and unmeasurable specifications in requirement documentation.
Input Artifacts: Agreed statements, elicitation notes, business rules.
Output Artifacts: Disciplined requirements document sections, decision tables, standardized requirement templates with fit criteria.
Participants & Roles: BA, Developer, Tester, Client.
Prerequisites: Elicited statements and business rules are available for formalization/structuring.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Apply local technical writing stylistic rules (short sentences, 'shall' for mandatory, define concepts before use, single requirement per sentence). 2. For complex logic: (a) Construct a Decision Table with input conditions on top and output actions on bottom; (b) Enumerate all 2^N truth value combinations; (c) Simplify table by eliminating impossible domain cases and merging redundant columns; (d) Verify completeness (column count). 3. Instantiate predefined requirement templates, including unique ID, category, specification, fit criterion, source, rationale, and priority.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Is this sentence ambiguous? What is the exact fit criterion to measure satisfaction? Are all 2^N combinations of input conditions accounted for in this rule?
Minimal Realistic Example: Replacing a vague 3-line paragraph on train braking with an 8-column decision table detailing exact full braking and alarm responses across combinations of speed, command age, and distance.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Completeness check on decision tables (column count = 2^N before reduction); non-ambiguity; testability via fit criteria; local style rule adherence.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Mixing 'and'/'or' connectives resulting in logical tautologies; overspecifying algorithmic implementation details instead of declarative rules; omitting fit criteria.
When NOT to Use: When full formal mathematical specification is required for ultra-critical safety proofs, or when informal quick notes suffice for low-risk agile iterations.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Free natural language prose, Diagrammatic notations (UML), Formal specification (Z, LTL, SCR).
Supported Decisions: Test case design, specification acceptance, baseline contract definition.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLM prompt pipelines can analyze unrestricted natural language requirements, rewrite them using controlled technical grammar, construct complete 2^N decision tables, and flag ambiguous logic.

Method Name: Context Diagrams and Problem Diagrams (Problem Frames)
Problem Solved: Reduces uncertainty regarding system scope, software-environment boundaries, shared phenomena, and misaligned machine assumptions.
Input Artifacts: System components, external devices, environmental phenomena, generic problem frames.
Output Artifacts: Context diagrams, problem diagrams, instantiated frame diagrams.
Participants & Roles: BA, System Architect, SME.
Prerequisites: System components, physical devices, and core interaction phenomena are known.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify the machine component to be built and surrounding environment components (causal, biddable, lexical). 2. Identify shared phenomena at component interfaces (events, state variables, commands). 3. Construct a Context Diagram showing components and directed shared phenomena. 4. Upgrade to a Problem Diagram by adding explicit requirement ovals, showing which components are referenced or constrained. 5. Alternatively, select a generic Frame Diagram (e.g., Simple Workpieces, Information Display), match parameters, and instantiate component/phenomena labels.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What phenomena are controlled by the machine vs monitored by the environment? Which components are constrained by this requirement? Which generic problem frame matches this domain problem?
Minimal Realistic Example: Instantiating the 'Information Display' frame for a meeting scheduler where the Machine monitors Date/Location from the Real World and issues Notifications to a Display component.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Clear separation of machine vs environment phenomena; accurate control/monitor interface labels; explicit mapping of requirements to constrained components.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confounding machine phenomena with world phenomena; omitting environmental components; fuzzy interface definitions.
When NOT to Use: When system boundaries and environmental interfaces are already rigidly fixed and fully specified.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: UML Use Case diagrams, Dataflow diagrams, Goal-derived Context diagrams.
Supported Decisions: System scope boundary, automation boundary, interface specification.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic modeling tools can parse natural language problem statements, classify environment components by frame type, and auto-generate problem diagrams with interface control annotations.

Problem Solved: Reduces structural ambiguity, concept duplication, and fuzzy data definitions across domain concepts.
Input Artifacts: Glossary of terms, goal definitions, domain properties, candidate concepts.
Output Artifacts: Entity-Relationship diagrams, UML Class diagrams (entities, associations, attributes, multiplicities, generalization hierarchies).
Participants & Roles: BA, Data Architect, SME.
Prerequisites: Domain concepts and their relationships have been elicited or derived from goals.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify entities (autonomous passive concepts) and define them. 2. Identify intrinsic attributes for each entity and define value ranges. 3. Identify associations (conceptual links) between entities, assigning role names and multiplicities (min..max). 4. Identify specialization/generalization hierarchies and apply default attribute inheritance. 5. Annotate diagram nodes/edges with precise Def, Has, and DomInvar textual specifications.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Is this concept an entity, attribute, or association? What is the minimum and maximum multiplicity on this side? What domain invariant constrains these linked objects?
Minimal Realistic Example: A class diagram showing 'Participant' (with attributes Name, Email) linked via a 'Constraints' association (attributes: excludedDates, preferredDates) to 'Meeting' (attribute: Date).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Precise Def/Has annotations for every element; accurate multiplicities reflecting domain laws; correct use of inheritance without semantic clashes.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Modeling attributes as pointers to other objects; confusing domain properties with prescriptive requirements in multiplicities; creating non-structural dynamic links.
When NOT to Use: For purely procedural/algorithmic problems involving no persistent conceptual data structures.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Goal-derived Object Modeling, SADT datagrams, Glossaries.
Supported Decisions: Data architecture design, database schema definition, domain rule enforcement.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLMs can extract entities, attributes, and relationships directly from goal definitions, auto-generate UML class diagrams in PlantUML syntax, and flag multiplicity inconsistencies.

Problem Solved: Reduces ambiguity regarding operational data transformations, inputs/outputs, and data dependencies between processes.
Input Artifacts: System activities, data flows, repositories, external components.
Output Artifacts: SADT Actigrams/Datagrams, Dataflow Diagrams (DFDs), process decomposition hierarchies.
Participants & Roles: BA, Systems Engineer, Developer.
Prerequisites: System operations and data stores are identified.
Step-by-Step Procedure: For SADT: (a) Construct Actigrams showing activities with Input (West), Output (East), Control (North), and Mechanism (South) arrows; (b) Construct dual Datagrams; (c) Perform hierarchical decomposition. 2. For DFD: (a) Identify process bubbles, data stores (double bars), external entities (boxes), and dataflows (arrows); (b) Refine complex bubbles into lower-level DFDs. 3. Verify interface consistency across refinement levels.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What data is required as input to produce this output? What activity controls this data store? Are all inputs in the parent process accounted for in the child DFD?
Minimal Realistic Example: A DFD showing 'AskConstraints' receiving 'meetingRequest' from 'Initiator' and storing 'copyOfConstraintsRequest' into a 'meetingConstraints' repository.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Conservation of dataflow across hierarchical decomposition levels; absence of black holes (processes with inputs but no outputs) or miracles (outputs without inputs).
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Including control flow/sequencing logic in DFDs; interface mismatch between parent and child bubbles; unlabelled dataflows.
When NOT to Use: When object-oriented encapsulated designs are strictly enforced and functional decomposition is forbidden, or for purely event-driven reactive state machines.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: UML Use Cases, Goal-derived Operation Models, Activity diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Functional decomposition, interface design, data dependency mapping.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Static analysis tools can automatically check DFD hierarchical levelling consistency and detect orphaned data stores or unlinked processes in a model database.

Method Name: Event Trace Diagrams & UML Sequence Diagrams
Problem Solved: Reduces confusion regarding the temporal sequence, message passing, and event ordering during component interactions.
Input Artifacts: System scenarios, agent instances, interaction events.
Output Artifacts: Event Trace diagrams, Message Sequence Charts (MSCs), UML Sequence Diagrams.
Participants & Roles: BA, System Architect, Developer, Tester.
Prerequisites: Interacting agent instances and candidate interaction events are identified.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify participating agent instances and represent them as vertical lifelines. 2. Arrange interaction events chronologically down the lifelines as horizontal directed arrows. 3. Annotate event arrows with event names and data attributes. 4. Represent optional/alternative branches using frames (opt, alt, neg). 5. Decorate lifelines with explicit state condition lists (monitored and controlled variables) if needed for synthesis or analysis.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Which agent controls this event? Which agent monitors it? What is the exact sequence of messages exchanged in this scenario?
Minimal Realistic Example: A sequence diagram showing 'Initiator' sending 'meetingRequest(dateRange)' to 'Scheduler', followed by 'Scheduler' sending '?constraints' to 'Participant'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Total ordering of events along individual lifelines; correct event attribute labeling; alignment with higher-level goals or state machines.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Including non-instantaneous macro-events without decomposition; depicting interactions controlled by agents incapable of controlling them; partial scenario misinterpretation as global system rules.
When NOT to Use: For specifying complete, exhaustive system-wide state transition rules (use State Machines instead).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: State Machines, Use Cases, Storyboards.
Supported Decisions: Communication protocol design, interaction validation, test case generation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: State machine synthesizers can ingest collections of sequence diagrams, automatically convert them into candidate Labelled Transition Systems (LTS), and ask interactive scenario questions to prune over-generalizations.

Problem Solved: Reduces incompleteness and ambiguity in reactive component behaviors across all possible event occurrences and state transitions.
Input Artifacts: Controlled state variables, events, guard conditions, operations, scenarios.
Output Artifacts: State Machine diagrams, UML Statecharts, Labelled Transition Systems (LTS), concurrent/hierarchical state diagrams.
Participants & Roles: BA, Software Engineer, Control Engineer, Verification Specialist.
Prerequisites: Controlled state variables, events, and candidate state transitions are identified.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify state variables controlled by the agent. 2. Define SM states as classes of snapshot states. 3. Define transitions between states, labelled by triggering events, guard conditions brackets, and auxiliary actions /slash. 4. Decompose complex states into sequential sub-states or parallel concurrent sub-states. 5. Define initial and final sub-states for entry/exit control. 6. Verify determinism, reachability, and absence of deadlocks.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What state is the component in? What event triggers this transition? What guard condition must hold for this transition to fire? What concurrent sub-states evolve in parallel?
Minimal Realistic Example: A statechart for 'Train' showing parallel states 'MovementState' (Stopped, Moving) and 'DoorsState' (Closed, Open), where 'Open' is guarded by Speed = 0.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Determinism (no identical event/guard causing multiple transitions from one state); reachability of all states; coverage of all valid event occurrences; absence of race conditions.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Combinatorial explosion of states due to flat representation of concurrent variables; non-deterministic transition definitions; un-synchronized parallel state machines causing implied scenarios.
When NOT to Use: For simple, non-reactive data-transformation applications without state-dependent behaviors.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Decision tables, R-net diagrams, Goal-derived State Machines.
Supported Decisions: Reactive controller design, code generation, model checking verification.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Model checkers (SPIN, NuSMV) can automatically parse statechart specifications, explore reachability graphs containing millions of states, and generate concrete counterexample traces when safety goals are violated.

Problem Solved: Reduces ambiguity regarding all required parallel and conditional operational responses triggered by a single external stimulus.
Input Artifacts: External stimulus events, conditional decision rules, operational responses.
Output Artifacts: R-net diagrams (response-net trees).
Participants & Roles: BA, Real-time Systems Engineer.
Prerequisites: External stimuli and required operational responses are identified.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify an external stimulus event and place it as the hexagon root of the R-net tree. 2. Define operational response nodes (boxes) triggered by the stimulus. 3. Insert condition decision points (circles) to branch responses based on guard conditions. 4. Connect operations and decision points in precedence order. 5. Terminate branches with end-state or event-generation markers.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What are all the required system responses when stimulus X occurs? Under what specific condition is response Y required vs response Z?
Minimal Realistic Example: An R-net rooted on 'MeetingRequest' branching via an 'Authorized' decision node to 'ValidateMeetingData' or 'DenyRequest'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Exhaustive coverage of all conditional response paths for the stimulus; consistency with state machine transitions.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Omitting required conditional response paths; confusing stimulus events with internal system actions.
When NOT to Use: For non-real-time systems where stimulus-response dynamics are irrelevant.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: State Machine diagrams, Use Cases, Decision tables.
Supported Decisions: Real-time stimulus handling, event-driven architecture design.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Automated tools can cross-check R-net response branches against decision tables to ensure every conditional response path is completely specified.

Problem Solved: Reduces imprecision, ambiguous interpretations, and lack of mathematical verifyability in declarative goals, requirements, assumptions, and domain properties.
Input Artifacts: Informal goal definitions, object model attributes/associations, time bounds.
Output Artifacts: Formal LTL specifications, formalized goal models, formal domain properties.
Participants & Roles: BA, Formal Methods Specialist, Verification Engineer.
Prerequisites: Object model provides typed variables, attributes, and associations; critical goals are selected for formalization.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify typed instance variables from the object model. 2. Formulate state assertions using first-order predicates, functions, and logical connectives. 3. Apply temporal operators (Always, Sooner-or-later, Until, Unless, Next, Previous) to specify state sequences over time. 4. Attach relative, absolute, or variable-dependent real-time bounds (e.g., <= 2s). 5. Match assertions against established goal specification patterns (Achieve, Maintain, Avoid) to ensure syntactic and semantic correctness.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Does this property hold in every future state or at least one future state? What is the exact relative time bound d? Is this variable evaluated in the current state or next state?
Minimal Realistic Example: Formalizing 'MaintainWorstCaseStoppingDistance' as: 'forall tr1, tr2: Train, Always (Following(tr2, tr1) => Dist(tr2, tr1) > WCS-Dist(tr2))'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Well-formed syntax; precise mapping to domain phenomena; absence of contradiction; realizability by assigned agents.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Writing unbounded Achieve goals assigned to single agents (unrealizable); nesting temporal operators awkwardly without using proven patterns; omitting variable-dependent time bounds.
When NOT to Use: For low-risk, non-critical requirements where structured natural language templates provide sufficient precision at lower cost.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Structured natural language with fit criteria, Z specification, SCR tabular specification.
Supported Decisions: Formal verification, safety case arguments, automated model checking.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLM formalization agents can automatically translate structured natural language goal definitions into well-formed LTL assertions using pattern-matching libraries, flagging un-realizable temporal operators.

Problem Solved: Reduces ambiguity, structural vagueness, and unverified state transformations in complex object-oriented transactional systems.
Input Artifacts: Object model entities, associations, system operations, domain invariants.
Output Artifacts: Z specification document (given types, data schemas, initialization schemas, operation schemas).
Participants & Roles: Formal Specification Engineer, BA, Software Architect.
Prerequisites: Conceptual objects and operations are identified.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Declare given types Book, Person. 2. Construct Data Schemas declaring state variables (sets, relations, functions) and framing state invariants. 3. Construct Initialization Schemas defining initial state values. 4. Construct Operation Schemas declaring input (?)/output (!) variables, Delta/Xi imported schemas, domain pre-conditions, and post-conditions relating primed (') output states to unprimed input states. 5. Compose schemas using schema calculus (conjunction, disjunction).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What state variables are modified (Delta) vs unchanged (Xi)? What is the exact mathematical relation defining this state transformation? What exception schemas must be disjoined to make this operation robust?
Minimal Realistic Example: A Z schema 'Checkout' importing 'Delta LibrarySystem', taking 'p?: Person' and 'bc?: BookCopy', with pre-conditions 'bc? in Available' and post-conditions 'OnLoan' = OnLoan union {bc?}'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Type correctness; schema consistency; satisfaction of data invariants by operation post-conditions; completeness of disjoined exception schemas.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Omitting prime (') notation on modified state variables; failing to handle the frame problem for unmentioned variables; writing un-satisfiable pre-conditions.
When NOT to Use: For reactive, real-time control systems where temporal ordering and event-driven triggers are dominant (use SCR or LTL instead).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: VDM, B-Method, Alloy, SCR, Real-Time LTL.
Supported Decisions: Transactional software architecture, formal refinement to code, theorem proving.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Z type-checkers and SAT solvers (like Alloy) can automatically parse Z schemas, verify invariant preservation across operations, and generate counterexamples when pre-conditions fail.

Problem Solved: Reduces incompleteness, non-determinism, and unhandled event combinations in reactive software controllers.
Input Artifacts: Four-variable model (monitored, controlled, input, output variables), mode classes, events, conditions.
Output Artifacts: SCR requirements specification (Mode Transition Tables, Event Tables, Condition Tables).
Participants & Roles: Software Requirements Engineer, Control Engineer, Verification Specialist.
Prerequisites: Monitored and controlled variables identified; synchrony hypothesis assumed.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Declare monitored, controlled, term, and mode class variables. 2. Construct Mode Transition Tables defining mode changes triggered by conditioned events (@T(V) WHEN C). 3. Construct Event Tables defining term/controlled variable outputs triggered by events in specific modes. 4. Construct Condition Tables defining output values as total functions of mode and conditions. 5. Perform automated consistency checks (disjointness and coverage) on every table row.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Under what mode does event X cause output Y? Are all condition entries in this table row pairwise disjoint? Do the condition entries in this row cover 100% of possible states?
Minimal Realistic Example: An SCR Condition Table for 'DoorsState' defining output 'Open' when mode is 'Stopped' and condition is 'AtPlatform or Emergency', and 'Closed' when 'NOT AtPlatform and NOT Emergency'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Row disjointness (no non-determinism: C1 AND C2 = false); row coverage (no missing cases: C1 OR C2 OR ... = true); type correctness.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Violating row disjointness (causing non-deterministic outputs); omitting cases in condition tables (causing incomplete requirements); violating the synchrony hypothesis.
When NOT to Use: For large, highly hierarchical transactional systems requiring complex object structuring and relational calculus.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: RSML, Statecharts, Real-time LTL, Z.
Supported Decisions: Embedded software controller specification, automated tabular consistency checking, test case generation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: The SCR toolset automatically checks tabular disjointness and coverage using embedded tautology checkers, runs model checkers, and auto-generates C source code from validated tables.

Problem Solved: Reduces implementation bias and state-representation overhead by defining domain concepts abstractly through equations on operation compositions.
Input Artifacts: Domain concepts, operations (generators, modifiers, observers), composition rules.
Output Artifacts: Algebraic specification units (signatures, conditional equations, pre-conditions).
Participants & Roles: Formal Specification Engineer, Software Mathematician.
Prerequisites: Domain concepts and applicable operations are identified.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Declare given types and parameterized type constructors. 2. Declare operation signatures (input/output sets). 3. Classify operations into Generators (minimal constructors), Modifiers, and Observers. 4. Construct conditional equations by systematically pairing every Observer and non-generator Modifier with every Generator. 5. Define equations for base cases (empty generator) and recursive cases (non-empty generator). 6. Specify pre-conditions or exception outputs for partial operations.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is the minimal set of generator operations? What is the effect of applying observer X to generator Y? What equation defines the composition of modifier A with generator B?
Minimal Realistic Example: Algebraically specifying a library stack where 'CopyExists(AddCopy(lib, bc'), bc)' evaluates to 'true' if bc = bc', and to 'CopyExists(lib, bc)' if bc != bc'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Completeness of operation pairings; consistency of equations; termination of term rewriting rules.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Failing to cover all Observer-Generator pairings; writing non-terminating recursive equations; over-complicating equations due to missing generators.
When NOT to Use: When system state dynamics and temporal event sequences are the primary concern of requirements engineering.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Z, VDM, LARCH, OBJ.
Supported Decisions: Abstract data type design, executable prototyping via term rewriting.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Term-rewriting engines (e.g., OBJ, MAUDE) can execute algebraic equations automatically to provide rapid functional prototypes and verify equational consistency.

Problem Solved: Reduces structural inconsistencies, unlinked elements, orphan requirements, and incomplete cross-view specifications across large multi-view models.
Input Artifacts: Model database (populated with goal, object, agent, operation, and behaviour model instances), database schema derived from meta-model.
Output Artifacts: Query result reports, inconsistency logs, orphan element lists, generated multi-view sub-models (e.g., load analysis views).
Participants & Roles: BA, Quality Assurance Specialist, System Architect.
Prerequisites: Model fragments are recorded as meta-concept/relationship instances in a model database.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select or write entity-relationship queries based on meta-model constraints (e.g., 'Find all leaf goals without assigned agents'). 2. Execute query engine over the model database. 3. Analyze returned error/inconsistency sets. 4. Update the multi-view model to resolve highlighted structural gaps. 5. Re-run queries in press-button mode during model evolution.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Which leaf goals have no operationalizing operations? Which objects in the object model are not concerned by any goal? Which agents are assigned responsibilities exceeding their capabilities?
Minimal Realistic Example: Executing a query 'unassignedGoals = Goal which not OR-RefTo Refinement and which not OR-AssTo Assignment' to flag all unassigned leaf goals.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Zero error results returned for mandatory structural consistency queries; complete meta-model coverage.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Failing to execute queries after model changes; ignoring query warnings; writing queries with incorrect meta-model role names.
When NOT to Use: When the model is tiny and easily inspected manually, or when no structured model database tool is used.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Manual inspection checklists, Xlinkit rule checking, static semantics compiling.
Supported Decisions: Model completeness sign-off, load balancing, structural QA verification.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Model database query engines can run continuously in the background of BA tools, auto-flagging structural violations as analysts edit diagrams and suggesting fix actions.

Problem Solved: Reduces requirements inadequacy, misunderstanding of formal specifications, and unhandled operational edge-cases by visually demonstrating executable models to stakeholders.
Input Artifacts: Executable formal specification (statecharts, SCR tables, B models, LTS, temporal logic operationalizations), simulation scenarios, domain scene graphics.
Output Artifacts: Visual animation execution traces, recorded animation test scenarios, identified adequacy defects, bug reports.
Participants & Roles: BA, End User, SME, Validation Engineer.
Prerequisites: Formal executable model extracted/compiled from specifications; animation tool with UI/domain scene capabilities.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Extract or compile an executable state machine model from formal specifications. 2. Instantiate model with specific test object instances. 3. Connect animator to visual domain scenes, control panels, or UI widgets. 4. Run simulation by feeding environment stimulus events (manually or via test scripts). 5. Observe dynamic evolution of highlighted states and visual domain scenes. 6. Identify adequacy defects with stakeholders and refine formal specifications.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Does the system behave as you expect when this stimulus occurs? Why did the simulated train move while doors were open? Is this visual response acceptable?
Minimal Realistic Example: Simulating a train control model in FAUST where an analyst clicks 'start' on a panel and visually observes on a 2D track scene that the train moves while doors remain open, exposing a missing guard.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Stakeholder validation of visual scene behaviors; complete coverage of key operational scenarios; absence of simulator execution deadlocks.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Animating non-representative test instances; relying on unvalidated simulation models that do not match the underlying formal specification; lack of stakeholder engagement during animation runs.
When NOT to Use: When no formal executable specification exists, or for purely non-functional static requirements (e.g., development cost).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Prototypes, Model Checking, Walkthroughs.
Supported Decisions: Requirements adequacy sign-off, operational workflow confirmation, acceptance test scripting.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Automated animators can generate edge-case event sequences, feed them into executable models, monitor for visual property violations, and auto-record failing animation traces for BA review.

Problem Solved: Reduces subtle concurrency errors, race conditions, deadlocks, and unhandled state combinations in complex reactive models.
Input Artifacts: Parallel state machine model (PROMELA, SMV, LTS), formal property to verify (LTL or CTL formula).
Output Artifacts: Verification result ('Property holds' or 'Property violated'), concrete counterexample trace.
Participants & Roles: Verification Specialist, Formal Methods Engineer, BA.
Prerequisites: State machine model and target properties are fully formalized.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Express system model as parallel state machines in model checker input language. 2. Formalize target safety/liveness property in LTL or CTL. 3. Execute model checker (e.g., SPIN, SMV, LTSA). 4. Tool exhaustively explores reachability graph. 5. If property holds, output 'Yes'. If property is violated, tool generates the shortest counterexample execution trace. 6. Analyze counterexample trace to pinpoint model defect and fix the specification.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Does this parallel state machine satisfy safety property P under all state combinations? What exact sequence of interleaving events led to the deadlock in this counterexample?
Minimal Realistic Example: Model checking a train door/movement controller against 'Always(Moving => DoorsClosed)', producing a 5-step counterexample trace showing doors opening while moving due to a missing guard.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Exhaustive reachability exploration; correctness of formalized target properties; validity of generated counterexample traces.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: State explosion problem on overly large state spaces; misinterpreting long counterexample traces; formalizing incorrect properties leading to false confidence.
When NOT to Use: For infinite-state systems without abstraction, or when models are informal and cannot be compiled into state machines.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Theorem Proving, Bounded SAT Solving, Specification Animation.
Supported Decisions: Safety/security verification sign-off, critical controller verification, bug elimination.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI diagnostic agents can analyze long model checker counterexample traces, automatically isolate the root cause transition in the source statechart, and suggest the missing guard condition.
