Problem Solved: Reduces unverified claims, subtle mathematical errors, and inconsistency in infinite-state declarative specifications.
Input Artifacts: Formal specification axioms (LTL, Z, PVS, B), candidate theorem (property/invariant to prove).
Output Artifacts: Formal proof script, verified invariant theorem, or unproved lemma log.
Participants & Roles: Formal Methods Specialist, Logic Engineer.
Prerequisites: System axioms, data schemas, and properties are fully formalized in a logic with a sound inference engine.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Load formal specification axioms and domain properties into theorem prover (e.g., PVS, STeP, Z/EVES). 2. Formulate target property as candidate theorem. 3. Apply inference rules (modus ponens, substitutivity, induction, pattern instantiation) interactively or via automated strategies. 4. Prove intermediate lemmas. 5. Complete proof sequence to establish theorem validity.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Does axiom set A entail theorem T? What induction step is required to prove this invariant over all states? Is this specification set mathematically consistent?
Minimal Realistic Example: Proving by induction in Z/EVES that the operation 'Checkout' maintains the data invariant 'Available intersect OnLoan = empty' across all valid system states.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Mathematical soundness and completeness of inference steps; complete coverage of initial and transition states in induction proofs.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Failing to complete proofs due to missing domain axioms; high human effort and skill required; lack of concrete counterexample generation when a proof fails.
When NOT to Use: When finite-state verification (model checking) can do the job automatically, or when team expertise in formal logic is absent.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Model Checking, Bounded SAT Solving, Formal Refinement Patterns.
Supported Decisions: Ultra-critical safety/security certification, formal invariant verification.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Automated tactic engines in modern provers use machine learning to select optimal proof strategies, auto-proving routine lemmas and reducing human interactive intervention.

Problem Solved: Reduces undocumented change impacts, orphan requirements, unverified design features, and costly maintenance overheads during system evolution.
Input Artifacts: RD items (goals, requirements, assumptions), downward software lifecycle items (architecture, code, test cases), traceability meta-model.
Output Artifacts: Traceability graph, traceability matrices/lists, impact analysis reports, coverage matrices.
Participants & Roles: BA, Traceability Manager, Change Review Board, System Architect, Test Lead.
Prerequisites: Traceable items have unique identifiers; project traceability policy is established.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Establish project traceability policy (scope, granularity, link types). 2. Assign unique identifiers to all traceable items. 3. Establish bi-directional links between source and target items (Dependency, Variant, Revision, Use, Derivation) manually, via model database, or using automated link generators. 4. Record links in a traceability database or matrix. 5. Exploit links for impact analysis, rationale analysis, coverage analysis, and defect tracking. 6. Maintain and update links when items are created, modified, or deleted.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Why does this requirement exist (backward traceability)? What design components and test cases are impacted if I change this requirement (forward traceability)? Is this requirement covered by test cases?
Minimal Realistic Example: Tracing goal 'Anywhere/anytime notification' to requirement 'SMS notification', then to architecture module 'SMSNotifier', and finally to test case 'TC-SMS-01'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: 100% coverage of critical requirements by test cases; accuracy of dependency links; bi-directional traversability.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Traceability overload (tracing everything at too fine a grain without policy); untracked manual link updates; vague link semantics.
When NOT to Use: Never skipped entirely, but restricted to coarse-grained items in low-risk, small-scale agile projects.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Traceability matrices, Feature diagrams, Traceability model databases, Information retrieval link generators.
Supported Decisions: Change request approval, impact assessment, release coverage verification, compliance audit.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Information retrieval AI agents can analyze semantic similarity between requirement text and source code to auto-generate candidate traceability links with precision/recall scoring.

Problem Solved: Reduces unmonitored scope creep, unexpected budget overruns, and system instability caused by ad-hoc, un-evaluated requirement changes.
Input Artifacts: Change requests, wishlists, existing RD baseline, impact analysis reports, traceability graph.
Output Artifacts: Evaluated/approved change requests, prioritized change log, baselined new RD version, change audit trail.
Participants & Roles: Change Review Board (CRB), BA, Project Manager, Sponsor, System Architect, Lead Developer.
Prerequisites: An approved baseline version of the RD exists; traceability links are established.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Initiate change: Collect change wishes and submit a structured Change Request (description, rationale, urgency, initial cost/impact estimate). 2. Evaluate change: CRB reviews request, assesses well-foundedness, traces forward/backward impact, detects conflicts, and estimates cost/feasibility. 3. Prioritize approved changes. 4. Consolidate change: Propagate approved changes through the RD, re-verify consistency, update traceability graph, and baseline the new RD version. 5. Implement changes in software revisions/variants.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is the rationale and urgency of this change? What other requirements and architectural components are impacted? Is the benefit worth the implementation cost?
Minimal Realistic Example: Evaluating a change request to add 'SMS notification' alongside 'e-mail notification', assessing its architectural impact on the 'Notifier' module, approving it, and updating the RD baseline.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Formal CRB approval sign-off; complete forward propagation across all dependent artifacts; maintained consistency in the new RD baseline.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Bypassing the CRB via informal developer-client agreements; failing to propagate changes to test cases and user manuals; un-documented change rationale.
When NOT to Use: In early exploratory prototyping phases before a formal requirement baseline has been established.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Agile backlog grooming, Configuration management, Feature toggles.
Supported Decisions: RD baselining, release scope adjustments, change request approval/rejection.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Change management agents can automatically parse incoming change requests, run forward impact analysis queries across the model database, and generate preliminary cost-benefit summaries for CRB review.

Problem Solved: Reduces system failure when real-world environment assumptions are violated or change dynamically after system deployment.
Input Artifacts: Mission-critical goals, volatile environment assumptions, formal temporal logic specifications, event logs.
Output Artifacts: Generated runtime assertion monitors, violation event logs, compensator reconfiguration rules, dynamic adaptation actions.
Participants & Roles: BA, System Architect, Software Engineer, Runtime Adaptation Engine.
Prerequisites: Critical/volatile environment assumptions are formally specified in temporal logic; alternative courses of action are designed.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify critical/volatile assumptions or requirements at RE time. 2. Formalize assertions in temporal logic. 3. Compile formal assertions into software monitors (as statecharts or event pattern checkers). 4. Design alternative recovery courses of action (compensators). 5. Deploy software with integrated monitors. 6. At runtime, monitor watches event streams; upon detecting assumption violation, it triggers compensator rules to dynamically reconfigure system behavior.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Which environment assumption is most likely to be violated at runtime? What alternative course of action should the software execute if assumption A fails?
Minimal Realistic Example: Monitoring the assumption 'Participant returns constraints within 3 days'; if violated > 3 times, the compensator engine automatically switches to fetching constraints directly from the participant's e-agenda.
Quality Criteria & Verification: 100% detection rate of specified assumption violations by monitors; correct rule-based execution of compensator reconfigurations; minimal runtime performance overhead.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Monitoring non-critical stable assumptions (causing excessive runtime overhead); failing to design alternative recovery actions; un-bounded monitoring loops.
When NOT to Use: For simple static systems operating in fully controlled, unchanging environments where assumptions never fail.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Static risk analysis, manual software updates, fault-tolerant architecture design.
Supported Decisions: Dynamic software reconfiguration, automated exception recovery, adaptive service execution.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Runtime monitoring agents can continuously evaluate streaming telemetry against formal LTL goal assertions, using machine learning to dynamically adjust reconfiguration thresholds.

Problem Solved: Provides a constructive, systematic method to build a complete, consistent, pertinent, and traceable multi-view system model combining WHY, WHAT, and WHO dimensions.
Input Artifacts: Preliminary documentations, interview transcripts, complaints, problem statements.
Output Artifacts: System Model (Goal model, Obstacle model, Object model, Agent model, Operation model, Behaviour model), generated Requirements Document.
Participants & Roles: BA, System Architect, SME, Business Owner, Developers, Testers.
Prerequisites: Access to domain stakeholders and initial problem descriptions.
Step-by-Step Procedure: System-as-is: (a) Build preliminary goal model illustrated by scenarios; (b) Derive preliminary object model. 2. System-to-be: (a) Update goal model with new goals and scenarios; (b) Derive updated object model; (c) Analyze obstacles, threats, and conflicts; (d) Analyze responsibilities and build agent model; (e) Make choices among alternative options; (f) Operationalize goals in operation model; (g) Build and analyze behaviour model (sequence and state diagrams); (h) Package model and generate requirements document.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: WHY is this goal needed? HOW can this goal be satisfied? WHO is capable of being responsible for this leaf goal? WHAT operations are required to operationalize this goal?
Minimal Realistic Example: Building a complete mine safety control model: refining 'Avoid Miners In Flooded Mine' down to 'PumpOnIfHighWater', deriving object 'Pump', assigning responsibility to 'SafetyController', operationalizing into 'SwitchPumpOn', and generating state diagrams.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Completeness of goal refinements; realizability of leaf goals by assigned agents; correctness of operation operationalizations; structural consistency across all views via meta-model rules.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confusing goals with operations; mixing case analysis with alternative options; building object models with non-structural dynamic links; omitting environment expectations.
When NOT to Use: For extremely small, low-risk, short-lived scripts or minor bug fixes where comprehensive multi-view modeling overhead is unjustified.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Use-case-driven analysis, Structured Analysis (SA), Tropos, NFR Framework.
Supported Decisions: System scope, automation boundary, architecture selection, risk countermeasure selection, release sign-off.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic RE platforms can orchestrate the entire KAOS pipeline: ingesting transcripts to build draft goal models, running automated obstacle/conflict regressors, generating UML class/sequence diagrams, and auto-formatting IEEE-830 compliant specifications.

Problem Solved: Provides a framework for investigating and analyzing external macro-environmental influences operating outside an organization's control, reducing uncertainty regarding future environmental threats and opportunities.
Input Artifacts: External environment data, research reports (e.g., Gartner, Dun & Bradstreet), domain knowledge.
Output Artifacts: Categorized list of key external influences, SWOT opportunities and threats.
Participants & Roles: BA, Business Owner, Senior Management, SME, Departmental Representatives (e.g., Legal, Finance).
Prerequisites: Pre-research on macroeconomic, political, legal, and technological trends affecting the business sector.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Convene a workshop with representatives from key departments. 2. Examine Political factors. 3. Examine Economic factors. 4. Examine Socio-cultural factors. 5. Examine Technological developments. 6. Examine Legal regulations. 7. Examine Environmental factors. 8. Evaluate and select key external factors that impact the organization.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What political changes or government initiatives could impact us? What economic trends affect our market? What socio-cultural changes alter consumer behavior? What new technologies exist? What legal/regulatory mandates affect us? What environmental issues present risks?
Minimal Realistic Example: A retail company evaluates plastic bag regulations (Legal/Environmental) affecting customer perception and costs, listing them as threats in a strategic review.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Identified factors must satisfy two criteria: they are completely outside the direct control of the organization, and they have a measurable potential impact on it.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confusing internal strategic responses (e.g., 'charge for carrier bags') with external factors (e.g., 'environmental pollution concerns'); spending excessive time debating exact categorization.
When NOT to Use: When analysing short-term operational tweaks without external market or environmental dependency, or when immediate low-risk hypotheses need rapid execution.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: SWOT Analysis, Porter's Five Forces, Resource Audit, MOST Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Strategic direction, market positioning, compliance strategies, product strategy.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI can continuously ingest global news, regulatory updates, and market reports to draft a dynamic PESTLE dashboard. Human-in-the-loop validates relevance to organizational strategic context.

Problem Solved: Determines the competitive intensity and profitability of an industry or market domain, reducing strategic blind spots regarding industry competitive pressures.
Input Artifacts: Industry data, market research reports, product/service portfolio descriptions.
Output Artifacts: Industry pressure assessment, competitive position summary, SWOT opportunities and threats.
Participants & Roles: BA, Product Manager, Business Owner, Senior Executives, Strategy Analysts.
Prerequisites: Clear definition of the specific industry or market domain being evaluated.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define the target industry/domain boundaries. 2. Assess threat of new entrants and barriers to entry. 3. Assess bargaining power of buyers. 4. Assess bargaining power of suppliers. 5. Assess threat of substitute products/services. 6. Evaluate rivalry among existing industry competitors. 7. Synthesize competitive pressures into strategic threats/opportunities.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is the level of competition? How easy is it for new players to enter? How much choice do buyers have? Do suppliers hold power over pricing? What alternative substitutes fulfill the same core need?
Minimal Realistic Example: A luxury handbag retailer defines its industry as 'luxury giftware' instead of 'leather bags', identifying fine jewelry and perfume as key competitive substitutes.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Comprehensive coverage of all five forces based on factual industry data rather than subjective organizational assumptions.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Defining the industry too narrowly or broadly; missing non-obvious substitute products; ignoring high-capital potential entrants such as mega-supermarkets.
When NOT to Use: In non-competitive internal process optimization or when analyzing internal team dynamics/operations.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: PESTLE analysis, SWOT analysis, Value Chain Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Market entry/exit, competitive strategy, pricing strategy, business model selection.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic scrapers monitor market entry, price changes, supplier consolidation, and consumer shift trends to populate force vectors automatically.

Problem Solved: Examines strategic direction alignment, ensuring tactics and operational efforts directly support higher-level mission and objectives, reducing strategic misalignment and conflicting priorities.
Input Artifacts: Corporate strategy documents, mission statements, business plans, stakeholder interviews.
Output Artifacts: MOST Matrix/Statement (Mission, Objectives, Strategy, Tactics), identified organizational strengths and weaknesses.
Participants & Roles: BA, Sponsor, Executive Leadership, Business Owner.
Prerequisites: Availability or definition of the corporate mission and strategic plans.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify and document the overall business Mission. 2. Identify measurable Objectives aligned to the Mission. 3. Identify medium-to-long term Strategies designed to achieve Objectives. 4. Identify short-term detailed Tactics that execute the Strategy. 5. Analyze alignment, clarity, definition, and staff commitment across all four levels.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is our business rationale/direction? What specific targets prove we met the mission? What strategic plans deliver those targets? What daily tactical activities execute those strategies?
Minimal Realistic Example: A retail company sets Mission 'Be top online fashion seller', Objective 'Increase online sales by 20%', Strategy 'Target youth market', and Tactic 'Launch TikTok marketing campaign'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Vertical alignment: every tactic maps to a strategy, every strategy to an objective, and every objective to the mission.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Assuming a published MOST equates to staff buy-in; defining vague objectives without clear targets; decoupling daily operations from strategic plans.
When NOT to Use: When performing pure low-level technical bug fixing or minor isolated operational changes with no strategic impact.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: VMOST, SWOT analysis, Balanced Business Scorecard, Resource Audit.
Supported Decisions: Scope definition, strategy validation, change prioritization, project initiation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLM agents analyze corporate communications and backlog items to detect misalignment between low-level task executions and strategic MOST goals.

Problem Solved: Identifies internal resource capability, highlights core competencies, and uncovers weaknesses that could prevent or undermine business change.
Input Artifacts: Financial reports, asset inventories, HR skill profiles, IT architecture diagrams, organizational charts.
Output Artifacts: Resource Audit profile categorized by Physical, Financial, Human, Reputation, and Know-how resources.
Participants & Roles: BA, Business Owner, HR Manager, Finance Manager, Operations SME.
Prerequisites: Access to organizational financial, physical, and human resource data.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Audit Physical resources (land, buildings, equipment). 2. Audit Financial resources (assets, cash flow, credit). 3. Audit Human resources (staff numbers, skills, motivation). 4. Audit Reputation (brand perception, goodwill). 5. Audit Know-how (data, information systems, IP). 6. Categorize findings into organizational strengths and weaknesses.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Do we have sufficient physical space and equipment? Is the business financially stable? Are staff skilled and motivated? What is our brand reputation? How effectively do we capture intellectual know-how?
Minimal Realistic Example: A consulting firm audits its resources, identifying high consultant motivation (Human Strength) but fragmented, unintegrated ad-hoc IT systems (Know-how Weakness).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Factual verification of resource existence, availability, and quality against objective benchmarks.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Underestimating the time and effort required for a thorough audit; ignoring intangible assets like organizational know-how and culture.
When NOT to Use: In small-scale, rapid hypothesis testing where resource constraints are well understood or negligible.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Resource Analysis, SWOT Analysis, McKinsey 7-S, Capability Modelling.
Supported Decisions: Feasibility decisions, build vs. buy, investment decisions, resource allocation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Automated data-mining agents summarize internal HR skills databases, asset management registers, and financial metrics into a consolidated resource dashboard.

Problem Solved: Evaluates product and service portfolios based on market share and market growth, reducing bad investment decisions in non-performing assets.
Input Artifacts: Product catalog, market share metrics, industry market growth trends, sales figures.
Output Artifacts: 2x2 Matrix mapping products into Star, Cash Cow, Wild Cat/Problem Child, and Dog quadrants.
Participants & Roles: BA, Product Manager, Marketing Manager, Business Owner, Sponsor.
Prerequisites: Reliable market share and industry growth metrics for all evaluated offerings.
Step-by-Step Procedure: List all products/services in the portfolio. 2. Determine market growth rate for each product's industry. 3. Determine relative market share for each product. 4. Map products onto the 2x2 grid (Star, Cash Cow, Wild Cat, Dog). 5. Formulate product investment/divestment strategies.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Which products operate in high-growth markets? Which products dominate their market share? Which offerings drain capital without growth prospects?
Minimal Realistic Example: A software vendor maps its legacy desktop software to 'Cash Cow' (funding new web apps) and an underperforming legacy utility to 'Dog' (flagged for retirement).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Accurate categorization reflecting objective market data rather than internal executive fondness for legacy products.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Forcing products that sit on quadrant boundaries into rigid categories; misjudging low market share as failure when it is caused by market timing.
When NOT to Use: For single-product startups or non-commercial internal IT systems without market competition.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: BCG Matrix, Ansoff's Matrix, Value Proposition Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Product portfolio investment, divestment, resource allocation, release priorities.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI analytics automatically categorize product lines by analyzing real-time sales velocity against industry market growth APIs.

Problem Solved: Consolidates and synthesizes internal strengths/weaknesses and external opportunities/threats, reducing unstructured, subjective strategy formulation.
Input Artifacts: PESTLE analysis, Porter's Five Forces, Resource Audit, MOST analysis results.
Output Artifacts: SWOT Matrix, strategic options for development and evaluation.
Participants & Roles: BA, Sponsor, Business Owner, Executive Management, Key SMEs.
Prerequisites: Completion of preliminary internal and external environmental investigations.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Input identified internal positive capabilities as Strengths. 2. Input internal negative capability gaps as Weaknesses. 3. Input external favorable possibilities as Opportunities. 4. Input external risks as Threats. 5. Cross-analyze SWOT quadrants to derive actionable strategic options.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What strengths enable us to seize these opportunities? What weaknesses make us vulnerable to threats? How can we overcome weaknesses to exploit opportunities?
Minimal Realistic Example: A retail firm combines its strong delivery fleet (Strength) with rising online shopping trends (Opportunity) to launch an express grocery delivery service.
Quality Criteria & Verification: SWOT entries must be explicitly derived from formal analytical models (e.g., PESTLE, Resource Audit) rather than ad-hoc opinions.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Conducting unstructured brainstorming without rigorous inputs; treating tactical project responses as external opportunities or threats.
When NOT to Use: As a standalone technique without prior formal environmental and internal capability analysis.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: TOWS analysis, PESTLE, Porter's Five Forces, Resource Audit.
Supported Decisions: Strategic options identification, change initiative initiation, business case development.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLMs can ingest multi-source analytical reports to draft a structured SWOT matrix, flagging ungrounded claims for human review.

Problem Solved: Structures product and market growth strategies, reducing uncertainty when identifying alternatives for strategic expansion.
Input Artifacts: SWOT Analysis, market research, product capability documentation.
Output Artifacts: 2x2 Growth Strategy Matrix (Market Penetration, Market Development, Product Development, Diversification).
Participants & Roles: BA, Product Manager, Business Owner, Marketing Director.
Prerequisites: Completed SWOT analysis and organizational growth objectives.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Evaluate existing products in existing markets (Market Penetration). 2. Evaluate existing products in new markets (Market Development). 3. Evaluate new products in existing markets (Product Development). 4. Evaluate new products in new markets (Diversification). 5. Assess risks and select strategic growth option.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Can we grow by selling more existing products to existing customers? Can we find new customer segments or regions for existing products? Can we build new features/products for current customers?
Minimal Realistic Example: An established UK training provider decides to sell its existing course portfolio in European markets (Market Development strategy).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Clear risk-return profiling of each quadrant option, backed by objective market feasibility research.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Choosing high-risk diversification without leveraging existing core competencies or existing customer relationships.
When NOT to Use: When analyzing purely internal process optimizations or non-growth compliance projects.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Ansoff's Box, SWOT Analysis, Boston Box, Value Proposition Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Scope definition, product roadmap decisions, market expansion strategy.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Generative AI simulates market responses and risk profiles for proposed expansion strategies across new geographic or demographic segments.

Problem Solved: Ensures holistic organizational alignment across 7 core areas during business change, reducing implementation failures caused by misaligned soft/hard factors.
Input Artifacts: Strategy definition, organizational structure, HR policies, business process maps, cultural audits.
Output Artifacts: 7-S Alignment Audit Report, impact analysis, change initiative recommendations.
Participants & Roles: BA, Sponsor, Change Manager, HR Lead, Enterprise Architect.
Prerequisites: A defined organizational strategy or proposed business change proposition.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Analyze Shared Values (superordinate goals). 2. Assess Hard elements: Strategy, Structure, Systems. 3. Assess Soft elements: Style, Staff, Skills. 4. Evaluate alignment and interdependencies between all 7 elements. 5. Identify misalignment gaps and required change interventions.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Do our internal structures support the new strategy? Are staff skills aligned with new system needs? Does management style fit our core shared values?
Minimal Realistic Example: A company shifting to high-volume low-cost sales uses 7-S to reveal that its highly paid, high-touch senior sales staff (Staff/Skills) conflict with the new low-cost strategy.
Quality Criteria & Verification: All 7 dimensions must demonstrate mutual reinforcement and explicit alignment with the shared values.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Focusing exclusively on hard elements (Structure, Systems) while ignoring soft elements (Style, Staff, Skills, Shared Values).
When NOT to Use: For isolated, localized software tweaks that have zero impact on staff, structure, or management culture.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: POPIT Model, Leavitt's Diamond, Cultural Web.
Supported Decisions: Target Operating Model design, organizational restructuring, change management strategy.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic systems monitor employee sentiment, process adherence, and skill distribution to report real-time alignment scores against corporate strategy.

Problem Solved: Analyzes proposed organizational changes holistically across four interdependent components, preventing project failure caused by isolated technological or structural changes.
Input Artifacts: Proposed change initiatives, process models, IT architecture plans, organizational charts.
Output Artifacts: Impact analysis matrix across Task, Structure, People, and Technology.
Participants & Roles: BA, Change Manager, IT Lead, Business Process Owner, HR SME.
Prerequisites: An initial change proposal originating in at least one component (e.g., new technology).
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify the primary driver component for change (e.g., Technology). 2. Analyze required changes to Tasks/processes. 3. Analyze required changes to People (skills, staffing, training). 4. Analyze required changes to Structure (roles, reporting lines). 5. Ensure all 4 components are balanced and harmonized.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How does this technology change affect daily tasks? What new skills do people need? Does this require restructuring teams or lines of communication?
Minimal Realistic Example: Introducing a workflow system (Technology) leads to redefined event-booking procedures (Task), staff training (People), and merging two administrative departments (Structure).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Demonstrated consideration of interdependencies across all four components so no component is modified in isolation.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Treating IT system deployment purely as a technical upgrade without adjusting human skills, tasks, or reporting structures.
When NOT to Use: For minor bug fixes or minor localized routine maintenance tasks.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: POPIT Model, McKinsey 7-S, Impact Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Implementation planning, change impact scope, training and organizational restructuring plans.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic impact models predict downstream disruption to tasks and required skill upgrades whenever a technology component change is introduced.

Problem Solved: Models what an organization needs to do to deliver value, independent of how, who, or where it is executed, reducing duplication and stability issues in business transformation.
Input Artifacts: Corporate strategy, business architecture blueprints, functional domains overview.
Output Artifacts: Hierarchical Business Capability Model (Strata, Foundation, Capability Groups, Business Capabilities taxonomy).
Participants & Roles: BA, Enterprise Architect, Business Architect, Executive Management.
Prerequisites: High-level understanding of the entire organizational business scope.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define Strategic, Core, and Support strata (Level 0). 2. Identify Level 1 Foundation capabilities (Operational and Environmental). 3. Decompose into Level 2 Capability Groups. 4. Decompose into Level 3/4 Business Capabilities. 5. Validate uniqueness and stability using the SUAVE checklist.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What ability does the business require to achieve this outcome? What (not how) does the business do? Is this capability unique across the entire organization?
Minimal Realistic Example: Decomposing 'HR Management' (Level 1) into 'Staff Recruitment' (Level 2) and further into 'Interviewing' and 'Induction' (Level 3).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Capabilities are named as nouns (not verbs), contain no process flow/arrows, are unique across the enterprise, and satisfy SUAVE criteria.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confusing capabilities with business processes or organizational units; using verb names; introducing process sequence arrows into capability maps.
When NOT to Use: When analyzing short-term procedural task sequences or temporary project task steps.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Value Streams, Business Process Modelling, Value Chain Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Target Operating Model design, enterprise architecture alignment, application portfolio rationalization, outsourcing decisions.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents map software tool functionality and organizational processes directly to standard business capability taxonomy nodes.

Problem Solved: Models end-to-end sequential stages that deliver value to stakeholders, reducing siloed process optimization that fails to deliver end-to-end value.
Input Artifacts: Stakeholder perspectives, Value Propositions, Capability Model.
Output Artifacts: Value Stream Model depicting sequential value stages, trigger events, and enabling business capabilities.
Participants & Roles: BA, Business Architect, Enterprise Architect, Customer Experience Lead, Sponsor.
Prerequisites: Identification of target stakeholder groups and their perceived value propositions.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify the primary target stakeholder and their desired value. 2. Work backward to define high-level sequential stages required to deliver that value. 3. Identify the triggering stakeholder event. 4. Map required enabling business capabilities to each stage. 5. Verify value accrual at each stage.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What value does the stakeholder expect? What sequential stages must occur to realize this value? What capability enables each stage?
Minimal Realistic Example: A passenger's value stream for 'Fly to holiday destination' includes stages: Park car -> Check in & bag drop -> Clear security -> Clear passport control -> Board flight -> Clear immigration -> Pick up bags.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Each stage must incrementally add value from the stakeholder's perspective; stages are high-level and distinct from low-level detailed process steps.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confusing value stream stages with detailed operational workflow diagrams; burying value streams inside internal departmental silos.
When NOT to Use: For micro-level task step analysis or purely technical system integration mapping.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Value Stream Mapping (Lean), Value Chain Analysis, Capability Modelling, Business Process Modelling.
Supported Decisions: Customer experience optimization, process re-engineering scope, capability investment prioritization.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Process mining agents analyze cross-system transaction logs to reconstruct real-world value stream execution times and friction points.

Problem Solved: Provides an holistic framework for identifying required business changes across four key dimensions, preventing single-dimensional (e.g. IT-only) project failure.
Input Artifacts: Gap analysis results, business strategy, requirements catalogue, system architecture.
Output Artifacts: POPIT Change Assessment across Processes, Organization, People, and Information/Technology.
Participants & Roles: BA, Sponsor, Change Manager, HR Lead, Enterprise Architect.
Prerequisites: Identification of proposed business or system changes.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Evaluate required changes to Business Processes. 2. Evaluate required changes to Information & Technology systems. 3. Evaluate required changes to People (skills, roles, communication). 4. Evaluate required changes to Organization (structure, management, resources). 5. Align all four areas to ensure coherent implementation.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: If we change this process, how does it affect IT systems? What training do people need? Does the organizational management structure support this?
Minimal Realistic Example: Redesigning a customer service process (Process) requires upgraded CRM screens (IT), staff training (People), and revised team supervisory roles (Organization).
Quality Criteria & Verification: All four quadrants are populated and cross-checked for mutual alignment and completeness.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Implementing technical changes without updating business processes or providing staff training.
When NOT to Use: For trivial bug fixes or micro-level task edits that carry no broader organizational impact.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Four-view model, McKinsey 7-S, Leavitt's Diamond, Impact Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Business case option design, change impact scope, target operating model specification.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: GenAI evaluates change request tickets to flag missing impact dimensions across People, Process, IT, or Organizational structure automatically.

Method Name: Critical success factors and key performance indicators
Problem Solved: Defines vital areas of performance and specific quantitative metrics to monitor progress toward organizational objectives, reducing ambiguity in performance evaluation.
Input Artifacts: MOST Analysis, CATWOE, Balanced Business Scorecard, corporate objectives.
Output Artifacts: CSF list (Industry-wide and Organization-specific), KPI targets with defined timeframes.
Participants & Roles: BA, Sponsor, Executive Leadership, Performance Manager.
Prerequisites: Clear definition of organizational Mission and Objectives.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Review corporate MOST and executive core beliefs (CATWOE). 2. Identify industry-wide Critical Success Factors (CSFs). 3. Identify organization-specific differentiator CSFs. 4. Define specific Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) for each CSF. 5. Set quantitative targets and timeframes for each KPI.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What critical factors are essential for our business to succeed? What specific metric measures if we achieved this success factor? What is the exact target and timeframe?
Minimal Realistic Example: For the CSF 'Excellent Customer Service', defining KPIs: 'Fewer than 2% customer complaints on quarterly survey' and 'More than 60% repeat purchases within 12 months'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: KPIs must be specific, measurable, actionable, relevant, and time-bound (SMART), directly linked to identified CSFs.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Creating KPIs that do not tie back to strategic CSFs; setting unmeasurable or vague performance targets; tracking too many vanity metrics.
When NOT to Use: When managing ad-hoc, exploratory research projects where quantifiable outcomes cannot be pre-defined.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Balanced Business Scorecard, Outcome Frame.
Supported Decisions: Performance management, business case evaluation, project success verification.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Autonomous monitoring agents stream real-time operational data to generate predictive KPI alerts and flag potential CSF breaches before they occur.

Problem Solved: Balances financial metrics with non-financial drivers of future success, reducing short-sighted over-reliance on past financial performance.
Input Artifacts: Corporate Strategy, CSFs and KPIs, Mission and Objectives.
Output Artifacts: Balanced Business Scorecard (BBS) covering Financial, Customer, Internal Business Process, and Learning & Growth perspectives.
Participants & Roles: BA, Executive Management, Sponsor, Finance Director, Operational Leads.
Prerequisites: Defined corporate vision, strategy, and strategic objectives.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Review corporate Vision and Strategy. 2. Define CSFs/KPIs for the Financial perspective. 3. Define CSFs/KPIs for the Customer perspective. 4. Define CSFs/KPIs for the Internal Business Process perspective. 5. Define CSFs/KPIs for Learning and Growth (Innovation). 6. Monitor performance holistically across all four quadrants.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How do we look to shareholders (Financial)? How do customers see us (Customer)? What must we excel at (Internal Business Process)? How can we continue to improve and create value (Learning & Growth)?
Minimal Realistic Example: A company measures supplier costs (Financial), price competitiveness (Customer), quality checking process speed (Internal Process), and new product introduction rates (Learning & Growth).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Balanced inclusion of quantitative metrics across all four perspectives, avoiding dominance by financial metrics.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Focusing exclusively on financial outcomes; treating the scorecard as a static reporting dashboard rather than an active strategic management tool.
When NOT to Use: For single minor feature enhancement projects without broad organizational reach.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: CSFs and KPIs, MOST Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Strategic performance monitoring, project portfolio selection, business model evaluation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI analytics engines compile cross-departmental data into unified Scorecard views, predicting future performance shifts across all four quadrants.

Problem Solved: Elicits qualitative facts, opinions, needs, tacit knowledge, and political perspectives through structured one-to-one discussions, reducing stakeholder misunderstanding and resistance.
Input Artifacts: Interview agenda, preliminary project documentation, stakeholder list.
Output Artifacts: Interview notes, confirmed facts/opinions, identified issues, initial requirements.
Participants & Roles: BA (Interviewer), Stakeholder (Interviewee - Sponsor, SME, Manager, or End User).
Prerequisites: Selection of interviewees, defined interview objectives, sent agenda.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Plan and prepare (agenda, venue, targeted questions). 2. Introduction and scene-setting (build rapport, state purpose, confirm note-taking). 3. Conduct main questioning (use open, probing, closed questions). 4. Summarize key points, gather sample documents, thank interviewee, explain next steps. 5. Write up notes promptly and send to interviewee for confirmation.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Please tell me about your daily process? What are your key pain points? What happens if an exception occurs? How would you like the new system to work?
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA interviews an order processing supervisor at their desk to understand manual entry bottlenecks and collect completed sample order forms.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Written interview notes validated and signed off by the interviewee for factual accuracy.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Asking overly leading or restrictive closed questions; failing to send an agenda beforehand; failing to write up notes immediately; taking no notes.
When NOT to Use: When quantitative statistical data is required from a large, widely dispersed population (use Surveys instead) or for resolving multi-stakeholder conflicts (use Workshops).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Workshops, Surveys, Observation, Shadowing, Repertory Grid.
Supported Decisions: Requirements baseline, problem definition, stakeholder engagement strategy.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents transcribe audio in real-time, generate automated summary notes, and extract entity-relationship or user story candidates automatically for analyst review.

Problem Solved: Elicits stakeholder constructs, attitudes, and unstated criteria without introducing analyst bias or leading questions, reducing researcher-induced distortion.
Input Artifacts: Identified list of domain elements (e.g., product lists, document types, process steps).
Output Artifacts: Rating grid matrix showing personal constructs rated on a 5- or 7-point scale.
Participants & Roles: BA (Researcher/Interviewer), Domain Expert / Stakeholder.
Prerequisites: Identification of a representative set of domain elements to compare.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify domain elements. 2. Present elements in triads to interviewee and ask how two are similar and different from the third. 3. Define the resulting similarity/contrast construct scales. 4. Rate all elements against each construct on a 5- or 7-point scale. 5. Analyze the completed grid matrix for key patterns and priorities.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Pick two items that are similar and tell me why. Which third item differs, and in what way? On a scale of 1 to 7, how does each item rate against this characteristic?
Minimal Realistic Example: A warehouse manager compares products using triads, uncovering unstated storage criteria: Weight (Light vs Heavy) and Shelf-life (1 Day vs Indefinite).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Constructs must originate entirely from the interviewee's expressions without analyst prompting.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Imposing pre-defined construct scales on the interviewee; choosing elements that are too abstract or unfamiliar to the respondent.
When NOT to Use: When rapid elicitation is required under strict time constraints, or when stakeholders are uncomfortable with abstract psychological frameworks.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Interviewing, Workshops, Surveys, Personas.
Supported Decisions: User interface design criteria, process prioritization, document management classification.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI tools process completed grid matrices using cluster analysis to discover hidden semantic categories and user preference vectors.

Problem Solved: Brings key stakeholders together to discover requirements, build consensus, and make rapid decisions, reducing delay and conflicting requirements.
Input Artifacts: Workshop agenda, objective statement, preliminary background models.
Output Artifacts: Workshop notes, validated process models, agreed requirements list, signed-off decisions.
Participants & Roles: Facilitator (BA or Independent), Scribe, Participants (Sponsor, SMEs, Users, Analysts).
Prerequisites: Clear workshop objectives, selected attendees with knowledge and authority, suitable venue and tools (flipcharts, sticky notes).
Step-by-Step Procedure: Plan (define objectives, invite key attendees, arrange venue). 2. Conduct (icebreaker, focus on objectives, use discovery techniques like brainstorming/Post-it exercises). 3. Keep on track, ensure participation, and document outputs visually. 4. Summarize key decisions. 5. Follow up by issuing notes promptly and gathering feedback.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What are the main issues we face? What ideas do you have for solving this? Do we all agree on this decision? What are our top priorities?
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA facilitates a 3-hour Post-it note workshop with marketing and operations leads to map out and agree on the end-to-end refund workflow.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Achievement of workshop objectives, active participation by all attendees, published and agreed outcome notes.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Inviting attendees without decision-making authority; allowing loud voices to dominate; facilitator pushing their own personal agenda; over-ambitious agenda; lacking a scribe.
When NOT to Use: When stakeholders are in deep toxic conflict requiring one-on-one negotiation, or when simple factual data collection from dispersed populations is needed.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Interviewing, Surveys, Brainstorming, Storyboarding, Hothousing.
Supported Decisions: Scope approval, requirements prioritization, process design choices, business case options approval.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Virtual workshop AI assistants organize digital sticky notes in real-time, generate summary reports, and highlight conflicting participant statements automatically.

Problem Solved: Gathers firsthand insights into actual business practices and uncovers tacit knowledge, reducing reliance on filtered or inaccurate verbal accounts.
Input Artifacts: Observation checklist, STROBE template, process description documents.
Output Artifacts: Observation notes, task timing data, identified process variations and tacit rules.
Participants & Roles: BA (Observer), Business User (Observed).
Prerequisites: Approval from management and staff/unions, clear observation objectives.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Prepare objectives and checklist (or STROBE sheet). 2. Brief the worker and management on the purpose. 3. Observe the worker performing tasks over an extended period. 4. Record normal flows, exceptions, interruptions, and environment. 5. Debrief worker to clarify observed actions. 6. Document findings.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Why did you perform that step? What triggers this exception? What information did you look up just now?
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA sits with a call center agent for half a day, noticing that agents manually copy data into an unrecorded Excel spreadsheet to bypass a system bug.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Observation conducted over a long enough period to mitigate the Hawthorne/Heisenberg effect.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Observing for too short a period; interrupting the worker constantly; failing to inform staff in advance; relying solely on structured checklists and missing unexpected events.
When NOT to Use: When studying highly cognitive, invisible mental work without verbalization, or when statistical quantitative task-time data is required.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Shadowing, Protocol Analysis, Ethnographic Studies, Activity Sampling.
Supported Decisions: Process improvement design, user interface optimization, tacit requirement definition.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Screen-recording AI process-mining tools observe digital user interactions to automatically map actual UI navigation paths and flag delays.

Problem Solved: Provides an extended form of observation where the analyst follows a worker through their entire role, reducing misunderstandings of role complexity and environmental pressures.
Input Artifacts: Role descriptions, observation checklist, project brief.
Output Artifacts: Detailed role execution logs, qualitative issue list, identified environmental constraints.
Participants & Roles: BA (Shadow), Business Worker (Subject), Line Manager.
Prerequisites: Permission from managers, trade unions (if applicable), and subject; agreed study etiquette.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify candidate complex jobs. 2. Explain study objectives and build rapport with subject. 3. Shadow the subject continuously over days/weeks, taking notes. 4. Observe customer/peer interactions and environmental factors. 5. Ask clarifying questions at appropriate non-intrusive moments. 6. Analyze qualitative findings.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What pressures are you experiencing right now? How do you decide how to handle this difficult customer? Why did you use that shortcut?
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA shadows an airport lost-baggage clerk for three days to experience firsthand customer hostility, system lag, and multi-tasking pressures.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Shadowing sustained long enough for the subject to revert to natural, un-staged working behaviors.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Interfering with critical or sensitive customer interactions; making the worker uncomfortable; drawing statistical conclusions from a single subject.
When NOT to Use: When quantitative statistical time measurements are required (use Activity Sampling), or when studying highly confidential 1-on-1 counseling/banking tasks where observers are barred.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Observation, Ethnographic Studies, Protocol Analysis, Personas.
Supported Decisions: Job design, process redesign, user training requirements, workplace environment improvements.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Wearable cameras or eye-tracking AI assistants summarize physical worker movement patterns and environmental interaction bottlenecks.

Problem Solved: Uncovers cognitive decision-making processes and tacit knowledge by having users give a running verbal commentary while performing a task.
Input Artifacts: Task checklist, recording equipment (optional), process documentation.
Output Artifacts: Verbal transcript, decision trees/flowcharts, documented business rules.
Participants & Roles: BA (Observer/Listener), Subject Matter Expert (Performative Commentator).
Prerequisites: Selection of an articulate SME performing a decision-intensive task; consent for commentary/recording.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select decision-heavy task. 2. Brief SME to speak thoughts aloud continuously while working. 3. Observe and record the running commentary and actions. 4. Gently prompt SME if they go silent. 5. Transcribe and analyze cognitive steps and decision rules. 6. Model as flowchart or decision table.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Please keep talking and tell me what you are looking at right now? What decision are you making? What rule made you choose that option?
Minimal Realistic Example: A bank loan officer speaks aloud while evaluating a loan application, explaining subtle red flags they look for that are not written in official manuals.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Successful capture of cognitive decision logic and tacit heuristics that were previously undocumented.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Using harsh questioning that unnerves the subject; performing protocol analysis on long, exhausting tasks without breaks; assuming commentary is 100% complete.
When NOT to Use: For simple, highly repetitive physical tasks requiring no cognitive decision-making, or with non-articulate subjects.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Observation, Shadowing, Decision Tables, Task Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Business rules specification, expert system logic design, decision process automation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Voice-recognition AI captures and parses the verbal commentary stream directly into candidate business rule specifications and decision trees.

Problem Solved: Immerses the analyst in the working culture over an extended period to understand social context, implicit norms, and naturalistic working behaviors.
Input Artifacts: Research objectives, environmental checklist, field notebooks.
Output Artifacts: Ethnographic field notes, cultural landscape analysis, validated requirements sanity check.
Participants & Roles: BA (Ethnographer/Researcher), Business Community Members.
Prerequisites: Organizational approval for extended immersion; researcher objectivity.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define scope and obtain access to the study area. 2. Immense analyst in the environment over days/weeks. 3. Observe processes, physical layouts, relationships, hierarchy, and informal behaviors. 4. Record comprehensive naturalistic field notes. 5. Analyze notes for cultural patterns, wastes, and underlying needs.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How do people interact here? What behaviors are rewarded or frowned upon? What informal workarounds exist in this culture?
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA spends two weeks immersed in a hospital ward observing nurse-doctor interactions, discovering that paper notes are preferred over mobile screens due to sterilization habits.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Grounded, unbiased naturalistic observations that reflect real-world execution rather than idealized procedures.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Imposing researcher bias or pre-conceived judgments; allowing formal pre-defined checklists to blind the analyst to unexpected cultural dynamics; taking too long without delivering actionable insights.
When NOT to Use: When rapid requirements delivery is required on tight project deadlines with low budget.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Shadowing, Contextual Inquiry, Personas, Cultural Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Change management strategy, user adoption planning, workplace design, software UI/UX architecture.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: NLP agents analyze unstructured field logs and communication channels to discover sub-cultural patterns and operational friction points automatically.

Problem Solved: Gathers quantitative and qualitative data from a large, geographically dispersed population, reducing sampling bias and validating findings from small sample groups.
Input Artifacts: Survey questionnaire, population distribution list, objective statement.
Output Artifacts: Aggregated survey response data, statistical summaries, validated requirement hypotheses.
Participants & Roles: BA (Survey Designer), Target Stakeholder Population (Respondents).
Prerequisites: Clear survey objectives, defined population sample, distribution mechanism (e.g., web tool).
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define purpose and scope. 2. Design structure (Title, Heading/Incentive, Classification, Data section). 3. Draft unambiguous open, closed, and limited-choice questions. 4. Pilot test questionnaire on a small sample. 5. Distribute survey. 6. Analyze collected responses using mean/mode/statistical tools.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How satisfied are you with the current process (Scale 1-5)? Which feature do you use most frequently? What is your main daily operational issue?
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA distributes an online survey to 500 remote sales reps to validate whether workshop claims regarding CRM slowness are shared across all regions.
Quality Criteria & Verification: High response rate, representative population sample, pre-tested unambiguous questions.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Asking overly complex or ambiguous questions; forcing binary answers without a 'Don't know' or comments option; low response rates leading to non-responder bias.
When NOT to Use: As a primary tool for discovering complex, ambiguous business rules or resolving deep stakeholder political conflicts.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Interviewing, Workshops, Sampling, Special-Purpose Records.
Supported Decisions: Requirements baseline validation, user prioritization, pain-point quantification.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI tools generate optimized survey questions based on project goals and automatically perform sentiment and statistical analysis on open-text responses.

Problem Solved: Measures transaction times and time allocation objectively across business tasks, reducing reliance on subjective staff estimates.
Input Artifacts: Activity sampling sheets, list of task activity codes, observation schedule.
Output Artifacts: Activity sampling summary sheets, moving average graphs, task time metrics.
Participants & Roles: BA (Sampler), Observed Staff Members, Line Manager.
Prerequisites: Agreement from management and staff/unions, established random or fixed sampling intervals.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Explain purpose to managers and staff. 2. Define standard activity codes. 3. Establish sampling intervals (e.g., every 15 mins). 4. Record observed activity code for each worker at each interval. 5. Summarize daily results and calculate moving averages. 6. Stop sampling when moving averages stabilize.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What specific activity is worker X performing at this precise sample moment?
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA conducts a 3-day activity sampling exercise across 7 bank call center staff, discovering that 34% of time is spent amending account details.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Stabilization of the calculated moving average across daily samples; sufficient sample size.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Sampling at predictable intervals that coincide with fixed breaks; stopping sampling before moving averages stabilize; worker behavior distortion.
When NOT to Use: When detailed qualitative reasons behind tasks are needed, or when sample populations are hostile to measurement.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Special-Purpose Records, Document Analysis, Observation.
Supported Decisions: Business case cost-benefit calculation, process bottleneck identification, resource capacity planning.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Automated system-event logging software continuously samples user system interactions to generate time-allocation metrics automatically.

Problem Solved: Gathers quantitative data on activity volumes and time spent directly from business users, reducing analyst observation overhead.
Input Artifacts: Special-purpose record sheet, tallies template, activity categories list.
Output Artifacts: Completed tally sheets, volume/time logs, aggregated task distribution data.
Participants & Roles: BA (Form Designer), Business Users (Record Keepers).
Prerequisites: Briefing session with users to explain form completion and secure buy-in.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify activity categories via preliminary interviews. 2. Design an easy-to-use tally/timesheet form. 3. Brief participating staff on how and when to record entries. 4. Staff keep tallies during their working week. 5. Collect forms and aggregate daily/weekly data. 6. Analyze volume and time trends.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How many times did issue X occur today? How much time was spent dealing with complaint category Y?
Minimal Realistic Example: Complaints handling staff use a daily 5-bar gate tally sheet for a week to record complaint volumes across 6 categories, revealing non-delivery as the top issue.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Consistent, real-time completion by staff throughout the day rather than end-of-day guesswork.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Designing overly complex forms with too many categories; user guesswork caused by end-of-day completion; staff inflating numbers to justify resources.
When NOT to Use: When staff are uncooperative or when high-precision objective timing is required.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Sampling, Document Analysis, Activity Sampling.
Supported Decisions: Process prioritization, workload distribution, business case savings estimation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Digital micro-logging widgets embedded in user dashboards allow 1-click activity tagging, feeding real-time analytics engines.

Problem Solved: Systematically extracts data requirements, data structures, and business rules from existing forms, screens, and reports, reducing missing data requirements in new IT systems.
Input Artifacts: Existing paper forms, screen layouts, report specifications, user records.
Output Artifacts: Document Specification forms, Data Dictionary entries, candidate entities/attributes.
Participants & Roles: BA (Analyst), SME / Document Owner.
Prerequisites: Access to sample completed forms, screens, and current system report outputs.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Gather sample filled-in documents/screens. 2. Log document metadata (Name, Filing sequence, Storage medium, Retention, Volumes). 3. Identify initial events and usage frequency. 4. Analyze each data item (Name, Description, Format, Value range, Source). 5. Map attributes to candidate data models.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Who completes this form? Where does this data item originate? How long is this document stored? What value ranges are valid?
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA analyzes a paper 'Training Record Sheet' (Form TR01), documenting its 7 data items (e.g. Payroll Number, Course Date, Result) to model the new HR database schema.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Complete document specification covering all metadata and data attribute definitions, validated against live filled-in samples.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Analyzing blank forms instead of completed ones; missing undocumented data items added manually in margins by workers; ignoring retention/security rules.
When NOT to Use: When creating a radical greenfield system where legacy data models are obsolete and misleading.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Entity Relationship Modelling, Class Modelling, Special-Purpose Records.
Supported Decisions: Database architecture specification, data migration scope, user access privileges.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: OCR and document-parsing AI tools automatically scan legacy forms/screens, extracting data fields, data types, and implicit validation rules into data dictionaries.

Problem Solved: Captures the holistic complexity, human relationships, emotions, culture, and structural issues of a business problem visually, reducing communication barriers created by long text.
Input Artifacts: Interview notes, observation logs, qualitative investigation data.
Output Artifacts: Rich Picture diagram capturing actors, processes, culture, conflict, and concerns.
Participants & Roles: BA (Diagrammer), Stakeholders (Reviewers).
Prerequisites: Preliminary qualitative investigation of the business situation.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify principal actors, structures, and systems. 2. Draw pictorial representations/symbols for actors, systems, and environment. 3. Add speech bubbles, emotions, and symbols for conflicts (e.g. crossed swords) and worries (e.g. time bombs). 4. Review diagram to summarize key problem areas.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Who are the main people involved? What worries them? Where are the conflicts or communication breakdowns? What is the organizational atmosphere?
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA draws a Rich Picture of a sales organization showing Bob worried about money down the drain, Alice frustrated by a slow mainframe (drawn as a snail), and crossed swords between Sales and Factory.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Captures soft human and cultural aspects alongside hard process structures; easily understood by the analyst team.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Treating rich pictures as formal process models; expecting non-authors to understand symbols without explanation; avoiding drawing due to lack of artistic confidence.
When NOT to Use: When communicating formal system specifications to technical developers or presenting to overly conservative formal stakeholders who reject non-formal diagrams.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Mind Maps, Fishbone Diagrams, Context Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Problem prioritization, investigation scope, stakeholder management strategy.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Generative image AI converts unstructured interview transcripts into rough cartoon-style rich picture sketches for analyst elaboration.

Problem Solved: Visually organizes and structures thoughts, concepts, and interview notes around a central theme, reducing information overload and unstructured note-taking.
Input Artifacts: Interview agenda, workshop topics, brainstorming notes.
Output Artifacts: Mind Map diagram showing central concept, main branches, sub-branches, and cross-connections.
Participants & Roles: BA (Note-taker/Facilitator), Workshop Participants / Interviewee.
Prerequisites: A defined central concept or agenda topic.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Place the central concept in the middle ('trunk'). 2. Draw major related themes radiating outwards as main 'branches'. 3. Add detailed ideas as sub-branches ('twigs'). 4. Use keywords, visual icons, and colors. 5. Draw cross-linking arrows between related sub-branches.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What are the main categories related to this topic? What sub-details belong to this branch? How does this concept connect to that branch?
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA structures a Mind Map for 'Making the Business Case' with branches for Situation, Options, Cost/Benefit, Risks, and Presentation.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Clear hierarchical branching from central topic; concise keyword usage; visual clarity.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Over-crowding branches with long textual sentences instead of keywords; forcing a rigid hierarchy where cross-links are needed.
When NOT to Use: When formal sequential system workflow specifications or strict database schemas are required.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Rich Pictures, Concept Maps, Fishbone Diagrams, Brainstorming.
Supported Decisions: Interview structuring, issue identification, workshop agenda planning.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI text parsers automatically convert meeting transcripts into interactive digital Mind Maps with auto-clustered thematic branches.

Problem Solved: Identifies and categorizes the root causes of a specific business problem or undesirable effect, reducing superficial problem solving that only targets symptoms.
Input Artifacts: Problem statement, investigation findings, workshop inputs.
Output Artifacts: Fishbone (Cause-and-Effect) Diagram mapping root causes into major categories.
Participants & Roles: BA (Facilitator), SMEs, Business Users, Operations Leads.
Prerequisites: A clear, agreed definition of the problem/effect placed at the 'head' of the fish.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Write the problem statement in the box at the 'head'. 2. Draw the main backbone and diagonal category spines (e.g. 6 Ps or 4 Ms). 3. Brainstorm specific causes and attach them as bones to the category spines. 4. Analyze secondary causes attached to primary bones. 5. Identify common or high-impact root causes.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is the specific undesirable effect? What People, Process, Place, or Technology factors contribute to this? Why did that primary cause happen?
Minimal Realistic Example: Analyzing 'Poor system availability' using the 6 Ps (People, Place, Processes, Physical evidence, Product, Performance measures) reveals offshore time zone lags and unclear SLAs as key root causes.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Distinguishes checked facts from believed facts/prejudices; identifies true root causes rather than symptoms.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confusing symptoms with root causes; relying on unverified assumptions/opinions ('believed facts') without factual data verification.
When NOT to Use: When the problem is simple, single-factor, and obvious without requiring multi-category diagnostic analysis.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Root Cause Analysis (5 Whys), Mind Maps, Rich Pictures.
Supported Decisions: Process improvement priorities, problem resolution strategy, business case problem statement.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Diagnostic AI analyzes operational incident logs and categorizes failure root causes onto an automated Fishbone diagram.

Problem Solved: Defines the high-level scope and boundary of an IT or business system and its external interfacing actors, reducing scope creep and missed system interfaces.
Input Artifacts: Project scope statement, stakeholder list, system boundary definition.
Output Artifacts: Context Diagram showing central system box, surrounding external actors (user roles, other systems, time), and association lines.
Participants & Roles: BA, System Architect, Business Users, Project Manager.
Prerequisites: High-level understanding of the proposed system's intent and environment.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Draw a central box representing the system. 2. Identify external user role actors (stick figures). 3. Identify other interfacing system actors (boxes). 4. Identify time-triggered actors (time boxes). 5. Draw un-arrowed association lines connecting actors to the system boundary. 6. Review boundary with stakeholders.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is the boundary of our system? Who are the human user roles interacting with it? What other IT systems send or receive data? What time events trigger system action?
Minimal Realistic Example: A Context Diagram for a 'Project Control System' showing interactions with Project Manager, Team Member, System Administrator, Finance System, and a Friday 22:00 time trigger.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Accurate system boundary definition; complete representation of all external interfacing actors without internal system detail.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Adding directional data flow arrows or internal system process detail inside the central system box.
When NOT to Use: When detailed internal process workflow or internal algorithmic logic needs to be documented.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Use Case Diagrams, Level-0 Data Flow Diagrams, Use Case Modelling.
Supported Decisions: System scope approval, interface architecture definition, project boundary agreement.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Architecture-parsing AI generates initial Context Diagrams by scanning system integration documentation and user access role matrices.

Problem Solved: Identifies initial project stakeholders through direct recommendation from leaders and interviewees, reducing missed key project contacts.
Input Artifacts: Sponsor list, preliminary project brief.
Output Artifacts: Initial stakeholder nomination list.
Participants & Roles: BA, Project Sponsor, Senior Managers.
Prerequisites: Access to project sponsor or commissioning manager.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Interview Project Sponsor to identify key business leads. 2. Interview named leads and ask them to nominate key team members. 3. Cascade nominations downward through organizational levels. 4. Compile master nominated stakeholder list.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Who else should I speak to about this? Who has detailed operational knowledge of this process? Who will be impacted by changes here?
Minimal Realistic Example: The BA interviews the Project Sponsor, who nominates the Operations Manager, who in turn nominates three senior claims handling clerks.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Coverage of key operational leads and decision-makers across the affected business areas.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Relying solely on nominated stakeholders, resulting in bias toward people who agree with the sponsor while missing critical or opposing perspectives.
When NOT to Use: As the sole method for stakeholder identification without combining with structured tools like the Stakeholder Wheel.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Stakeholder Wheel, Background Research, Organization Diagram.
Supported Decisions: Interview planning, workshop participant selection, stakeholder engagement strategy.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Organizational chart parsing tools suggest cascading lists of candidate stakeholders based on initial manager nominations.

Problem Solved: Uncovers hidden, external, or non-obvious stakeholders and organizational context by systematically analyzing existing project and organizational documentation.
Input Artifacts: Project Initiation Document (PID), feasibility reports, terms of reference, org charts, organization diagrams.
Output Artifacts: Expanded stakeholder list, organizational structure maps.
Participants & Roles: BA (Researcher).
Prerequisites: Access to relevant organizational, pre-project, and historical project documentation.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Gather pre-project documents (Feasibility studies, Terms of Reference, PIDs). 2. Review Organization Charts and Organization Diagrams. 3. Identify departments, external groups, or managers mentioned. 4. Add identified individuals and groups to the stakeholder list.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What previous studies examined this area? Which external suppliers or customer groups are mapped in organization diagrams? Which departments appear on org charts as linked to this process?
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA reads a 2-year-old feasibility study, discovering that the legal compliance team and an external auditing partner were listed as key impacted parties.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Thorough extraction of all named internal and external groups from available project documentation.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Failing to look for pre-project documents; ignoring org chart units that appear peripherally related.
When NOT to Use: When no prior documentation exists for a completely novel greenfield startup venture.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Stakeholder Nomination, Stakeholder Wheel, Organization Diagram.
Supported Decisions: Stakeholder engagement scope, risk analysis, project boundary setting.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Document-mining AI agents ingest repositories of legacy project files and org charts to output a consolidated list of historical stakeholders.

Problem Solved: Provides a comprehensive categorization checklist across 8 internal and external groups, preventing omission of critical external stakeholders.
Input Artifacts: Project context description, business domain overview.
Output Artifacts: Categorized Stakeholder Map covering Owners, Managers, Employees, Regulators, Suppliers, Partners, Customers, and Competitors.
Participants & Roles: BA, Sponsor, Key Business Leads.
Prerequisites: Understanding of the organizational operating model and business domain.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Review the 8 categories of the Stakeholder Wheel. 2. Identify Owners (shareholders, ministers). 3. Identify Managers and Employees. 4. Identify Regulators and Standards bodies. 5. Identify Suppliers and Partners. 6. Identify Customers and Competitors. 7. Compile comprehensive stakeholder list.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Who regulates this business? Who supplies raw materials/services? Who are our delivery partners? Who are our customer groups and competitors?
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA on a conference-booking project uses the wheel to identify venue suppliers, keynote speakers, external event partners, and regulatory safety bodies.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Systematic evaluation of all 8 categories of the wheel, ensuring external stakeholders are not neglected.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Focusing exclusively on internal managers/employees while ignoring regulators, partners, or suppliers.
When NOT to Use: When analyzing a tiny internal micro-task with no external interactions or organizational dependencies.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Stakeholder Nomination, Background Research, Power/Interest Grid.
Supported Decisions: Stakeholder management planning, communication strategy, risk identification.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Web-scraping AI agents automatically search regulatory registers, partner listings, and market landscapes to populate external wheel categories.

Problem Solved: Categorizes stakeholders based on their level of power and interest, reducing communication failures and resistance by establishing tailored management strategies.
Input Artifacts: Identified stakeholder list, organizational context, CATWOE outputs.
Output Artifacts: Power/Interest Grid Matrix (2x2 or 3x3), baseline stakeholder management categories.
Participants & Roles: BA, Project Sponsor, Project Manager.
Prerequisites: Completed stakeholder identification exercise.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Estimate each stakeholder's level of power/influence (Low/Medium/High). 2. Estimate each stakeholder's level of interest (Low/Medium/High). 3. Plot stakeholders onto the grid. 4. Assign management strategies: High Power/High Interest (Manage Actively), High Power/Low Interest (Keep Satisfied/Watch), Low Power/High Interest (Keep Informed/Onside), Low Power/Low Interest (Ignore/Minimal Effort). 5. Re-evaluate grid periodically.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How much power does this stakeholder have to influence or block the project? How interested are they in the project outcome? How might their power or interest change?
Minimal Realistic Example: Operational clerks are plotted as Low Power/High Interest ('Keep Informed') while the Finance Director is plotted as High Power/Low Interest ('Keep Satisfied').
