Quality Criteria & Verification: Accurate assessment of actual influence vs formal title; regular review to catch shifting power/interest levels.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Assuming operational staff have no power and ignoring them (leading to collective resistance/unions); treating the grid as a static one-off artifact.
When NOT to Use: When working with a single business user on a localized personal productivity tool.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Social Network Analysis, RASCI Charts, CATWOE, Stakeholder Management Plan.
Supported Decisions: Stakeholder communication plans, risk management, project governance structure.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Sentiment analysis engines monitor stakeholder emails and project communications to automatically adjust power/interest grid coordinates.

Problem Solved: Maps informal relationships and communication pathways between individuals, reducing disruption caused by missing informal influencers and information brokers.
Input Artifacts: Interviews, observation notes, email flow tracking, surveys.
Output Artifacts: Social Network Map identifying Central Connectors, Boundary Spanners, Information Brokers, and Peripheral Specialists.
Participants & Roles: BA (Analyst), Departmental Staff.
Prerequisites: Understanding of informal workplace communication flows.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Gather interaction data via interviews, observation, or email tracking. 2. Map nodes (people) and directional interaction lines. 3. Identify Central Connectors (high interaction hubs). 4. Identify Boundary Spanners (cross-departmental bridges). 5. Identify Information Brokers (information conduits). 6. Identify Peripheral Specialists (isolated experts). 7. Formulate communication strategies based on network roles.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Who do you go to first when you need information from another department? Who really holds this team together? Who possesses specialized knowledge?
Minimal Realistic Example: Mapping a manufacturing firm reveals Vicky (a junior clerk) as the Central Connector binding Design, Sales, and Production together.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Accurate mapping of actual informal advice and communication channels rather than official organigram hierarchy lines.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Assuming official management hierarchy reflects actual informal communication channels; ignoring peripheral specialists leading to lost expert knowledge.
When NOT to Use: In small 2-person projects or highly rigid automated environments with zero human interaction.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Power/Interest Grid, Stakeholder Map, Ethnographic Studies.
Supported Decisions: Change agent selection, communication routing, key-person risk management, training distribution.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Enterprise collaboration analytics (e.g. Slack/Teams graph analysis) automatically generate dynamic social network maps.

Problem Solved: Creates realistic fictional user archetypes to embody user goals, behaviors, and motivations, reducing selfish or biased user interface design assumptions.
Input Artifacts: User analysis, market analytics, stakeholder interviews, domain knowledge.
Output Artifacts: Persona Profiles (1-2 page descriptions detailing demographics, professional background, motivations, tech comfort, preferences).
Participants & Roles: BA, UX Designer, Business Users, Domain Experts.
Prerequisites: Research into the target user/customer community.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Research stakeholder user community. 2. Identify common behavioral patterns and characteristics. 3. Define 3-5 representative fictional personas. 4. Populate persona templates (Personal, Professional, Motivations, Dislikes, Tech literacy). 5. Use personas to evaluate proposed system designs, wireframes, and workflows.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Who is this user? What are their goals and frustrations? How tech-literate are they? Would 'Susan' find this screen layout intuitive?
Minimal Realistic Example: Creating 'Susan', a 57-year-old busy Sales Manager who wants quick luxury purchases and hates low-value cheap gift items, to evaluate an e-commerce gift site.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Personas represent research-backed archetypes rather than false user stereotypes or the analyst's personal preferences.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Creating too many personas (>5); treating personas as a static paper exercise without using them to validate actual screen designs.
When NOT to Use: When designing fully automated back-end machine-to-machine interfaces with no human user interaction.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: User Analysis, Scenarios, Wireframes, Ethnographic Studies.
Supported Decisions: UI/UX design choices, feature prioritization, accessibility specifications, value proposition alignment.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI models generate synthetic user personas based on live customer behavioral analytics and simulate persona navigation through proposed wireframe prototypes.

Problem Solved: Categorizes business situations into 4 contexts (Simple, Complicated, Complex, Chaotic) to guide the selection of appropriate leadership, analysis, and decision-making approaches.
Input Artifacts: Problem descriptions, stakeholder viewpoints, situational investigation data.
Output Artifacts: Categorized Situational Context (Simple, Complicated, Complex, Chaotic, or Disorder) and selected analytical/development approach.
Participants & Roles: BA, Sponsor, Executive Leadership, Project Manager.
Prerequisites: Investigation into the cause-and-effect predictability of the business situation.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Analyze situation predictability and cause-and-effect visibility. 2. Categorize as Simple (Sense-Categorize-Respond / Best Practice), Complicated (Sense-Analyze-Respond / Good Practice), Complex (Probe-Sense-Respond / Emergent Practice), or Chaotic (Act-Sense-Respond / Novel Practice). 3. Identify if the situation sits in Disorder. 4. Select matching BA approach (e.g., Waterfall for Simple/Complicated; Agile/Prototyping for Complex; Pragmatic fast intervention for Chaotic).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Is cause-and-effect clear to everyone? Are there 'known unknowns' requiring expert analysis? Are there 'unknown unknowns' requiring experimentation? Is immediate action needed to stop panic?
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA categorizes a disruptive new market entry as 'Complex', recommending an Agile prototyping approach rather than a rigid upfront waterfall specification.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Accurate assessment of situational complexity, preventing over-simplification of complex problems.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Applying rigid best-practice waterfall specifications to Complex problems; over-analyzing Chaotic situations instead of taking immediate action; remaining in Disorder.
When NOT to Use: When the project approach and domain complexity are already thoroughly understood and fixed.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Sensemaking, Risk Analysis, Gap Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Project lifecycle selection (Agile vs Waterfall), leadership style selection, decision-making approach.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Decision-support AI evaluates project risk parameters and historic success factors to classify new change initiatives into Cynefin quadrants.

Problem Solved: Uncovers and analyzes underlying stakeholder worldviews, values, and assumptions, reducing hidden conflicts, contradictory requirements, and strategic misalignment.
Input Artifacts: Stakeholder interviews, background research, stakeholder list.
Output Artifacts: CATWOE Analysis breakdown (Customer, Actor, Transformation, Worldview, Owner, Environment), Root Definition statement.
Participants & Roles: BA, Key Stakeholders (Sponsors, Department Leads, SMEs).
Prerequisites: Identification of key stakeholders whose perspectives need to be evaluated.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify the stakeholder's Worldview (W) - their underlying beliefs and values. 2. Define the core Transformation (T) process that fulfills W. 3. Identify the Customer (C) benefiting or affected by T. 4. Identify the Actors (A) performing T. 5. Identify the Owner (O) with authority over T. 6. Identify Environmental (E) constraints surrounding T. 7. Assemble into a concise Root Definition statement.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is this stakeholder's core belief about the business purpose (W)? What core transformation process fulfills this (T)? Who is the recipient (C)? Who carries out the work (A)? Who can stop it (O)? What constraints exist (E)?
Minimal Realistic Example: A retail operations director's CATWOE defines W as 'fashionable clothes must be inexpensive', T as 'sell cheap trendy clothes', C as 'young consumers', and O as 'the board'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Clear derivation of Transformation directly from the Worldview; explicitly validated Root Definition signed off by the stakeholder.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Omitting the Worldview (W) and jumping straight to process details; defining generic actors like 'staff' without role specificity; drafting Root Definitions without stakeholder validation.
When NOT to Use: For low-level, non-contentious technical coding tasks where stakeholder worldviews are identical and unproblematic.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: VOCATE, PARADE, Business Activity Modelling (BAM), Root Definition.
Supported Decisions: Business activity model baseline, conflict resolution strategy, gap analysis alignment, requirements prioritization.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLM agents analyze interview transcripts across different department leads to construct draft CATWOE matrices and highlight conflicting worldviews automatically.

Problem Solved: Creates a conceptual model of activities required to fulfill a specific stakeholder worldview, independent of current operational execution, reducing legacy process bias during gap analysis.
Input Artifacts: CATWOE outputs, Root Definition statement.
Output Artifacts: Business Activity Model (BAM) diagram showing Plan, Enable, Do, Monitor, and Control activities with logical dependency links.
Participants & Roles: BA, Key Stakeholder / SME group.
Prerequisites: Agreed CATWOE analysis and Root Definition.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify 1-2 core 'Doing' (D) primary task activities. 2. Identify required 'Enabling' (E) activities for resources. 3. Identify 'Planning' (P) activities that set performance targets. 4. Identify 'Monitoring' (M) activities to track Doing tasks against targets. 5. Add 'Control' (C) action activities fed by Monitoring outputs. 6. Draw logical dependency arrows.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What are the primary doing tasks? What resources must be enabled before doing can happen? What planning sets targets? What monitors performance? What control action occurs if targets are missed?
Minimal Realistic Example: A retail BAM shows 'Sell clothes' (Doing), enabled by 'Design clothes' and 'Acquire stores', planned by 'Define customer profile', monitored by 'Monitor sales profits', and controlled by 'Take control action'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Model is conceptual (what, not how); includes Plan, Enable, Do, Monitor, and Control activity types; contains unique activity definitions.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Modeling current physical reality ('as is') instead of a conceptual ideal model; adding process flow arrows or swimsuit lanes prematurely; creating too many 'Doing' tasks.
When NOT to Use: When analyzing low-level physical IT system interface interactions or detailed step-by-step procedure flowcharts.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: BAM, Conceptual Model, Business Process Modelling, Gap Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Gap analysis target setting, target operating model design, business process scope boundary.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI modeling tools auto-generate candidate BAM activity structures from input CATWOE root definitions, verifying logical activity dependencies.

Problem Solved: Maps stakeholder roles and responsibilities across project tasks or business processes, reducing role confusion, unassigned ownership, and overlapping authority.
Input Artifacts: Task list, process models, stakeholder list, job descriptions.
Output Artifacts: RASCI Matrix (Tasks on vertical axis, Roles on horizontal axis, populated with R, A, S, C, I letters).
Participants & Roles: BA, Project Sponsor, Project Manager, Operations Leads.
Prerequisites: List of tasks/work areas and defined stakeholder roles.
Step-by-Step Procedure: List tasks along matrix rows (using active verbs). 2. List stakeholder roles along matrix columns. 3. For each task, assign Responsible (R - owns/does work), Accountable (A - ultimate sign-off), Supportive (S - provides resources/help), Consulted (C - provides input), Informed (I - notified of outcome). 4. Verify matrix completeness.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Who is ultimately Accountable for this task? Who is Responsible for doing the work? Who provides Support? Who must be Consulted? Who needs to be Informed?
Minimal Realistic Example: For the task 'Document Requirements', BA is Responsible (R), Sponsor is Accountable (A), Sales Clerk is Consulted (C), and Project Manager is Informed (I).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Exactly one 'Accountable' role per task; at least one 'Responsible' role per task; balanced workload distribution across roles.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Assigning multiple Accountable roles to a single task; assigning too many Responsible roles; confusing Accountable (sign-off) with Responsible (execution).
When NOT to Use: For micro-level internal algorithmic coding steps with a single developer.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: RACI, ARCI, Power/Interest Grid, User Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Project governance definition, role design, approval workflows, communication routing.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Governance AI parses workflow models and project plans to draft RASCI matrices, highlighting tasks with missing or duplicate Accountable roles.

Problem Solved: Establishes structured, ongoing action and communication plans for each stakeholder, reducing project resistance and maintaining executive buy-in.
Input Artifacts: Power/Interest Grid, RASCI Chart, CATWOE outputs, stakeholder list.
Output Artifacts: Stakeholder Management Plan table (Name, Power, Interest, Issues/Interests, Current Attitude, Desired Support, Desired Role, Desired Actions, Messages, Communications).
Participants & Roles: BA, Project Sponsor, Project Manager, Change Manager.
Prerequisites: Completed stakeholder analysis (Power/Interest, CATWOE, RASCI).
Step-by-Step Procedure: List stakeholder names and roles. 2. Record Power and Interest levels. 3. Document key issues and interests. 4. Classify Current Attitude (Champion, Supporter, Neutral, Critic, Opponent, Blocker). 5. Define Desired Support, Role, and Actions. 6. Formulate tailored Messages and Communication actions.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is this stakeholder's current attitude? What support do we need from them? What key messages will resonate with them? How frequently should we communicate?
Minimal Realistic Example: Creating a plan for Marketing Director Steven Lewis (High Power/High Interest / Champion), scheduling bi-weekly meetings to review web marketing objectives.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Tailored communication strategies aligned with power/interest grid positions; actionable communication schedules.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Treating the management plan as a static document; sending generic mass-emails to high-power stakeholders instead of personalized engagement.
When NOT to Use: In trivial, single-person projects with no wider organizational impact.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Stakeholder Map, Power/Interest Grid, Communication Plan.
Supported Decisions: Communication strategy, governance schedule, risk mitigation, change management intervention.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: CRM-style stakeholder AI engines log engagement interactions, track attitude changes, and trigger automated reminders for scheduled communications.

Problem Solved: Identifies five conflict resolution modes (Avoiding, Accommodating, Competing, Compromising, Collaborating) based on assertiveness and cooperativeness, reducing unhelpful conflict handling.
Input Artifacts: Stakeholder analysis outputs, conflict observations.
Output Artifacts: Conflict resolution strategy assessment.
Participants & Roles: BA (Facilitator/Negotiator), Conflicting Stakeholders.
Prerequisites: Identification of a disagreement or conflict situation between stakeholders.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Assess the assertiveness and cooperativeness of conflicting parties. 2. Identify current conflict modes (Avoiding, Accommodating, Competing, Compromising, Collaborating). 3. Evaluate the significance of the issue. 4. Guide parties toward an appropriate mode (e.g., Collaborating for high-value win-win, Compromising for fast balance).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Is this issue critical enough to justify deep collaboration? Can we find a creative win-win option? Is a compromise acceptable here?
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA recognizes two leads taking a 'Competing' stance over UI layouts, guiding them toward 'Collaborating' by brainstorming creative new layout alternatives.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Selection of a conflict mode appropriate to the strategic importance and relationship needs of the situation.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Assuming 'Competing' vs 'Accommodating' are the only choices; relying habitually on 'Avoiding' for major conflicts, causing festering resentment.
When NOT to Use: When technical specifications are governed by strict non-negotiable legal regulations.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Principled Negotiation, BATNA, CATWOE.
Supported Decisions: Conflict resolution strategy, requirement trade-offs, negotiation approaches.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI negotiation assistants analyze participant phrasing in chat/email to classify active conflict modes and suggest de-escalation strategies.

Problem Solved: Resolves stakeholder disagreements by focusing on interests rather than positions, separating people from the problem, and using objective criteria, reducing destructive positional bargaining.
Input Artifacts: Stakeholder positions, CATWOE outputs, requirement trade-offs.
Output Artifacts: Negotiated Agreement, defined BATNA (Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement) and warning levels.
Participants & Roles: BA (Negotiator/Facilitator), Disagreeing Stakeholders.
Prerequisites: A disagreement over requirements, scope, or project choices.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Separate the people from the problem (manage emotions/perceptions). 2. Focus on underlying interests rather than stated positions (ask 'Why?'). 3. Brainstorm a variety of creative options for mutual gain. 4. Establish objective evaluation criteria. 5. Define BATNA and warning levels for all parties. 6. Agree on option satisfying criteria.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Why is that position important to you? What underlying interest does that satisfy? What objective benchmark can we use to evaluate options? What is your BATNA if we don't agree?
Minimal Realistic Example: Instead of arguing over a demand for 'instant phone repairs' (position), the BA asks 'Why?', uncovers the interest ('preventing missed client calls'), and agrees on 'call-forwarding during repairs'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Agreement satisfies the true underlying interests of all parties based on objective criteria; clear pre-defined BATNAs.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Entrenching in positional arguments; making personal attacks; accepting bad deals below the pre-set BATNA warning level.
When NOT to Use: When dealing with strict non-negotiable statutory legal mandates.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: BATNA, Thomas-Kilmann Instrument, CATWOE.
Supported Decisions: Requirements trade-offs, scope approval, vendor contract terms, consensus building.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI mediation bots analyze conflicting interests, evaluate objective benchmarks, and generate win-win candidate solution options automatically.

Problem Solved: Analyzes customer perspectives on value across Timing, Financial, and Quality categories for Owners, Partners, and End Customers, reducing misalignment between business processes and customer expectations.
Input Artifacts: Customer feedback, market research, business strategy, CATWOE outputs.
Output Artifacts: Value Proposition Matrix mapping customer types against value categories.
Participants & Roles: BA, Marketing Manager, Product Manager, Business Owner.
Prerequisites: Identification of key customer groupings (Owners, Partners, End Customers).
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify target customer types (Owners/Managers, Partners/Resellers, End Customers). 2. Analyze value expectations across Timing, Financial, and Quality categories for each type. 3. Map value proposition criteria into a matrix. 4. Evaluate current and proposed business processes against the matrix.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Why do customers choose us over competitors? What do Owners expect (dividends, reports)? What do Partners expect (discounts, service)? What do End Customers expect (price, speed, quality)?
Minimal Realistic Example: Mapping supermarket end-customers who prioritize 'high quality and reasonable price', contrasting with owners who demand 'timely financial returns and high profit margins'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Clear distinction between the differing value propositions of Owners, Partners, and End Customers; alignment of business processes to value criteria.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Focusing solely on internal cost-cutting (Owner value) while degrading product quality/speed (End Customer value).
When NOT to Use: For purely technical internal infrastructure maintenance projects with no customer-facing or commercial dimensions.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Value Chain Analysis, Value Streams, Personas, Organization Diagram.
Supported Decisions: Business process redesign priorities, service level target setting, product positioning.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Customer analytics AI processes review streams and feedback metrics to dynamically map and update customer value proposition matrices.

Problem Solved: Groups organizational activities into Primary (Inbound logistics, Operations, Outbound logistics, Marketing/Sales, Service) and Support activities, reducing siloed operational thinking.
Input Artifacts: High-level business architecture, departmental workflow summaries, value propositions.
Output Artifacts: Value Chain Diagram showing primary and support activity chains.
Participants & Roles: BA, Enterprise Architect, Operations Director, Business Process Owner.
Prerequisites: High-level understanding of the enterprise business model.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify core 'Operations' activity (the main value delivery). 2. Identify 'Inbound logistics' (inputs/preparation). 3. Identify 'Outbound logistics' (delivery/distribution). 4. Identify 'Marketing and Sales' (promotion/registration). 5. Identify 'Service' (post-sales support). 6. Identify 'Support activities' (Procurement, Tech, HR, Infrastructure). 7. Link primary activities sequentially.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is our primary operations activity? What inbound activities prepare for this? How do we distribute outputs? How do we market and sell? What support functions enable these primary activities?
Minimal Realistic Example: An examination body maps primary activities: Research qualification requirements & Promote qualifications (Sales) -> Define syllabus, Write exams, Set schedule (Inbound) -> Examine candidates (Operations) -> Issue results (Outbound) -> Handle appeals (Service).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Complete end-to-end representation of primary activities delivering customer value, clearly distinguished from support functions.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Applying rigid manufacturing value chain labels to service organizations without adapting the category definitions.
When NOT to Use: When analyzing micro-level algorithmic system code or localized single-task desk procedures.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Value Streams, Capability Modelling, Business Activity Modelling, Organization Diagram.
Supported Decisions: Process hierarchy structuring, process improvement prioritization, target operating model design.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Enterprise process mining tools auto-map cross-departmental workflows into high-level Primary and Support Value Chain architectures.

Problem Solved: Integrates external environment factors (PESTLE, Competitors, Suppliers, Customers) with the internal Value Chain, providing complete organizational context for process improvement.
Input Artifacts: PESTLE analysis, Value Chain, Supplier lists, Customer segments, Competitor analysis.
Output Artifacts: Completed Organisation Diagram showing external forces surrounding the internal Value Chain.
Participants & Roles: BA, Executive Management, Enterprise Architect, Strategy Lead.
Prerequisites: Completed PESTLE analysis and initial internal Value Chain map.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Draw central box representing the organization containing its Value Chain. 2. Map top box for PESTLE external forces. 3. Map left boxes for Resource Suppliers (People, Capital, Technology). 4. Map right boxes for Customer types (Owners, Partners, End Customers). 5. Map bottom box for Competitor organizations. 6. Draw interaction arrows.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What PESTLE factors pressure us? Who supplies our people, technology, and capital? Who competes for those suppliers and customers? How does our internal value chain deliver to those customers?
Minimal Realistic Example: An Organization Diagram for an examination body showing external PESTLE pressures at the top, Tech/People suppliers at the left, Competitors at the bottom, and Candidates/Employers at the right, surrounding the central exam Value Chain.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Complete visual integration of external environment forces with the internal value chain activities.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Modeling internal organization departments inside the value chain box instead of business process activities.
When NOT to Use: When analyzing a minor, isolated internal software utility with no external environmental dependencies.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Organisation Model, Value Chain Analysis, PESTLE Analysis, Context Diagram.
Supported Decisions: Process improvement context setting, organizational alignment, project scope boundary setting.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents continually ingest external market threat data and internal process metrics to update dynamic Organization Diagrams.

Problem Solved: Identifies external, internal, and time-based triggers that initiate business processes, reducing missing process triggers and scope gaps.
Input Artifacts: Context Diagram, Stakeholder list, Value Chain, process domain scope.
Output Artifacts: Business Event List categorized by External, Internal, and Time-based triggers, with named responses/processes.
Participants & Roles: BA, SMEs, Business Process Owners, System Users.
Prerequisites: High-level understanding of the business domain boundary.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify external stakeholders (using Stakeholder Wheel/Context Diagram). 2. Identify External business events triggered by stakeholders. 3. Identify Internal business events triggered by management decisions or staff actions. 4. Identify Time-based events triggered by calendars/deadlines. 5. Define the required outcome and process response for each event.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What occurrences outside the business require a response? What internal decisions trigger new work? What regular calendar deadlines trigger reporting or processing?
Minimal Realistic Example: Identifying External event 'Customer purchase request', Internal event 'Manager revises quote format', and Time-based event 'End-of-month reconciliation'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Event names expressed in past/event tense ('Invoice reminder issued'); clear mapping of every event to a specific process response and outcome.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Naming events as process verbs ('Issue invoice') instead of triggering occurrences ('Invoice required'); missing time-based triggers.
When NOT to Use: When modeling static data structures with no behavioral or event-driven requirements.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Context Diagram, Business Process Modelling, Use Case Modelling.
Supported Decisions: Process scope partitioning, process trigger design, SLA definition.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Event-driven system monitors parse incoming messaging queues and logs to auto-discover and categorize business event triggers.

Problem Solved: Models detailed task steps, decision paths, and iterations using standardized UML flowchart notation, reducing procedural ambiguity in task execution.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Analyse Needs / Business Process Analysis / Specification
Input Artifacts: Task descriptions, business rules, scenario scripts.
Output Artifacts: UML Activity Diagram (Start state, Activity steps, Decision diamonds with guard conditions, Merge points, End state).
Participants & Roles: BA, SMEs, System Users, Developers, Testers.
Prerequisites: Identification of the specific task or procedure to be modeled.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Draw Start solid circle. 2. Draw rounded boxes for task steps in sequence. 3. Add decision diamonds where choices occur, labeling outbound flows with bracketed guard conditions e.g. code known. 4. Model iterations/loops where steps repeat. 5. Connect to End bulls-eye circle.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is the initial step? What choice occurs here? What is the guard condition for this path? Which steps repeat until a condition is met?
Minimal Realistic Example: Modeling a mail-order task: Ask customer for products -> Decision code known vs code unknown -> Display details -> Enter quantity -> Decision more products loop back vs no more -> Confirm order -> End.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Clear logical sequence; all decision diamond outbound paths labeled with mutually exclusive guard conditions; clear start and end points.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Missing guard conditions on decision branches; creating infinite loops without exit conditions; mixing high-level business workflow with micro-level task steps.
When NOT to Use: For high-level conceptual business activity mapping (use BAM instead) or static data structure design.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Flowcharting, Business Process Modelling, Task Analysis, Use Case Descriptions.
Supported Decisions: Procedural task design, test script generation, user training manual documentation, exception handling logic.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Code-generation AI parses UML Activity Diagrams directly into executable workflow code and automated test scripts.

Problem Solved: Models cross-functional end-to-end workflows across actor swimlanes, reducing functional silo bottlenecks, handoff failures, and lack of customer focus.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Analyse Needs / Business Process Analysis / Specification
Input Artifacts: Business Events, Value Chain, Task descriptions, stakeholder input.
Output Artifacts: Business Process Model / Swimlane Diagram (Event trigger, Actor swimlanes, Tasks, Decisions, Sequences, Outcomes, Timeline).
Participants & Roles: BA (Facilitator), Actors / SMEs from participating departments.
Prerequisites: Identification of the initiating business event and expected process outcome.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define initiating business event and end outcome. 2. Identify participating actor roles and create horizontal swimlanes. 3. Plot tasks in appropriate actor swimlanes in sequential flow order. 4. Add decision points and alternative pathways. 5. Rationalize steps into discrete tasks. 6. Add timeline performance measures. 7. Number tasks hierarchically.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What event starts this process? Who performs the first task? To whom is the work handed off next? What decision routes exist? What is the final outcome?
Minimal Realistic Example: A 'Record booking' process model showing initiating event 'Booking received' in Sales Clerk swimlane, handoff to Event Organiser swimlane for 'Complete booking arrangements', leading to end outcome.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Cross-functional visibility across swimlanes; clear event start and outcome end; rationalized tasks (one actor at one point in time); hierarchical task numbering.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Over-detailing micro-steps inside swimlanes instead of rationalizing into tasks; creating 'silo' models contained in a single swimlane; omitting handoff triggers.
When NOT to Use: For static data modeling or high-level conceptual business activity mapping.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Swimlane diagrams, Process maps, Activity Diagrams, Value Streams.
Supported Decisions: End-to-end process redesign, handoff optimization, job role design, SLA definition, IT automation boundaries.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Process mining tools automatically ingest cross-departmental log data to generate 'as is' swimlane models and highlight real-world handoff delays.

Problem Solved: Defines the detailed execution steps, input/output data, triggers, prerequisites, and business rules for a single business process task, reducing operational ambiguity.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Analyse Needs / Business Process Analysis / Specification
Input Artifacts: Business Process Model, task list, business rules, document specs.
Output Artifacts: Task Description document (Identifier, Name, Actor, Prerequisites, Trigger, Inputs, Outputs, Goals, Performance Measures, Steps, Rules).
Participants & Roles: BA, Task Actor / SME.
Prerequisites: Identification of the task within a business process model.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Record task identifier (e.g., 2/1) and name ('imperative verb noun'). 2. Identify actor role and prerequisites. 3. Identify triggering business event (distinct from inputs). 4. List input and output information/documents. 5. Define task goals and performance measures. 6. Document detailed steps (using text or Activity Diagram) and embedded business rules.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What triggers you to start this specific task? What must be true before you start? What information do you need? What steps do you take? What rules govern your decision?
Minimal Realistic Example: Documenting Task 2/1 'Review complaint' performed by Customer Services Manager, triggered by 'Formal complaint received', requiring account/call records, outputting decision/compensation.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Clear distinction between triggering event and input data; measurable performance targets; complete step-by-step procedural description covering exceptions.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confusing input data arrival with the actual triggering event; omitting prerequisites; failing to document embedded business decision rules.
When NOT to Use: For high-level corporate strategic option planning or macro value chain mapping.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Task modelling, Activity Diagrams, Use Case Descriptions, Decision Tables.
Supported Decisions: Job description design, user training curriculum, operational performance target setting, automated user interface requirements.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI task-capture assistants log user desktop actions to draft initial task step descriptions, inputs, and outputs automatically.

Problem Solved: Identifies and categorizes operational constraints, policies, and statutory laws that govern business decisions and process execution, reducing compliance failures and invalid decisions.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Analyse Needs / Business Process Analysis / Specification
Input Artifacts: Legal regulations, corporate policy documents, process models, data models.
Output Artifacts: Business Rules Catalogue categorized by Statutory/Regulatory, Organizational Policy, and Operational Procedures.
Participants & Roles: BA, Compliance/Legal Officer, Business Owner, Policy SME.
Prerequisites: Identification of business processes, decisions, or data structures.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify external Legal/Regulatory constraints (non-negotiable). 2. Identify internal Organizational Policy constraints (strategic). 3. Identify internal Operational Procedures (tactical/flexible). 4. Document rules explicitly. 5. Challenge operational procedures to eliminate legacy bad habits. 6. Map rules to process decision points and data model relationships.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What law compels us to do this? What corporate policy dictates this rule? Is this rule a strict policy or just an old habit? What rule determines this data relationship?
Minimal Realistic Example: Analyzing ticket booking rules: identifying mandatory legal age limits (Statutory), group booking limits (Policy), and discount eligibility rules (Operational Procedure).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Clear categorization by constraint type; explicit mapping to corresponding process decision points and data model cardinality constraints.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Mistaking long-standing informal habits for unchangeable corporate policies; failing to challenge outdated operational procedures; mixing non-negotiable legal rules with flexible operational guidelines.
When NOT to Use: In unconstrained creative brainstorming or visioning sessions where rules are deliberately set aside.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Constraints Analysis, Decision Tables, Decision Trees, Entity Relationship Modelling.
Supported Decisions: Compliance validation, process logic design, database integrity constraint specification.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Regulatory-compliance AI engines scan new statutory legislation text to extract candidate business rules and flag impacted corporate process steps automatically.

Problem Solved: Models complex combinations of conditions and their resulting actions in a rigorous grid or tree format, eliminating logic gaps, ambiguities, and redundant rules.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Analyse Needs / Business Process Analysis / Specification
Input Artifacts: Business rules, task steps, policy specifications.
Output Artifacts: Limited-entry or Extended-entry Decision Table (Condition stub/entries, Action stub/entries), or Decision Tree diagram.
Participants & Roles: BA, SMEs, Business Rules Developer, Tester.
Prerequisites: Identification of a task or process step containing multiple decision conditions.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify all decision conditions and list in Condition Stub. 2. Calculate required combinations (2^c for limited entry). 3. Populate Condition Entries systematically (Y/N patterns). 4. List all possible outcomes in Action Stub. 5. Check action boxes for each combination column. 6. Rationalize redundant columns if identical actions result. 7. Alternatively, draw as a branching Decision Tree.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What conditions affect this decision? What are the possible Y/N answers? What exact action results from this specific combination of conditions?
Minimal Realistic Example: A rail fare decision table with 2 conditions ('Travel after 10am?', 'Aged 60+?') generating 4 condition columns mapping to 4 distinct ticket price actions (Full, Full-20%, Off-peak, Off-peak-20%).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Completeness (all 2^c condition combinations accounted for); elimination of logical contradictions and redundant rules.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Creating massive un-nested tables for >5 conditions without using hierarchical sub-tables; missing condition combination columns.
When NOT to Use: For simple 1-condition binary choices (use a basic activity diagram decision diamond instead).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Activity Diagrams, Business Rules Analysis, Task Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Complex decision logic design, business rule automation, test case scenario generation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI rule-engine tools convert natural language policy documents directly into verified, gap-free Decision Tables and executable business rules code.

Problem Solved: Compares the current 'as is' business situation with the conceptual 'to be' desired model to identify required change actions across Process, IT, People, and Organization.
Input Artifacts: Current state models (Rich Pictures, Mind Maps, 'As Is' Process Maps), Desired state models (BAM, 'To Be' Process Maps), Scope definition.
Output Artifacts: Gap Analysis Report, categorized change actions list across POPIT (Process, IT, People, Organization).
Participants & Roles: BA, Business Owner, Sponsor, Enterprise Architect, Change Manager.
Prerequisites: Completion of both 'as is' investigation and 'to be' conceptual modeling.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Compare each activity in the BAM against the current situation. 2. Categorize activities: Existing & Satisfactory, Existing & Unsatisfactory, or Missing. 3. Prioritize unsatisfactory and missing activities. 4. Analyze detailed process gaps and IT support needs. 5. Map required change actions across POPIT (Process, IT, People, Organization). 6. Compile list of change actions.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Does this desired activity exist today? Is it done satisfactorily? What are the gaps in process, technology, staff skills, or structure? What specific actions will close this gap?
Minimal Realistic Example: Comparing a desired BAM activity 'Monitor staff performance' reveals it is 'Missing' currently, generating change actions to create a new reporting process (Process), build a KPI dashboard (IT), and train team leads (People).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Holistic coverage of gaps across all 4 POPIT dimensions; clear traceability from missing/unsatisfactory activities to proposed change actions.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Focusing exclusively on IT system gaps while ignoring necessary changes to staff skills, business processes, or organizational structure.
When NOT to Use: When the project is a pure technical infrastructure replacement with zero change to business processes, human roles, or organization.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: POPIT Model, Process Redesign Patterns, Feasibility Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Business case option formulation, change initiative scoping, target operating model design.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents compare current process logs against target capability maps to automatically highlight operational gap areas and draft proposed change action lists.

Problem Solved: Provides four structured analytical approaches (Reengineering, Simplification, Value-add analysis, Gaps/Disconnects) to guide process improvement and elimination of waste.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Analyse Needs / Change Identification / Process Design
Input Artifacts: 'As Is' Business Process Models, Task analysis records, Customer Value Propositions.
Output Artifacts: Redesigned 'To Be' Business Process Models, process waste elimination report.
Participants & Roles: BA, Business Process Owner, SMEs, Operations Lead.
Prerequisites: Documented 'as is' process models and identified customer value targets.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select redesign pattern(s). 2. For Reengineering: discard current process, work backward from end goals/events using technology. 3. For Simplification: examine tasks for redundancy, duplication, and bottlenecks. 4. For Value-add: classify tasks as Value-adding, Value-enabling, or Non-value-adding (eliminate/streamline non-value tasks). 5. For Gaps/Disconnects: analyze communication handoffs and conflicting metrics between actors.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: If we started from scratch today, how would we achieve this goal (Reengineering)? Is this step redundant (Simplification)? Would the customer pay for this step (Value-add)? Where do handoff failures occur (Disconnects)?
Minimal Realistic Example: Applying Value-add analysis to an invoice approval process: classifying 'Manager Sign-off' on small invoices as Non-value-adding control waste, replacing it with random sampling.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Demonstrated reduction in process cycle time, cost, or handoff errors while preserving or enhancing end customer value.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Automating an inherently flawed, redundant process without simplifying it first; eliminating essential compliance/control tasks during aggressive value-add trimming.
When NOT to Use: When process rules are strictly mandated by external statutory laws that forbid procedural alterations.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Business Process Reengineering (BPR), Lean Value Stream Mapping, Gap Analysis.
Supported Decisions: To-be process model design, IT feature automation scope, operational waste elimination.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Process mining AI applies Value-add and Disconnect patterns to real-time event logs to automatically highlight redundant steps and handoff bottlenecks.

Problem Solved: Generates a comprehensive longlist of potential business and technical solution options, preventing premature commitment to a single unexamined solution.
Input Artifacts: Gap Analysis results, problem statement, business strategy, MOST analysis.
Output Artifacts: Options Longlist covering business and technical possibilities (including 'Do Nothing').
Participants & Roles: BA, Sponsor, Business Owner, Technical Architect, SMEs.
Prerequisites: Clear definition of the business problem and change gap.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Convene creative workshop with key stakeholders. 2. Brainstorm business solution options (e.g. outsource, change strategy, manual process). 3. Brainstorm technical solution options (e.g. buy package, build bespoke, enhance existing). 4. Ensure 'Do Nothing' option is included. 5. Compile un-filtered longlist of options.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What are all the different ways we could solve this problem? What if we bought a package? What if we outsourced? What happens if we do nothing?
Minimal Realistic Example: A firm facing legacy system obsolescence brainstorms a longlist: 1. Buy package, 2. Enhance existing, 3. Revert to manual, 4. Outsource, 5. Exit business, 6. Share competitor system, 7. Do nothing.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Broad longlist covering diverse business and technical dimensions without premature filtering or dismissals.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Prematurely rejecting 'off-the-wall' options before evaluation; blindly accepting the sponsor's pet solution without generating alternative options; omitting 'Do Nothing'.
When NOT to Use: When the solution option is strictly dictated by mandatory statutory legal compliance with zero alternative choices.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Brainstorming, Hothousing, SWOT Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Business case scope options, solution approach selection.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Generative AI parses the problem statement and industry benchmarks to generate a broad candidate list of innovative business and technical options.

Problem Solved: Evaluates shortlisted options across Business, Technical, and Financial dimensions, reducing the risk of selecting unviable, unaffordable, or technically impossible options.
Input Artifacts: Options longlist, business strategy, technical architecture, budget constraints.
Output Artifacts: Feasibility Assessment Report evaluating shortlisted options against Business, Technical, and Financial criteria.
Participants & Roles: BA, Business Owner, Technical Architect, Finance Manager, HR Lead.
Prerequisites: Shortlist of candidate options.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Evaluate Business feasibility (Strategic fit, market conditions, timeliness, culture, org fit, competencies, legal). 2. Evaluate Technical feasibility (Availability, reliability, maintainability, performance, security, scalability, skills, compatibility). 3. Evaluate Financial feasibility (Budget, funds, ROI, cash flow, payback). 4. Document feasibility findings for each option.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Does this option fit our business strategy? Is it culturally acceptable? Is the technology reliable and scalable? Do we have the technical skills? Is it within budget?
Minimal Realistic Example: Evaluating a proposed software package: finding high business fit, but revealing technical infeasibility due to incompatibility with legacy databases and lack of internal support skills.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Comprehensive assessment across all three dimensions (Business, Technical, Financial) backed by factual evidence.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Evaluating only technical feasibility while ignoring organizational culture and staff competency fit; presenting over-optimistic financial projections.
When NOT to Use: During initial creative brainstorming where feasibility filtering would stifle idea generation.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Force-Field Analysis, PESTLE, SWOT, Investment Appraisal.
Supported Decisions: Option shortlisting, business case recommendation, risk identification.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Automated feasibility evaluators cross-check option parameters against enterprise architecture rules, regulatory databases, and financial constraints.

Problem Solved: Identifies driving forces (+ positive) and restraining forces (- negative) acting upon a proposed change option, guiding strategies to strengthen drivers and reduce resistance.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Evaluate Options / Shortlist Options / Change Management
Input Artifacts: Shortlisted option description, stakeholder analysis, cultural analysis.
Output Artifacts: Force-Field Diagram mapping driving forces and restraining forces, with force-mitigation strategy.
Participants & Roles: BA, Sponsor, Change Manager, Key Stakeholders.
Prerequisites: Definition of a specific proposed change option.
Step-by-Step Procedure: State the proposed change option in the center. 2. Identify driving forces (+ favoring change, e.g. regulator pressure, customer demands). 3. Identify restraining forces (- opposing change, e.g. tight budget, manager hostility). 4. Estimate the relative strength of each force. 5. Formulate actions to weaken negative forces and leverage positive forces.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What forces are pushing this change forward? What forces are resisting or blocking it? How powerful is each force? How can we weaken the negative forces?
Minimal Realistic Example: Analyzing an IT upgrade option: identifying positive forces (regulator pressure, CEO enthusiasm) vs negative forces (poor financial climate, CFO hostility), leading to strategies to engage the CFO.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Honest identification of negative cultural/political restraining forces alongside positive drivers.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Ignoring powerful negative stakeholder forces; assuming positive forces will automatically overcome negative resistance without targeted action.
When NOT to Use: When selecting purely technical algorithms where human/organizational forces are absent.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Kurt Lewin's Change Model, Risk Analysis, Stakeholder Management Planning.
Supported Decisions: Option selection, change management plan formulation, risk mitigation strategy.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Sentiment analysis systems evaluate project communications to identify and rate emerging negative organizational forces automatically.

Problem Solved: Identifies, quantifies, and contrasts the expected costs and benefits of a proposed solution option across Tangible/Intangible and Immediate/Longer-term categories.
Input Artifacts: Option descriptions, vendor quotes, HR day rates, market research, operational metrics.
Output Artifacts: Cost-Benefit Statement categorized by Tangible Immediate/Longer-term Costs and Tangible/Intangible Immediate/Longer-term Benefits.
Participants & Roles: BA, Sponsor, Finance Manager, Business User Leads, Solution Vendors.
Prerequisites: Selected option definition and access to organizational financial/resource cost data.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify one-off initial tangible costs (Hardware, software, development, training, data cleanup). 2. Identify ongoing tangible costs (Maintenance, support, salaries). 3. Identify intangible costs (Recruitment, short-term productivity loss). 4. Identify tangible benefits (Staff savings, reduced effort, avoided costs). 5. Identify intangible benefits (Job satisfaction, customer satisfaction, brand image). 6. Quantify tangible items in financial terms.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What are the one-off startup costs? What are the ongoing maintenance costs? What tangible cost savings result? What intangible benefits will be realized? Can this benefit be credibly monetized in advance?
Minimal Realistic Example: Quantifying a new system: One-off costs (£350k hardware/software, £60k ongoing support) vs Tangible benefits (£80k staff savings/yr, £100k increased sales/yr) and Intangible benefit (Improved brand image).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Tangible claims must be backed by credible, pre-verifiable evidence; clear distinction between features and actual benefits.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Claiming intangible benefits as tangible without credible pre-quantification; falling for the 'FTE fallacy' (aggregating fractional staff time savings that cannot actually be realized as real cash savings); double-counting accommodation costs.
When NOT to Use: When evaluating mandatory regulatory options where execution is legally compulsory regardless of cost-benefit ratios.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: CBA, BCA, Benefits Categorisation, Investment Appraisal.
Supported Decisions: Business case financial justification, project authorization, option comparison.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Financial AI tools analyze historical project expenditure and operational metrics to predict cost-benefit figures for new option proposals automatically.

Problem Solved: Classifies business benefits into four distinct categories (Financial, Quantifiable, Measurable, Observable), providing a nuanced framework beyond simple tangible/intangible labels.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Evaluate Options / Prepare Business Case / Benefits Management
Input Artifacts: Cost-Benefit Analysis, Business Case, stakeholder input.
Output Artifacts: Categorized Benefits List (Financial, Quantifiable, Measurable, Observable) with defined evaluation mechanisms.
Participants & Roles: BA, Benefit Owner, Finance Lead, Sponsor.
Prerequisites: Identification of proposed project benefits.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Review proposed benefits. 2. Categorize as Financial (provable in advance in cash terms). 3. Categorize as Quantifiable (provable in advance in non-cash metrics, e.g. lives saved). 4. Categorize as Measurable (measurable after the event, e.g. website sales increase). 5. Categorize as Observable (assessed via expert judgment/agreed criteria, e.g. staff morale). 6. Define evaluation mechanisms for each.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Is this benefit provable in cash terms in advance (Financial)? Is it provable in advance using non-cash metrics (Quantifiable)? Can we measure it before and after (Measurable)? Must it be judged by experts using criteria (Observable)?
Minimal Realistic Example: Categorizing benefits for a level-crossing safety project: 'Closing crossings' is Quantifiable (saves X lives/yr based on statistics), but assigning cash value is separate.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Appropriate categorization based on proof availability and measurement timing; clear pre-defined evaluation mechanism for every category.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Attempting to force fake financial values onto purely observable benefits; failing to establish baseline metrics before project execution for measurable benefits.
When NOT to Use: When preparing a simple informal rough estimate with no formal benefits management framework.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Cost-Benefit Analysis, Benefits Dependency Framework, Benefits Realisation.
Supported Decisions: Business case justification, benefits management plan design, post-project evaluation criteria definition.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI analytics engines match proposed benefits against historic enterprise tracking data to classify them accurately into the four categories.

Problem Solved: Identifies and presents non-cost organizational, cultural, and procedural impacts of a proposed change, ensuring decision-makers have a complete picture beyond financial numbers.
Input Artifacts: Selected solution option description, process models, organization charts, POPIT assessment.
Output Artifacts: Impact Analysis Report detailing non-cost impacts (Org structure, Interdepartmental relations, Working practices, Management style, Recruitment, Promotion, Customer focus, Supplier relations).
Participants & Roles: BA, Change Manager, HR Lead, Operations Leads, Sponsor.
Prerequisites: Definition of the recommended solution option.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Analyze impact on Organizational Structure and interdepartmental relations. 2. Analyze impact on Working Practices and union agreements. 3. Analyze impact on Management Style (e.g. shift to coaching). 4. Analyze impact on Recruitment, Promotion criteria, and Skills. 5. Analyze impact on Customer Focus and Supplier relations. 6. Formulate mitigation actions for negative impacts.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How does this option change daily working practices? Does it require shifting management style from command-and-control to coaching? How does it affect supplier or union relationships?
Minimal Realistic Example: Identifying that flattening management layers (Option impact) requires supervisors to shift from 'command-and-control' to a 'coaching' style, requiring targeted leadership development.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Holistic coverage of soft organizational and human impacts alongside hard structural changes; actionable mitigation proposals.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Omitting non-cost cultural/political impacts from the business case, leading to executive surprise and project rejection during rollout.
When NOT to Use: For minor isolated technical bug fixes with zero process or human footprint.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: POPIT Model, McKinsey 7-S, Leavitt's Diamond, Force-Field Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Business case approval, target operating model design, change management intervention planning.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Impact prediction AI scans proposed solution feature lists against historical HR and process data to highlight probable cultural and working practice friction areas.

Problem Solved: Systematically identifies, assesses (impact & probability), and formulates responses/owners for risks threatening a proposed project option, increasing business case credibility.
Input Artifacts: Option descriptions, feasibility report, stakeholder input, risk breakdown structures.
Output Artifacts: Risk Log / Risk Matrix detailing Risk description, Impact (Large/Moderate/Small), Probability (High/Medium/Low), Response (Avoidance, Mitigation, Transference, Acceptance), and Risk Owner.
Participants & Roles: BA, Project Manager, Sponsor, Technical Lead, Risk Owner.
Prerequisites: Selected option definition and access to key technical/business stakeholders.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify risks via interviews, workshops, or checklists. 2. Determine potential impact if risk occurs. 3. Assess scale of Impact (Large/Moderate/Small) and Probability (High/Medium/Low). 4. Formulate response actions (Avoidance, Mitigation, Transference, Acceptance). 5. Assign a specific named Risk Owner for each action.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What could go wrong with this option? What is the impact if it happens? How likely is it? How can we avoid or mitigate it? Who owns this risk?
Minimal Realistic Example: Identifying risk 'Selecting wrong software package' (Large impact / Medium probability), defining Avoidance action 'Mandate rigorous requirements spec and objective selection criteria', assigned to BA Lead.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Every identified risk has an assigned response strategy and a named individual Risk Owner with authority to act.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Downplaying or hiding major risks to make the business case look artificially attractive; assigning risk ownership to people without authority.
When NOT to Use: During initial unconstrained creative brainstorming sessions.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Risk Management, Risk Identification, Feasibility Analysis, Force-Field Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Business case authorization, contingency budget allocation, risk response planning.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Risk analytics AI scans project parameters against historical project failure databases to identify candidate risks and suggest proven mitigation strategies automatically.

Problem Solved: Evaluates project options using quantitative financial models (Payback/Breakeven, Discounted Cash Flow / Net Present Value, Internal Rate of Return), proving financial viability.
Input Artifacts: Cost-Benefit Analysis figures, corporate discount rates, project timeframe constraints.
Output Artifacts: Financial Investment Appraisal Report showing Payback period, Net Present Value (NPV), and/or Internal Rate of Return (IRR).
Participants & Roles: BA, Finance Manager / Management Accountant, Sponsor.
Prerequisites: Quantified tangible cost and benefit figures from Cost-Benefit Analysis.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Compile annual cash flow table (Benefits minus Costs per year starting at Year 0). 2. Calculate Payback period (when cumulative cash flow becomes positive). 3. Apply corporate Discount Factors to calculate Discounted Cash Flows for each year. 4. Sum discounted cash flows to calculate Net Present Value (NPV). 5. Calculate Internal Rate of Return (IRR) where NPV=0 to compare against interest benchmarks.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: When does the project achieve payback? What is the Net Present Value using our corporate discount rate? What is the Internal Rate of Return compared to bank interest rates?
Minimal Realistic Example: Calculating an investment: Initial £410k cost with £120k net annual benefit shows 4-year Payback, but applying a 10% discount rate reveals a negative NPV of -£29,720 (failing financial appraisal).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Discount factors correctly aligned with corporate management accounting standards; rigorous inclusion of all tangible capital and ongoing costs.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Relying solely on simple payback while ignoring the time value of money (DCF/NPV); using inaccurate discount rates; misinterpreting IRR on different scale projects.
When NOT to Use: For non-financial mandatory compliance projects where options are dictated by law regardless of financial return.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Payback analysis, DCF/NPV, IRR, Cost-Benefit Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Project authorization, capital allocation, option selection.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Financial modeling AI automatically executes multi-scenario DCF/NPV and IRR calculations, running sensitivity analyses across varying discount rates.

Problem Solved: Assembles all analytical findings, option evaluations, cost-benefit models, and impact/risk assessments into a structured, convincing written business report for executive decision-makers.
Input Artifacts: Gap Analysis, Option evaluations, Cost-Benefit Analysis, Investment Appraisal, Impact/Risk analysis outputs.
Output Artifacts: Written Business Case Report (Introduction, Management Summary, Background, Options, Benefits & Costs, Investment Appraisal, Impacts, Risks, Recommendations, Appendices).
Participants & Roles: BA (Author), Sponsor (Reviewer/Owner), Decision-Makers (Audience).
Prerequisites: Completion of option evaluation, cost-benefit, and risk analysis.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Write Background and Introduction. 2. Document Options considered and rejection reasons. 3. Document Benefits and Costs (benefits first). 4. Include Investment Appraisal summary. 5. Detail Impacts and Risks with mitigations. 6. State clear Recommendations and required decision. 7. Move detailed calculations to Appendices. 8. Write concise 3-paragraph Management Summary last. 9. Proofread thoroughly.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is the core recommendation? What decision is required from executive management? Are the financial details accessible in appendices? Is the Executive Summary concise and focused?
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA drafts a 10-page Business Case Report with a 1-page Management Summary recommending option 1 (buy package), attaching 40 pages of detailed DCF tables in appendices.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Concise, active-voice writing style; clear 3-paragraph Management Summary; explicit recommendation and requested decision; zero typos.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Writing an overly long, verbose report without a clear Executive Summary; burying key recommendations in dense text; passive academic writing style ('It is recommended that...'); draft errors.
When NOT to Use: When presenting micro-level operational tweaks where a simple verbal briefing or email request is sufficient.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Business Case Presentation, 4As Communication Model.
Supported Decisions: Project authorization, capital expenditure approval, strategic option selection.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: GenAI report-authoring tools compile underlying analytical models into a standardized, beautifully formatted Business Case Report draft.

Problem Solved: Delivers a short, sharp, persuasive executive briefing to decision-makers, summarizing the business case recommendations and securing approval.
Input Artifacts: Business Case Report, executive stakeholder profiles.
Output Artifacts: Slide Deck / Executive Presentation, approved business case decision.
Participants & Roles: BA (Presenter), Project Sponsor, Executive Decision-Makers (Audience).
Prerequisites: Completed Business Case Report; booked executive presentation slot.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Understand executive audience interests and available time slot (e.g. 15 mins). 2. Create minimal, highly visual slides (<5 slides). 3. Start with an impactful opening statement ('Start with a bang!'). 4. Present main issues and solution option. 5. State explicit recommendations and required decision ('End on a high'). 6. Rehearse with colleagues acting as critical managers. 7. Deliver presentation and answer questions.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What headline message will hook these executives immediately? What decision do I need from them today? What tough questions will they ask?
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA opens a 15-minute board presentation stating: 'This proposal will save our firm £12m/year in operating expenses', presenting 4 visual slides and securing project sign-off.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Delivered strictly within time limits; concise visual slides; active engagement and confident handling of executive questions.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Reading the text of the report word-for-word off dense slides ('death by PowerPoint'); taking too many slides; lacking rehearsed answers to tough financial/risk questions.
When NOT to Use: When decision-makers require only a formal written report submission without a live meeting.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Business Case Report Creation, 4As Communication Model.
Supported Decisions: Project authorization, budget sign-off, option selection.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI presentation tools auto-generate visual slide decks directly from written business case reports and simulate executive Q&A sessions for rehearsal.

Problem Solved: Provides a 4-part planning structure (Aim, Audience, Arrangement, Appearance) for developing effective presentations and business documents.
Input Artifacts: Presentation topics, stakeholder list, venue details.
Output Artifacts: Structured Presentation Plan / Document Layout (Aim, Audience analysis, Arrangement outline, Appearance specifications).
Participants & Roles: BA (Presenter/Author), Target Audience / Stakeholders.
Prerequisites: Need to communicate business analysis findings, proposals, or business cases.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define Aim (why is presentation required, desired outcome). 2. Analyze Audience (who are they, what are their aims/expectations, background). 3. Plan Arrangement (structure: Tell 'em what you'll tell 'em -> Tell 'em -> Tell 'em what you told 'em). 4. Design Appearance (presenter attire, slide readability, font consistency, visual style).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is my specific aim? Who is in my audience and what do they want? How should I arrange the logical flow? How should the slides/document visually appear?
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA uses 4As to structure a project update: setting Aim (secure extra budget), analyzing Audience (CFO/Sponsor needs), Arrangement (Problem -> Solution -> ROI), and Appearance (clean visual charts).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Explicit alignment between presenter aim and audience needs; clear logical arrangement; readable visual design.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Ignoring audience expectations; creating unreadable slides with bad fonts/colors; lacking a structured opening/closing arrangement.
When NOT to Use: For casual, informal 1-on-1 chats where formal communication planning is unnecessary.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Business Case Presentation, Business Case Report Creation.
Supported Decisions: Presentation structure approval, document format design, communication strategy execution.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI communication assistants evaluate presentation drafts against 4As criteria, highlighting unreadable fonts, missing audience hooks, or weak logical flows.

Problem Solved: Identifies and classifies user populations into user classes, analyzing their characteristics, demographics, tasks, and working environments to guide UI/UX and work practice design.
Input Artifacts: Stakeholder list, process maps, user profiles, market analytics.
Output Artifacts: User Classification Document detailing user classes, attributes (type, experience, frequency, motivation, numbers, training, tasks), and usability considerations.
Participants & Roles: BA, Usability/UX Specialists, Business Users, System Actors.
Prerequisites: Identification of user groups interacting with proposed systems/processes.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify user populations interacting with system (direct, intermediaries, customers). 2. Group users into similar User Classes. 3. Analyze attributes for each class (Tech literacy, expectations, motivation - mandatory/discretionary, population size, training, tasks, environment). 4. Document usability considerations. 5. Input findings into UI/UX design and requirements catalog.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Who will use this system? Is usage mandatory or discretionary? How tech-literate are they? What environment do they work in? What tasks do they perform daily?
Minimal Realistic Example: Documenting User Class 'Hotel Reception Desk Staff': High frequency (80/day), mandatory usage, high time-pressure with waiting clients, driving UI requirements for fast-access keys and high system responsiveness.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Usability decisions backed by objective user attributes rather than developer assumptions; complete coverage of all user classes.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Assuming all users possess high tech-literacy; ignoring discretionary users who can easily abandon a site; designing interfaces based on developer preferences.
When NOT to Use: For purely automated back-end batch interface systems with zero human interaction.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Personas, Scenarios, Wireframes, Prototyping.
Supported Decisions: UI/UX design architecture, training program design, non-functional usability requirement specification, job role design.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: User analytics AI processes real-time user session logs to automatically cluster users into attribute classes and generate candidate usability profiles.

Problem Solved: Walks through concrete examples of specific situation threads from a user's perspective, uncovering missing requirements, edge cases, and tacit knowledge.
Input Artifacts: Process models, user analysis, business events, context diagrams.
Output Artifacts: Scenario Descriptions (Background/Situation narrative, Script step sequence, Exceptions), Scenario Coverage Model.
Participants & Roles: BA, Business Users, SMEs, Testers.
Prerequisites: Identification of key business events and user tasks.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select specific task/event. 2. Define background situation (role, frequency, specific context). 3. Draft step-by-step user script (happy day flow). 4. Identify exception threads at specific steps. 5. Validate script with business users. 6. Build Scenario Coverage Model (user population, environment, frequency) to ensure comprehensive test coverage.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Can you walk me through a specific example of this task? What happens first? What if the customer doesn't have a loyalty card? What exceptions occur?
Minimal Realistic Example: Writing a scenario for 'Customer buying fuel & shop items using credit card with separate VAT receipt', walking through attendant actions, credit card swipe, and VAT receipt generation exceptions.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Written from user perspective; covers happy day and exceptions; validated against Scenario Coverage Model to ensure sufficient coverage across frequent, critical, and difficult tasks.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Focusing only on 'happy day' paths while ignoring exceptions; writing abstract general descriptions instead of specific concrete examples; neglecting low-frequency critical events.
When NOT to Use: When analyzing purely static data structures or high-level strategic corporate goal definitions.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Use Case Descriptions, Storyboarding, Prototyping, Activity Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Requirements specification validation, test script design, user acceptance criteria definition, training scenario creation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Generative AI parses business event maps to auto-generate comprehensive scenario scripts covering edge cases and exception branches for analyst review.

Problem Solved: Captures system requirements as short, simple user-focused sentences supported by conversations and confirmation criteria, reducing bloated, unreadable specification documents.
Input Artifacts: User analysis, Scenarios, Product Backlog, business goals.
Output Artifacts: User Story Cards ('As a role, I want feature, So that benefit'), Acceptance Criteria / Confirmations, Story Point estimates.
Participants & Roles: BA, Business User / Product Owner, Developer, Tester.
Prerequisites: Identification of user roles and required business features.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Write user story using standard format ('As a... I want to... So that...'). 2. Conduct collaborative Conversations between BA, users, developers, and testers to explore detail. 3. Document Confirmations (Acceptance Criteria / business rules). 4. Estimate Story Points (using Planning Poker). 5. Verify story against INVEST criteria (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Who needs this feature? What specific feature is needed? What business value or benefit does it deliver? What specific acceptance criteria prove it works?
Minimal Realistic Example: Writing Story 150: 'As a customer, I want to amend my credit card payment details so that I can continue to purchase items via the website', with rules on card security and order despatch states.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Adheres to INVEST criteria; includes clear confirmation rules/acceptance criteria; estimated in story points; captures a conversation rather than acting as a static specification.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Writing bloated technical specifications on cards; omitting the 'So that' business value statement; treating cards as static documentation without holding conversations; missing acceptance criteria.
When NOT to Use: For complex legal contracts or heavy outsourcing agreements where formal legally binding written specifications are required upfront.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Use Case Descriptions, Requirements Catalogue, Planning Poker, Product Backlog.
Supported Decisions: Iteration planning, backlog prioritization, development scope allocation, test case design.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: GenAI assistants convert scenario transcripts into INVEST-compliant User Stories complete with candidate acceptance criteria.

Problem Solved: Estimates the relative size and complexity of user stories/requirements using consensus-based card voting, reducing individual estimator bias and unvetted estimates.
Input Artifacts: User stories, Acceptance Criteria, baseline estimation unit.
Output Artifacts: Agreed Story Point estimates per user story.
Participants & Roles: Moderator/BA, Estimating Team (Developers, Testers, Designers), Product Owner.
Prerequisites: Selected user stories with clear descriptions and acceptance criteria; decks of planning poker cards (Fibonacci sequence: 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20, 40, 100).
Step-by-Step Procedure: Moderator presents user story. 2. Team discusses requirement to clarify scope. 3. Each estimator privately selects a numbered card. 4. All cards revealed simultaneously. 5. High and low estimators explain their reasoning. 6. Group discusses insights (e.g. reusability, hidden complexity). 7. Re-vote until consensus is reached.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How complex is this story compared to our baseline? Why did you pick a 13 while others picked a 3? What hidden technical or business tasks exist?
Minimal Realistic Example: A team plays Planning Poker for a payment story: initial votes range 2 to 8. Discussion reveals reusable code exists, leading to a second-round consensus estimate of 5 story points.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Achieved through true team consensus and open dialogue rather than forced voting or manager imposition.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Converting story points directly into fixed developer hours; forcing a vote majority instead of consensus; allowing senior leads to dominate initial card selection.
When NOT to Use: When well-understood, routine repetitive tasks with historical precise time data are being estimated.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Wideband Delphi, Expert Judgment, Function Point Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Iteration scope selection, velocity planning, release schedule estimating.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Estimation AI analyzes historical team velocity and past story complexity to offer baseline story point suggestions during poker sessions.

Problem Solved: Illustrates navigation routes and screen sequences for user scenarios using low-fidelity visual sketches or index cards, reducing misinterpretation of user interface workflows.
Input Artifacts: Scenarios, User analysis, Context definitions, UI layout ideas.
Output Artifacts: Storyboard diagram / slide deck showing sequential interface frames, user actions, and system navigation links.
Participants & Roles: BA, Solution Designer, UX Designer, Business Users.
Prerequisites: Defined user scenarios and key interface interaction goals.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Input user scenario. 2. Brainstorm UI ideas on whiteboards/Post-its. 3. Select top ideas. 4. Sketch sequential screen frames showing pictures, text, buttons, and navigation arrows. 5. Walk through storyboard frames with business users to validate navigation flow. 6. Convert to digital slides if helpful.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What does the user see first? What button do they click next? What screen appears in response? How do they navigate back?
