Minimal Realistic Example: Creating a 6-frame travel agent storyboard: Customer enquiry -> Main booking screen -> Flight details popup -> Location map -> Insurance window -> Final airline ticket generation.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Demonstrates clear navigation sequences; validated by business users as accurately reflecting their scenario workflow.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Getting bogged down in fine graphic design details (fonts, colors) instead of focusing on navigation and functional sequence; designing in isolation without user feedback.
When NOT to Use: For non-visual, non-interactive back-end database scripts or batch processing systems.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Wireframes, Prototyping, Scenarios, Activity Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: UI navigation flow design, prototype scope selection, scenario validation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI design tools automatically convert text scenario scripts into visual interactive Storyboard slide decks.

Problem Solved: Constructs working models (Throwaway or Evolutionary) of proposed software/screens to clarify requirements and test usability, reducing post-implementation rework.
Input Artifacts: Scenarios, Storyboards, Wireframes, User analysis, functional specs.
Output Artifacts: Working Prototype (Throwaway or Evolutionary), Business/Usability/Capacity test feedback, refined requirements.
Participants & Roles: BA, Solution Developer, UX Designer, Business Users / Testers.
Prerequisites: Selected scope, agreed fidelity level (low/high), and clear session objectives (Business, Usability, or Capacity).
Step-by-Step Procedure: Agree prototype objectives, scope, fidelity, and type (Throwaway or Evolutionary). 2. Construct prototype model (Horizontal scope or Vertical depth). 3. Demonstrate prototype to users in structured sessions. 4. Gather user feedback and observe interaction difficulties. 5. Refine prototype iteratively or update requirements catalogue.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Does this screen layout meet your needs? Is this navigation intuitive? What information is missing from this view?
Minimal Realistic Example: Developing a vertical evolutionary prototype of an online flight booking screen, refining button placement and field validation based on live user feedback.
Quality Criteria & Verification: User expectations managed regarding prototype performance and final system delivery; complete capture of user feedback into requirement updates.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Allowing throwaway prototypes to turn into unmaintainable production code; creating over-promising prototypes with unrealistic response times; failing to document requirements learned.
When NOT to Use: When requirements are already 100% stable, standardized, and non-visual (e.g. standard file format conversion).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Wireframes, Storyboarding, Hothousing, Use Case Modelling.
Supported Decisions: UI/UX design sign-off, functional requirement baseline, usability acceptance criteria validation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Generative UI tools convert user story descriptions instantly into functional HTML/JS prototypes for live user testing.

Problem Solved: Creates simple 2D structural illustrations of screen layouts focusing on content allocation and navigation without visual style distractions, reducing UI design confusion.
Input Artifacts: Scenarios, Storyboards, User analysis, functional specifications.
Output Artifacts: Wireframe Diagrams (Hand-drawn low-fidelity or digital high-fidelity screen layout diagrams with content blocks, search fields, headers, footers, and links).
Participants & Roles: BA, UX/UI Designer, Business Users, Developers.
Prerequisites: Identification of screen functional requirements and key content types.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify key content blocks, search areas, headers, and actions. 2. Draw 2D structural layout using grayscale boxes (use 'x' box for images). 3. Use generic single font sizes for headers/text. 4. Position primary content and navigation paths. 5. Review wireframe layout with users to agree content distribution.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Where should the primary content block sit? How much space should be allocated to search vs navigation? Is the contact form clearly positioned?
Minimal Realistic Example: Drawing a grayscale web wireframe for a 'Contact Us' page showing header logo, global navigation bar, search box, map placeholder (box with x), and input form fields.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Focuses purely on structural content layout and navigation pathways, omitting color, graphics, and specific fonts.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Adding colors, fancy fonts, and real graphics that distract users from structural layout feedback; treating wireframes as final graphic design.
When NOT to Use: For non-visual back-end systems or when testing complex interactive micro-animations (use high-fidelity prototypes instead).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Storyboarding, Prototyping, Personas.
Supported Decisions: Screen layout sign-off, content prioritization, navigation structure approval.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI sketching tools transform hand-drawn napkin wireframe sketches into clean digital UI layouts and responsive code templates.

Problem Solved: Accelerates requirement clarification and solution prototyping through an intensive 3-day off-site workshop with competing teams, significantly shortening delivery timescales.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Define Requirements / Elicitation / Analysis / Solution Design
Input Artifacts: Business problems, Use case scenarios, PIR 'handshake' metrics.
Output Artifacts: Selected Working Prototype, PIR Handshake document (measurable targets & 90-day objectives), Cost-Benefit Analysis, Metrics.
Participants & Roles: BA, Facilitators, Cross-functional Teams (Developers, Business Users, Partners, Customers), Judges/Sponsors.
Prerequisites: Off-site venue, technical infrastructure, clear business problem statement, 3-day commitment.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Day One: Present business problem, teams brainstorm approaches, present outlines, score/rank. 2. Day Two: Teams build working prototypes with direct user feedback, score/rank. 3. Day Three: Fine-tune prototypes, evaluate final solutions, select winning prototype. 4. Establish 90-day release timebox and PIR handshake.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How can we solve this business problem in 3 days? What is the core working prototype we can build? What measurable targets define success for our 90-day release?
Minimal Realistic Example: A retail bank holds a 3-day off-site hothouse where 3 cross-functional teams compete to build a mobile loan application prototype, selecting the winning app for a 90-day rollout.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Working prototype delivered within 3 days; explicit PIR handshake defining measurable targets for the subsequent 90-day release timebox.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Failing to secure off-site isolation leading to work distractions; lacking real business decision-makers during the event; over-scoping beyond the 3-day limit.
When NOT to Use: For routine, minor system maintenance or when key business users and developers cannot commit to 3 days off-site.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Hackathons, Agile Prototyping, Facilitated Workshops, Timeboxing.
Supported Decisions: Solution architecture selection, 90-day release scope approval, business case metrics sign-off.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI coding assistants accelerate hothouse prototype generation, allowing teams to build complex working features in hours during the 3-day sprint.

Problem Solved: Fixes delivery deadlines and budgets, flexing scope via prioritisation rather than allowing schedules to slip, ensuring timely delivery.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Define Requirements / Requirements Analysis / Project Execution
Input Artifacts: Prioritised Requirements List (MoSCoW), Outer timebox schedule, product definitions.
Output Artifacts: Timebox Plan (Kick-off/Planning, Investigate 15%, Refine 70%, Consolidate 15%, Close-out/Review), delivered product increments.
Participants & Roles: BA, Project Manager, Development Team, Business Users / Product Owner.
Prerequisites: Agreement that deadlines are fixed and scope is flexible using MoSCoW priorities.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Agree fixed end date for outer/inner timebox. 2. Kick-off / Planning (select MoSCoW prioritised requirements). 3. Investigate (15% - clarify detail). 4. Refine (70% - build & test iteratively). 5. Consolidate (15% - finalize & review). 6. Close-out / Review (evaluate delivered items against goals). 7. If time runs short, drop 'Could/Should haves' to guarantee 'Must haves'.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is the fixed end date for this timebox? Which 'Must haves' are included? If time runs short, which 'Should/Could haves' will we drop?
Minimal Realistic Example: Executing a 4-week inner timebox: allocating 15% to Investigate, 70% to Refine (building stories), and 15% to Consolidate, dropping a 'Could have' report to hit the 4-week deadline.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Timebox ends strictly on the agreed date; 100% of 'Must haves' delivered; scope flexed using lower priorities.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Allowing timebox deadlines to slip when work falls behind; attempting to timebox without MoSCoW prioritization; treating timeboxing as an ad-hoc panic measure.
When NOT to Use: When fixed-scope legal compliance mandates require 100% of all listed requirements to be delivered on a single non-negotiable date.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: MoSCoW Prioritisation, Product Backlog, Planning Poker.
Supported Decisions: Release scope management, iteration planning, resource allocation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Project management AI engines track velocity during timeboxes, alerting teams early if 'Must have' delivery is threatened so scope flexing can occur.

Problem Solved: Categorizes requirements into Must have, Should have, Could have, and Want to have (WONT) based on clear definitions, enabling flexible scope management during fixed timeboxes.
Input Artifacts: Requirements Catalogue, User Stories, Timebox constraints.
Output Artifacts: Prioritised Requirements List categorized by M, S, C, and W.
Participants & Roles: BA (Facilitator), Sponsor, Business Owner, Users, Developers.
Prerequisites: Decomposed requirements defined in sufficient detail.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define MoSCoW rules clearly to stakeholders. 2. Evaluate 'Must haves' (M - critical minimum usable subset, guaranteed). 3. Evaluate 'Should haves' (S - important, short-term workaround exists). 4. Evaluate 'Could haves' (C - desirable, easily dropped). 5. Evaluate 'Want to have but WONT get this time' (W - valuable, deferred to future releases). 6. Ensure 'Must haves' do not exceed ~60% of total effort.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Is the system unusable without this (Must)? Is there a manual workaround for this (Should)? Can this be easily left out without major pain (Could)? Can this wait for a later release (WONT)?
Minimal Realistic Example: Prioritizing bank balance features: 'View balance' (Must), 'Up-to-date daily transactions' (Should), 'View in Euros' (Could), 'Multi-language views' (WONT).
Quality Criteria & Verification: 'Must haves' comprise <=60% of total effort; unambiguous categorization backed by clear business criteria; agreement from all key stakeholders.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Classifying >80% of requirements as 'Must have'; treating 'Should haves' as optional fluff; prioritizing high-level undecomposed requirements.
When NOT to Use: When prioritizing a tiny list of 2 items where simple binary ranking is sufficient.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Timeboxing, Product Backlog, Planning Poker, Weighted Scoring.
Supported Decisions: Release scope selection, timebox scope flexing, trade-off analysis.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Prioritization AI analyzes requirement descriptions against business goals and historical timebox velocity to suggest candidate MoSCoW tags.

Problem Solved: Structures, clusters, and links large sets of requirements, and resolves conflicting stakeholder requirements, reducing unmanageable, contradictory specifications.
Input Artifacts: Raw elicited requirements list, stakeholder lists, domain maps.
Output Artifacts: Structured Requirements Specification (clustered by Functional, Non-functional, General, Technical), documented requirement links, negotiated conflict agreements.
Participants & Roles: BA, Sponsor, Stakeholders, Technical Leads.
Prerequisites: Elicited list of candidate requirements.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Cluster requirements into high-level groups (Functional, Non-functional, General, Technical). 2. Sub-group into lower-level categories (by business process, non-functional type, etc.). 3. Document links and dependencies between requirements. 4. Perform hierarchical decomposition. 5. Identify conflicting requirements. 6. Conduct 3-step negotiation (Discussion, Prioritisation, Agreement).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Which category does this requirement belong to? What other requirements depend on this? How can we resolve the contradiction between User A and User B's requests?
Minimal Realistic Example: Structuring 200 raw requirements into Functional (by booking process) and Non-functional (Performance/Security), resolving a conflict between open access vs tight security via role-based rules.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Logical partitioning; explicit dependency linking; complete resolution of conflicting requirements through consensus.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Leaving requirements as an un-categorized flat list of 500 items; ignoring conflicts until technical build starts; mixing non-functional constraints inside functional requirements.
When NOT to Use: In micro-projects with under 10 straightforward requirements.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Requirements Catalogue, MoSCoW Prioritisation, CRUD Matrix, Traceability Matrix.
Supported Decisions: Requirements specification baseline, release packaging, conflict resolution.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Clustering AI parses unstructured requirement lists, automatically categorizing them into Functional/Non-functional buckets and flagging conflicting statements.

Problem Solved: Maintains a dynamic, prioritized list of features, user stories, and bug fixes for development, providing a constant stream of prioritized work for development teams.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Define Requirements / Requirements Analysis / Backlog Management
Input Artifacts: High-level business requirements, User Stories, Customer feedback, Defect logs.
Output Artifacts: Product Backlog (Task board or digital repository of prioritized stories, estimates, and acceptance criteria).
Participants & Roles: BA, Product Owner, Development Team, Scrum Master.
Prerequisites: High-level understanding of system goals and user needs.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Compile initial backlog from business requirements and user stories. 2. Sequence items based on value, risk, dependencies, and delivery target. 3. Continuously maintain/groom backlog (analyze customer feedback, add/split user stories, refine acceptance criteria). 4. Re-estimate story points (Planning Poker). 5. Select top backlog items for upcoming iteration timebox.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What item delivers the highest business value next? Are the top backlog stories refined and ready for development? How does customer feedback alter backlog priorities?
Minimal Realistic Example: Maintaining an e-commerce backlog: ranking 'Credit card payment' story at the top (Priority 1, 8 points), followed by 'PayPal integration' (Priority 2, 5 points), grooming acceptance rules weekly.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Top backlog items are fully estimated and meet INVEST criteria; clear prioritization backed by business value; continuous grooming by BA/PO and dev team.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Treating the backlog as a static upfront specification; letting the backlog become un-groomed and full of stale, ambiguous stories; technical team prioritizing without Product Owner/business input.
When NOT to Use: In traditional rigid waterfall projects where scope is fixed upfront and change requests are strictly controlled via formal board procedures.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Requirements Catalogue, User Stories, Timeboxing, MoSCoW.
Supported Decisions: Iteration planning, feature release sequence, development resource allocation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Backlog management AI continuously analyzes production telemetry and user feedback to recommend backlog re-prioritizations automatically.

Problem Solved: Provides a standard, consistent structure for capturing the overall requirements set and detailed individual requirements, ensuring clear communication and auditability.
Input Artifacts: Elicited requirements, process models, data models, stakeholder inputs.
Output Artifacts: Requirements Specification document (Introduction, Functional model, Data model, Catalogue, Glossary) and Requirements Catalogue entries.
Participants & Roles: BA (Author), Sponsor/Owner (Sign-off), Developers, Testers.
Prerequisites: Elicitation and initial analysis of requirements.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Draft Requirements Specification overview (Business context, Scope, Drivers, Constraints). 2. Attach Functional and Data Models. 3. Create Requirements Catalogue entries for each requirement (ID, Name, Domain, Description, Source, Owner, Priority, Stakeholders, Type, Non-functional links, Acceptance criteria, Justification, Resolution). 4. Compile Glossary. 5. Maintain catalogue resolution status throughout project.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is the unique ID for this requirement? Who is the named business Owner? What is the explicit business justification? What is the current resolution status?
Minimal Realistic Example: Creating Catalogue Entry F-073 'Book a flight' for Head of Internet Booking (Owner), marked 'Must have', detailing description, associated non-functional speed rules, acceptance criteria, and resolution 'Release 1'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: All catalogue fields completed; explicit named business owner assigned; clear resolution audit trail recorded for every requirement.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Leaving catalogue fields blank (e.g. no Owner or Justification); documenting vague descriptions without unique IDs; failing to update resolution status.
When NOT to Use: In lightweight informal prototyping spikes where visual models replace formal document logs.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Requirements Catalogue, User Stories, Product Backlog.
Supported Decisions: Requirements baselining, scope sign-off, solution verification, audit compliance.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Requirement documentation AI automatically formats raw interview transcripts into standardized Requirements Catalogue entries.

Problem Solved: Defines specific, objective, and measurable criteria for each requirement, bridging the gap between business needs and solution testing.
Input Artifacts: Requirements Catalogue, User Stories, Scenarios, Use Case Descriptions.
Output Artifacts: Measurable Acceptance Criteria / Fit Criteria per requirement (including PLUME usability metrics for non-functional items).
Participants & Roles: BA, Business Customer/Owner, Developers, Testers.
Prerequisites: Identification and description of individual requirements.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Review requirement description and scenarios. 2. Formulate specific, quantifiable benchmark criteria. 3. Define functional fit criteria (inputs, expected outputs, state changes). 4. Define non-functional criteria (response times, PLUME usability metrics: Productivity, Learnability, User satisfaction, Memorability, Error rates). 5. Validate criteria with customer and tester.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How will we prove this requirement has been met? What specific quantifiable metric defines success? What is the exact response time limit? How will testers verify this?
Minimal Realistic Example: Defining acceptance criteria for 'Book a flight': 'System confirms booking by displaying reservation reference code, notes date/time, and response time <=10 seconds for 95% of transactions'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Criteria are specific, objective, quantifiable, and testable; agreed by both business customer and testing lead.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Writing vague, unmeasurable criteria like 'system must be fast and user-friendly'; defining acceptance criteria after testing has already started.
When NOT to Use: During initial exploratory visioning workshops before specific requirements have been formulated.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Fit Criteria, Test Cases, PLUME Usability Metrics, Scenarios.
Supported Decisions: User acceptance test sign-off, requirement completion validation, solution verification.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Test-generation AI engines parse acceptance criteria text directly to generate automated Gherkin test scripts (Given-When-Then) automatically.

Problem Solved: Verifies that requirements are correctly specified (Verification) and validates that they deliver real business value (Validation), reducing costly defects in delivered solutions.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Define Requirements / Requirements Development / Quality Assurance
Input Artifacts: Requirements Specification, Requirements Catalogue, Business Objectives, CRUD Matrix.
Output Artifacts: Verified/Validated Requirements Document, Quality Review Logs, Sign-off Records.
Participants & Roles: BA, Quality Reviewers, Domain Experts, Business Owner, Sponsor.
Prerequisites: Documented draft requirements specification.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Check individual requirements against Quality Criteria (Unambiguous, Clear, Complete, Consistent, Testable, Feasible, etc.). 2. Check requirement set for completeness using CRUD matrix. 3. Conduct Necessity Checking against business goals. 4. Execute Static Testing (Peer reviews, Walkthroughs, Technical reviews, Inspections). 5. Obtain formal stakeholder sign-off.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Is this requirement unambiguous and testable? Does it contribute to our business goals? Is it consistent with other requirements? Are there any missing CRUD aspects?
Minimal Realistic Example: Conducting a formal Inspection review of a 50-item Requirements Catalogue against a quality checklist, uncovering 3 ambiguous statements and 2 missing delete operations.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Requirements satisfy all 18 quality criteria (Unambiguous, Clear, Complete, Consistent, etc.); documented defect log resolved; formal stakeholder sign-off achieved.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confusing verification (doing things right) with validation (doing the right thing); skipping reviews due to schedule pressure; conducting reviews without checklists.
When NOT to Use: In informal exploratory brainstorming where quality filtering would choke creative idea generation.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Peer Reviews, Inspections, Walkthroughs, CRUD Matrix, Prototyping.
Supported Decisions: Requirements baselining approval, quality gateway progression, development phase authorization.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Static analysis AI tools audit requirements catalogue text against quality rules, flagging passive voice, ambiguity, contradictions, or un-testable statements automatically.

Problem Solved: Applies configuration control, version numbering, baseline management, and formal change control to requirements, preventing scope creep and un-tracked modifications.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Define Requirements / Requirements Management / Change Control
Input Artifacts: Requirements Catalogue, Change Requests, Baseline specifications, Traceability Matrix.
Output Artifacts: Requirements Management Plan, Version-controlled Requirements Catalogue, Change Control Logs, Baseline Audit Trail.
Participants & Roles: BA, Change Control Board / Approval Authority, Project Manager, Librarian.
Prerequisites: Formal baselining of the initial requirements specification.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Establish configuration identification rules (naming, version numbering, item levels). 2. Formally baseline the requirements set. 3. Place items in a controlled repository/library. 4. Process new Change Requests via 4 steps: Document request, Assess impact/cost/effort, Review by approval authority (Approve/Reject/Defer), Implement and update version numbers.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What version of the requirement is this? Has the baseline been formally established? What is the cost/effort impact of this proposed change? Was this change approved by the Change Board?
Minimal Realistic Example: A user requests a new report post-baseline: the BA logs Change Request CR-012, performs impact analysis (£5k cost, 3-day delay), the Change Board approves it, and the catalogue version advances to v2.1.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Complete audit trail for every change; all stakeholders working to the identical current baseline version; zero unauthorized scope additions.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Allowing informal 'off-the-record' scope changes without impact analysis; failing to baseline requirements; allowing developers to work from outdated document versions.
When NOT to Use: During early discovery/elicitation before an initial baseline has been established.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Configuration Management, Traceability Matrix, Change Control Board.
Supported Decisions: Change request approval/rejection/deferral, baseline release scope definition.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Requirements management AI tools automatically track requirement edits, link change requests to impacted design modules, and assess downstream cost/schedule impacts.

Problem Solved: Tracks requirements bi-directionally (backwards to business sources/goals, forwards to design, code, and test cases), ensuring all requirements are delivered and no unneeded features are built.
Input Artifacts: Requirements Catalogue, Use Cases, System Design docs, Test Scripts.
Output Artifacts: Requirements Traceability Matrix mapping Requirement ID -> Source -> Use Case -> Design Module -> Code Component -> Test Case ID -> Test Result.
Participants & Roles: BA, Project Manager, System Architect, Developers, Testers.
Prerequisites: Uniquely identified requirements in a requirements catalogue.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Create standard matrix template. 2. Populate row IDs from Requirements Catalogue. 3. Map backward links to original business sources/goals. 4. Map forward links to Use Cases and Design modules as created. 5. Map forward links to Test Case IDs and code modules. 6. Update test result status. 7. Use matrix for impact analysis when changes occur.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Which business goal spawned this requirement? Which use case implements this requirement? Which test case verifies this requirement? What code/design components are impacted if this requirement changes?
Minimal Realistic Example: Mapping Requirement F-073 ('Book flight'): Source (Focus Group) -> Use Case (UC-04) -> Design Module (Mod-9) -> Test Case (TC-102) -> Result (Pass).
Quality Criteria & Verification: 100% bi-directional traceability for every requirement; zero 'orphan' requirements without test cases or sources.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Creating the matrix at the end of the project as a fake compliance exercise; maintaining complex matrices manually in flat spreadsheets without repository support.
When NOT to Use: In tiny, 1-week single-developer scripts where formal matrix tracking creates excessive overhead.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Requirements Catalogue, CRUD Matrix, Use Case Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Scope verification sign-off, change impact assessment, test coverage validation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: ALM AI systems parse requirements, architecture models, and automated test suites to maintain dynamic, bi-directional traceability matrices automatically.

Problem Solved: Models high-level business services provided by an organization/domain to actors, independent of technology or internal execution mechanics, clarifying strategic business scope.
Input Artifacts: Organization Diagram, Value Chain, CATWOE outputs, stakeholder list.
Output Artifacts: Business Use Case Diagram (Actors, Business Use Cases, Associations, optional system boundary) and Business Use Case Descriptions.
Participants & Roles: BA, Business Architect, Enterprise Architect, Business Owners.
Prerequisites: High-level understanding of business domain goals and services.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify high-level business services required by stakeholders. 2. Represent services as Business Use Cases (ovals, using standard or striped Podeswa notation). 3. Identify human/external system Business Actors (stick figures). 4. Draw association lines connecting actors to business use cases. 5. Review business services with stakeholders.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What core business services does this organization provide to its clients? Who are the primary actors accessing these services? What business value is delivered?
Minimal Realistic Example: A Business Use Case Diagram for an HR domain showing actors HR Manager and HR Officer interacting with business use cases 'Recruit staff member', 'Induct staff member', and 'Conduct annual appraisal'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Models business-level services (what), not IT software functions or physical step procedures; covers all core stakeholder services.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confusing high-level business use cases with low-level IT system software functions; adding technical screen details.
When NOT to Use: When analyzing micro-level software coding logic or database schema architecture.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Use Case Modelling, Value Streams, Capability Modelling, Business Activity Modelling.
Supported Decisions: Business domain scope definition, target operating model design, service delivery channel selection.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Enterprise architecture AI parses corporate strategy documents to draft candidate Business Use Case Diagrams automatically.

Method Name: Use case diagrams and use case descriptions
Problem Solved: Models IT system functional scope via Use Case Diagrams and details actor-system interactions via structured Use Case Descriptions, providing clear developer and user specifications.
Input Artifacts: Context Diagram, Business Use Cases, Scenarios, User Analysis.
Output Artifacts: Use Case Diagram (System Boundary, Actors, Use Cases, Associations, <>, <>) and Use Case Descriptions (Preconditions, Trigger, Guarantees, Main Success Scenario, Extensions).
Participants & Roles: BA, Business Users, System Architect, Developers, Testers.
Prerequisites: Defined IT system boundary and user roles.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Draw System Boundary box and System Name. 2. Position Actors outside boundary (User roles, Other systems, Time). 3. Draw Use Case ovals inside boundary. 4. Draw un-arrowed Association lines. 5. Add <> (mandatory common sub-use cases) and <> (optional sub-use cases) links. 6. Write detailed Use Case Descriptions (Scope, Actors, Preconditions, Trigger, Guarantees, Main Success Scenario, Extensions).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What does the user want the IT system to do? What is the main 'happy day' sequence between actor and system? What exceptions or alternative flows occur?
Minimal Realistic Example: Diagram for 'Project Control System' showing Project Manager actor linked to Use Cases 'Create project', 'Amend project' (including 'Identify project'), and optional extension 'Print assignment', supported by detailed tennis-match narrative descriptions.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Clear system boundary; user-perspective interaction narrative; complete exception coverage in extension section; unambiguous <> (mandatory) and <> (optional) usage.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Over-using <> and <> to turn diagrams into complex functional decomposition flowcharts; writing internal technical coding steps inside use case descriptions.
When NOT to Use: For purely non-functional infrastructure performance specifications or static database schema design.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Activity Diagrams, User Stories, Business Process Modelling, Task Analysis.
Supported Decisions: IT system scope approval, software architecture design, test case generation, user training documentation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Requirement AI tools generate complete Use Case Diagrams and structured Descriptions directly from input scenario transcripts.

Problem Solved: Models the conceptual data structure (entities, attributes, relationships, cardinalities) and business data rules of an organization, reducing database errors and redundant data.
Input Artifacts: Document analysis outputs, domain forms, business rules, requirements specification.
Output Artifacts: Entity Relationship Model / Diagram (Entities, Relationships, Cardinality, Optionality, Link Entities, Subtypes/Supertypes) and Supporting Entity/Attribute Descriptions.
Participants & Roles: BA, Data Architect, Database Designer, SMEs.
Prerequisites: Identification of key business data items and operational business rules.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify candidate Entities (nouns: physical, conceptual, active). 2. Identify Relationships between entities. 3. Determine Cardinality (one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many) and Optionality. 4. Resolve many-to-many relationships by inserting Link Entities. 5. Model Recursive or Exclusive relationships and Subtypes/Supertypes. 6. Define Entity attributes and primary keys.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What things do we need to store data about (Entities)? How many B's can relate to one A (Cardinality)? Must an A have a B (Optionality)? What business rule governs this relationship?
Minimal Realistic Example: Modeling a garage data domain: Car entity linked to Service entity via a resolved many-to-many Link Entity 'Car Service', connected to Technician.
Quality Criteria & Verification: All many-to-many relationships resolved; correct cardinality and optionality reflecting real business data rules; primary keys defined.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Leaving unresolved many-to-many relationships in the model; confusing entity instances with entity classes; designing physical database tables prematurely.
When NOT to Use: When analyzing purely procedural workflow timing or non-data UI visual layouts.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Class Modelling, Data Dictionary, Document Analysis, CRUD Matrix.
Supported Decisions: Database architecture specification, data migration design, enterprise data governance, business rule definition.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI data-modeling engines parse business specs and legacy database schemas to generate normalized Entity Relationship Diagrams automatically.

Problem Solved: Models object-oriented data structures, attributes, associations, multiplicities, and operations, providing an enriched data specification for modern software architectures.
Input Artifacts: Entity Relationship Models, Document Analysis, Use Cases, domain rules.
Output Artifacts: Class Diagram (Classes with Name, Attribute, and Operation compartments, Multiplicities, Association Classes, Reflexive Associations, Generalizations).
Participants & Roles: BA, System Architect, Software Developer, Data Architect.
Prerequisites: Identification of domain objects, attributes, and system functionality.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify Classes (3-compartment box: Name, Attributes, Operations). 2. Draw Association lines between classes. 3. Specify Multiplicity (e.g. 0..*, 1..1, 0..4). 4. Create Association Classes for many-to-many relationships holding attributes. 5. Model Generalizations (inheritance super-classes) and Reflexive associations.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What are the object classes? What attributes describe them? What are the minimum and maximum association numbers (Multiplicity)? What general super-class unites these sub-classes?
Minimal Realistic Example: Class diagram showing Car class linked 0..* to Service class via Association Class CarService (holding dateOfService, recordedMileage), connected 0..4 to Technician class.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Correct UML lower/upperCamelCase naming syntax; accurate multiplicity numbers; clear generalisation hierarchies.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Over-populating operations prematurely before software design; confusing UML class multiplicity notation with SSADM entity relationship crow's foot notation.
When NOT to Use: When working in non-object-oriented legacy relational database environments where traditional ERD notation is preferred.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Entity Relationship Modelling, Data Dictionary, CRUD Matrix.
Supported Decisions: Object-oriented software design, database schema design, application architecture.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: UML AI assistants parse user story descriptions to auto-generate class diagrams with candidate attributes and multiplicity associations.

Problem Solved: Cross-references system use cases against data entities/classes to map Create, Read, Update, and Delete operations, ensuring data-process model completeness and consistency.
Input Artifacts: Use Case Diagrams, Class Models / Entity Relationship Models.
Output Artifacts: CRUD Matrix (Classes/Entities on vertical axis, Use Cases on horizontal axis, populated with C, R, U, D letters).
Participants & Roles: BA, System Architect, Developers, Testers.
Prerequisites: Draft Use Case Model and draft Data Model.
Step-by-Step Procedure: List Classes/Entities down vertical matrix rows. 2. List Use Cases across horizontal matrix columns. 3. For each intersection, indicate whether the use case Creates (C), Reads (R), Updates (U), or Deletes (D) instances of the class. 4. Check rows: ensure every class has at least one C and D. 5. Check columns: ensure every use case accesses data.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Does this use case create, read, update, or delete this data class? Are there any data classes that are never created or never deleted by any use case?
Minimal Realistic Example: Mapping a library system: 'New borrower' use case Creates Borrower class; 'Borrow book' Reads Borrower, Updates Book, and Creates Loan class.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Every class has at least one 'C' (Create) and 'D' (Delete) across its row; every use case interacts with at least one data class.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Failing to check for orphan classes with no Create or Read operations; ignoring CRUD validation until late in software testing.
When NOT to Use: In simple projects with under 3 use cases and 2 data tables where manual inspection is trivial.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Requirements Traceability Matrix, Use Case Modelling, Class Modelling.
Supported Decisions: Model completeness validation, development iteration sequencing, work package packaging, effort estimation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Modeling AI engines automatically compare Use Case text against Class Diagrams to compile verified CRUD matrices and highlight missing data operations.

Problem Solved: Models the permissible states, state transitions, triggering events, and guard conditions for a specific business entity/class over its lifecycle, eliminating invalid state changes.
Input Artifacts: Class Model, Task Descriptions, Business Rules, Use Cases.
Output Artifacts: State Machine Diagram / Statechart (Initial state, States, Transition arrows, Events, Guard conditions, Actions, Final state).
Participants & Roles: BA, System Architect, Business Rules SME, Developers, Testers.
Prerequisites: Identification of a complex entity/class with multiple lifecycle states.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Draw Initial state (solid circle). 2. Identify valid lifecycle States (rounded boxes). 3. Draw directional Transition arrows between valid states. 4. Label transitions with syntax: Event Guard condition / Action. 5. Draw Final state (bulls-eye circle). 6. Verify illegal transitions are blocked.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What states can this object exist in? What event triggers a transition from State A to State B? What guard condition must be true? What state transitions are illegal?
Minimal Realistic Example: Modeling 'Order' class: Placed -> Picked -> Despatched -> Delivered -> If <28 days Refunded vs 28 days after delivery -> Finalised, blocking 'Cancel' after 'Despatched'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Complete lifecycle coverage from initial to final state; explicit guard conditions on conditional transitions; impossible illegal transitions explicitly prevented.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Creating state charts for simple entities with only 2 trivial states; cluttering diagrams with obvious redundant event labels; missing exit guard conditions.
When NOT to Use: For simple stateless data lookups or static reference tables with no lifecycle state changes.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Statecharts, State Transition Diagrams, Activity Diagrams, Business Rules Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Entity lifecycle business rule specification, system state validation logic, negative test case generation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI code generators convert State Machine Diagrams directly into executable state-machine software classes and negative test scripts.

Problem Solved: Analyzes organizational corporate culture (Deal & Kennedy, Handy, Hofstede, Johnson & Scholes Cultural Web), reducing change rejection caused by cultural incompatibility.
Input Artifacts: Organizational context, cultural observations, leadership style data, Cultural Web components.
Output Artifacts: Cultural Analysis Report / Cultural Web Matrix (Paradigm, Stories, Rituals, Symbols, Org Structures, Control Systems, Power Structures).
Participants & Roles: BA, Change Manager, HR Director, Executive Sponsor.
Prerequisites: Understanding of informal organizational norms, stories, and power dynamics.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Analyze central Paradigm (core assumptions/mission). 2. Audit Stories and myths. 3. Audit Rituals and Routines. 4. Audit visual Symbols and dress codes. 5. Audit formal/informal Organizational Structures. 6. Audit Control Systems and metrics. 7. Map Power Structures. 8. Evaluate cultural gap between current and required culture.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is the core paradigm? What stories are told to newcomers? What rituals are valued? Where does real power lie? How does our proposed change fit this culture?
Minimal Realistic Example: Analyzing Virgin Atlantic using the Cultural Web: defining Paradigm ('profitable airline people love'), un-earthing Richard Branson stories, flat structures, informal dress (Symbols), and visible punctuality metrics (Controls).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Holistic audit covering both subjective (stories, rituals) and objective (controls, structures) cultural dimensions; clear gap identification between current and required culture.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Treating culture as an irrelevant soft factor; attempting to impose changes that directly contradict the un-addressed core organizational paradigm.
When NOT to Use: For micro-level technical bug fixes with zero cultural or human impact.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Cultural Web, Handy's Cultural Types, Hofstede's Dimensions, POPIT Model.
Supported Decisions: Change management strategy, organizational redesign, leadership engagement approach, communication strategy.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: NLP agents analyze internal communications, employee surveys, and news archives to construct initial Cultural Web models and flag cultural risk areas.

Method Name: Kurt Lewin’s model of organisational change
Problem Solved: Provides a 3-stage framework (Unfreeze -> Transition -> Freeze) to guide change implementation, reducing change rejection and reversion to old habits.
Input Artifacts: Force-Field Analysis, Change strategy, POPIT assessment.
Output Artifacts: Change Implementation Plan structured into Unfreeze, Transition, and Freeze stages.
Participants & Roles: BA, Change Manager, Sponsor, Line Managers, Business Users.
Prerequisites: Definition of required business changes and force-field assessment.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Unfreeze stage: overcome inertia, dismantle old mindsets, communicate urgency and evidence for change. 2. Transition stage: execute changes, support staff through uncertainty, handle errors with sensitivity. 3. Freeze stage: anchor new working practices, establish new stability, reinforce behaviors so staff do not revert to old habits.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How will we unfreeze current habits and demonstrate the need for change? How will we support people during transition confusion? How will we freeze the new process so staff don't revert?
Minimal Realistic Example: Implementing a public smoking ban: Unfreezing via health evidence campaigns -> Transitioning on the implementation date with support -> Freezing as non-smoking becomes the new socially accepted norm.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Explicit activities planned and executed for all three stages; demonstrated stability (permanency) achieved during the Freeze stage.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Skipping the Unfreeze stage and forcing change on unprepared staff; failing to Freeze the new state, allowing staff to revert to legacy habits.
When NOT to Use: When managing continuous micro-iterations where a permanent frozen state is intentionally avoided.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Kotter's 8-Step Change, Force-Field Analysis, SARAH Model.
Supported Decisions: Change management plan design, user readiness evaluation, post-implementation stabilization.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Change analytics AI tracks user adoption metrics during Transition to advise managers when an organization is ready to move to the Freeze stage.

Problem Solved: Maps the emotional journey individuals experience during major change (Shock -> Anger -> Rejection -> Acceptance -> Hope), guiding empathetic change support strategies.
Input Artifacts: Stakeholder Analysis, Change impact assessment, communication plan.
Output Artifacts: Stakeholder Emotional Support Strategy / Timeline.
Participants & Roles: BA, Change Manager, Line Managers, Affected Staff.
Prerequisites: Announcement or implementation of significant business change.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Recognize initial Shock upon change announcement. 2. Empathize with resulting Anger directed at change/analysts. 3. Patiently manage Rejection stage without overreacting or forcing rational arguments. 4. Support staff as they reach Acceptance. 5. Leverage dawning Hope to gather user suggestions for future enhancements.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What emotional stage is this stakeholder currently experiencing? How can we support them through Anger/Rejection without overreacting? Are they ready for training to reach Acceptance?
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA encounters user anger and rejection during a new system rollout, remaining patient and empathetic until staff complete training, reach Acceptance, and suggest new ideas (Hope).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Demonstrated empathy and patience during early negative emotional stages; successful progression of staff to Acceptance and Hope.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Arguing rationally with stakeholders experiencing emotional Anger/Rejection; expecting instant enthusiasm without allowing staff to process the emotional curve.
When NOT to Use: For minor, unnoticeable system tweaks that trigger no emotional impact on workers.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Kurt Lewin's Change Model, Conscious Competence Model, Kotter's 8-Step Change.
Supported Decisions: Change communication timing, training plan scheduling, stakeholder support strategy.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Sentiment-analysis AI engines evaluate employee feedback channels during rollout to map staff distribution across the SARAH curve in real-time.

Problem Solved: Provides a comprehensive 8-step framework (Urgency, Coalition, Vision, Communicate, Remove obstacles, Short-term wins, Build, Anchor) for leading successful organizational change.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Manage Change / People Change / Organisational Change
Input Artifacts: Business Case, Strategy definition, Stakeholder analysis, POPIT assessment.
Output Artifacts: 8-Step Change Execution Roadmap and Communication Plan.
Participants & Roles: BA, Executive Sponsor, Guiding Coalition Leads, Change Manager.
Prerequisites: High-level authorization for major business change.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Create sense of Urgency (get ~75% manager buy-in). 2. Form a powerful Guiding Coalition. 3. Create Vision and Strategy. 4. Communicate Vision broadly. 5. Remove obstacles (align structures, systems, rewards). 6. Create Short-Term Wins. 7. Build on change (don't declare victory early). 8. Anchor changes in Corporate Culture.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Have we created a true sense of urgency? Who forms our guiding coalition? What is our concise vision strap line? What short-term win can we deliver first?
Minimal Realistic Example: Implementing automated airport border control: 1. Build urgency around queues -> 2. Form coalition (ministers, border leads) -> 3. Define vision 'Speed & Security' -> 4. Communicate -> 5. Align staff -> 6. Pilot short-term win -> 7. Roll out -> 8. Anchor in culture.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Sequential execution of all 8 steps; >75% management buy-in established in Step 1; early short-term wins achieved and celebrated.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Declaring victory after the first short-term win; skipping Step 1 (Urgency) and rushing straight to execution; lacking a powerful guiding coalition.
When NOT to Use: For small, routine micro-tasks or isolated technical maintenance with no organizational reach.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Kurt Lewin's Change Model, POPIT Model, Cultural Web, SARAH Model.
Supported Decisions: Change roadmap planning, stakeholder coalition assembly, change communication execution.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Change management platforms track progress metrics across all 8 Kotter steps, alerting leaders if steps are skipped or short-term wins are lacking.

Problem Solved: Shifts planning and negotiation mindsets from problem/blame orientation to a positive, future-focused outcome orientation (What do I want?, How will I know?, What resources?).
BA Lifecycle Phase: Manage Change / People Change / Planning / Negotiation
Input Artifacts: Problem statements, negotiation contexts, stakeholder disputes.
Output Artifacts: Outcome Plan (Desired Outcome, Rationale, Timing, Verification criteria, Current state, Resource needs, Action steps, Impact assessment).
Participants & Roles: BA, Stakeholders, Negotiating Parties.
Prerequisites: Identification of a desired goal, change objective, or negotiation dispute.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Answer: What outcome do I want? 2. Why do I want it? 3. When do I want it? 4. How will I know I achieved it? 5. Where am I now? 6. What resources do I need? 7. What action steps are required? 8. What else is affected?
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What specific positive outcome do we want to achieve? How will we verify success? What resources are needed? What are the step-by-step actions?
Minimal Realistic Example: Resolving a requirements dispute between two leads: using Outcome Frame questions to shift focus from past arguments to agreeing on a consensus outcome within 5 days using data analysis.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Future-focused, positive outcome definition; explicit verification criteria; actionable step-by-step execution plan.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Falling back into problem-blame thinking ('Who caused this bug?'); defining vague outcomes without verification criteria.
When NOT to Use: When performing forensic root-cause auditing of past financial fraud where identifying past problem culpability is mandatory.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Outcome Thinking, NLP Planning, Principled Negotiation, SMART Objectives.
Supported Decisions: Negotiation resolution, change initiative goal definition, project planning.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI coaching tools guide analysts through interactive Outcome Frame prompts during dispute resolution or project planning sessions.

Problem Solved: Explains how individuals learn skills through a 4-stage cycle (Concrete Experience, Reflection, Abstract Concepts, Testing) and 4 Learning Styles (Activist, Reflector, Theorist, Pragmatist).
BA Lifecycle Phase: Manage Change / People Change / Training / Workshop Facilitation
Input Artifacts: Training needs analysis, stakeholder profiles, workshop plans.
Output Artifacts: Tailored Training Curriculum, Balanced Workshop Facilitation Strategy.
Participants & Roles: BA (Facilitator/Trainer), Business Users / Workshop Attendees.
Prerequisites: Planning of training programs or stakeholder workshops.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Understand the 4 cycle stages (Concrete Experience, Observation & Reflection, Abstract Concepts, Testing). 2. Recognize participant Learning Styles (Activist - jump in; Reflector - analyze data; Theorist - assimilate logic; Pragmatist - practical application). 3. Design balanced training/workshops catering to all 4 styles.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What learning style dominates this stakeholder group? How can we balance jump-in exercises (Activists) with quiet reflection (Reflectors) and practical application (Pragmatists)?
Minimal Realistic Example: Designing a workshop for mixed styles: combining a fast Post-it exercise (Activists/Pragmatists) with pre-circulated reading materials and quiet reflection time (Reflectors/Theorists).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Training/workshop design incorporates activities for all 4 learning cycle stages and styles.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Designing workshops exclusively for Activists (e.g. non-stop loud brainstorming), alienating Reflectors and Theorists; presenting pure theory without practical exercises.
When NOT to Use: When delivering fully automated machine-executable script updates requiring zero human learning.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Kolb's Cycle, Honey & Mumford's Learning Styles, Conscious Competence Model.
Supported Decisions: User training curriculum design, workshop facilitation technique selection, change adoption planning.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Adaptive AI learning platforms monitor user interaction habits to deliver dynamically tailored training modules matching individual learning styles.

Problem Solved: Tracks skill acquisition across 4 stages (Unconscious Incompetence -> Conscious Incompetence -> Conscious Competence -> Unconscious Competence), guiding user training and support.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Manage Change / People Change / Training / Support
Input Artifacts: Training plans, role descriptions, SARAH model outputs.
Output Artifacts: Competency Transition Plan (Awareness, Training/Coaching, Practice/Mentoring, Mastery).
Participants & Roles: BA, Trainers, Mentors, Business Users.
Prerequisites: Introduction of new business processes or IT systems requiring new skills.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Unconscious Incompetence: sensitively raise awareness of new required skills. 2. Conscious Incompetence: provide formal training and support to alleviate fear/anxiety. 3. Conscious Competence: provide coaching/mentoring as users practice (accepting short-term productivity dips). 4. Unconscious Competence: celebrate mastery and capture new improvement ideas.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What stage of competence are users currently at? How do we support them through Conscious Incompetence without causing panic? Have we allowed for short-term productivity dips during Conscious Competence?
Minimal Realistic Example: Supporting users during a CRM rollout: acknowledging anxiety at Stage 2, providing intensive desk-side coaching during Stage 3 (where productivity temporarily dips), until system use becomes second nature at Stage 4.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Demonstrated progression of users through to Unconscious Competence; planned allowance for temporary productivity dips during Stage 3.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Expecting instant Stage 4 mastery immediately post-training; treating Stage 2 anxiety as incompetence; criticizing users during the Stage 3 learning dip.
When NOT to Use: For automated system-to-system interfaces requiring no human operator learning.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: The Learning Cycle, SARAH Model, Training Needs Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Training schedule design, post-go-live support planning, productivity impact estimation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI performance-support assistants provide real-time in-app guidance to users during Stage 3 (Conscious Competence) to accelerate progression to mastery.

Problem Solved: Manages a project continuously against a formal Benefits Plan and Benefits Dependency Framework, maximizing the probability that business benefits are actually achieved.
Input Artifacts: Business Case, Objectives, Benefit descriptions, Enabling and Business changes list.
Output Artifacts: Benefits Dependency Framework / Map, Benefits Plan (Vision, Maps, Timeline Bar Chart, Metrics, Financials, Accountabilities/Owners, Review tracking).
Participants & Roles: BA, Project Sponsor, Change Manager, Benefit Owners (Line Managers).
Prerequisites: Identification of expected business benefits and business case approval.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify overall business Objectives. 2. Identify required Benefits. 3. Identify necessary Business Changes. 4. Identify required Enabling Changes. 5. Construct Benefits Dependency Framework/Map. 6. Map against timeline bar chart. 7. Assign named Benefit Owners. 8. Manage project against Benefits Plan, reviewing at stage gates.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What core business objective are we serving? What specific benefits achieve this objective? What business and enabling changes are required? Who is the named Benefit Owner?
Minimal Realistic Example: Creating a Benefits Map for customer support: Enabling changes (tech spec, training) -> Business changes (adopt new service) -> Benefits (online support, faster response) -> Objective (Improved Customer Satisfaction).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Complete logical chain from Enabling Changes -> Business Changes -> Benefits -> Objectives; named Benefit Owners with authority assigned to every benefit.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Focusing purely on IT system delivery while neglecting necessary business/enabling changes; failing to assign benefit owners; treating benefits as a static business case appendix.
When NOT to Use: In small, non-investment experimental research spikes where benefits cannot be structured.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Benefits Dependency Framework, Benefits Realisation, Cost-Benefit Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Project stage-gate approval, scope change impact evaluation, benefit owner assignment.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Benefits tracking AI engines monitor project execution milestones and operational metrics, dynamically updating Benefits Dependency Maps and alerting owners to risks.

Problem Solved: Evaluates whether business benefits were actually achieved post-implementation, identifying corrective actions if shortfalls occur and capturing lessons learned for future projects.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Manage Change / Benefits Realisation / Post-Project Review
Input Artifacts: Business Case, Benefits Plan, Evaluation criteria, Operational performance metrics.
Output Artifacts: Benefits Realisation Report, Corrective Action Plan, Organizational Lessons Learned log.
Participants & Roles: BA, Project Sponsor, Benefit Owners, Line Managers, Post-Project Reviewer.
Prerequisites: Completed project implementation and sufficient operational running time.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Review original Business Case and Benefits Plan evaluation criteria. 2. Collect post-implementation operational performance data. 3. Compare actual realized benefits against target metrics. 4. Identify shortfalls and investigate root causes. 5. Formulate corrective action plans (e.g. extra training, publicity) to salvage benefits. 6. Publish Benefits Realisation Report and archive organizational lessons learned.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Did we achieve the expected benefits outlined in the business case? What is the actual metric value today vs the baseline? If benefits were missed, why? What corrective action can salvage them?
Minimal Realistic Example: A post-implementation review of a customer support portal reveals online usage is lower than targeted; the review identifies lack of customer awareness, initiating a publicity campaign to salvage the benefit.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Objective measurement of actual post-implementation metrics against pre-set evaluation criteria; actionable salvage plans for missed benefits.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Failing to conduct post-implementation reviews; conducting 'witch hunts' instead of objective evaluations; measuring benefits too early before operational stabilization.
When NOT to Use: Immediately post-go-live before the system has had sufficient operational running time to generate measurable benefits data.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Benefits Management, Post-Implementation Review (PIR), Cost-Benefit Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Corrective action intervention, future project selection/estimation refinement, organizational learning.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Post-implementation telemetry AI automatically audits live operational KPIs against business case targets, drafting Benefits Realisation Reports and highlighting shortfalls.

Problem Solved: Reduces uncertainty and ambiguity regarding architecturally significant quality attribute requirements prior to completing the architecture design.
Input Artifacts: Business/mission context, high-level system requirements, initial architectural plans (if available).
Output Artifacts: Consolidated and prioritized quality attribute scenarios, list of key architectural drivers, refined 6-part quality attribute scenarios.
Participants & Roles: Facilitators, Architect, Business/Mission Stakeholders, Project Manager, Developers, Testers.
Prerequisites: Identified system stakeholders and a presentation of the business/mission vision and goals.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Present QAW overview. 2. Present business/mission needs. 3. Present architectural plan. 4. Identify architectural drivers. 5. Brainstorm quality attribute scenarios. 6. Consolidate similar scenarios. 7. Prioritize scenarios using voting. 8. Refine top scenarios into six-part scenario format.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What stimulus initiates the scenario? What is the source of the stimulus? What environment is the system in? What artifact is affected? What is the expected response? How is the response measured?
Minimal Realistic Example: Stakeholders brainstorm and refine a scenario: 'When a peak load of 2,000 requests occurs during normal operation, the system processes all requests with an average latency of under 2 seconds.'
Quality Criteria & Verification: Six-part scenario completeness check, stakeholder consensus, voting results, review of response measures for testability.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Creating untestable scenarios, focusing exclusively on functional features instead of quality attributes, lack of key stakeholder representation.
When NOT to Use: Small projects with trivial quality requirements or well-known, fully established domains without stakeholder uncertainty.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Quality Attribute Utility Trees, Requirements Document Mining, PALM (Pedigreed Architecture Analysis Method for Business Goals).
Supported Decisions: Scope definition, prioritization of quality attribute drivers, preliminary architectural design strategy.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: An AI agent can ingest raw stakeholder transcripts to auto-generate 6-part scenarios, suggest scenario consolidations, and run automated ambiguity/testability checks. Human-in-the-loop is required for final scenario prioritization and validation.

Method Name: Pedigreed Architecture Analysis Method for Business Goals (PALM)
Problem Solved: Reduces uncertainty regarding business goals and aligns architectural decisions directly with business motivations.
Input Artifacts: Business strategy documents, corporate vision statements, executive mandates.
Output Artifacts: Prioritized business goal scenarios, identified quality attribute requirements linked to business goals.
Participants & Roles: Facilitator, Software Architect, Executive/Business Stakeholders, Product Manager.
Prerequisites: Availability of business leaders capable of articulating strategic business goals.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Present PALM overview. 2. Present business drivers and context. 3. Elicit business goals using standard categories. 4. Consolidate and refine business goals into structured business goal scenarios. 5. Prioritize business goal scenarios. 6. Map prioritized business goals to specific quality attribute requirements.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What are the growth, financial, market, and process goals of the organization? How does this system contribute to meeting those organizational business goals?
Minimal Realistic Example: Eliciting a business goal to 'reduce annual operating costs by 30%', which maps to a quality attribute requirement for energy efficiency and resource auto-scaling.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Traceability between business goal scenarios and corresponding quality attribute scenarios; stakeholder consensus on goal priorities.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confusing technical features with business goals; focusing only on short-term project objectives rather than organizational business goals.
When NOT to Use: Projects where business goals are already explicit, fixed, and clearly mapped to technical requirements.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Quality Attribute Workshop (QAW), Utility Tree Construction, Balanced Scorecard.
Supported Decisions: Scope decisions, architecture investments, build vs. buy decisions, risk mitigation priorities.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can analyze strategic corporate artifacts to draft candidate business goal scenarios. Human oversight is mandatory to confirm strategic priorities and business alignment.

Problem Solved: Solves prioritization conflicts and lack of specificity in quality attribute requirements by organizing and quantifying them.
Input Artifacts: Business goals, quality attribute requirements, system context documents.
Output Artifacts: Utility Tree (hierarchical structure mapping Utility -> Quality Attributes -> Attribute Refinements -> Concrete Scenarios with (Importance, Risk) ratings).
Participants & Roles: Software Architect, Lead Analysts, Key Business/Technical Stakeholders.
Prerequisites: High-level understanding of required quality attributes and business goals.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define 'Utility' as the root node representing overall system goodness. 2. Identify main quality attribute categories (e.g., Performance, Security). 3. Refine categories into specific sub-attributes. 4. Write concrete 6-part scenarios at the leaves. 5. Prioritize leaf scenarios based on Business Importance (H/M/L) and Technical Risk (H/M/L).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How do we define overall system utility? What specific quality sub-attributes drive success? What concrete stimulus-response scenario exemplifies this sub-attribute? What is its business value and technical risk?
Minimal Realistic Example: Utility -> Performance -> Latency -> 'Under peak load, a user updates an address and receives confirmation in < 0.75s' rated as (High Importance, High Risk).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Every leaf scenario must have a measurable response measure; high-importance/high-risk (H,H) scenarios must be explicitly highlighted for architectural focus.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Leaving leaf nodes as vague statements (e.g., 'High Availability') without 6-part concrete scenarios; failing to involve business decision-makers in importance rating.
When NOT to Use: Extremely small systems with no significant or complex quality attribute requirements.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Quality Attribute Workshop (QAW), Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method (ATAM).
Supported Decisions: Architectural driver selection, iteration goal setting, trade-off decisions between conflicting quality attributes.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLMs can automatically generate draft utility trees from unstructured requirements specifications. Human-in-the-loop validation is required to assign risk and importance ratings.

Problem Solved: Eliminates design uncertainty and arbitrary decision-making by systematically designing software architecture based on prioritized quality attribute requirements and architectural drivers.
Input Artifacts: Design purpose, primary functional requirements, quality attribute scenarios, constraints, architectural concerns.
Output Artifacts: Architectural views (sketches of Module, C&C, Allocation views), instantiated elements with assigned responsibilities, documented design decisions and rationale, updated design backlog.
Participants & Roles: Software Architect, Design Team, Technical Lead.
Prerequisites: Prioritized architecturally significant requirements (ASRs) and clear definition of design purpose.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Review inputs. 2. Establish iteration goal by selecting drivers. 3. Choose system elements to refine. 4. Choose design concepts (patterns/tactics) satisfying drivers. 5. Instantiate elements, allocate responsibilities, and define interfaces. 6. Sketch views and record design decisions. 7. Analyze current design and review goal achievement.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Which drivers are highest priority for this iteration? What patterns or tactics address these drivers? What responsibilities does each instantiated element hold? What interfaces are required?
Minimal Realistic Example: In Iteration 1 for a web app, select 'High Availability' driver, choose 'Active Redundancy' pattern, instantiate primary and backup server elements, assign failover responsibilities, and sketch C&C view.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Verification against selected drivers using lightweight architecture analysis, tactics questionnaires, or prototyping.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Big Design Up Front (BDUF); designing without explicit quality attribute drivers; failing to record design decisions and rationale.
When NOT to Use: Trivial systems where standard reference architectures can be directly instantiated without adaptation or trade-offs.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Domain-Driven Design (DDD), Rational Unified Process (RUP) architecture design, Agile Spikes.
Supported Decisions: Structural decisions, technology stack selection, pattern and tactic adoption, interface specifications.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can analyze ASRs to recommend candidate design patterns/tactics and draft structural views. Human architects must review and approve final design trade-offs.

Problem Solved: Uncovers architectural risks, sensitivity points, and tradeoff points that threaten business goals before system deployment.
Input Artifacts: Architecture documentation, business goals presentation, quality attribute requirements.
Output Artifacts: ATAM evaluation report containing identified risks, non-risks, sensitivity points, tradeoff points, risk themes, and refined utility tree.
Participants & Roles: Evaluation Team (Leader, Scribe, Questioners), Project Decision Makers (Architect, Project Manager, Customer), Architecture Stakeholders (Developers, Testers, Users).
Prerequisites: Documented or presentable software architecture and available business/technical stakeholders.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Present ATAM. 2. Present business goals. 3. Present architecture. 4. Identify architectural approaches. 5. Generate quality attribute utility tree. 6. Analyze architectural approaches. 7. Brainstorm and prioritize scenarios with stakeholders. 8. Re-analyze architectural approaches against top brainstormed scenarios. 9. Present results and risk themes.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How does the architecture satisfy scenario X? Which architectural decisions affect this response? What is the impact if a component fails or load doubles?
Minimal Realistic Example: Analyzing a switch failover scenario reveals a risk: 'No backup data channel exists', exposing a tradeoff between hardware cost reduction and 0.999999 availability.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Traceability of risks to business goals, agreement among stakeholders on prioritized scenarios, clear justification of sensitivity and tradeoff points.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Evaluating without an architect present; treating evaluation as an adversarial audit; failing to convert discovered risks into actionable remediation plans.
When NOT to Use: Very early stages before any candidate architecture exists, or on small, low-risk systems where evaluation cost exceeds system risk exposure.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Lightweight Architecture Evaluation (LAE), Tactics-based Questionnaires, Peer Reviews.
Supported Decisions: Architecture acceptance, risk mitigation planning, refactoring priorities, resource reallocation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can pre-screen architecture documentation using tactics-based rules to detect potential risks and sensitivity points prior to the workshop. Human facilitation remains necessary for stakeholder consensus.

Problem Solved: Provides a low-cost, fast-turnaround peer review mechanism to detect architectural risks during iterative development.
Input Artifacts: Current architecture sketches/documentation, updated utility tree, recent design changes.
Output Artifacts: List of discovered architectural risks, non-risks, sensitivities, and trade-offs.
Participants & Roles: Lead Architect (Facilitator), Peer Developers, Testers, Internal Technical Stakeholders.
Prerequisites: Existing architectural baseline and familiarity of participants with system context.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Review business goals. 2. Review architecture changes. 3. Review/update quality attribute utility tree. 4. Brainstorm/select high-priority scenarios. 5. Analyze architectural approaches against scenarios. 6. Capture risks, non-risks, and action items.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What architectural changes were made in the recent iteration? Do these changes introduce risks for our top quality attribute scenarios?
Minimal Realistic Example: A 2-hour peer review analyzes a new database caching layer and identifies a risk regarding stale data during concurrent writes.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Peer consensus on identified risks and agreement on remediation actions for high-priority drivers.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Superficial review without probing design decisions; cognitive bias/groupthink due to lack of external perspective.
When NOT to Use: High-risk, mission-critical systems requiring formal external validation, or initial architecture reviews of complex systems.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: ATAM, Tactics-Based Questionnaires, Code Reviews.
Supported Decisions: Iteration sign-off, refactoring identification, local design adjustments.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic systems can automatically track architecture modifications between iterations and generate targeted evaluation prompts for the peer review team.

Problem Solved: Rapidly identifies missing architectural mechanisms and design risks for a specific quality attribute.
Input Artifacts: Architecture design, code base locations, quality attribute specific tactics questionnaire.
Output Artifacts: Completed tactics questionnaire documenting support status (Y/N), design locations, risk levels (H/M/L), and rationale.
Participants & Roles: Software Architect, Technical Reviewer / Analyst.
Prerequisites: Knowledge of system design decisions related to the target quality attribute.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select a quality attribute tactics questionnaire. 2. For each tactic question, determine if supported (Y/N). 3. If Yes, record design decisions and location in code/design. 4. Rate implementation risk (H/M/L). 5. Document rationale and assumptions for using or omitting the tactic.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Does the system use ping/echo to detect failure? Does the system support data encryption in transit and at rest? Does the system use heartbeat messages?
Minimal Realistic Example: Asking 'Does the system encrypt data in transit?' reveals that data is XOR'ed rather than encrypted using standard algorithms, highlighting a high-risk security vulnerability.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Complete coverage of all tactics in the questionnaire; explicit documentation of locations in code/artifacts for supported tactics.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Answering 'Yes' without verifying physical realization in code; treating omitted tactics automatically as defects without considering rationale.
When NOT to Use: When holistic trade-off analysis across multiple competing quality attributes is required simultaneously.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: ATAM, Lightweight Architecture Evaluation, Static Code Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Selection of specific architectural tactics, identification of technical debt, security/availability auditing.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLM agents can scan code repositories and architecture documentation to auto-fill draft answers for tactics questionnaires, flagging unverified tactic implementations for human review.

Method Name: Architecture Debt Analysis via Hotspot Discovery
Problem Solved: Identifies, quantifies, and calculates the ROI for refactoring architectural debt caused by design anti-patterns and high maintenance churn.
Input Artifacts: Source code repository, version control revision history (commits/churn), issue tracking database (bugs/tickets).
Output Artifacts: Design Structure Matrix (DSM), identified architectural anti-patterns/hotspots, quantified debt cost (person-months), refactoring ROI business case.
Participants & Roles: Software Architect, Maintenance Leads, Software Engineering Manager.
Prerequisites: Access to source code, commit history, and issue tracking history spanning a sufficient operational period.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Extract static structural dependencies from source code. 2. Extract evolutionary co-change dependencies from revision history. 3. Build combined Design Structure Matrix (DSM). 4. Scan DSM for architecture anti-patterns (Cliques, Unhealthy Inheritance, Modularity Violations, Crossing, Unstable Interfaces). 5. Overlay bug/churn data from issue tracker onto identified hotspots. 6. Calculate refactoring effort vs. maintenance savings (ROI).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Which files change together frequently despite having no structural link? Are there cyclic dependencies among components? Which modules generate the highest proportion of defects?
Minimal Realistic Example: Identifying an Unhealthy Inheritance anti-pattern between SSTable and SSTableReader with 68 co-commits; refactoring costs 14 person-months but saves 41 person-months annually.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Hotspot identification validated by architect agreement; quantitative ROI calculation demonstrating positive financial payback for refactoring.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Focusing purely on static code metrics (e.g., LOC, cyclomatic complexity) while ignoring evolutionary co-change and defect history.
When NOT to Use: New greenfield projects without sufficient commit or issue history.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Code Refactoring Inspections, Static Code Analysis (e.g., SonarQube), Architecture Reconstruction.
