Supported Decisions: Refactoring prioritization, technical debt payoff justification, maintenance budget allocation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Fully automatable pipeline where agentic scripts mine Git/Jira, build DSMs, flag anti-pattern hotspots, and generate refactoring ROI reports for architect approval.

Problem Solved: Reduces functional ambiguity, goal misalignment, unhandled exception/failure modes, scope creep, and communication barriers between technical teams, business stakeholders, and users.
Input Artifacts: Vision Statement, In/Out List, Actor Profile Table, System Architecture/Scope Drawings, Usage Narratives, Stakeholder Request/Interviews
Output Artifacts: Actor-Goal List, Fully Dressed Use Case Specification, Casual Use Case, Use Case Briefs, Test Scenario Outlines, Requirements Matrix (Hub-and-Spoke)
Participants & Roles: Primary Actor, Supporting/Secondary Actors, Offstage Stakeholders, Business Analyst / Use Case Author, Subject Matter Expert (SME), Developer / Architect, Tester / QA, Sponsor / Executive
Prerequisites: Defined System Scope (System Under Discussion), identified Primary Actors, identified Offstage Stakeholders and their key Interests, and agreed-upon writing standards/level of formality.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Establish system boundaries using an In/Out List and Design Scope diagram. 2. Brainstorm and list all primary actors over the life of the system. 3. Brainstorm and exhaustively list user goals for each primary actor (Actor-Goal List). 4. Capture outermost summary-level use cases to set operational context. 5. Select a user-goal level use case to expand. 6. Identify stakeholders, interests, preconditions, and guarantees (minimal and success). 7. Write the Main Success Scenario (MSS) in 3 to 9 simple, action-oriented steps. 8. Brainstorm and exhaustively list failure and alternate extension conditions. 9. Write extension-handling steps detailing system recovery, fallback, or goal failure. 10. Extract complex subgoals into sub-use cases or merge trivial steps as needed.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Can the primary actor go away happy after having done this?" (Coffee break test) "Does your job performance depend on how many of these you do today?" "Why is the actor doing this?" (To raise goal level) "How is this goal accomplished?" (To lower goal level) "What would make this stakeholder unhappy at the end of a successful run?" (To find success guarantees) "What does the system detect when something goes wrong?" "What is the human backup to system failure?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Use Case: Buy Stocks over the Web Primary Actor: Purchaser Scope: Personal Advisors / Finance package (PAF) Level: User Goal Precondition: User has PAF open. MSS: 1. Purchaser selects to buy stocks over the web. 2. PAF gets name of web site to use from user. 3. PAF opens web connection to site. 4. Purchaser buys stock from web site. 5. PAF intercepts response and updates portfolio. 6. PAF shows new portfolio standing. Extensions: 3a. Web failure during setup: System reports failure, backs up to step 2.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Pass/Fail checklist against template fields: Active-verb goal title, black-box view of SuD, 3 to 9 MSS steps, clear actor intent without UI/GUI mechanics ('Who has the ball?'), complete coverage of detectable extension conditions, validation by stakeholder walkthrough and test-case derivation.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Including UI mechanics (clicks, screen layouts) instead of user intent ('Too much UI'); missing system actions or missing primary actor actions; writing underwater/indigo subfunctions as standalone specs ('Fleas on fleas'); writing 'checks whether' instead of 'validates'; assuming unverified preconditions; missing failure recovery logic.
When NOT to Use: Small/zero-risk feature tweaks, purely algorithmic/mathematical processing (e.g., matrix calculations, compiler passes, batch data transformation without interactive logic), or when stakeholder communication is real-time/colocated with no requirement for durable specifications (e.g., raw XP user stories on index cards).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary Prior: Vision Statement, Usage Narratives, In/Out List, Domain Data Model. Complementary Subsequent: UI Design / Wireframes, Test Case Design, CRC Cards / Responsibility-Driven Design. Alternatives: User Stories (XP), Feature Lists, State Transition Diagrams, Activity Diagrams / BPMN.
Supported Decisions: Scope inclusion/exclusion, release staging/prioritization, architecture/subsystem allocation, acceptance testing criteria, project effort estimation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Roles: Agentic AI as Primary Actor (autonomous caller) or Supporting Actor (external intelligence/llm service). Inputs: Structured JSON payloads or semantic prompts replacing free-form textual inputs. Guardrails: Deterministic verification steps (validation gates) explicitly added to handle LLM non-determinism or timeout/hallucination failures in extension steps. Human-in-the-loop: Escalation extension conditions where AI confidence drops below a threshold, routing execution to a human operator. Audit Trail: System logs must capture agent decisions, prompt context, and token outputs for compliance and rollback.

Problem Solved: Defines testable conditions to judge whether a solution is acceptable to stakeholders and provides a framework to compare and rank multiple alternative solutions or designs objectively.
BA Lifecycle Phase: analysis / specification / prioritisation / validation / change management
Input Artifacts: Requirements (specified and modelled), design options, business needs, contractual obligations.
Output Artifacts: Acceptance criteria (pass/fail statements), evaluation criteria (measurable parameters and scoring matrices), test plans/cases.
Participants & Roles: Sponsor, business owner, SME, end user, BA, developer, tester, compliance/legal.
Prerequisites: Agreed value attributes and stakeholder consensus on success measures/constraints.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify value attributes relevant to stakeholders (cost, usability, performance, etc.). 2. Formulate acceptance criteria as pass/fail conditions for a single solution. 3. Formulate evaluation criteria with continuous/discrete measurement scales for multiple solutions. 4. Design assessment tools, instructions, and scoring metrics. 5. Conduct evaluation or testing (e.g., UAT) against the defined criteria. 6. Record and process results to determine acceptance or rank solutions.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What are the minimum conditions under which this solution is acceptable?", "How will we measure whether value attribute X is met?", "Which criteria take precedence when comparing trade-offs between options?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Evaluating two vendor CRM systems where acceptance requires 99.9% uptime (pass/fail) and evaluation ranks them on usability (1-5 scale) and implementation cost.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Criteria must be atomic, testable (true/false or measurable on a clear scale), unambiguous, and agreed upon by key stakeholders.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Defining untestable or vague criteria (e.g., 'system must be fast'); locking in rigid contractual criteria that cannot adapt to change.
When NOT to Use: When requirements are highly exploratory, stakeholders cannot agree on value metrics, or formal acceptance is unnecessary for low-risk changes.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Prototyping, Decision Analysis, User Stories (Acceptance Criteria), and Metric/KPI definitions.
Supported Decisions: Acceptance (sign-off) of a delivered solution, selection among vendor/design options, release readiness.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: An AI agent can automatically convert user story statements into testable Gherkin-style acceptance criteria, run automated verification against designs, and prompt human-in-the-loop sign-off for policy compliance.

Problem Solved: Manages overload when work items exceed team capacity, reducing uncertainty about delivery order and ensuring high-value items are addressed first.
Input Artifacts: User stories, use cases, change requests, defects, risk items, business needs, iteration plans.
Output Artifacts: Prioritized backlog, refined user story descriptions, release plans, estimates.
Participants & Roles: Product Manager / Product Owner, BA, Sponsor, Developer, Tester, Customer.
Prerequisites: A defined product vision, authorization mechanism for adding items, and capacity for periodic reviews.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Capture work items (stories, defects, tasks) in the backlog repository. 2. Review items periodically with stakeholders to assess relevance and business value. 3. Re-prioritize backlog items relative to each other based on shifting needs and dependencies. 4. Elaborate and estimate high-priority items near the top of the backlog in detail. 5. Select top items for implementation based on team capacity. 6. Remove completed or obsolete items from the backlog.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Which items deliver the highest immediate business value?", "What dependencies block this backlog item?", "Has the priority of item X changed since the last review?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A software team maintains 50 feature requests in Jira; top 5 items are fully detailed for the next 2-week sprint while bottom items remain high-level summary notes.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Top backlog items are detailed and estimated; relative ordering reflects current business value and stakeholder priorities.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Allowing the backlog to grow unmanaged into thousands of obsolete items; fully elaborating low-priority items prematurely.
When NOT to Use: In strict predictive Waterfall initiatives where full up-front scope freeze is mandatory, or when there is no dedicated role/capacity to maintain the queue.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Prioritization, User Stories, Relative Estimation, Story Mapping, and Kanban.
Supported Decisions: Scope selection for iterations/releases, priority of enhancements vs. bug fixes, resource allocation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can analyze user usage data and defect reports to suggest backlog item priorities, auto-deconstruct high-level epics into user stories, and track velocity while requiring Product Owner human approval for final ordering.

Problem Solved: Mitigates narrow financial focus by balancing performance evaluation across four perspective dimensions: Financial, Customer, Business Process, and Learning & Growth.
Input Artifacts: Enterprise vision, strategic plans, business goals and objectives, operational performance metrics.
Output Artifacts: Balanced Scorecard matrix/dashboard, strategy map, target KPIs, performance reports.
Participants & Roles: Executive Sponsor, Business Owner, BA, Product Manager, Operational Support.
Prerequisites: A clearly articulated organizational vision and strategic plan.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Translate vision and strategy into tangible strategic objectives. 2. Categorize objectives across 4 dimensions: Financial, Customer, Internal Business Process, Learning & Growth. 3. Define leading and lagging measures (KPIs) for each objective. 4. Establish baseline values and target metrics for specified timeframes. 5. Define strategic initiatives to achieve the target outcomes. 6. Continuously monitor progress and adapt strategy as needed.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "To succeed financially, how should we appear to shareholders?", "To achieve our vision, how should we appear to our customers?", "What business processes must we excel at?", "How will we sustain our ability to change and improve?"
Minimal Realistic Example: An e-commerce firm sets target KPIs: Financial (+15% ROI), Customer (90% satisfaction score), Process (order fulfillment < 24 hrs), Learning (100% staff trained on new platform).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Measures are quantitative, explicitly linked to enterprise strategy, balanced between leading/lagging indicators, and clearly communicated.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Treating the scorecard as a static reporting tool rather than an active strategic management framework; lacking a clear strategy to align the four dimensions.
When NOT to Use: For small, isolated tactical projects where organizational strategic alignment is not relevant or where no overarching business strategy exists.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by SWOT Analysis, Benchmarking, Metrics & KPIs, and Business Model Canvas.
Supported Decisions: Strategic investment decisions, project portfolio prioritization, organizational alignment, operational change strategy.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic systems can ingest operational data logs to dynamically calculate leading indicators, detect cross-dimensional performance variances, and simulate strategy adjustments with human executive sign-off.

Problem Solved: Reduces uncertainty about competitive standing, market trends, and organizational efficiency gaps by comparing internal performance against external baselines or market demands.
Input Artifacts: Existing process metrics, published industry benchmarks, competitor reports, RFI responses, market research data.
Output Artifacts: Gap analysis report, market research summary, best practice recommendations, RFI evaluation.
Participants & Roles: Sponsor, Business Owner, BA, Domain SME, Marketing/Strategy Lead.
Prerequisites: Clear definition of internal operational focus areas and access to reliable market/competitor data sources.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify specific operational processes or market questions to evaluate. 2. Identify industry leaders, competitors, or best-in-class standard baselines. 3. Collect data via surveys, RFIs, market research, or site visits. 4. Analyze gaps between internal performance and external best practices/customer expectations. 5. Identify market trends, customer segment preferences, and competitor strengths/weaknesses. 6. Develop proposals or strategy adjustments based on findings.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Who are the leaders in our industry and what practices make them successful?", "What features do competitors offer that we lack?", "What are the emerging market trends and customer buying preferences?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A retail bank conducts a benchmark study on customer onboarding time against top 3 fintech competitors, discovering an average 3-day gap, which drives a digital transformation initiative.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Data sources must be credible and recent; market segments must be properly differentiated to avoid misleading comparisons.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Copying competitor practices blindly without accounting for internal context; spending excessive time/budget on research without actionable outcomes.
When NOT to Use: When seeking novel, ground-breaking innovations (benchmarking only reproduces existing practices), or when fast action is required on immediate hypotheses without market research budget.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by SWOT Analysis, Competitive Analysis, Focus Groups, and Survey/Questionnaire.
Supported Decisions: Market entry/exit decisions, capability investment priorities, solution selection, change strategy definition.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLM agents can scrape and analyze web data, competitor offerings, and industry reports to generate automated market summaries and gap matrices, flagged for analyst review.

Problem Solved: Mitigates creative blocks and limited perspectives by producing a broad, non-judgmental set of ideas and options for problem solving or feature generation.
Input Artifacts: Problem statement, area of interest definition, evaluation criteria.
Output Artifacts: Categorized and rated idea list, action item list, mind map/affinity diagram.
Participants & Roles: Facilitator, Scribe, BA, Sponsor, SME, End User, Developer, Tester (6–8 participants recommended).
Prerequisites: A clearly defined topic or problem statement and pre-agreed evaluation criteria.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Develop a concise definition of the area of interest and establish time limits. 2. Select participants representing diverse backgrounds and set ground rules (no criticism during generation). 3. Conduct session: share and visibly record ideas rapidly without discussion or judgment. 4. Encourage participants to build on and combine each other's ideas. 5. Wrap up: review, discuss, and evaluate ideas against criteria. 6. Consolidate, eliminate duplicates, rate ideas, and distribute final list.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What options are available to resolve this issue?", "What factors are constraining us?", "What crazy or exaggerated ideas might spark a practical solution?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A 30-minute cross-functional workshop generates 45 ideas to reduce customer checkout drop-offs, which are then grouped and rated to select the top 3 for prototyping.
Quality Criteria & Verification: High volume of diverse ideas generated; non-judgmental atmosphere maintained during generation; clean rated output produced.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Debating or criticizing ideas during the generation phase; dominance by vocal participants suppressing reserved team members.
When NOT to Use: When technical constraints demand a strict deterministic outcome, or when organizational politics prohibit open expression.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Alternatives include Mind Mapping, Collaborative Games, Focus Groups, and Focus Group/Surveys.
Supported Decisions: Solution option selection, risk identification, change strategy approach.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can act as virtual participants in brainstorming sessions, generating 20+ divergent ideas instantly based on prompt criteria, which human facilitators then refine.

Problem Solved: Reduces organizational misalignment and duplication by defining what an enterprise can do independent of how it is executed or structured.
Input Artifacts: Enterprise strategy, organizational models, business goals, current state description.
Output Artifacts: Capability Map, performance gap assessment, risk model, product/release roadmap.
Participants & Roles: Executive Sponsor, Business Owner, BA, Enterprise/Business Architect, SME.
Prerequisites: Executive consensus to collaborate on a holistic enterprise model.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify and name the business capabilities required to fulfill business goals (what the business does). 2. Organize capabilities into a hierarchical Capability Map (categorized by strategic, core, supporting). 3. Assess target performance expectations against current performance to find performance gaps. 4. Evaluate business, technology, and market risks associated with capability performance. 5. Associate business value/outcomes with each capability. 6. Prioritize capability gaps to guide investment and release roadmaps.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What core capabilities does the organization need to deliver its value proposition?", "Where are the biggest performance gaps in our capabilities?", "Which capabilities are redundant across business units?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A retail company maps its 'Order Fulfillment' capability, identifying a 'High Performance Gap' in 'Same-Day Delivery' that justifies funding a new logistics application.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Each capability appears only once on the map; capabilities describe 'what' not 'how'; cross-functional agreement achieved on gaps.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confusing capabilities with business processes or organizational structures; creating capability models in a silo without stakeholder buy-in.
When NOT to Use: For micro-level bug fixes or minor tactical changes where enterprise-level alignment offers no value.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Functional Decomposition, Value Stream Mapping, Business Model Canvas, and Process Architecture.
Supported Decisions: Strategic investment allocation, IT portfolio prioritization, M&A integration scope, release planning.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic systems can process enterprise documentation to propose initial capability hierarchies and flag overlapping capability descriptions across business units for architect review.

Problem Solved: Reduces financial and strategic uncertainty by providing a formal justification for investing resources in a proposed solution compared to alternative options or doing nothing.
Input Artifacts: Business need, current state description, solution options, cost-benefit estimates, risk analysis.
Output Artifacts: Business Case document/presentation (containing need assessment, desired outcomes, alternative analysis, and recommended solution).
Participants & Roles: Sponsor, Business Owner, BA, Project Manager, Financial Analyst, Domain SME.
Prerequisites: Clearly defined business problem/opportunity and preliminary estimation of costs/benefits.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define the core business need and align it with strategic objectives. 2. Detail desired measurable outcomes independent of the specific solution. 3. Identify and assess solution alternatives (including scope, feasibility, risks, and financial ROI/NPV). 4. Evaluate the 'Do Nothing' option as a baseline. 5. Select and justify the recommended solution with cost and timeline estimates. 6. Present to decision makers for approval and funding.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What business problem are we solving?", "What are the quantifiable financial and non-financial benefits?", "What is the cost and risk of doing nothing?", "What is the ROI and payback period?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A business case demonstrates that spending $200k on automated invoice processing will save $100k/year in labor, breaking even in 2 years with a net positive NPV.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Clear linkage to strategy; realistic and verifiable financial assumptions; objective assessment of risks and alternatives.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Author bias exaggerating benefits and underestimating costs; failing to update the business case after funding is approved.
When NOT to Use: For small, mandatory low-cost changes (e.g., urgent regulatory patch) where the cost of writing the business case exceeds the change cost.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Financial Analysis, Decision Analysis, Feasibility Study, and SWOT Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Project funding/approval, solution alternative selection, go/no-go change strategy decisions.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can pull cost data and historical project metrics to draft financial models and risk sections, leaving strategic justification and approval to human executives.

Problem Solved: Reduces strategic misalignment by mapping on a single page how an enterprise creates, delivers, and captures value across operational, financial, and customer dimensions.
Input Artifacts: Organizational strategy, market analysis, current state description, value proposition ideas.
Output Artifacts: Business Model Canvas (9 building blocks), diagnostic assessment, target business model blueprint.
Participants & Roles: Sponsor, Executive/Business Owner, BA, Product Manager, Domain SME.
Prerequisites: High-level understanding of the enterprise's current or proposed offering and customer base.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define the 9 building blocks: Customer Segments, Value Propositions, Channels, Customer Relationships, Revenue Streams, Key Resources, Key Activities, Key Partnerships, and Cost Structure. 2. Map the current state ('as-is') canvas to diagnose resource allocation and value flow. 3. Identify pain points, gaps, or strategic opportunities across the building blocks. 4. Design future state ('to-be') canvas options. 5. Evaluate inter-dependencies (e.g., how key activities support the value proposition). 6. Use the canvas to guide project portfolio mapping and change strategy.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What value do we deliver to the customer?", "Which customer segments are we serving?", "What are our key revenue streams and cost drivers?", "What key activities drive value creation?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A software startup drafts a canvas identifying 'Small Businesses' as Customer Segment, 'Cloud Accounting' as Value Proposition, 'Subscription' as Revenue Stream, and 'AWS Infrastructure' as Key Resource.
Quality Criteria & Verification: All 9 building blocks are completed and logically connected; clear alignment between Key Activities/Resources and Value Propositions.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Treating the canvas as a complete strategy tool while ignoring broader environmental factors; focusing solely on product features instead of holistic value creation.
When NOT to Use: For micro-level technical tasks or isolated software feature specs with no impact on the overall business model.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by SWOT Analysis, Balanced Scorecard, Value Stream Mapping, and Business Capability Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Strategic pivot decisions, target operating model selection, product-market fit evaluation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can auto-populate a draft canvas for competitors or new product concepts by analyzing market data and filing reports, providing an instant baseline for human review.

Problem Solved: Reduces ambiguity and operational inconsistency by identifying, expressing, and managing actionable, testable business directives separately from processes and technology.
Input Artifacts: Business policies, regulations, contracts, subject matter expertise, current process models.
Output Artifacts: Business rules catalog/repository, definitional and behavioral rules statements, decision tables/trees.
Participants & Roles: BA, Domain SME, Business Owner, Compliance/Legal, Developer, Tester.
Prerequisites: Established business glossary and vocabulary relevant to the domain.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Elicit business policies and directives from documentation or SMEs. 2. Distinguish definitional rules (knowledge/inferences) from behavioral rules (governing conduct). 3. Express rules at an atomic level using standard, business-friendly terminology. 4. Specify enforcement levels for behavioral rules (e.g., strictly enforced, override with explanation). 5. Map rules to the business decisions and processes they constrain or enable. 6. Validate rules for consistency, completeness, and non-contradiction in a repository.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What rule determines whether a customer is eligible for discount X?", "Is this directive a definitional fact or a behavioral constraint?", "What is the consequence/enforcement if this rule is violated?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Definitional rule: 'A customer placing >10 orders/month is a Preferred Customer.' Behavioral rule: 'Orders over $1,000 must not be placed without manager override.'
Quality Criteria & Verification: Rules are atomic, practicable (no further interpretation needed), declarative, single-sourced, and free from implementation logic.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Embedding business rules directly into process flow diagrams or code; creating long lists of ambiguous, contradictory rules.
When NOT to Use: When business operations are completely ad-hoc and non-repeatable, or when procedural workflow matters more than decision logic.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Concept Modelling, Decision Modelling, Decision Analysis, Data Dictionary, and Glossary.
Supported Decisions: Operational business decisions, compliance verification, business process logic execution.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agents can parse regulatory documents to extract candidate declarative rules, run cross-validation checks for rule conflicts, and feed verified rules into automated Business Rules Management Systems (BRMS).

Problem Solved: Reduces stakeholder communication barriers, hidden assumptions, and reserved participation by using structured game play to foster collaboration and creative insight.
Input Artifacts: Elicitation topic/problem statement, game rules, physical/virtual collaboration tools (sticky notes, boards).
Output Artifacts: Group-generated feature lists, affinity maps, visual product boxes, identified hidden assumptions.
Participants & Roles: Facilitator (neutral), BA, Stakeholders, SMEs, End Users, Developers.
Prerequisites: Clear objective for the game session and a comfortable, safe collaborative environment.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select an appropriate game (e.g., Product Box, Affinity Map, Fishbowl) matching the objective. 2. Explain the purpose and process/rules of the game to participants. 3. Opening step: engage participants and begin rapid idea generation. 4. Exploration step: engage participants in testing, connecting, and experimenting with ideas. 5. Closing step: evaluate, synthesize, and prioritize the ideas generated. 6. Record and document the outcomes for follow-up decision making.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "If this product were sold in a retail store, what key features would be printed on its box?", "How do these features group together naturally?", "What assumptions are we making?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Participants design a physical 'Product Box' for an internal IT portal, revealing that 'Instant Chat Support' is considered the top selling feature by end users.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Active participation across reserved and vocal team members; clear identification of shared themes and hidden perspectives.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Perceiving games as silly/unproductive due to poor framing; failing to synthesize game results into actionable business analysis artifacts.
When NOT to Use: In rigid, highly formal corporate cultures hostile to game play, or when quick deterministic technical decisions are needed.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Alternatives include Brainstorming, Focus Groups, Workshops, and Mind Mapping.
Supported Decisions: Product feature scoping, assumption validation, team consensus building.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Virtual collaboration boards driven by AI can auto-cluster sticky notes during affinity mapping games and sentiment-analyze participant discussions in real time.

Problem Solved: Reduces semantic ambiguity and vocabulary conflicts across stakeholders by organizing core domain terms and their structural connections independently of technical data design.
Input Artifacts: Glossary terms, domain SME input, regulatory texts, core business concepts.
Output Artifacts: Concept Model diagram/text (noun concepts, verb concepts, categorizations, roles).
Participants & Roles: BA, Domain SME, Business Architect, Compliance/Legal.
Prerequisites: Initial business glossary and commitment to design-independent semantic precision.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify core noun concepts (givens of the domain space). 2. Identify verb concepts connecting noun concepts to form basic structural statements. 3. Add categorizations, classifications, and roles to capture rich semantic meaning. 4. Define concepts cleanly without implementation or data-design biases. 5. Render the concept model graphically or textually. 6. Validate the model with business SMEs to ensure exact, unambiguous business language.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What are the core 'things' in this domain?", "How does noun A relate to noun B in natural business language?", "Is term X identical to term Y or is there a subtle distinction?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A concept model defines 'Member', 'Policy', and 'Claim', linking them via verb concepts: 'Member holds Policy', 'Claim is filed against Policy'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Model is free of technical database artifacts (foreign keys, physical types), rich in business semantics, and validated by SMEs.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confusing concept models with physical database ERDs; using overly technical terminology that alienates business stakeholders.
When NOT to Use: For simple systems with universally understood, non-complex terminology, or where data design normalization is the immediate goal.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Alternatives/Complements include Glossary, Data Dictionary, Data Modelling, and Business Rules Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Business terminology standardization, complex decision logic definition, compliance alignment.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLM agents can analyze domain documentation to automatically discover noun/verb concept triples and propose candidate concept maps for domain expert validation.

Problem Solved: Reduces data inconsistency and misinterpretation across solutions and stakeholders by standardizing definitions, primitive elements, and composite structures.
Input Artifacts: Elicitation results, source system data specs, domain terminology, Data Models.
Output Artifacts: Data Dictionary / Metadata Repository (defining primitive elements and composite structures).
Participants & Roles: BA, Data Analyst/Architect, Developer, SME.
Prerequisites: Identification of data elements requiring standardization across solutions.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify target data elements (primitive and composite). 2. For primitive elements, document Name, Aliases, Description, and allowable Values/Meanings. 3. For composite elements, define structural compositions (sequences, repetitions, optional elements). 4. Validate definitions with domain SMEs and data stewards. 5. Store definitions in a centralized metadata repository or spreadsheet. 6. Maintain the dictionary continuously throughout the solution life cycle.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What is the exact definition and format of data element X?", "What are the allowed values for field Y?", "How is composite structure Z constructed from primitive fields?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Data Dictionary defines 'Customer Name' = First Name (min 2 chars) + Middle Name (optional) + Last Name (min 2 chars).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Definitions are complete, clear, consistent across systems, and actively maintained by designated stewards.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Failing to maintain the dictionary over time, leading to obsolete metadata; documenting fields in isolation without considering enterprise reuse.
When NOT to Use: On small, single-use scripts or throw-away prototypes where formal data stewardship adds unnecessary overhead.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Glossary, Data Modelling, Concept Modelling, and Business Rules Analysis.
Supported Decisions: System integration design, data migration scope, compliance/data governance enforcement.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agents can scan database schemas and sample datasets to auto-generate baseline data dictionaries including inferred data types, nullability, and field formats.

Problem Solved: Reduces functional and data boundary ambiguity by visually portraying how data is transformed by processes, stored, and exchanged with external entities.
Input Artifacts: Elicitation results, existing process documentation, system interfaces, Data Dictionary.
Output Artifacts: Context Diagram (Level 0), Level 1+ Data Flow Diagrams (Gane-Sarson or Yourdon notation).
Participants & Roles: BA, Systems Analyst, Developer, SME, Operational Support.
Prerequisites: Understanding of system boundaries, inputs, outputs, and external actors.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify externals (entities/sources/sinks) outside the system. 2. Create a Context Diagram (Level 0) depicting the system as a single process with external data flows. 3. Decompose into Level 1 diagram showing major processes, data stores, and data flows. 4. Further decompose complex processes into Level 2+ diagrams as needed. 5. Ensure all data flows connect to/from a process and are labelled with nouns. 6. Verify diagram consistency against data dictionaries and process models.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Where does input data X originate?", "What transformation process modifies data X into output Y?", "Where is data stored for future use?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A Level 1 DFD shows 'Customer' sending 'Order Data' to process '1.0 Validate Order', which checks 'Customer DB' data store and outputs 'Valid Order' to '2.0 Process Payment'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Diagrams follow strict notation rules (no flow directly between two stores or two externals); inputs and outputs balance across levels.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Including sequence/timing logic in DFDs (confusing DFD with flowchart); over-complicating diagrams with too many levels.
When NOT to Use: When the sequence of activities or timing/workflow control is the primary focus of analysis (use Process Modelling instead).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Alternatives/Complements include Process Modelling, Use Cases, Interface Analysis, and Sequence Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: System boundary definition, data architecture design, scope allocation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can parse process specifications or user stories to construct draft DFDs, verifying data conservation (balancing inputs and outputs) automatically.

Problem Solved: Reduces decision uncertainty by extracting hidden patterns, correlations, and predictive insights from large datasets.
Input Artifacts: Large transactional datasets, historical logs, decision models, business objectives.
Output Artifacts: Data mining models (descriptive, diagnostic, predictive), scorecards, discovered business rules, dashboards.
Participants & Roles: BA, Data Analyst/Scientist, Business Owner, SME, IT/Database Admin.
Prerequisites: Access to high-volume, high-quality data and clear decision requirements or pattern discovery goals.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Establish goals/scope (top-down decision-driven or bottom-up pattern discovery). 2. Prepare analytical dataset by merging, cleaning, and partitioning data (training, testing, validation sets). 3. Analyze data distributions, missing values, and calculated characteristics. 4. Apply modelling techniques (decision trees, regression, clustering, neural networks). 5. Validate model accuracy on independent test datasets. 6. Deploy model as visual reports, mathematical formulas, or executable business rules.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What historical patterns predict customer churn?", "Why does this performance variance exist?", "Which data fields offer the highest predictive value for fraud detection?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A telecom firm mines 2 years of customer usage logs using decision trees, discovering that customers with >3 support calls and falling data usage have an 80% probability of churning.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Model replicates successfully on independent validation data; insights are actionable and deployable within decision processes.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Applying data mining without understanding the business decision context; assuming correlation implies causation.
When NOT to Use: When available dataset volume or quality is inadequate, or when business decision logic is simple and fully known.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Decision Modelling, Business Rules Analysis, Metrics & KPIs, and Root Cause Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Automated operational decisions (credit scoring, fraud detection), marketing strategy, customer segmentation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic AI natively executes end-to-end data mining (data cleaning, feature engineering, AutoML model selection), outputting natural language insight summaries for analysts.

Problem Solved: Reduces software and system design errors by defining the logical and physical data structures, attributes, and entity relationships required by a domain.
Input Artifacts: Elicitation results, Concept Models, Data Dictionary, business rules, legacy database schemas.
Output Artifacts: Entity-Relationship Diagrams (ERD) or UML Class Diagrams (Conceptual, Logical, Physical), object diagrams, metadata definitions.
Participants & Roles: BA, Data Architect/Modeller, Developer, SME, Database Admin.
Prerequisites: Understanding of business domain entities, relationships, and attributes.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify core entities/classes (things about which data is kept). 2. Define attributes for each entity and specify unique primary identifiers. 3. Establish relationships/associations between entities. 4. Define cardinality/multiplicity (minimum and maximum occurrences, e.g., 0, 1, many). 5. Apply normalization rules for logical data models. 6. Validate model completeness with business SMEs and technical developers.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What data must we store about entity X?", "How many occurrences of entity B can relate to one instance of entity A?", "Is attribute Y dependent solely on the primary key?"
Minimal Realistic Example: An ERD models 'Customer' (1) to 'Order' (0..*) relationship, where each Order must have exactly 1 Customer, and an Order contains multiple 'Order Items'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Model accurately reflects business rules; logical model is normalized; entities and relationships are clearly named and documented.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Creating overly complex physical models prematurely during business analysis; violating normalization rules leading to data redundancies.
When NOT to Use: When analyzing purely procedural workflows with no persistent data requirements.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Concept Modelling, Data Dictionary, Glossary, Class Diagrams, and State Modelling.
Supported Decisions: Database architecture design, software system specification, application integration.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can convert text requirements or form specs into normalized logical ERDs, generating database DDL scripts while requesting human review of complex relationships.

Problem Solved: Reduces decision bias and uncertainty when evaluating complex, high-risk alternatives with conflicting objectives and multi-criteria outcomes.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Strategy / prioritisation / Solution Evaluation / change management
Input Artifacts: Problem statement, solution options, risk assessment results, evaluation criteria, financial estimates.
Output Artifacts: Simple/weighted decision matrices, decision trees, trade-off rankings, recommended action report.
Participants & Roles: Decision Maker, Sponsor, BA, SME, Project Manager.
Prerequisites: Clearly defined problem statement, list of alternatives, and pre-agreed evaluation criteria.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Clearly define the decision problem statement. 2. Identify all possible alternatives or courses of action. 3. Establish decision criteria and assign importance weightings. 4. Evaluate each alternative against criteria using decision matrices or decision trees. 5. Eliminate dominated alternatives and evaluate trade-offs. 6. Select the optimal alternative to implement and document rationale.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What are the key criteria governing this decision and their relative weights?", "What is the expected value of option A under uncertain condition X?", "Which alternative dominates the others?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A weighted decision matrix evaluates 3 ERP vendors across Cost (weight 5), Usability (weight 3), and Security (weight 4); Option 2 wins with a score of 40 vs 37 and 28.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Evaluation criteria are agreed upon up-front; trade-off calculations are transparent and reproducible; decision maker accepts remaining uncertainty.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Analysis paralysis by spending excessive effort on probabilistic modelling; forcing emotional decisions into a matrix to justify a preconceived choice.
When NOT to Use: When decisions must be made instantaneously in emergencies, or when information is too scarce to establish meaningful criteria.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Alternatives/Complements include Decision Modelling, Business Cases, Financial Analysis, and SWOT Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Vendor selection, design option selection, change strategy recommendations, risk treatment response.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agents can evaluate multi-attribute decision matrices automatically based on parsed vendor proposals, conducting sensitivity analysis to highlight key trade-off variables.

Problem Solved: Reduces process complexity and maintainability issues by extracting repeatable operational decision logic and business rules out of process flows into standalone models.
Input Artifacts: Business rules, process models, data elements, business knowledge sources.
Output Artifacts: Decision Tables, Decision Trees, Decision Requirements Diagrams (DRD).
Participants & Roles: BA, Business Rules Developer, Domain SME, Compliance Lead.
Prerequisites: Identification of discrete operational decision points within a process.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify discrete decision points within business processes. 2. Decompose complex decisions into input data, sub-decisions, and business knowledge models. 3. Create a Decision Requirements Diagram (DRD) linking decisions, inputs, and knowledge sources. 4. Represent atomic decision logic using Decision Tables or Decision Trees. 5. Ensure decision tables cover all input condition combinations without gaps or overlaps. 6. Link decision models to process models and business rules engines.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What decision is made at step X in the process?", "What input data is required to make this decision?", "What combination of rules leads to outcome Y?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A Decision Table evaluates 'Loan Amount' and 'Applicant Age': If Amount <= $1,000 and Age > 18 -> Outcome = 'Eligible'; If Age <= 18 -> Outcome = 'Ineligible'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Decision tables are complete (no missing condition rows) and consistent (no conflicting outcomes for identical inputs); standalone readability by business SMEs.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Mixing process flow logic with decision logic; capturing decision rules without standardizing underlying business terminology.
When NOT to Use: For one-off strategic decisions (use Decision Analysis instead) or simple processes with no conditional branching.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Business Rules Analysis, Process Modelling, Concept Modelling, and Data Dictionary.
Supported Decisions: Automated operational decisions (loan approval, pricing, claim validation, tax calculation).
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can convert decision requirements diagrams directly into DMN-compliant XML for automated execution, verifying table completeness programmatically.

Problem Solved: Reduces elicitation gap risks and subject matter expert availability bottlenecks by extracting business analysis background information, business rules, and current state specs from existing artifacts.
Input Artifacts: Existing documentation (policies, specs, user manuals, org charts, audit reports, regulations, contracts).
Output Artifacts: Document analysis chart, research notes, current state specs, confirmed elicitation inputs, identified information gaps.
Participants & Roles: BA, Domain SME (for clarification/validation).
Prerequisites: Access to relevant, credible, and current documentation assets.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify and procure candidate background documentation sources. 2. Evaluate sources for relevance, currency, credibility, and authenticity. 3. Review material systematically and record findings/notes in a document analysis chart. 4. Identify duplicate notes, conflicts between documents, and knowledge gaps. 5. Transform findings into visual models or structured requirements. 6. Validate findings and resolve discrepancies with domain SMEs.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What current state rules are documented in this manual?", "Is this system documentation still accurate?", "Where are the gaps between documented procedures and actual practices?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA reviews an outdated system user manual and training guide to extract 30 baseline business rules for a legacy billing system migration.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Findings are validated against current SME practices; source references are cited; conflicts between docs are highlighted and resolved.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Assuming outdated documentation represents actual current state without verification; getting mired in information overload without focused objectives.
When NOT to Use: When documentation is completely absent, or when defining entirely novel future state capabilities with no existing baseline.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Observation, Interviews, Data Mining, and Process Modelling.
Supported Decisions: Current state baseline definition, migration scope boundaries, gap analysis.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLMs excel at document analysis—scanning hundreds of PDF manuals to auto-extract business rules, interface parameters, and term definitions into structured tables in seconds.

Problem Solved: Reduces budget and timeline forecasting uncertainty by using structured, mathematical, or expert-driven techniques to predict cost, effort, and duration.
Input Artifacts: Work Breakdown Structure (WBS), user stories, scope models, historical project performance data.
Output Artifacts: Cost/effort estimates, confidence intervals (ROM or definitive ranges), estimation assumptions.
Participants & Roles: BA, Project Manager, Developer, Tester, Implementation SME, Estimator.
Prerequisites: Decomposed work scope (WBS or feature list) and agreed estimation method.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Decompose scope into estimable work elements (WBS or backlog). 2. Select estimation method (Top-down, Bottom-up, Parametric, PERT, Delphi, ROM, Rolling Wave). 3. Gather historical performance data and consult experts. 4. Compute estimates and establish confidence intervals (ranges, e.g., PERT = (O + 4M + P)/6). 5. Document all underlying assumptions, risks, and constraints. 6. Revisit and refine estimates continuously as work progresses and uncertainty drops.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What is the optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic effort for task X?", "What historical data do we have for similar work?", "What confidence interval applies to this ROM estimate?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Using PERT for a module design: Optimistic = 4 days, Most Likely = 6 days, Pessimistic = 14 days -> PERT Estimate = (4 + 24 + 14)/6 = 7 days.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Estimates express ranges/confidence intervals rather than single point figures; underlying assumptions are explicitly documented; history calibrates estimates.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Treating early Rough Order of Magnitude (ROM) estimates as fixed binding commitments; relying on single-person uncalibrated guesses.
When NOT to Use: When scope is completely undefined with zero domain knowledge (conduct exploratory experiments first).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Functional Decomposition, Relative Estimation (Story Points), PERT, and Financial Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Project budgeting, iteration/release scheduling, resource allocation, business case justification.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can analyze historic code commits or Jira ticket completion times to generate automated parametric effort estimates with probabilistic confidence bands.

Problem Solved: Reduces financial investment risk by evaluating expected costs, total cost of ownership (TCO), and projected value realization of solution options.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Strategy / prioritisation / Solution Evaluation / change management
Input Artifacts: Projected solution costs, expected benefits timeline, discount rate, operational cost estimates.
Output Artifacts: Cost-Benefit Analysis, ROI, Present Value (PV), Net Present Value (NPV), Internal Rate of Return (IRR), Payback Period.
Participants & Roles: BA, Financial Analyst, Sponsor, Business Owner, Executive.
Prerequisites: Quantified cost and benefit estimates spread across defined timeframes.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Estimate initial cost of change and ongoing Total Cost of Ownership (TCO). 2. Estimate annual tangible/intangible value realization across project horizon. 3. Construct Cost-Benefit Analysis table detailing net annual cash flows. 4. Apply discount rate to compute Present Value (PV) and Net Present Value (NPV = PV - Initial Investment). 5. Calculate Return on Investment (ROI = Net Benefits / Cost) and Payback Period. 6. Compare metrics against organizational hurdle rates to support solution recommendation.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What is the Total Cost of Ownership over 5 years?", "What discount rate should be used for present value calculations?", "When will this initiative achieve breakeven (payback)?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A $100k investment yields $40k net benefits/year for 3 years. At a 10% discount rate, PV of benefits =  $99,474, NPV = -$ 526, requiring re-evaluation.
Quality Criteria & Verification: All financial assumptions are explicitly stated; TCO includes ongoing support/licensing; standard formulas used consistently across options.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Ignoring ongoing maintenance/operating costs in TCO; treating intangible benefits as absolute facts without accounting for risk uncertainty.
When NOT to Use: For minor, non-monetary operational tweaks where financial calculation overhead outweighs the change scope.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Business Cases, Decision Analysis, Estimation, and Value Stream Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Capital allocation, solution recommendation, project continuation/cancellation (stage-gate review).
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can run automated NPV, IRR, and Monte Carlo sensitivity simulations across multiple cost/benefit variables, instantly producing executive financial summaries.

Problem Solved: Reduces customer and user adoption risk by collecting qualitative feedback, attitudes, and emotional responses about a product or topic in an interactive group setting.
Input Artifacts: Focus group plan, discussion guide (script/questions), product prototypes/concepts, participant criteria.
Output Artifacts: Focus group report, transcribed qualitative findings, identified user themes/attitudes.
Participants & Roles: Moderator (unbiased), Recorder, BA, Participants (6–12 pre-qualified users/customers), Observers.
Prerequisites: Clearly stated session objective, pre-qualified participants matching target demographic, discussion guide.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define clear objective and target participant demographics. 2. Create Focus Group Plan (logistics, location, incentives, discussion guide). 3. Assign an experienced neutral Moderator and a Scribe/Recorder. 4. Conduct 1–2 hour session: moderator leads discussion using open-ended script. 5. Recorder captures comments, non-verbal cues, and interaction dynamics. 6. Transcribe notes, analyze qualitative themes, and publish summary report.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What are your immediate impressions of this product concept?", "How does feature X fit into your daily routine?", "Why do you prefer option A over option B?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A 90-minute focus group of 8 mobile banking users tests a new app interface prototype, revealing that users find the transfer workflow confusing.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Unbiased moderation allowing all participants to speak; clear synthesis of qualitative themes; qualified demographic representation.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Allowing one vocal participant to dominate the group; treating qualitative opinions as statistically significant quantitative data.
When NOT to Use: When quantitative statistical proof is required, or when topic matter is highly sensitive/confidential so participants won't speak openly.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Survey/Questionnaire, Interviews, Observation, and Prototyping.
Supported Decisions: User experience design, feature scoping, product market positioning.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI transcription tools can process focus group audio in real-time, performing sentiment analysis and auto-clustering user responses by theme.

Problem Solved: Reduces system complexity and size uncertainty by breaking down complex processes, systems, or deliverables into smaller, independent, manageable sub-components.
Input Artifacts: High-level business outcomes, scope statements, business processes, system specs.
Output Artifacts: Functional Decomposition Diagram (tree or nested diagram), Work Breakdown Structure (WBS), component hierarchy.
Participants & Roles: BA, Domain SME, Systems Architect, Project Manager.
Prerequisites: Identification of the high-level subject or system to be decomposed.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define the decomposition objective (e.g., designing, estimating, optimizing, scope definition). 2. Identify the top-level parent component or subject. 3. Decompose parent into lower-level sub-components (functions, processes, activities, or tasks). 4. Ensure each sub-component has only one parent component. 5. Repeat decomposition until a manageable, understandable level of detail is reached. 6. Represent results visually (tree diagram, nested boxes, or outline list) and validate completeness.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What sub-functions make up this overarching business function?", "Can task X be broken down into smaller sub-tasks?", "Do these sub-components completely cover the parent component?"
Minimal Realistic Example: The function 'Manage Account' is decomposed into sub-functions: '1.1 Create Account', '1.2 Modify Account', '1.3 Close Account', where 1.1 further breaks down into specific steps.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Parent components are fully described by their sub-components without gaps; sub-components are distinct with clear single-parent hierarchy.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Over-decomposing to an absurd level of detail ('analysis paralysis'); allowing a sub-component to belong to multiple parents in a strict hierarchy.
When NOT to Use: When analyzing highly complex adaptive systems where emergent behavior cannot be captured by simple hierarchical decomposition.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Process Modelling, Scope Modelling, Use Cases, and Work Breakdown Structure (WBS).
Supported Decisions: Scope boundaries, work allocation, effort estimation, modular architecture design.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can analyze high-level project specs and automatically construct draft 3-tier functional decomposition trees for analyst refinement.

Problem Solved: Reduces miscommunication and terminology conflicts by defining key business terms and acronyms in a single, accessible repository.
Input Artifacts: Elicitation results, domain documentation, regulatory texts, stakeholder conversations.
Output Artifacts: Glossary (alphabetical list of domain terms, definitions, acronyms, and synonyms).
Participants & Roles: BA, Domain SME, Glossary Owner/Data Steward, All Stakeholders.
Prerequisites: Early initiative agreement to maintain standardized terminology.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify terms unique to the domain, terms with multiple definitions, or acronyms. 2. Draft clear, concise definitions for each term. 3. Resolve definition conflicts among different stakeholder groups. 4. Document standard synonyms and acronym expansions. 5. Publish glossary in a centralized, easily accessible location. 6. Assign an owner for continuous glossary maintenance throughout the lifecycle.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What does term X mean in this business context?", "Are there conflicting definitions for word Y across departments?", "What does acronym Z stand for?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Glossary entry: 'Premium' - The periodic payment required to keep an insurance policy active. Synonym: 'Policy Fee'. Not to be confused with 'Premium Service'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Definitions are concise, clear, agreed upon by diverse stakeholders, and continuously maintained by a single owner.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Failing to maintain the glossary so it becomes obsolete; allowing multiple uncoordinated glossaries to exist across business units.
When NOT to Use: Rarely inappropriate, though minimal effort is needed if an industry-standard ontology is already universally adopted without variation.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Data Dictionary, Concept Modelling, and Business Rules Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Domain vocabulary alignment, requirements validation, stakeholder communication.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can continuously monitor project chats and spec docs, auto-detecting undefined jargon or ambiguous terms and drafting glossary entries for SME confirmation.

Problem Solved: Reduces system integration failures and missing requirements by identifying where, what, why, when, how, and for whom data/messages are exchanged across solution boundaries.
Input Artifacts: Context diagrams, solution scope models, existing system specs, stakeholder requirements.
Output Artifacts: Interface specs (inputs, outputs, validation rules, message formats, triggers, communication frequency).
Participants & Roles: BA, Systems Architect, Developer, SME, External Vendor/Regulator.
Prerequisites: Identification of connecting solution components, hardware, external systems, or user roles.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify all potential interfaces (user, external system, hardware, API, business process) using context diagrams. 2. For each interface, clarify the purpose (why) and participants (who/what). 3. Define message content (what information is exchanged) and volume. 4. Specify timing, event triggers, and frequency of data exchange (when). 5. Define exchange mechanism, protocol, and message format (how). 6. Specify input/output validation rules and exception handling flows.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What data must be passed across this boundary?", "What event triggers the interface exchange?", "What happens if the receiving system fails to respond?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Interface spec defines an API connecting Web Portal to Payment Gateway: sends 'Order ID + Amount' via HTTPS POST on 'Checkout Click'; expects 'Success/Fail Code' within 2 seconds.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Interface inputs and outputs are explicitly defined; validation and error/exception paths are fully specified.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Focusing solely on happy-path data exchange while omitting error/timeout handling; defining technical implementation details prematurely.
When NOT to Use: When analyzing standalone monolithic applications with zero external connections, human workflows, or hardware interactions.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Context Diagrams, Data Flow Diagrams, Sequence Diagrams, and Use Cases.
Supported Decisions: System architecture allocation, vendor integration scope, non-functional performance design.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can analyze API schemas (e.g., OpenAPI specs) and UI wireframes to auto-generate structured interface mappings and edge-case validation rules.

Problem Solved: Reduces requirement gaps and stakeholder misalignment by directly eliciting business analysis information, concerns, and goals through structured or unstructured dialogue.
Input Artifacts: Interview guide/script, business needs, stakeholder list, background documents.
Output Artifacts: Interview notes, confirmed elicitation results, stakeholder rapport/buy-in.
Participants & Roles: Interviewer (BA), Interviewee(s) (SME, End User, Sponsor, Customer), Scribe (optional).
Prerequisites: Clear interview goals, pre-identified interviewees, and scheduled logistics.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Establish clear interview goals based on business needs. 2. Select appropriate interviewees and choose structured, unstructured, or hybrid format. 3. Design interview questions (open-ended for exploration, closed for confirmation) and interview guide. 4. Opening: explain purpose, roles, and how data will be recorded. 5. Conduct interview: ask questions, practice active listening, and record responses. 6. Closing: summarize main points, invite follow-up, and thank interviewee. 7. Follow-up: organize notes and send to interviewee for confirmation.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Why do you perform step X in your process?", "What challenges do you face with the current system?", "What would success look like for this solution?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A 45-minute structured interview with a Claims Manager uncovers 5 unwritten business rules governing high-value insurance claim approvals.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Interview results documented prompt after session; written notes confirmed/signed off by interviewee; objective non-leading questions used.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Asking leading questions that bias responses; failing to validate interview notes with the interviewee afterwards.
When NOT to Use: When eliciting consensus from large, disparate groups (>15 people) simultaneously (use Surveys or Workshops instead).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Alternatives include Workshops, Surveys/Questionnaires, Observation, and Focus Groups.
Supported Decisions: Requirement validation, process gap identification, stakeholder expectation alignment.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI meeting assistants can record, transcribe, and extract action items and requirements from interview audio, flagging conflicting statements across multiple interviews.

Problem Solved: Reduces the risk of overlooked issues, requirements conflicts, and unaddressed stakeholder concerns by capturing, classifying, and tracking items to resolution.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Planning / elicitation / analysis / prioritisation / validation / change management
Input Artifacts: Stakeholder concerns, review feedback, defect reports, change requests, risk logs.
Output Artifacts: Item Record / Tracker (unique ID, category, impact, priority, owner, resolver, status, resolution history).
Participants & Roles: BA, Item Owner, Item Resolver, Sponsor, Stakeholders.
Prerequisites: Agreed item tracking tool/spreadsheet and defined escalation lifecycle.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Capture stakeholder concern or issue as a tracked item record. 2. Assess viability and classify item type (action, assumption, constraint, defect, risk, enhancement). 3. Assign priority, impact level, target resolution date, and item owner/resolver. 4. Formulate agreed strategy (e.g., accept, mitigate, resolve, avoid). 5. Track progress through status changes (Open, Assigned, Resolved, Closed). 6. Log resolution history and escalate to management if target date is missed.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Who is the assigned owner for resolving issue X?", "What is the impact on project scope if this item is not resolved by date Y?", "What is the current status of concern Z?"
Minimal Realistic Example: An issue raised during review ('Unclear tax calculation logic') is logged as Item #104, assigned to Tax SME, prioritized High, and tracked to resolution within 3 days.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Every item has an assigned owner, target date, and priority; tracking log is accessible and regularly updated until all items reach closure.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Logging excessive trivial details leading to tracking overhead; allowing items to remain open indefinitely without escalation.
When NOT to Use: On minor tasks where informal direct communication resolves questions immediately without formal tracking overhead.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Risk Management, Defect Tracking Systems, Backlog Management, and Reviews.
Supported Decisions: Issue escalation, sign-off readiness, risk mitigation prioritization.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agents integrated into communication channels can detect unresolved questions in chat threads, auto-create tracked issues, assign team owners, and ping for status updates.

Problem Solved: Prevents repeating past mistakes and amplifies project successes by systematically compiling, documenting, and applying team retrospectives.
Input Artifacts: Project deliverables, performance metrics, issue logs, process assessments.
Output Artifacts: Lessons Learned report / Retrospective log (successes, improvement opportunities, root causes, actionable recommendations).
Participants & Roles: Facilitator, BA, Project Manager, Agile Team, Key Stakeholders.
Prerequisites: Completion of a project phase, iteration, or milestone in a psychological safe environment.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Schedule a retrospective meeting at a key milestone or iteration end. 2. Set an open, non-blaming tone focused on continuous improvement. 3. Identify what worked well (successes to reinforce). 4. Identify what didn't work well (problems, variances, failures). 5. Perform root cause analysis on identified challenges. 6. Formulate concrete, actionable recommendations for future work and store in an accessible repository.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What went well during this iteration that we should continue?", "What caused our review cycle to take longer than estimated?", "What should we do differently next time?"
Minimal Realistic Example: In a sprint retrospective, the team identifies that missing wireframes caused developer rework; they agree to require wireframe sign-offs prior to sprint planning.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Atmosphere remains constructive without personal blame; recommendations are actionable and integrated into organizational process assets.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Turning sessions into finger-pointing 'blame games'; documenting lessons learned in reports that are archived and never read again.
When NOT to Use: When team trust is completely absent and facilitation cannot guarantee a psychological safe, constructive discussion.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Alternatives/Complements include Retrospectives, Root Cause Analysis, Process Analysis, and Collaborative Games.
Supported Decisions: BA process improvements, future project estimation adjustments, team working agreement updates.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can summarize retrospective meeting notes across multiple teams, flagging recurring organizational bottlenecks and suggesting process rule adjustments.

Problem Solved: Reduces performance evaluation subjectivity by defining quantifiable indicators to track solution performance and strategic progress over time.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Strategy / Solution Evaluation / analysis / change management
Input Artifacts: Business objectives, strategic goals, current baseline metrics, solution specs.
Output Artifacts: KPI framework, target metrics, monitoring & evaluation plan, performance dashboards/reports.
Participants & Roles: BA, Business Owner, Executive Sponsor, Operational Support, Data Analyst.
Prerequisites: Clear business goals, established baseline metrics, and data collection mechanisms.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify business concerns, goals, and strategic objectives. 2. Define good indicators (clear, relevant, economical, adequate, quantifiable, trustworthy). 3. Establish target metrics (points, thresholds, or ranges) and timeframes. 4. Design data collection, analysis, and reporting procedures. 5. Gather baseline data prior to change implementation. 6. Continuously track actual performance metrics against baselines and targets.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What specific indicator proves that objective X has been achieved?", "What is our baseline starting point for metric Y?", "Is this indicator reliable and economical to collect?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Target KPI for a helpdesk portal: 'Reduce average ticket resolution time from baseline 48 hours to target < 12 hours within 6 months.'
Quality Criteria & Verification: Indicators are valid, reliable, and timely; targets align directly with higher-level strategic goals.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Collecting excessive 'vanity' metrics that add collection overhead without driving decisions; perverse incentives where users game the metric.
When NOT to Use: When data collection costs vastly outweigh the value of monitoring, or when measuring purely ad-hoc creative activities.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Balanced Scorecard, Value Stream Mapping, Solution Performance Analysis, and Benchmarking.
Supported Decisions: Solution performance evaluation, strategy adjustment, process optimization investments.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic systems can continuously monitor live telemetry data, auto-detecting KPI trend anomalies and triggering real-time alerts or corrective process flows.

Problem Solved: Reduces information overload and creative blocks by visually capturing and structuring complex ideas, concepts, and relationships in a non-linear diagram.
Input Artifacts: Central thought/topic, brainstorming ideas, elicitation notes.
Output Artifacts: Mind map diagram (main topic, branches, sub-topics, keywords, visual icons, color groupings).
Participants & Roles: BA (author/facilitator), Stakeholders, SMEs, Team Members.
Prerequisites: A central topic or complex problem statement to explore.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Place the main central topic or image in the center of the canvas. 2. Draw primary branches radiating outward for key secondary topics. 3. Add sub-branches for detailed sub-topics radiating from secondary topics. 4. Assign a single keyword or image to each branch to explain the connection. 5. Use colors and visual symbols to categorize, prioritize, and group related branches. 6. Review and consolidate map structure to present complex concepts clearly.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What are the main categories radiating from our core business problem?", "How does sub-topic Y connect to main branch X?", "What keyword best describes this relationship?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A mind map centered on 'Portal Redesign' branches into 'User Roles', 'Security', 'Content', and 'Integrations', with 'Security' branching into 'OAuth' and 'MFA'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Map clearly presents complex associations; concise keyword usage; visually engaging layout that aids rapid recall.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Over-complicating branches with long sentences instead of keywords; using mind mapping during strict linear estimation exercises.
When NOT to Use: When strict formal notation standards (like UML or BPMN) are required for contractual specification.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Alternatives/Complements include Concept Modelling, Brainstorming, Affinity Diagrams, and Scope Modelling.
Supported Decisions: Exploratory problem scope definition, workshop agenda structuring, feature categorization.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLMs can convert unstructured interview text into structured JSON mind map trees, auto-categorizing topics and generating visual node charts.

Problem Solved: Reduces solution failure risks related to quality of service by specifying constraints and operational attributes (e.g., performance, security, availability) that functional features must meet.
Input Artifacts: Functional requirements, architectural constraints, regulatory standards, SLA objectives.
Output Artifacts: Non-functional requirements statements/matrices (quantified quality attributes and constraints).
Participants & Roles: BA, Systems Architect, Developer, Tester, Security/Compliance Lead, Operational Support.
Prerequisites: Understood functional requirements and business context.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify relevant non-functional categories (Availability, Security, Performance Efficiency, Usability, Maintainability, Scalability, Compliance, etc.). 2. Elicit specific quality expectations and constraints from business and technical stakeholders. 3. Quantify vague expectations into testable declarative statements (e.g., response time in seconds, uptime %)... 4. Evaluate context and potential conflicts between non-functional attributes (e.g., Security vs. Usability). 5. Document requirements in matrices or specifications alongside functional stories. 6. Validate testability with QA testers and architects.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What is the maximum acceptable downtime for this system?", "How many concurrent users must the system support at peak load?", "What regulatory compliance standards (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA) apply?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Requirement: 'The payment search function must return results in < 1.5 seconds for peak loads of up to 5,000 concurrent users with 99.9% uptime.'
Quality Criteria & Verification: Requirements are quantified and testable (e.g., specific metrics instead of 'fast'); clear constraints on solution architecture.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Using vague qualitative phrases like 'user-friendly' or 'system must be fast'; specifying overly strict targets that unnecessarily inflate cost.
When NOT to Use: Rarely omitted, though deep technical NFR specification may be deferred in very early conceptual prototypes.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Acceptance Criteria, SLA definitions, Prototyping, and Use Cases.
Supported Decisions: Technical architecture selection, infrastructure sizing, vendor platform evaluation, acceptance testing sign-off.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can analyze functional specs to auto-suggest missing NFRs based on domain industry standards (e.g., security NFRs for fintech apps).

Problem Solved: Reduces requirements inaccuracies and missing details caused by unstated worker habits or inaccurate self-reporting by directly viewing work activities in context.
Input Artifacts: Observation objectives, schedule, process documentation, performance standards.
Output Artifacts: Observation notes, time/motion logs, process workarounds identified, contextual inquiry report.
Participants & Roles: Observer (BA), Participant (Worker/End User), Manager/Sponsor.
Prerequisites: Clear observation objective, scheduled session, participant consent.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define clear observation objectives (e.g., process flow understanding, pain point identification). 2. Select approach: Active/Noticeable (ask questions during work) or Passive/Unnoticeable (silent observation). 3. Prepare participant: explain purpose, reassure performance is not being judged, get consent. 4. Conduct session: observe tasks, record steps, execution time, tools used, and workarounds. 5. Follow up with participant to ask clarifying questions and fill knowledge gaps. 6. Synthesize notes and validate findings with participants and management.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Why did you perform that manual workaround step?", "What tool or cheat-sheet did you just reference?", "How frequently does this exception occur?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA passively shadows a warehouse worker for 2 hours, discovering that workers manually re-key order numbers into an Excel sheet because system auto-sync fails.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Findings validated by the observed participant; objective evidence recorded; workarounds and unwritten steps captured.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Causing the 'Hawthorne Effect' where worker alters normal behavior because they feel evaluated; interrupting passive observation excessively.
When NOT to Use: For evaluating unobservable knowledge-based or cognitive-only thinking activities (e.g., high-level strategic decision making).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Interviews, Process Modelling, Document Analysis, and Time/Motion studies.
Supported Decisions: Usability design, process automation scope, training plan formulation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Video AI agents can process screen recordings of user task execution to auto-generate process maps and log task completion cycle times.

Problem Solved: Reduces structural misalignment and communication gaps by defining roles, responsibilities, reporting hierarchies, and formal/informal interaction networks.
