Input Artifacts: Job descriptions, org charts, procedure manuals, stakeholder analysis.
Output Artifacts: Organizational Charts (Org Charts), Matrix Models, role descriptions, interface definitions, influencer network map.
Participants & Roles: BA, Executive Management, HR, Business Unit Owner, SME.
Prerequisites: Access to organizational structure records and key leadership stakeholders.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify organizational design model (Functionally-oriented, Market-oriented, or Matrix). 2. Map formal reporting relationships (who reports to whom) and organizational unit boundaries. 3. Define roles, required skills, and key responsibilities for each position. 4. Map unit interfaces (work packages and communication flows exchanged between units). 5. Identify informal lines of authority, communication, and key organizational influencers. 6. Validate model accuracy and evaluate alignment with enterprise strategy.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Who holds final operational decision authority for this department?", "Where are the silos causing cross-functional handoff delays?", "Who are the informal influencers people go to for guidance?"
Minimal Realistic Example: An org chart identifies that 'Customer Support' reports to 'Operations' while 'Billing' reports to 'Finance', explaining a key cross-departmental approval bottleneck.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Accurately depicts both formal structures and informal influencer networks; clear boundaries and role responsibilities defined.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Relying strictly on outdated official org charts while ignoring informal authority structures; creating models in a vacuum without HR/management sign-off.
When NOT to Use: On small, single-team software bug fixes where organizational structures have zero impact.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by RACI Matrix, Roles and Permissions Matrix, Stakeholder Mapping, and Process Modelling.
Supported Decisions: Organizational redesign, change management planning, governance escalation paths, role authority allocation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can analyze corporate communication metadata (e.g., Slack/email interaction graphs) to map informal influencer networks and cross-departmental communication bottlenecks automatically.

Problem Solved: Reduces conflict and resource waste by determining the relative importance and implementation order of business analysis information based on value, risk, and constraints.
BA Lifecycle Phase: prioritisation / planning / Requirements Life Cycle Management
Input Artifacts: Unprioritized requirements/backlog, business goals, risk logs, cost estimates, dependencies.
Output Artifacts: Prioritized requirements/designs (ranked, grouped, or budgeted).
Participants & Roles: BA, Product Owner/Sponsor, Customer, SME, Developer, Project Manager.
Prerequisites: Agreed prioritization criteria (benefit, penalty, cost, risk, dependencies, urgency).
Step-by-Step Procedure: Agree on prioritization basis/criteria with key stakeholders (e.g., value, risk, cost). 2. Select prioritization approach: Grouping (High/Med/Low), Ranking (1 to N), Time-boxing/Budgeting, or Negotiation. 3. Evaluate requirements against selected basis and dependencies. 4. Facilitate stakeholder consensus and trade-off discussions. 5. Sequence requirements in order of priority. 6. Re-evaluate priorities continually as business context and constraints change.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Which requirements deliver the highest value relative to cost?", "What is the penalty for not implementing feature X in this release?", "Which technical dependency requires requirement A to precede requirement B?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A team uses MoSCoW grouping to classify 20 release features: 8 Must Haves, 6 Should Haves, 4 Could Haves, and 2 Won't Haves for current budget.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Stakeholder consensus achieved on top priorities; prioritization criteria transparent and consistently applied; technical dependencies respected.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Classifying 100% of requirements as 'High' priority; allowing vocal stakeholders to manipulate priorities without objective criteria.
When NOT to Use: When all requirements are legally mandatory with unlimited budget and fixed hard deadline.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Backlog Management, Decision Analysis, MoSCoW, Kano Analysis, and Financial Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Release scope planning, budget allocation, iteration backlog ordering.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can auto-score requirements against multi-criteria risk/value algorithms, presenting ranked backlogs for Product Owner review.

Problem Solved: Reduces operational waste, bottlenecks, and hand-off errors by systematically evaluating a business process for efficiency, effectiveness, and alignment.
Input Artifacts: Current state process models, performance metrics, cycle time data, pain points.
Output Artifacts: Gap analysis report, root cause identification, process improvement options, VSM/SIPOC maps.
Participants & Roles: BA, Process Owner, Process Analyst, Process Participants, Operational Support.
Prerequisites: Documented current state process flow and baseline performance metrics.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify gaps and non-value-added steps in current process. 2. Perform root cause analysis on identified bottlenecks and error points. 3. Apply specialized methods (SIPOC, Value Stream Mapping, Cycle-time analysis, Value Added analysis). 4. Evaluate hand-offs between roles to eliminate wait times and redundant steps. 5. Generate and analyze process improvement options (automation, task simplification). 6. Formulate future state process recommendations.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Which steps in this process add value for the customer?", "Where does work sit waiting in queue (bottle-neck)?", "What is the root cause of rework in step X?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Value Stream Analysis reveals that an invoice approval process takes 5 days total, but actual work processing time is only 15 minutes (99.8% wait time waste).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Distinguishes value-add vs non-value-add steps; root causes of bottlenecks identified; improvement options backed by quantitative cycle time data.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Automating a bad process without fixing underlying process flaws ('automating waste'); analyzing processes without involving actual frontline workers.
When NOT to Use: On highly ad-hoc, creative, non-repeatable human processes where fixed workflow analysis cannot apply.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Process Modelling, Root Cause Analysis, SIPOC, Value Stream Mapping, and Benchmarking.
Supported Decisions: Process re-engineering scope, automation target selection, operational cost reduction strategy.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Process mining agents can ingest system event logs (e.g., SAP/Salesforce logs) to construct accurate real-time process execution maps and pinpoint exact bottleneck latencies automatically.

Problem Solved: Reduces operational ambiguity and alignment gaps by creating a visual, standardized sequential flow of work across roles, tasks, and system boundaries.
Input Artifacts: Elicitation notes, worker interviews, observation logs, current procedures.
Output Artifacts: Process Maps / Flowcharts (BPMN, UML Activity Diagrams, Swimlane Diagrams, As-Is/To-Be models).
Participants & Roles: BA, Process Modeller, Process Owner, Process Participants, Developer.
Prerequisites: Understanding of process trigger events, participating roles, activities, and outcomes.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify process boundary (trigger event, initial inputs, final outputs/outcomes). 2. Identify participating roles and represent them as swimlanes or pools. 3. Map sequential activities, tasks, and sub-processes in chronological flow. 4. Add decision gateways (exclusive/parallel) and conditional branching logic. 5. Annotate data inputs/outputs and data store interactions. 6. Validate model flow ('As-Is' or 'To-Be') with process participants and owners.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What event triggers this process?", "Who is responsible for executing step X?", "What decision rule governs this gateway branch?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A BPMN diagram maps 'Order Processing': 'Customer' places order -> 'Sales Swimlane' validates order -> 'Gateway' checks inventory -> 'Warehouse Swimlane' ships product.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Follows standard notation syntax (e.g., BPMN 2.0); clear start/end events; validated for accuracy by actual process workers.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Mixing process flow with complex embedded business rules (make decision rules separate); drawing unwieldy monolithic diagrams without sub-process decomposition.
When NOT to Use: When describing static entity relationships (use Data Modelling) or high-level organizational structures (use Org Modelling).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Business Rules Analysis, Decision Modelling, Use Cases, Value Stream Mapping, and Sequence Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Target operating model design, automation workflow spec, role responsibility assignment.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI models can translate natural language process descriptions directly into valid BPMN XML diagrams, validating structural syntax automatically.

Problem Solved: Reduces misinterpretation and unsubstantiated user assumptions by providing an early visual or functional approximation of the proposed solution for rapid feedback.
Input Artifacts: User requirements, screen flows, storyboards, UI guidelines, usability goals.
Output Artifacts: Prototypes (Throw-away or Evolutionary; Paper, Wireframe, Form Study, Usability, Visual, or Functional simulations).
Participants & Roles: BA, UX/UI Designer, Developer, End User, SME, Customer.
Prerequisites: Initial understanding of target user tasks and interface goals.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Determine prototyping approach (Throw-away vs. Evolutionary) and fidelity level (low/paper vs. high/functional). 2. Select prototyping method (Storyboarding, Paper Prototyping, Workflow Modelling, Interactive Simulation). 3. Draft initial interface screens or workflow mock-ups. 4. Present prototype to end users and elicit feedback on navigation, layout, and functionality. 5. Refine prototype iteratively based on user interactions and usability feedback. 6. Document confirmed user interface requirements or convert evolutionary model into development code.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "How does this screen layout feel for completing task X?", "What information is missing on this dashboard view?", "Does this navigation path match your expectations?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA drafts a 3-page interactive wireframe in Figma for a mobile claims app; user testing reveals that the 'Upload Photo' button needs to be on the primary screen.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Elicits active user feedback; clarifies ambiguous interface requirements; keeps users focused on 'what' rather than nitpicking minor styling in low-fidelity stages.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Setting unrealistic expectations where users mistake high-fidelity prototypes for finished, fully coded applications; spending excessive time polishing throw-away mockups.
When NOT to Use: When solution logic is purely back-end batch processing with zero user interface or user interaction.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Use Cases, User Stories, Storyboarding, Usability Testing, and Interface Analysis.
Supported Decisions: User experience design approval, UI feature scope selection, technical feasibility validation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Generative AI agents can instantly convert text prompts or hand-drawn whiteboards into working HTML/CSS front-end prototypes for immediate user testing.

Problem Solved: Reduces defect leaks and quality errors by systematically evaluating business analysis work products with peers and stakeholders.
BA Lifecycle Phase: validation / verification / Requirements Life Cycle Management
Input Artifacts: Work product / deliverable package (requirements spec, models, user stories), review checklist, objectives.
Output Artifacts: Logged defects, review findings report, approved deliverable, requested rework items.
Participants & Roles: Author (BA), Reviewer(s) (Peer, SME, Tester, Architect), Facilitator, Scribe.
Prerequisites: Completed draft work product and defined review objectives/checklists.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define review objectives and select technique (Inspection, Formal Walkthrough, Single Issue Review, Desk Check, Pass Around, Ad-hoc). 2. Identify participants (Author, Reviewers, Facilitator, Scribe) and distribute work product in advance. 3. Reviewers individually inspect work product against checklists and log preliminary defects. 4. Conduct joint review meeting: walk through document, discuss findings, and log agreed defects/action items. 5. Author performs required rework to correct logged defects. 6. Facilitator/Reviewers verify rework and approve final deliverable.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Does this requirement conform to our quality standards?", "Are there ambiguous or untestable statements in section X?", "Do all reviewers agree on the correctness of model Y?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A 1-hour formal walkthrough of a Software Requirements Specification (SRS) with a Lead Developer and Tester catches 4 missing edge-case exceptions prior to development.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Defects identified and logged objectively; work product checked against quality characteristics (atomic, unambiguous, testable); sign-off achieved.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Turning reviews into personal attacks on the author; conducting walkthroughs without advance reviewer preparation.
When NOT to Use: When work products are in early, highly volatile brainstorming draft stages where formal review adds rigid friction.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Alternatives/Complements include Verification checklists, Approval tasks, and Inspection.
Supported Decisions: Requirement baseline sign-off, deliverable verification, quality gate approval.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can pre-screen requirement docs against verification quality checklists (checking for ambiguous terms, passive voice, missing test criteria) before human peer review.

Problem Solved: Reduces the negative impact of internal and external uncertainties on project and solution value by identifying, analyzing, evaluating, and planning risk responses.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Planning / Strategy / Solution Evaluation / change management
Input Artifacts: Business objectives, strategy, elicitation results, influences, historical project lessons learned.
Output Artifacts: Risk Register (Risk event, probability, impact, overall level, response strategy, risk owner, residual risk).
Participants & Roles: BA, Project Manager, Sponsor, Risk Owner, Technical SME, Regulator.
Prerequisites: Understanding of business objectives and organizational risk tolerance levels.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Risk Identification: discover potential risk events/conditions through expert judgment and elicitation. 2. Risk Analysis: estimate probability of occurrence and negative value impact (cost, timeline, quality). 3. Priority & Level: calculate overall risk level (Probability x Impact) and rank risks. 4. Risk Evaluation: compare risk levels against organizational risk tolerance thresholds. 5. Risk Treatment: select response strategy (Avoid, Transfer, Mitigate, Accept, Increase/Pursue Opportunity) and assign Risk Owner. 6. Develop response plan and continuously monitor residual risks throughout the lifecycle.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What uncertain event could prevent us from realizing solution value?", "What is the probability and impact of risk X?", "What is our risk response strategy and who owns it?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Risk Identified: 'SME unavailable during testing' (Prob: Med, Impact: High). Mitigation Plan: 'Schedule 2-week block in advance with manager approval'; Residual Risk: Low.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Comprehensive risk coverage; actionable mitigation plans assigned to individual owners; residual risk brought within acceptable tolerance.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Logging unmanageably huge lists of trivial risks while missing critical ones; treating risk registration as a one-time exercise never updated.
When NOT to Use: Never omitted entirely, though low-impact micro-tasks require only brief informal risk consideration.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Decision Analysis, SWOT Analysis, Lessons Learned, and Root Cause Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Change strategy selection, contingency budget allocation, solution go/no-go decisions.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can continuously monitor project health telemetry (velocity drops, turnover, code bugs) to auto-raise elevated risk flags in the Risk Register for PM review.

Problem Solved: Reduces security breaches, governance failures, and activity gaps by defining role authorities, data access permissions, and segregation of duties.
Input Artifacts: Org models, job descriptions, process models, use cases, security policies.
Output Artifacts: Roles and Permissions Matrix (Role groups vs. Activities/Data; CRUD or RACI designations), authority delegation rules.
Participants & Roles: BA, Security/Compliance Lead, System Admin, SME, Business Owner.
Prerequisites: Identified organizational user roles and system activities/data entities.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify distinct user roles sharing common functions and permissions. 2. Identify system activities, functions, or data entities (e.g., Create, Read, Update, Delete). 3. Map authority permissions for each role across each activity/data entity in a matrix. 4. Define security levels, segregation of duties, and authorization constraints. 5. Specify delegation and organizational hierarchy inheritance rules. 6. Validate permission matrix with security leads and business owners.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Which roles are authorized to perform action X?", "Does role A have permission to Delete record Y?", "Are there segregation of duty conflicts between role A and B?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A CRUD matrix defines that 'Sales Rep' role has 'Create/Read' permissions on 'Orders', while 'Sales Manager' has 'Create/Read/Update/Delete' permissions.
Quality Criteria & Verification: All system activities covered; no security policy or segregation-of-duties violations; explicit authority for every role.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Creating an overly granular matrix that becomes an administrative nightmare; neglecting to define delegation and revoking procedures.
When NOT to Use: On open-access public systems where all users possess identical, unrestricted permissions.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by RACI Matrix, Organizational Modelling, Use Cases, and Security NFR Analysis.
Supported Decisions: System security design, compliance/audit approval, user access control configuration.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can audit roles and permissions matrices automatically against corporate compliance rules, flagging segregation-of-duty policy violations.

Problem Solved: Prevents superficial symptom-fixing by systematically identifying and evaluating the underlying fundamental origin of a problem.
Input Artifacts: Problem statement, defect reports, performance variance data, process observation notes.
Output Artifacts: Fishbone (Ishikawa) Diagrams, 5 Whys analysis trace, corrective action plan.
Participants & Roles: BA, Facilitator, SME, Process Worker, Quality Engineer.
Prerequisites: A clearly defined, observable problem statement.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define Problem Statement clearly (describe issue, impact, and location). 2. Collect data regarding the magnitude and timing of the problem. 3. Choose technique: Fishbone Diagram (for category analysis) or 5 Whys (for iterative drill-down). 4. Fishbone: draw spine, add category bones (People, Process, Tools, Policy), brainstorm causes. 5. 5 Whys: repeatedly ask 'Why did this occur?' (typically 5 levels deep) until the fundamental root cause is reached. 6. Identify and evaluate corrective/preventive action plans to eliminate the root cause.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Why did problem X occur?", "What is the fundamental underlying cause behind this symptom?", "Will addressing factor Y permanently prevent recurrence?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Problem: 'Invoice paid late'. Why 1: Delay in approval. Why 2: Manager missed email. Why 3: No auto-reminder system. Why 4: Process was never automated -> Root Cause: Lack of workflow automation.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Analysis identifies root causes rather than superficial symptoms; proposed corrective action permanently eliminates or mitigates recurrence.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Stopping analysis at first-level symptoms; placing personal blame on workers instead of fixing faulty system/process designs.
When NOT to Use: For simple, known one-off glitches where root cause is self-evident without investigation.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Process Analysis, Fishbone Diagram, 5 Whys, Failure Mode & Effects Analysis (FMEA), and SWOT Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Corrective action plan selection, process redesign priorities, quality improvement investments.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI diagnostic agents can analyze error logs and operational data to automatically trace cause-and-effect chains and present draft 5 Whys trees to analysts.

Problem Solved: Reduces scope creep and boundary ambiguity by explicitly defining what elements fall inside and outside the limits of a change, solution, or business need.
Input Artifacts: Business needs, vision statements, stakeholder lists, initial feature requests.
Output Artifacts: Scope models (Context Diagrams, In-Scope/Out-of-Scope lists, Use Case Diagrams, Feature breakdowns, Venn diagrams).
Participants & Roles: BA, Sponsor, Project Manager, Key Stakeholders, Systems Architect.
Prerequisites: High-level understanding of the business need and initiative goals.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify the scope objective (scope of control, need, solution, or change). 2. Select appropriate scope modelling techniques (Context Diagram, Functional Decomposition, Use Case Diagram, In/Out lists). 3. Identify boundary elements: people, processes, systems, data, and organizational units. 4. Classify elements explicitly as In-Scope or Out-of-Scope. 5. Explore relationships and dependencies between boundary elements. 6. Document critical scope assumptions and gain stakeholder agreement.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Is process X explicitly included or excluded from this initiative?", "What external systems touch our solution boundary?", "What assumptions define this scope boundary?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A Context Diagram places 'New E-Commerce Engine' in center, with In-Scope flows to 'Payment Gateway' and 'Shipping API', and explicitly marks 'ERP Accounting System' as Out-of-Scope.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Scope boundaries are clear and agreed upon by sponsors; explicit Out-of-Scope list prevents creep; assumptions documented.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Failing to document Out-of-Scope items; creating high-level scope models that lack sufficient detail to guide development.
When NOT to Use: On open-ended exploratory research initiatives where rigid boundaries impede initial ideation.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Context Diagrams, Functional Decomposition, Use Case Diagrams, and Value Stream Mapping.
Supported Decisions: Contractual obligations, project estimation boundaries, requirement inclusion/exclusion, release planning.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can evaluate project communications and proposal text to draft In-Scope vs Out-of-Scope matrices, flagging boundary ambiguities for BA review.

Problem Solved: Reduces object interaction and logic errors in technical software design by visually depicting message exchanges between objects/systems over time in a chronological scenario.
Input Artifacts: Use cases, scenarios, Class Diagrams, interface specs.
Output Artifacts: Sequence Diagram (Lifelines, Activation Boxes, Synchronous/Asynchronous Messages, Calls, Responses, Destruction).
Participants & Roles: BA, Systems Analyst, Software Developer, Systems Architect.
Prerequisites: Defined use case scenario and participating software objects/classes.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify scenario/use case path to model. 2. Lay out participating objects/systems as boxes horizontally across top. 3. Draw vertical dashed lifelines descending from each object. 4. Draw activation boxes on lifelines to show when operation executes. 5. Draw horizontal message arrows between lifelines in top-down chronological order. 6. Label messages (synchronous calls, asynchronous signals, return responses, destruction).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Which object initiates the first message in this scenario?", "Is this call synchronous (blocking) or asynchronous?", "What response message is returned to object A?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Sequence diagram shows 'User' -> (submits login) -> 'UI' -> (validates) -> 'Auth Server' -> (returns token) -> 'UI' -> (displays dashboard) -> 'User'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Strict UML notation syntax; chronological top-down message order; logic matches use case scenario steps accurately.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Over-complicating diagrams by trying to represent every possible alternate flow in a single diagram; creating sequence diagrams for non-technical business stakeholders.
When NOT to Use: When communicating high-level business process workflows to non-technical business users (use BPMN or Flowcharts instead).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Alternatives/Complements include Use Cases, Activity Diagrams, Data Flow Diagrams, and Interface Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Detailed software design specification, API call structure, technical feasibility verification.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can generate PlantUML or Mermaid sequence diagram code directly from narrative use case steps automatically.

Problem Solved: Reduces stakeholder oversight, communication breakdowns, and misalignment by identifying, categorizing, mapping, and profiling stakeholders and their characteristics.
Input Artifacts: Business need, org charts, process models, project charter.
Output Artifacts: Stakeholder List, Stakeholder Matrix (Influence vs Impact), Stakeholder Onion Diagram, RACI Matrix, Personas.
Participants & Roles: BA, Sponsor, Project Manager, All Stakeholder Groups.
Prerequisites: Initial initiative goal and access to organizational information.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Brainstorm and list all internal/external stakeholders affected by or influencing the change. 2. Analyze characteristics: authority, attitude/interest, influence, decision authority. 3. Map stakeholders using matrices (Influence vs Impact) or Onion Diagrams (level of involvement). 4. Assign responsibility levels using a RACI matrix (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed). 5. Develop Personas (archetypal fictional user profiles) for major end-user groups. 6. Formulate tailored collaboration, communication, and engagement strategies.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Who is impacted directly/indirectly by this change?", "What is stakeholder X's level of influence and interest?", "What are the key goals and pain points of Persona Y?"
Minimal Realistic Example: An Influence/Impact matrix maps 'Finance Director' as High Influence/High Impact (Key Player - closely engage), and 'Field Reps' as Low Influence/High Impact (Keep informed/consult).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Exhaustive coverage of affected parties; RACI assigns exactly 1 Accountable role per task; Personas grounded in real user research data.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Forgetting key stakeholder groups leading to late requirements; treating stakeholder analysis as a static one-time activity.
When NOT to Use: Rarely omitted, though minimal lightweight listing is sufficient for simple single-user tasks.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Organizational Modelling, RACI, User Stories, and Communication Plans.
Supported Decisions: Stakeholder engagement plan, communication delivery format, change management strategy.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agents can analyze user telemetry and feedback text to auto-synthesize realistic user Personas and map RACI matrices based on workflow roles.

Problem Solved: Reduces logic gaps and invalid status transition errors by analyzing the distinct lifecycle states of an entity, allowed transitions, and triggering events.
Input Artifacts: Data Models, business rules, process models, use cases.
Output Artifacts: State Transition Diagram, State Table (States, Transitions, Events, Conditions, Actions).
Participants & Roles: BA, Systems Analyst, Domain SME, Developer, Tester.
Prerequisites: Identification of a complex business entity with multiple distinct status states.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify the core entity with complex lifecycle behaviour (e.g., Order, Claim, Account). 2. Elicit all possible valid states the entity can inhabit from creation to retirement. 3. Identify initial start state and final end state. 4. Define valid transitions from one state to another. 5. Specify events, guard conditions, and resulting actions for each transition. 6. Document visually via State Diagram or structurally via State Table, and validate with SMEs.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What states can entity X be in?", "What event triggers a transition from state A to state B?", "Under what condition is a transition prohibited?"
Minimal Realistic Example: An 'Order' entity states: 'New' -> (event: Payment Received) -> 'Paid' -> (event: Ship) -> 'Shipped' -> (event: Deliver) -> 'Closed'. If Payment Fails -> 'Cancelled'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: All valid entity states accounted for; no 'dead end' states (except final state); transitions governed by explicit events/rules.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confusing state diagrams with process flow diagrams; missing exception transition paths.
When NOT to Use: For simple entities that possess no complex status changes or lifecycle rules.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Data Modelling, Business Rules Analysis, Process Modelling, and Use Cases.
Supported Decisions: System status logic specification, data lifecycle governance, exception handling design.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can analyze entity specs to generate state transition tables automatically, verifying that no invalid state transitions or orphan states exist.

Problem Solved: Reduces data collection costs and time bottlenecks when gathering structured feedback, customer preferences, or work practice data from large or geographically dispersed groups.
Input Artifacts: Survey objective, target group profile, sample size plan, questions list.
Output Artifacts: Survey document/tool, raw response data, statistical summary report, categorized qualitative themes.
Participants & Roles: BA (author/analyst), Respondents (SMEs, Customers, End Users), Statistician (optional).
Prerequisites: Clear objective, identified target population, and distribution channel.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define clear survey objective and target survey population. 2. Select question types: Close-ended (quantitative, easy to analyze) and Open-ended (qualitative insights). 3. Determine sample group size and distribution method (online, email, phone). 4. Write clear, non-leading questions and conduct usability test/pilot on survey. 5. Distribute survey with clear deadline, purpose statement, and confidentiality assurance. 6. Collate responses, perform statistical analysis on quantitative items, categorize qualitative themes, and publish summary report.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "On a scale of 1-5, how satisfied are you with feature X?", "Which of the following options best describes your daily usage?", "What specific improvements would you suggest?"
Minimal Realistic Example: An online survey with 10 closed-ended questions sent to 500 remote store managers yields a 60% response rate, proving that 80% want automated inventory replenishment.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Questions are unbiased and unambiguous; statistical sample size is representative of target population; high response rate achieved.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Writing ambiguous or leading questions that bias results; surveying an unrepresentative sample group.
When NOT to Use: When deep, open-ended qualitative exploration or complex back-and-forth negotiation is required (use Interviews or Workshops instead).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Alternatives/Complements include Focus Groups, Interviews, Observation, and Metrics & KPIs.
Supported Decisions: Customer satisfaction evaluation, feature prioritization, broad operational gap identification.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can design survey questions based on research goals, auto-analyze free-text survey responses using NLP sentiment analysis, and generate statistical chart summaries.

Problem Solved: Reduces strategic blind spots by evaluating an organization's internal Strengths and Weaknesses alongside external Opportunities and Threats.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Discovery / Strategy / Solution Evaluation / change management
Input Artifacts: Market research, current state assessments, industry trends, internal performance metrics.
Output Artifacts: SWOT Matrix (2x2 grid: Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats), strategic action strategies (SO, ST, WO, WT strategies).
Participants & Roles: BA, Executive Sponsor, Business Owner, Strategic Planner, SME.
Prerequisites: Defined evaluation context (enterprise, division, project, or product).
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define the specific evaluation context and objective. 2. Identify external Opportunities (O) and Threats (T) in the market/environment. 3. Identify internal Strengths (S) and Weaknesses (W) of the organization. 4. Construct 2x2 SWOT Matrix. 5. Brainstorm matching strategies: SO (use strengths to exploit opportunities), ST (use strengths to ward off threats), WO (overcome weaknesses by using opportunities), WT (minimize weaknesses and avoid threats). 6. Summarize findings and incorporate into change strategy or business case.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What internal advantages or core capabilities do we possess?", "What external market trends present growth opportunities?", "What internal weaknesses expose us to external threats?"
Minimal Realistic Example: SWOT analysis for a retailer identifies Strength (Strong Brand) and Opportunity (E-commerce growth) -> SO Strategy: 'Launch mobile shopping app using brand equity'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: SWOT entries are brief, specific, realistic, and supported by objective evidence; actionable strategies derived from combinations.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Conducting SWOT at a vague level without a defined context; listing subjective opinions without factual evidence.
When NOT to Use: For micro-level software component specification where enterprise strategy and environment are irrelevant.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Benchmarking, PESTLE/5 Forces, Business Model Canvas, and Risk Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Strategic direction selection, change strategy formulation, business case justification.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can analyze industry news and internal performance reports to populate a draft SWOT matrix and propose initial SO/WT strategies for executive review.

Problem Solved: Reduces requirements ambiguity by describing narrative step-by-step interactions between primary actors and a solution to achieve a specific goal.
Input Artifacts: Elicitation results, actor profiles, scope models, process models.
Output Artifacts: Use Case Diagrams, Use Case Specifications (Name, Goal, Actors, Preconditions, Triggers, Basic Flow, Alternate Flows, Exception Flows, Post-conditions).
Participants & Roles: BA, Primary/Secondary Actors, Developer, Tester, SME.
Prerequisites: Identified system boundary, primary actors, and actor goals.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify actors and their specific goals interacting with the solution. 2. Create Use Case Diagram showing actors, use cases, <>, and <> relationships. 3. For each use case, write brief goal description, primary actor, preconditions, and triggers. 4. Document Basic/Primary Success Flow as chronological numbered steps. 5. Document Alternate Flows (optional success paths) and Exception Flows (failure paths). 6. Specify Post-conditions (minimal and success guarantees) and validate with stakeholders.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What is the primary actor's goal?", "What step-by-step path achieves this goal?", "What exception occurs if input X is invalid?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Use Case 'Withdraw Cash': Actor = Cardholder. Basic Flow: Insert Card -> Enter PIN -> Select Amount -> Dispense Cash. Exception 3a: Invalid PIN -> Eject Card -> End.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Written from actor's point of view; covers basic, alternate, and exception flows; post-conditions hold true; easily testable by QA.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Embedding UI design details or business rules directly inside use case steps instead of referencing separate rule tables; creating overly complex nested flows.
When NOT to Use: When lightweight user stories are preferred in short-iteration agile teams without formal documentation requirements.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Alternatives/Complements include User Stories, Process Modelling, Sequence Diagrams, Prototyping, and Activity Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Functional scope definition, test case design, user acceptance criteria verification.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLMs can convert narrative use case flows automatically into automated test scripts (Cucumber/Gherkin) or sequence diagrams.

Problem Solved: Reduces heavy documentation overhead and rigid upfront scoping by capturing concise statements of stakeholder value to invite ongoing collaborative exploration.
Input Artifacts: Stakeholder needs, personas, product vision, backlog.
Output Artifacts: User Stories ('As a , I need to , so that '), detailed Acceptance Criteria, story maps.
Participants & Roles: Product Owner, BA, Agile Team (Developers, Testers), Customer/User.
Prerequisites: Understood user personas and product vision.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify user role or persona (Who). 2. Express necessary action, behavior, or feature desired (What). 3. Express business value or benefit received (Why). 4. Format as standard sentence: 'As a , I need to , so that '. 5. Attach testable Acceptance Criteria (e.g., Given/When/Then format). 6. Refine, elaborate, and decompose stories iteratively during team discussions.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Who needs this feature?", "What goal are they trying to accomplish?", "What is the measurable benefit delivered?", "How do we know when this story is complete (acceptance criteria)?"
Minimal Realistic Example: 'As a Shopper, I want to save items to a wishlist, so that I can purchase them later.' Acceptance Criteria: Wishlist holds max 50 items; accessible across logins.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Follows INVEST criteria (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable); clear acceptance criteria attached.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Treating user stories as rigid specs without team discussion; omitting the 'Why' (statement of value); writing huge monolithic stories ('epics') that cannot fit in an iteration.
When NOT to Use: For long-term knowledge retention, or highly regulated contractual specs requiring comprehensive formal documentation upfront.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Acceptance Criteria, Story Mapping, Personas, Use Cases, and Backlog Management.
Supported Decisions: Iteration scope selection, feature prioritization, developer work estimation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can generate user stories and Gherkin acceptance criteria from high-level feature prompts, estimating relative story point complexity based on historical team velocity.

Problem Solved: Reduces third-party procurement risk by formally evaluating vendor stability, capability, licensing models, and compliance before committing to a commercial solution.
Input Artifacts: RFI, RFP, RFQ, RFT, vendor proposals, non-functional requirements, SLA expectations.
Output Artifacts: Vendor assessment report, vendor scorecard, licensing/pricing model comparison, risk evaluation.
Participants & Roles: BA, Procurement Lead, Sponsor, Technical Architect, Compliance/Legal.
Prerequisites: Clear business and non-functional requirements for the third-party product/service.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Issue procurement request (RFI/RFP/RFQ) detailing business requirements and SLAs. 2. Evaluate vendor knowledge, domain expertise, and technical capability. 3. Analyze vendor licensing, pricing models, and total cost of ownership. 4. Assess vendor market position, experience, reputation, and financial stability. 5. Evaluate legal terms, IP rights, data protection, and product roadmap. 6. Score vendors against evaluation criteria and make selection recommendation.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Does the vendor meet our security and regulatory compliance standards?", "What is the vendor's financial stability and market reputation?", "What are the total licensing and customization costs over 5 years?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A vendor evaluation scorecard rates 3 Cloud CRM vendors across Security (30%), TCO (30%), and Feature Coverage (40%); Vendor B achieves highest score of 88/100.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Objective scoring criteria used; due diligence performed on financial/legal terms; non-functional SLAs evaluated.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Selecting a vendor based purely on low initial price while ignoring ongoing TCO and vendor stability risks; subjective biased scoring.
When NOT to Use: When building an in-house custom solution with no third-party software, hardware, or consulting vendor involvement.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complemented by Decision Analysis, Acceptance & Evaluation Criteria, Financial Analysis, and RFPs.
Supported Decisions: Vendor selection, commercial software procurement, outsourcing contracts, SLA approval.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can ingest hundreds of pages of vendor RFP responses to auto-extract pricing models, SLA terms, and compliance matrices for analyst review.

Problem Solved: Reduces project delays and conflicting stakeholder priorities by bringing key stakeholders together in a structured, facilitated event to achieve an agreed-upon goal.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Discovery / Planning / elicitation / analysis / prioritisation / validation / change management
Input Artifacts: Workshop agenda, purpose statement, background materials, pre-workshop interview notes.
Output Artifacts: Workshop deliverables (models, agreed requirements, decision logs, action items, meeting record).
Participants & Roles: Facilitator (neutral), Scribe, Timekeeper, Sponsor, BA, Key Stakeholders, SMEs.
Prerequisites: Defined workshop goal, agenda, invited key stakeholders, and room/tool logistics.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Prepare: define goal, outcomes, agenda, select neutral facilitator/scribe, and distribute pre-read materials. 2. Opening: state purpose, desired outcomes, and establish ground rules (respect, active contribution). 3. Conduct: lead interactive exercises, facilitate collaborative discussions, and manage conflicts. 4. Maintain focus on agenda items and record deferred topics in a 'parking lot'. 5. Document decisions, outputs, and open action items in real time via scribe. 6. Wrap-up: review outcomes, assign action item owners, and distribute post-workshop documentation.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Do all participants agree on this proposed scope boundary?", "What concerns remain regarding option X?", "Who owns action item Y resulting from this decision?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A 4-hour requirements scoping workshop brings together Marketing, IT, and Finance leads to resolve conflicting priorities, successfully agreeing on 12 core MVP features.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Predefined workshop goal achieved; active participation across all represented stakeholder groups; documented decisions and action items distributed promptly.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Lacking a neutral facilitator causing biased discussions; inviting too many participants (>12-15) slowing down decision making; failing to follow up on action items.
When NOT to Use: When individual confidential feedback is needed (use Interviews) or when simple quantitative polling is sufficient (use Surveys).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Alternatives/Complements include Focus Groups, Interviews, Brainstorming, Collaborative Games, and JAD workshops.
Supported Decisions: Scope definition approval, requirements consensus, risk/priority trade-offs, architecture direction sign-off.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can act as virtual co-facilitators—transcribing multi-party audio, auto-summarizing agreed decisions, and populating action item boards live during the workshop.

Problem Solved: Specifies stored data structure and relationships precisely, reducing ambiguity about business entities and data logic.
Input Artifacts: Stakeholder interviews, domain concepts, existing forms/documents, database schemas.
Output Artifacts: E/R diagram, class diagram, entity definitions.
Participants & Roles: BA, architect, developer, SME.
Prerequisites: Basic understanding of key domain entities and business concepts.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify core domain entities (boxes). 2. Define essential fields/attributes for each entity. 3. Identify relationships and connectors between entities. 4. Determine cardinalities (e.g., 1:m, m:m). 5. Normalize the model to remove duplicate data and fixed-size constraints. 6. Review and validate against domain rules and task needs.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How many stays can a guest have? Is a company considered a guest or a separate entity? Can a room be used for multiple stays at once?
Minimal Realistic Example: Entity 'Guest' with attributes (name, address) connected via 1:m relationship to entity 'Stay' with attributes (stay#, paymethod).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Normalization check, CRUD matrix check against user tasks, developer review.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Over-modeling non-essential connection objects, mixing dynamic user roles into static sub-classes, failing to normalize variable-length data.
When NOT to Use: Standard off-the-shelf COTS purchasing where standard schema is fixed and unchangeable.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Data Dictionary, Virtual Windows, Data Expressions, Class Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Database architecture, data schema design, COTS fit-gap analysis.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Prompt AI with domain entity descriptions to automatically draft normalized E/R diagrams and detect missing relationships.

Problem Solved: Eliminates ambiguity regarding individual data fields, special values, domain business rules, and field lengths.
Input Artifacts: Domain concepts, draft data models, SME interviews, existing user interface screens.
Output Artifacts: Structured textual data catalog with entity and attribute descriptions.
Participants & Roles: BA, SME, developer, tester.
Prerequisites: Basic list of entities and fields identified.
Step-by-Step Procedure: List entity classes alphabetically or by structural grouping. 2. Define each entity class with synonyms, purpose, and realistic examples. 3. List all attributes for each entity. 4. Specify data type, size, allowable values, and special value handling. 5. Explain non-trivial business logic, origin, and usage for each attribute.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Where do these values originate? What is the maximum character length needed? What happens if this field is left blank?
Minimal Realistic Example: Class: Guest. Attribute: 'name' (Text, 50 chars), stated by guest, truncated at registration to prevent printout overflow.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Peer review, SME walkthrough, checking completeness against non-trivial questions guide.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Writing trivial definitions (e.g., 'guestName is the name of the guest') instead of capturing domain logic.
When NOT to Use: Small, trivial domain where field meanings are completely self-explanatory.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Data Model, Data Expressions, Virtual Windows.
Supported Decisions: Database schema design, input validation logic, UI field constraints.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Feed AI raw data samples to auto-generate data dictionary entries including inferences on field types, constraints, and descriptions.

Problem Solved: Reduces ambiguity in nested, sequence-dependent, or composite data structures and message protocols.
Input Artifacts: Interface descriptions, data flow inputs, message format definitions.
Output Artifacts: Data expression formulas (BNF/Regular expressions).
Participants & Roles: BA, system architect, developer, tester.
Prerequisites: Identification of composite data flows or structured message protocols.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify composite data elements or message exchanges. 2. Define sequential composition using concatenation operators (+ or implicit). 3. Mark optional data using brackets . 4. Mark repeated data structures using braces {}. 5. Define choices/alternatives using vertical bars ( | ). 6. Define literal value options.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: In what order do these data fields appear? Which fields are optional? How many times can this group repeat?
Minimal Realistic Example: booking request = guest data + period + room type; guest data = guest name + address + passport number.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Verification against syntax rules; syntax-driven test case generation for boundary testing.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Attempting to model cyclic/recursive domain data structures leading to infinite loops.
When NOT to Use: Describing large, non-sequential entity-relationship databases.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Data Model, Data Dictionary, Sequence Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Technical message protocol design, API payload validation rules.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Utilize AI parser agents to translate raw interface specs or XML/JSON samples into BNF expressions.

Problem Solved: Bridging the communication gap between users and developers by visually representing stored domain data without committing to UI button/menu design prematurely.
Input Artifacts: E/R model, task descriptions, domain entities.
Output Artifacts: Idealized screen representations showing realistic data layout without functional controls.
Participants & Roles: BA, UI designer, SME, end user.
Prerequisites: Preliminary data model and list of core user tasks.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify data needs for a core user task. 2. Compose a visual virtual window containing all necessary fields with realistic sample data. 3. Expand existing windows or create new ones for subsequent tasks to minimize total screen count. 4. Perform an understandability test with users to verify data clarity. 5. Cross-check data coverage against the E/R data model.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Does this screen show all the information you need to make this decision? Can you understand what this sample data represents?
Minimal Realistic Example: A 'Guest Window' displaying guest contact info, stays history, current room numbers, and room rates without any action buttons.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Early user understandability test, CRUD verification against E/R model.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Designing functional UI components (buttons, dropdowns) too early; spending excessive time making mockups visually pretty.
When NOT to Use: COTS acquisitions where existing screens cannot be altered.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Data Model, Screens & Prototypes, Tasks with Data.
Supported Decisions: UI architecture, confirmation of complete domain data modeling.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic UI generators can take entity models and task goals to synthesize candidate virtual window layouts automatically.

Problem Solved: Defines product boundaries (scope) and reduces misunderstandings regarding external systems and user group interfaces.
Input Artifacts: Stakeholder lists, project inception documents, interface lists.
Output Artifacts: Black-box system context diagram with external entities and data/event flows.
Participants & Roles: BA, system architect, project manager, sponsor.
Prerequisites: High-level understanding of system purpose and surrounding environment.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Draw the product as a central black box. 2. Identify surrounding user groups and external technical systems. 3. Draw arrows representing data or event flows entering and leaving the central system. 4. Annotate each arrow with clear data descriptions. 5. Review and validate scope boundaries with stakeholders.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Is system X included inside our deliverable or is it external? What exact information flows between the user and the system?
Minimal Realistic Example: Central 'Hotel System' box connected via arrows to 'Receptionist' (booking data), 'Guest' (invoice), and 'Accounting System' (account records).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Stakeholder review, boundary confirmation against project scope statement.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Including internal system functions or internal modules inside the context box.
When NOT to Use: When the project scope is entirely isolated and has zero external actors or systems.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Use Case Diagrams, High-level Dataflow Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Project scope boundaries, external API integration requirements, vendor responsibility boundaries.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Extract external actors and data exchanges from project charters using LLMs to automatically generate Mermaid or PlantUML context diagrams.

Problem Solved: Prevents missing functionality and clarifies triggers initiating system or domain processing.
Input Artifacts: Context diagram, stakeholder requests, domain task lists.
Output Artifacts: Categorized catalog of domain business events or product functions/messages.
Participants & Roles: BA, developer, SME.
Prerequisites: Context diagram or defined system boundaries.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify external triggers/events arriving from surroundings (domain events). 2. Map business events to corresponding user tasks or activities. 3. (For product-level) Derive product events/messages required across each interface. 4. Organize functions by interface or subsystem. 5. Conduct CRUD completeness check against the data model.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What event triggers this action? How does the product know it needs to perform this calculation?
Minimal Realistic Example: Domain Event: 'Guest arrives to check in' maps to Product Functions: 'Find free room', 'Record guest', 'Print confirmation'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: CRUD completeness check against database entities, developer interface verification.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confusing domain business triggers with internal product function execution; treating product event lists as domain requirements in COTS projects.
When NOT to Use: COTS acquisition projects where internal product event structures are already fixed.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Task Descriptions, Use Cases, State Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Scope determination, functional coverage, testing case cataloging.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Parse unstructured feature requests into structured trigger-response event catalogs automatically.

Problem Solved: Communicates required product functionality clearly in traditional textual format for simple extensions or technical component purchases.
Input Artifacts: Stakeholder wishlists, event lists, domain problems.
Output Artifacts: Numbered textual feature requirement statements ('The product shall...').
Participants & Roles: BA, developer, customer.
Prerequisites: Clear domain understanding by the analyst.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify required product capabilities from task studies or domain problems. 2. Draft textual feature statements specifying product capability. 3. Add domain context and 'why' background rationale to resolve potential ambiguities. 4. Review feature statements with developers and SMEs for clarity and feasibility.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Why do you need this feature? What specific problem does this functionality solve in your task?
Minimal Realistic Example: R1: The product shall be able to record that a room is occupied for repair in a specified period.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Verification testing (pass/fail per feature), developer code review.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Creating endless feature 'wishlists' disconnected from real business tasks, leading to bloated, unusable systems.
When NOT to Use: COTS business application tenders where feature lists lock out superior standard software workflows.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Task Descriptions, Tasks & Support, Use Cases.
Supported Decisions: Software build specifications, acceptance test verification lists.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Refactor raw user feature requests into precise 'shall' statements enriched with domain rationale prompts.

Problem Solved: Eliminates ambiguity in complex user interface designs and ensures high usability prior to programming.
Input Artifacts: Task descriptions, Virtual Windows, screen sketches, user profiles.
Output Artifacts: Screen mockups/prototypes, process descriptions for buttons/menus, error message lists.
Participants & Roles: BA, UI designer, developer, tester, end user.
Prerequisites: Detailed task analysis and clear understanding of workflow sequences.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Draft screen layouts based on task data requirements. 2. Define logic/pseudo-code for interactive controls (buttons, menus). 3. Define error messages and validation checks. 4. Conduct usability testing on the prototype using realistic tasks. 5. Iterate prototype based on observed user failures. 6. Freeze prototype as a design-level requirement.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What should happen when this button is clicked? What error message should be displayed if this input is invalid?
Minimal Realistic Example: R1: The product shall use screen pictures in Appendix XX; Check-in button executes pseudo-code logic in Appendix YY.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Usability testing with target end users, direct visual verification against prototype during delivery testing.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Specifying prototypes as rigid requirements without prior usability testing; using fixed screen prototypes for COTS acquisitions.
When NOT to Use: COTS acquisition projects, or early elicitation phases where project scope is volatile.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Task Descriptions, Virtual Windows, Tasks & Support.
Supported Decisions: UI design freezing, front-end software architecture, delivery acceptance criteria.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Generate runnable HTML/CSS prototypes directly from textual pseudo-code and task inputs using LLMs.

Problem Solved: Specifies user work requirements at the domain level without restricting product design or specifying premature user interface mechanics.
Input Artifacts: User interviews, workplace observations, business process models.
Output Artifacts: Structured task descriptions (Purpose, Trigger/Preconditions, Frequency, Criticality, Sub-tasks, Variants).
Participants & Roles: BA, SME, end user, developer, vendor.
Prerequisites: Identification of user roles and closed business work goals.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify closed user work goals (closure rule). 2. Describe work environment and user profile in the work area header. 3. Define task purpose, triggers, frequency, and critical scenarios. 4. Detail essential sub-tasks (domain level: human and computer combined). 5. List realistic sub-task variants and exception cases.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is the ultimate goal of this work session? When do you feel this task is complete? What special or unusual cases happen?
Minimal Realistic Example: Task 1.2: Checkin. Purpose: Give guest a room, mark occupied. Trigger: Guest arrives. Sub-tasks: 1. Find room 2. Record guest 3. Deliver key. Variants: 1a. Guest pre-booked.
Quality Criteria & Verification: User validation walkthrough, CRUD matrix check, task execution walkthrough during system test.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Writing low-level programming steps instead of domain goals; defining tasks that lack closure (e.g., 'enter text').
When NOT to Use: Purchasing low-level technical components or maintenance projects focused strictly on isolated software bug fixes.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Tasks & Support, Use Cases, Activity Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: COTS vendor selection, business process redesign, user acceptance test planning.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Analyze user transcriptions or observation logs to generate structured task templates with variants.

Problem Solved: Balances domain-level user task demands against candidate software product features, bridging problem specification and solution evaluation.
Input Artifacts: Domain task descriptions, stakeholder problem lists, vendor proposals.
Output Artifacts: Two-column task tables detailing domain sub-tasks/problems on the left and proposed/agreed software support on the right.
Participants & Roles: BA, SME, product vendor/developer, customer project team.
Prerequisites: Domain task identification and SME availability.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Document domain sub-tasks and operational problems in the left column using imperative language. 2. Detail task triggers, frequency, and critical situations. 3. Provide candidate product support features or example solutions in the right column. 4. Submit table to vendors/developers during tender or design phases. 5. Evaluate proposals and convert the right column to agreed project commitments.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is the main problem with how you do this step today? How could a computer best support you here?
Minimal Realistic Example: Sub-task: 1. Find room. Problem: Guest wants neighboring rooms. Example Solution: System shows free rooms on visual floor map.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Stakeholder review, vendor proposal scoring, task walkthrough verification during acceptance testing.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Writing traditional feature specifications directly inside the left column; failing to update column headings during contract lifecycle.
When NOT to Use: Pure technical sub-contracting projects where no human interface exists.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Task Descriptions, Features from Task Descriptions, Use Cases.
Supported Decisions: Vendor selection in tenders, COTS fit-gap analysis, scope vs. cost trade-off decisions.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Auto-populate candidate technical solutions in the right-hand column by prompting AI agents with domain sub-tasks and vendor feature sheets.

Problem Solved: Provides vivid illustration of real-world user situations to sharpen developer intuition and create realistic test cases.
Input Artifacts: User stories, workplace observation logs, critical incident reports.
Output Artifacts: Vivid narrative case stories or specific instance test cases.
Participants & Roles: BA, end user, developer, tester.
Prerequisites: Basic understanding of user tasks and work environment.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify a critical, frequent, or stressful work situation. 2. Write a narrative story detailing a specific user acting in a realistic context. 3. Incorporate realistic details (time, stress, environment, interrupts). 4. Use narrative to derive domain requirements, variants, or test cases.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Can you tell me a story about a particularly difficult shift you had recently? What happened step-by-step?
Minimal Realistic Example: Story of receptionist Doug preparing for 50 bus tourists at 7 PM while handling a walk-in family asking for adjoining rooms.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Verification as valid test cases during usability or acceptance testing.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Treating vivid narrative scenarios as formal requirements specifications.
When NOT to Use: Formal contractual specifications requiring complete coverage.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Task Descriptions, Use Cases, Activity Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Test case generation, developer domain orientation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Generate realistic persona-driven narrative stories from structured task descriptions using LLMs.

Problem Solved: Identifies overarching client business processes to enable Business Process Re-engineering (BPR) and avoid local sub-optimization.
Input Artifacts: Business goals, client journey maps, high-level process flows.
Output Artifacts: High-level task descriptions centered around the end-client's total business case.
Participants & Roles: BA, business owner, client/end-user, consultant.
Prerequisites: Identification of end-clients and strategic business goals.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify the ultimate end-client's goal (e.g., 'A stay at the hotel'). 2. Outline client sub-tasks from start to finish. 3. Identify client pain points and operational bottlenecks across sub-tasks. 4. Brainstorm radical BPR solutions (e.g., self-service Web options). 5. Decompose validated high-level tasks into operational user tasks.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is the client trying to achieve from start to finish? Where do clients experience delays or friction in this journey?
Minimal Realistic Example: Task 1: A stay at the hotel. Client Sub-tasks: 1. Select hotel 2. Book 3. Check in 4. Receive service 5. Check out 6. Reimburse expenses.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Traceability matrix connecting high-level tasks to business goals and operational sub-tasks.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Designing system features around existing clerical staff steps without considering the client's high-level workflow.
When NOT to Use: Small maintenance projects or minor software enhancements.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Tasks & Support, Value Stream Mapping, Goal-Domain Tracing.
Supported Decisions: Business process re-engineering, strategic IT investment choices, system scope boundaries.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Map end-to-end customer journey maps to high-level BPR tasks using strategic AI prompts.

Problem Solved: Specifies product-centric functional interactions and system boundary behaviors for software developers.
Input Artifacts: Context diagrams, task descriptions, domain event lists.
Output Artifacts: Use case diagrams, textual use case specifications (Actor/System interaction steps).
Participants & Roles: BA, system architect, developer, tester.
Prerequisites: Clear definition of system boundaries and actors.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify actors and system boundaries. 2. Define use case bubbles representing product-provided functional units. 3. Specify interaction steps (User Action / System Response). 4. Detail preconditions, postconditions, and alternative execution branches. 5. (Optional) Define include and extend relationships between use cases.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What input does the user send to the system? What specific validation and response does the product execute?
Minimal Realistic Example: Use Case: Check in booked guest. User: Enters booking number. System: Displays guest details. User: Pushes checkin. System: Allocates room, displays room number.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Developer code review, automated system test scripting.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Creating hundreds of trivial, tiny use cases (e.g., 'Enter name'); specifying premature UI dialog details in domain use cases.
When NOT to Use: COTS acquisition projects where internal system interaction sequences are already built.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Task Descriptions, Tasks & Support, Activity Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Software object architecture, system test case design.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Convert user stories or task descriptions into formal UML use case specifications using AI agents.

Problem Solved: Ensures that all visible data required by a user to complete each sub-task variant is explicitly identified for screen design and verification.
Input Artifacts: Task descriptions, E/R data model, Virtual Windows.
Output Artifacts: Three-column table listing Sub-tasks/Variants, Visible Data Needs, and Related Screen Windows.
Participants & Roles: BA, UI designer, SME, developer.
Prerequisites: Completed task descriptions and draft E/R data model.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Take sub-tasks and sub-task variants from task descriptions. 2. For each sub-task/variant, detail the specific data items the user must see or enter. 3. Cross-check data items against the E/R model. 4. Map data needs to candidate screen windows and search criteria. 5. Review mappings with UI designers.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What exact pieces of data do you need to see on the screen to decide which room to choose?
Minimal Realistic Example: Sub-task 1a (No suitable room): Visible Data = All free rooms, price, available discounts; Virtual Window = Rooms (Criteria: dates).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Traceability check against E/R model fields; UI layout verification during prototype reviews.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Listing technical database fields instead of user-perceived domain information.
When NOT to Use: Projects purchasing standard COTS software without custom screen development.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Virtual Windows, Task Descriptions, CRUD Matrix.
Supported Decisions: UI screen layout, UI data binding specifications.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Map entity model attributes automatically to sub-task steps using domain reasoning prompts.

Problem Solved: Models processes, data stores, and data flows to specify exact data transformations and information movements across domain or product boundaries.
Input Artifacts: Context diagram, event lists, data expressions, existing process docs.
Output Artifacts: Dataflow diagrams (Bubbles, Data Stores, Data Flows, External Entities) and Data Expressions.
Participants & Roles: BA, system architect, developer.
Prerequisites: Defined context boundary and system interfaces.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify external entities and top-level process bubbles. 2. Draw data flow arrows carrying named data structures between processes, stores, and entities. 3. Specify incoming and outgoing data flows using data expressions. 4. Decompose complex bubbles into second-level dataflow diagrams. 5. (For product level) Split domain bubbles into separate user and computer bubbles.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What data enters this process? Where is this data stored? What transformed data leaves this function?
Minimal Realistic Example: Bubble 'FindFreeRoom' receives 'period+room type' from user, queries 'Rooms' data store, and outputs 'free rooms' list to user.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Data balance checks between hierarchy levels, CRUD check against data stores.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Over-specifying strict process execution sequences inside DFDs (DFDs show data flow, not control flow).
When NOT to Use: Describing event-driven user interface screens with complex, non-sequential user interactions.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Activity Diagrams, Task Descriptions, Use Cases.
Supported Decisions: System architecture, system data interface definitions, workflow engine configuration.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Convert process descriptions into structured DFD dataflow connections and syntax trees using LLMs.

Problem Solved: Transfers detailed regulatory, platform, or interface specifications to external standard documents, avoiding redundant specification writing.
Input Artifacts: Industry regulations, corporate style guides, technical interface manuals.
Output Artifacts: Textual requirement statements referencing external standards.
Participants & Roles: BA, compliance officer, legal advisor, developer.
Prerequisites: Identification of applicable legal, regulatory, or technical standards.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify applicable external domain or technical standards. 2. Verify the relevance and version of the standard. 3. Draft requirement statements referencing the specific standard and release. 4. Define compliance and certification responsibilities (e.g., supplier must obtain certificate). 5. Specify ongoing maintenance obligations for evolving standards.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Which union agreements or accounting laws apply? Which specific version of the platform style guide must be enforced?
Minimal Realistic Example: R4: The product shall follow good accounting practice. The supplier shall obtain the necessary certification.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Third-party certification, compliance audit reviews.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Blindly referencing standards without understanding their business goals or practical verification costs.
When NOT to Use: When custom, project-specific behavior is required that contradicts public standards.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Feature Requirements, Process Descriptions.
Supported Decisions: Legal compliance, technical architecture alignment, platform selection.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Scan requirement documents for regulatory gaps against pre-loaded compliance standard frameworks using AI agents.

Problem Solved: Mitigates high requirement uncertainty or scope volatility by specifying the development and change management process rather than fixed product features.
Input Artifacts: Project charter, risk management plan, agile development methodology outlines.
Output Artifacts: Contractual process requirements (e.g., prototyping iterations, change management rules, unit pricing formulas).
Participants & Roles: BA, project manager, customer, supplier.
Prerequisites: High project uncertainty where fixed-price feature specification is unfeasible.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify volatile or highly uncertain system requirement areas. 2. Define required iterative development processes (e.g., 3 prototype iterations). 3. Establish change management procedures and bi-weekly review boards. 4. Define unit pricing structures (e.g., price per additional screen or Function Point). 5. Incorporate process requirements into the contract.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How will we evaluate change requests? What unit pricing formula will govern unforeseen additions?
Minimal Realistic Example: R1: System development shall use iterative development based on prototypes. R2: Supplier shall deliver additional screens at $X per screen.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Process audit, joint review sign-offs, adherence to change board protocols.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Committing to fixed-price development without locking down either features or process pricing rules.
When NOT to Use: Simple, well-known COTS purchases with fixed, non-negotiable scopes.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Tasks & Support, Open Target / Open Metric Requirements.
Supported Decisions: Contract pricing structure, vendor engagement model, change management governance.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Monitor change request logs automatically and calculate impact estimates based on contractual unit pricing rules.

Method Name: Decision Tables and Informal Rules Tables
Problem Solved: Specifies non-trivial business logic, conditional rules, and complex calculations unambiguously without writing code.
Input Artifacts: Business policy documents, SME interview notes, pricing rules.
Output Artifacts: Decision tables (Conditions vs. Actions matrix) or informal business rule tables.
Participants & Roles: BA, SME, developer, tester.
Prerequisites: Identification of conditional business logic with multiple combinations.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify all basic input conditions affecting the decision. 2. List all possible outcome actions. 3. Create a matrix grid with conditions on top and actions below. 4. Populate condition columns with Yes/No/Don't Care combinations. 5. Mark the corresponding actions for each condition column. 6. Check table for completeness, contradictions, and redundant rules.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What conditions determine this discount? What action happens if condition A is true but condition B is false?
Minimal Realistic Example: Matrix listing 6 discount conditions (e.g., 'Before 6pm', 'Hotel <50% booked') mapped to specific discount percentage actions (e.g., 'Room discount 25%').
Quality Criteria & Verification: Logical completeness check (2^N conditions check), test case generation covering all table columns.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Attempting to model sequential program loops or procedural workflows inside decision tables.
When NOT to Use: Simple, unconditional functions or highly algorithmic code with loops.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Textual Process Descriptions (Pseudo-code), Activity Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Business rules engine configuration, pricing logic specification, automated test case design.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Automatically generate complete decision tables from raw business policy text using AI logic parsers.

Problem Solved: Provides precise algorithmic specifications for semi-complex functions, buttons, or methods where developer guessing is risky.
Input Artifacts: UI prototypes, event lists, decision tables, data dictionary.
Output Artifacts: Textual mini-specifications / pseudo-code detailing Input, Entry State, State Changes, and Output.
Participants & Roles: BA, developer, tester.
Prerequisites: Selected UI screens or defined product-level functions.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify non-trivial product functions or UI event buttons. 2. Specify input parameters and explicit/implicit entry state conditions. 3. Write algorithmic steps detailing state changes (database updates). 4. Specify output parameters or screen state updates. 5. Review pseudo-code with developers for clarity.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What entry state is required before this function runs? What exact database updates occur step-by-step?
Minimal Realistic Example: Function Checkin(CurrentStay, CurrentRooms): If CurrentStay is booked, record rooms as occupied. If guest not recorded, check data complete, record guest.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Developer code review, unit test execution against algorithm steps.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Over-specifying obvious, trivial functions (e.g., standard field entry); attempting to specify mathematically impossible or expert-level algorithms.
When NOT to Use: Trivial CRUD functions or highly complex expert-level algorithms (e.g., 3D graphics rendering).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Decision Tables, Activity Diagrams, Sequence Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Detailed program logic design, unit test case creation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Translate pseudo-code specifications directly into candidate programming code blocks or test scripts.

Problem Solved: Models entity life cycles and identifies missing state-transition functions or illegal event sequences.
Input Artifacts: Data model, event list, business rules.
Output Artifacts: State transition diagram (State boxes, Event transition arrows, Start/End markers).
Participants & Roles: BA, system architect, developer, SME.
Prerequisites: Identification of entities with multi-state life cycles.
