Step-by-Step Procedure: Select a complex entity or dialog object. 2. Identify all valid operational states of the entity (rounded boxes). 3. Draw arrows between states representing allowable event transitions. 4. Annotate arrows with the triggering event names. 5. Identify dead ends, missing transition events, or unreachable states. 6. Validate life cycle transitions with SMEs.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What state does this room enter when cancelled? Can a booked room transition directly to repair?
Minimal Realistic Example: Entity 'RoomState' with states (Free, Booked, Occupied, Repair) connected by event arrows (book, checkin, checkout, cancel, repair).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Verification against developer implementation code, state coverage test design.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Creating state diagrams for simple entities that have trivial two-state life cycles (Exists/Deleted).
When NOT to Use: Simple data entities without multi-state transitions.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: State-Transition Matrices, Activity Diagrams, Sequence Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Entity life cycle design, UI navigation map design, event validation logic.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Extract entity states and valid transition triggers from requirement text to construct PlantUML state diagrams automatically.

Problem Solved: Exhaustively analyzes all combinations of states and events to uncover hidden requirements, edge cases, and illegal operations.
Input Artifacts: State diagram, event list, data model.
Output Artifacts: State-Transition Matrix (Events on Y-axis, States on X-axis, cell actions/next-states).
Participants & Roles: BA, system architect, developer, tester.
Prerequisites: Complete list of entity states and possible system events.
Step-by-Step Procedure: List all entity states along the horizontal axis. 2. List all possible system events along the vertical axis. 3. Systematically evaluate every intersecting matrix cell. 4. Specify the resulting new state, error action, or invalid indicator (-) in each cell. 5. Add explanatory footnotes for complex cell actions or edge cases. 6. Review edge cases with SMEs.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What happens if a 'Cancel' event arrives while the room is in 'Occupied' state? What if 'ChangeRoom' occurs during 'Booked' state?
Minimal Realistic Example: Matrix with 4 states and 7 events; cell for Event 'Checkin' in State 'Booked' transitions to State 'Occupied' with footnote explaining stay date handling.
Quality Criteria & Verification: 100% matrix cell coverage check, edge-case test suite generation.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Applying to huge systems with hundreds of states, resulting in massive, sparse, unreadable matrices.
When NOT to Use: Simple entities or large systems where a state diagram gives a cleaner visual overview.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: State Diagrams, Decision Tables.
Supported Decisions: Robust event handling architecture, error handling design, complete test suite generation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Automatically populate state-transition matrix cells and flag undefined state-event combinations using AI logic engines.

Problem Solved: Models complex workflows involving parallel execution threads, swim lanes, and control/data synchronization across actors.
Input Artifacts: Task descriptions, workflow models, event lists.
Output Artifacts: UML Activity Diagram (Swim lanes, Action barrels, Control flows, Objects, Fork/Join bars, Guard conditions).
Participants & Roles: BA, workflow architect, developer, SME.
Prerequisites: Identification of actors and workflow steps across boundaries.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define swim lanes representing actors or subsystems. 2. Place action/activity rounded boxes in appropriate swim lanes. 3. Draw solid arrows showing sequential flow of control. 4. Add decision diamonds with guard conditions in brackets . 5. Add synchronization bars for parallel fork and join operations. 6. Draw dashed arrows for object/data flows between activities.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Which steps occur in parallel? Which conditions trigger this branch? What data object is passed between these actors?
Minimal Realistic Example: Workflow across 'Guest', 'Hotel', and 'Bank' swim lanes showing room checking, credit checks, and booking confirmation with fork/join synchronization.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Workflow walkthrough with SMEs, business process simulation.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Drawing control arrows across actor swim lanes instead of passing data objects; using activity diagrams as a replacement for structured programming flowcharts.
When NOT to Use: Simple, single-user sequential screen interactions.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Dataflow Diagrams, Task Descriptions, Sequence Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Workflow engine configuration, cross-system process integration, parallel processing architecture.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Convert process descriptions into structured PlantUML activity diagrams complete with swimlanes and synchronization bars using LLMs.

Problem Solved: Models internal software object structures by encapsulating data attributes and operational methods into object classes.
Input Artifacts: Data model, process descriptions, system architecture notes.
Output Artifacts: UML Class Diagram (Class boxes with attributes and operations, Association lines with numeric cardinalities).
Participants & Roles: System architect, developer, BA.
Prerequisites: Detailed understanding of object-oriented software design.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify object classes based on system domain or software artifacts. 2. List class attributes and data types in the middle compartment. 3. List operations/methods and parameters in the bottom compartment. 4. Connect classes with association lines annotated with explicit numeric cardinalities (e.g., 1..*). 5. (For business applications) Separate data objects from complex service/observer objects.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What methods operate on this data? Which class is responsible for executing this calculation?
Minimal Realistic Example: Class 'Stay' with attributes (stay#, paymethod) and operations (checkout, recordService) connected 1..* to Class 'RoomState'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Object design review, automated unit test coverage.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Mixing human domain tasks into object methods; attempting to encapsulate complex business logic directly inside database data objects.
When NOT to Use: Domain-level requirements specifications for business application procurement.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Data Model (E/R), Collaboration Diagrams, Sequence Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Object-oriented software architecture, database persistence framework design.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Auto-generate class diagrams and Java/C++ class boilerplates from pseudo-code specs using coding AI agents.

Problem Solved: Visualizes how software objects co-operate and exchange numbered message calls to complete a specific system function.
Input Artifacts: Class diagram, textual process descriptions, use cases.
Output Artifacts: UML Collaboration Diagram (Object boxes, structural links, numbered message call arrows).
Participants & Roles: System architect, developer.
Prerequisites: Completed static class diagram.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify the software objects involved in executing a specific function. 2. Draw structural link lines between co-operating objects. 3. Draw message arrows along the links indicating call direction. 4. Number messages sequentially (e.g., 1, 1.1, 1.1.1) to show call hierarchy. 5. Annotate messages with operation names and parameters.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Which object calls which method to gather this invoice line item? In what sequence do these sub-routine calls occur?
Minimal Realistic Example: Object 'Stay' sends numbered message 1.1 *getService to 'Service', which in turn sends 1.1.1 getServicePrice to 'ServiceType'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Code walkthrough, object interaction testing.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Attempting to use collaboration diagrams for user interface requirements or non-technical stakeholder reviews.
When NOT to Use: User interface requirements elicitation or high-level business process modeling.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Sequence Diagrams, Activity Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Internal object interaction design, API internal sub-routine routing.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Parse multi-object execution traces into PlantUML collaboration diagrams automatically.

Problem Solved: Specifies dynamic, time-ordered message sequences, synchronous/asynchronous events, and protocol handshakes between actors or technical components.
Input Artifacts: Use cases, interface specifications, event lists.
Output Artifacts: UML Sequence Diagram (Actor lifelines, activation bars, synchronous/asynchronous arrows, reply lines).
Participants & Roles: System architect, developer, integration engineer.
Prerequisites: Identification of communicating components and message types.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Place communicating actors/components horizontally across the top. 2. Draw vertical dashed lifelines extending downwards representing time. 3. Draw horizontal message arrows between lifelines in chronological order. 4. Use solid black arrowheads for synchronous calls and half arrowheads for asynchronous messages. 5. Add activation boxes on lifelines showing execution duration. 6. Draw dashed return arrows for reply messages.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Does the sender wait for a reply before continuing? What exact data payload is returned in the handshake reply?
Minimal Realistic Example: Sequence showing 'Product' sending 'Transfer' event to 'Account System', receiving 'OK' reply, followed by sequential data packet messages and a 'Done' notification.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Protocol conformance testing, interface verification testing.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Failing to distinguish synchronous blocking calls from asynchronous events; using for broad, flexible user workflows.
When NOT to Use: Flexible, non-deterministic user interface screen workflows.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Collaboration Diagrams, Activity Diagrams, State Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Technical interface protocol design, dynamic API sequencing, sub-system integration design.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Generate PlantUML sequence diagrams automatically from API documentation or message trace logs using AI agents.

Problem Solved: Systematically prioritizes quality factors (non-functional requirements) and identifies critical business quality concerns before specifying metrics.
Input Artifacts: List of quality factors (McCall, ISO 9126), project charter.
Output Artifacts: Quality Grid table (Quality Factors vs. Priority levels: Critical, Important, As Usual, Unimportant) with annotated business concerns.
Participants & Roles: BA, sponsor, business owner, architect, QA manager.
Prerequisites: Understanding of business goals and overall project constraints.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select a comprehensive list of quality factors (e.g., McCall's 11 factors). 2. Evaluate and mark the priority level for each factor relative to normal standards. 3. Force stakeholders to balance priorities (not everything can be Critical). 4. For every 'Critical' or 'Important' factor, document the specific business concern behind the rating. 5. Use the prioritized grid to guide detailed quality metric selection.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Why is availability critical in this project? What specific business loss occurs if this quality factor is at a normal level?
Minimal Realistic Example: Grid rating Reliability/Availability as 'Critical' with Concern: 'Hard to run hotel if system is down; room status not visible.'
Quality Criteria & Verification: Sponsor sign-off, alignment with project budget and resource constraints.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Rating every quality factor as 'Critical' without budget justification, leading to unrealistic project scope.
When NOT to Use: Small, trivial projects where quality needs are standard and self-evident.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Planguage, Risk Assessment.
Supported Decisions: Quality requirement prioritization, QA resource allocation, architectural trade-offs.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Prompt AI to evaluate project charters against quality taxonomies to draft initial candidate quality grids.

Method Name: Open Metric and Open Target Requirements
Problem Solved: Prevents arbitrary or unrealistically expensive quality targets by inviting suppliers to specify achievable metrics or performance targets based on their expertise.
Input Artifacts: Quality grid, stakeholder expectation notes.
Output Artifacts: Textual quality requirements with open blanks for suppliers to fill in, combined with customer expectation anchors.
Participants & Roles: BA, customer project manager, vendor.
Prerequisites: Identification of a non-mandatory or soft quality factor.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify a quality factor where the exact target value is uncertain or cost-sensitive. 2. Define the measurement scale and test procedure. 3. Leave the target value blank for the supplier to specify in their proposal. 4. Optionally append the customer's benchmark expectation in parentheses. 5. Evaluate supplier proposals during tender based on offered target vs. price.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What response time can your standard product guarantee? What forecast accuracy can you commit to for a business of our size?
Minimal Realistic Example: R5: Product shall compute a room occupation forecast within ___ minutes. (Customer expects one minute.)
Quality Criteria & Verification: Verification testing against supplier's proposed value during system/acceptance testing.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Using open targets for physically mandatory constraints (e.g., real-time valve control) where a fixed limit is non-negotiable.
When NOT to Use: Hard real-time technical systems where targets are governed strictly by physical laws.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Planguage, Standard Quality Requirements.
Supported Decisions: Vendor proposal comparison, cost vs. quality trade-offs, contract target negotiations.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Analyze vendor response proposals to automatically extract and benchmark filled-in open targets across competitors.

Problem Solved: Defines quality requirements with extreme quantitative precision using a structured syntax for scales, meters, baseline values, and target benchmarks.
Input Artifacts: Quality grid, stakeholder goals, benchmark metrics.
Output Artifacts: Planguage requirement statements (Tag, Gist, Scale, Meter, Must, Plan, Wish, Past).
Participants & Roles: BA, system architect, QA manager, vendor.
Prerequisites: Identification of key quality factors needing quantitative control.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define a unique Tag and brief Gist for the quality requirement. 2. Define the exact measurement Scale. 3. Define the practical test procedure (Meter). 4. Specify baseline historic performance (Past). 5. Define mandatory survival threshold (Must), target goal (Plan), and ideal goal (Wish). 6. Review parameters with stakeholders and suppliers.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is the worst acceptable performance before the system is rejected (Must)? How exactly will we measure this in practice (Meter)?
Minimal Realistic Example: Tag: Forecast Speed. Scale: Seconds from button push to report. Meter: Stopwatch during peak hours. Must: 8 min. Plan: Supplier fill. Wish: 2 min. Past: 1 hour.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Quantitative verification testing according to the defined Meter specification.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Over-specifying Planguage for trivial quality factors, creating overly complex documents.
When NOT to Use: Simple projects where standard informal quality targets suffice.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Open Metric & Open Target Requirements, Quality Grid.
Supported Decisions: Contractual acceptance criteria, architectural trade-offs, quantitative SLA definitions.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Convert informal quality statements into fully structured Planguage parameter blocks using AI syntax templates.

Problem Solved: Identifies real user interface usability problems, task failures, and learnability roadblocks before code is locked in.
Input Artifacts: Realistic task scenarios, UI prototypes/mockups, user profile definitions.
Output Artifacts: Usability problem log (categorized by severity: Task Failure, Critical, Medium, Minor) and task time measurements.
Participants & Roles: Facilitator, log keeper, test subject (end user), developer.
Prerequisites: Paper mockup or functional UI prototype and representative end users.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Prepare realistic, closed test tasks without giving step-by-step instructions. 2. Brief the representative test user on the session rules. 3. Instruct the user to perform tasks while thinking aloud. 4. Facilitate without guiding or helping the user prematurely. 5. Log all observed user hesitation, misunderstandings, and task failures. 6. Classify problem severity and prioritize repair based on cost/benefit.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What are you thinking right now? What do you expect will happen if you click that button?
Minimal Realistic Example: Testing a hotel check-in prototype with 5 users, logging 3 task failures where users failed to locate the 'F10' search key.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Problem list classification, verification testing on revised prototypes.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Conducting system demos instead of tests; using internal developers as test subjects; testing late in the project after code is written.
When NOT to Use: Evaluating internal back-end algorithmic calculations with no human interface.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Heuristic Evaluation, Keystroke-Level Model, Usability Requirements.
Supported Decisions: UI design approval, front-end refactoring priorities, release readiness.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Analyze video/audio transcripts of usability sessions using AI to automatically extract and classify problem severity logs.

Problem Solved: Predicts and calculates the exact task execution time for experienced users on a computer interface without requiring user testing.
Input Artifacts: UI prototypes/screens, standard execution operators (Keystroke, Pointing, Homing, Mental preparation, System response).
Output Artifacts: Calculated task execution time predictions.
Participants & Roles: BA, UI designer, developer.
Prerequisites: Defined UI interaction sequence for an experienced user.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Break down the user's task interaction into standard primitive operators (K, P, H, M, R). 2. Assign standard time constants to each operator (e.g., K=0.2s, M=1.35s, H=0.4s). 3. Sum the operator times for the complete task sequence. 4. Add non-overlapped system response time (R). 5. Compare calculated times against usability efficiency targets.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How many keystrokes and mouse movements are required to complete this daily entry? Where do mental pauses occur?
Minimal Realistic Example: Calculating 100 room entries: (3 Keystrokes × 0.3s + 1 Mental × 1.35s + 0.35s Response) × 100 = 260 seconds (4.3 minutes).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Mathematical validation against standard KLM time tables.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Failing to account for mental preparation pauses (M=1.35s) or non-overlapped system response delays.
When NOT to Use: Predicting learnability for novice users who do not follow predictable expert keystroke paths.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Usability Testing (Task Time), Usability Requirements (Keystroke Counts).
Supported Decisions: UI layout optimization, comparison of candidate UI designs for high-frequency tasks.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Auto-calculate KLM execution times for proposed screen workflows directly from wireframe UI models using AI scripts.

Problem Solved: Identifies threat vulnerabilities, estimates financial losses per incident, and calculates annual expected losses to prioritize security safeguards.
Input Artifacts: System context diagram, threat catalogs, business asset values.
Output Artifacts: Security Risk Assessment Table (Threats, Annual Frequency, Loss per Hit, Total Loss per Year, Proposed Safeguards).
Participants & Roles: BA, security specialist, business owner, IT operations manager.
Prerequisites: Identification of critical system assets and data flows.
Step-by-Step Procedure: List potential threats across Input, Storage, and Output processes. 2. Estimate annual occurrence frequency for each threat (e.g., 10, 1, 0.1). 3. Estimate financial loss per hit ( $). 4. Multiply frequency by loss per hit to calculate total expected annual loss ($ /year). 5. Identify high-loss threat areas and evaluate cost-effective safeguards (Prevention, Detection, Repair).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is the financial impact if our database is completely lost? How frequently do we expect virus or credit fraud attacks?
Minimal Realistic Example: Threat: Disk crash. Frequency: 0.3/year. Loss per hit: $100,000. Annual Loss: $30,000/year. Proposed Safeguard: RAID mirrored disks.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Review by certified security auditors, financial risk alignment.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Ignoring soft threats (like internal fraud) while over-investing in extreme, low-probability threats (like nuclear attack).
When NOT to Use: Minor non-critical applications holding no sensitive data or financial assets.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Quality Grid, Threat and Safeguard Catalogs.
Supported Decisions: Security budget allocation, safeguard selection, disaster recovery planning.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Analyze system architecture diagrams using security AI agents to automatically flag threat vectors and estimate risk scores.

Problem Solved: Identifies all individuals or groups necessary for project success, along with their goals, risks, and potential resistance.
Input Artifacts: Project charter, organization charts, business goals.
Output Artifacts: Stakeholder Matrix/Catalog (Roles, Goals, Contributions, Risks, Perceived Rewards).
Participants & Roles: BA, project sponsor, project manager, candidate stakeholders.
Prerequisites: Initiation of a new IT project.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Brainstorm all internal and external groups affected by the project. 2. Interview key representatives from each stakeholder role. 3. Document their primary goals, expected rewards, and perceived risks/costs. 4. Identify potential conflicts between stakeholder groups. 5. Ensure each stakeholder group receives tangible benefits in the project scope.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Who pays for the system? Who will use it daily? What do you gain or fear from this new system?
Minimal Realistic Example: Matrix identifying Sponsor (wants cost savings), Receptionists (fear complex UI, want easy check-in), and IT Dept (want low maintenance).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Sponsor review, stakeholder coverage check.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Only consulting appointed middle managers while ignoring daily end users who operate the system.
When NOT to Use: None; applicable to all projects.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Focus Groups, Brainstorming, Context Diagram.
Supported Decisions: Change management strategy, user involvement planning, project scope trade-offs.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Extract stakeholder roles and potential resistance areas from meeting transcripts using LLMs.

Problem Solved: Elicits current problems, generates creative future visions, and establishes joint commitment across conflicting stakeholder groups.
Input Artifacts: Meeting room, flipcharts/whiteboard, stakeholder list.
Output Artifacts: Prioritized list of top stakeholder issues, problems, and future wishes (with rationale 'why').
Participants & Roles: Facilitator, log keeper, representatives from multiple stakeholder groups.
Prerequisites: Selection of 6–18 diverse stakeholders.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Invite 6–18 representatives across stakeholder groups. 2. Open session and establish ground rules (no criticism allowed). 3. Conduct roundtable on bad experiences and current problems; log on board. 4. Conduct visioning phase: Imagine the ideal future solution and capture 'why'. 5. Consolidate and edit the issue list in front of participants. 6. Have each stakeholder group select their top 10 non-prioritized issues. 7. Review selection to ensure every stakeholder group gains key benefits.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is the most annoying problem in your work today? If you could get whatever you wanted, what would the ideal system do and why?
Minimal Realistic Example: A 3-hour session with secretaries, engineers, and IT staff producing 40 issues, resulting in secretaries prioritizing 'automatic filing by subject' as a top wish.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Joint stakeholder agreement on top issue lists, balance of benefits across groups.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Allowing technical staff to criticize user wishes during the session; taking an mathematical average of priorities across groups.
When NOT to Use: When extreme interpersonal hostility prevents stakeholders from sitting in the same room.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Brainstorming, Group Interviews, Tasks & Support.
Supported Decisions: System vision freezing, high-level scope trade-offs, change management alignment.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Cluster and summarize raw focus group whiteboard notes into organized problem/wish categories using LLMs.

Problem Solved: Verifies that every business goal is supported by specific domain tasks/requirements, and that every specified task serves a business purpose.
Input Artifacts: Business goals list, task descriptions / work areas list.
Output Artifacts: Goal-Domain Matrix (Goals vs. Work Areas/Tasks) or Quality Function Deployment (QFD) House of Quality matrix.
Participants & Roles: BA, business owner, QA manager, system architect.
Prerequisites: Explicit list of business goals and defined domain tasks.
Step-by-Step Procedure: List business goals along matrix rows. 2. List domain work areas, tasks, or quality factors along matrix columns. 3. Evaluate intersections and mark cells where a task supports a goal. 4. Check for unlinked goals (missing requirements) and unlinked tasks (unjustified scope). 5. (For QFD) Add goal values, support weights, and function cost calculations.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Which specific task enables us to achieve this business goal? Why are we building this feature if it supports no stated goal?
Minimal Realistic Example: Matrix mapping Goal 'Use experience data for quotation' to Tasks 'Quotation' and 'Cost Registration', revealing that experience data capture was missing.
Quality Criteria & Verification: 100% trace coverage for all business goals; sign-off by business owner.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confusing functional requirements with business goals inside the QFD rows.
When NOT to Use: Small, simple projects where business goals and features are directly obvious.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Goal-Requirements Analysis, Traceability Matrix.
Supported Decisions: Scope verification, detection of missing requirements, feature justification.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Automatically map business goals to candidate task descriptions using semantic matching prompts.

Problem Solved: Evaluates project financial viability and compares hard monetary returns against soft quality factors to justify IT investments.
Input Artifacts: Business goals, vendor price quotes, operational cost estimates.
Output Artifacts: Cost/Benefit Table (Hard Benefits, Hard Costs, Net Present Value, Payback Period, Soft Factors score).
Participants & Roles: BA, sponsor, financial manager, IT manager.
Prerequisites: Estimates of project costs and quantifiable business benefits.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify hard benefits ($/year saved or gained). 2. Identify hard costs (supplier price, hardware, training, operational maintenance). 3. Discount future cash flows to calculate Net Present Value (NPV), Payback Period, and ROI. 4. Identify soft benefit factors (e.g., IT flexibility, stress reduction) and rate on a 0–5 scale. 5. Present combined hard/soft analysis to executive management.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How much money do we lose annually from these errors? What is the expected payback period for this investment?
Minimal Realistic Example: Hard Benefits ( $9M) minus Hard Costs ($ 1.7M) yielding NPV = $7.3M and payback in 2.5 years, alongside Soft Factor gains in stress reduction.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Financial audit review, ROI/payback threshold check.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Manipulating soft factors artificially to force a positive net value for a non-viable project.
When NOT to Use: Mandatory legal/regulatory compliance projects where the system must be built regardless of cost.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Goal-Domain Tracing, QFD.
Supported Decisions: Project charter approval, go/no-go investment decisions, vendor selection.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Run multi-variable NPV, payback, and sensitivity analyses automatically based on estimated cost parameters using financial AI models.

Problem Solved: Uncovers missing user tasks, missing system functions, or unmaintained database entities by systematically cross-checking data lifecycle operations.
Input Artifacts: Data model (entities), task descriptions / event list.
Output Artifacts: CRUD Matrix (Tasks/Events vs. Database Entities) with identified lifecycle gaps.
Participants & Roles: BA, developer, tester.
Prerequisites: Draft data model and draft task descriptions/event list.
Step-by-Step Procedure: List database entities along columns. 2. List user tasks or system functions along rows. 3. Populate cells with C (Create), R (Read), U (Update), D (Delete), or O (Overview). 4. Analyze bottom summary row for each entity. 5. Flag entities missing Create, Update, or Delete coverage. 6. Add missing tasks or retention requirements to resolve gaps.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How does this entity get created? Which task allows a user to update or delete this record?
Minimal Realistic Example: Matrix check revealing that 'Guest' entities had no 'Delete' task, leading to the creation of a data retention requirement.
Quality Criteria & Verification: 100% CRUD lifecycle coverage for all database entities.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Performing CRUD checks late in the development cycle after database schemas are frozen.
When NOT to Use: None; essential analysis technique for all data-centric applications.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Data Model, Tasks with Data, Event List.
Supported Decisions: Completeness verification, missing task discovery, data retention policy definitions.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Evaluate entity models against task lists to auto-detect missing CRUD operations using logic agents.

Problem Solved: Validates requirements completeness, correctness, and feasibility prior to contracting, identifying high-risk requirements for mitigation.
Input Artifacts: Draft requirements specification, review checklists, risk rating scales.
Output Artifacts: Review defect log, Risk Assessment Matrix (Customer Risk vs. Developer Risk per requirement), risk mitigation plan.
Participants & Roles: BA, customer review team, developer review team, QA manager.
Prerequisites: Completed draft requirements specification.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Customer and developer teams review draft spec independently. 2. Customer rates each requirement for risk (risk of not getting real needs met). 3. Developers rate each requirement for risk (risk of cost overruns or technical unfeasibility). 4. Conduct joint review meeting to log defects and discuss high-risk requirements. 5. Apply risk mitigation strategies (change requirement style, specify prototypes, isolate risk). 6. Update requirements specification.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Are you confident you can deliver this at a fixed price? Does this requirement truly reflect your operational need?
Minimal Realistic Example: Review flagging a rigid 0.5s max response time requirement as high-risk for developers, resulting in a change to a 95% statistical response time style.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Checklist sign-off, removal of high-risk items.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Debating solutions during the review meeting instead of logging defects; ignoring developer feasibility concerns.
When NOT to Use: None; mandatory prior to signing delivery contracts.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Prototype Testing, Walkthroughs, Checklists.
Supported Decisions: Contract sign-off, risk mitigation strategy, requirement style selection.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Scan requirements specifications against quality checklists to flag ambiguities, missing sections, and high-risk phrasing automatically.

Problem Solved: Reduces omission of critical non-operational stakeholders (regulators, beneficiaries, negative stakeholders) and clarifies project context/boundaries.
Input Artifacts: Sponsor requests, organization charts, project vision, context models
Output Artifacts: Stakeholder map (onion diagram), stakeholder matrix, influence diagrams, stakeholder responsibility lists
Participants & Roles: BA, Sponsor, Client, SME, Product Manager, Architect
Prerequisites: Project mission, sponsor brief, initial domain/context knowledge
Step-by-Step Procedure: Place the product/service at the center of the concentric ring model. 2. Identify operational roles in the innermost ring ('The System'). 3. Identify functional, financial, political, and social beneficiaries in 'The Containing System'. 4. Identify regulators, champions, purchasers, developers, and negative stakeholders in 'The Wider Environment'. 5. Label connections and draw influence/interaction arrows between roles. 6. Validate the diagram with project sponsors and domain experts.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Who has a valid interest in this product? Who will operate it? Who will benefit financially or functionally? Who regulates this domain? Who might oppose or be harmed by this system? Who interacts with or influences this role?
Minimal Realistic Example: Mapping a city tram service: innermost system includes tram drivers and mechanics; containing system includes passengers (functional beneficiaries) and the tram operating firm (financial beneficiary); wider environment includes city councils, safety regulators, and local residents (potential negative stakeholders).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Checked against context diagrams and interviews; covers operational, beneficiary, regulatory, and negative roles exhaustively; verified via stakeholder walkthroughs.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Focusing only on direct software users; treating surrogate roles as end-users without validation; ignoring negative stakeholders or regulatory bodies.
When NOT to Use: In extremely trivial or well-understood internal tasks where stakeholders are strictly fixed and known.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Organization charts, Soft Systems Methodology (Rich Pictures), Context Diagrams, i* Strategic Dependency Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Scope definition, stakeholder engagement strategy, project governance, resource allocation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic role discovery: LLM agents analyze project documentation, organizational charts, and regulations to automatically generate draft Onion Models and identify overlooked regulatory or security stakeholders. Human-in-the-loop validation is required to confirm stakeholder power and alignment.

Problem Solved: Resolves lack of clarity on project purpose, uncovers hidden conflicts between stakeholder desires, and prevents scope creep.
Input Artifacts: Mission statements, vision documents, stakeholder interview notes, problem statements
Output Artifacts: Goal diagrams, goal hierarchy tree, i* strategic dependency/rationale diagrams, list of obstacles and threats
Participants & Roles: BA, Sponsor, Product Manager, Business Owner, SME, End User, Compliance/Legal
Prerequisites: Identified list of key stakeholders and project mission.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify the top-level mission or business goal. 2. Decompose high-level goals into sub-goals (functional or quality) by asking 'How?'. 3. Trace sub-goals upwards to parent goals by asking 'Why?'. 4. Identify goal dependencies, support (+), and conflicts (-). 5. Identify obstacles and threats impeding goals. 6. Reconcile goal conflicts through design trade-offs or stakeholder negotiation.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What are you trying to achieve? Why do you want this feature? What does success look like? What could get in the way of achieving this goal?
Minimal Realistic Example: A spacecraft mission has a top-level goal 'Do Worthwhile Space Science'. Sub-goals include 'Carry Many Scientific Instruments' and 'Ensure Long Lifetime', which conflict through mass and power constraints with 'Affordable Launch Price'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Goals must be agreed upon by stakeholders, verifiable when refined into requirements, and free of unhandled conflicts.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Mistaking premature design solutions for goals; ignoring negative goals/threats; failing to resolve goal conflicts prior to specification.
When NOT to Use: When the project scope, technical solution, and requirements are fully known, standardized, and routine.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Problem Pyramid, Soft Systems Methodology, Rationale Modeling, Trade-Off Analysis (Optioneering).
Supported Decisions: Scope baseline, feature inclusion, design trade-offs, release priority.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLM agents extract goals and implicit conflicts from stakeholder transcripts and documentation, building automated Goal/Obstacle graphs. Human-in-the-loop review resolves trade-offs and negotiates conflicting objectives.

Problem Solved: Clarifies ill-defined, messy problem situations involving political, social, emotional, and organizational factors before fixing boundaries.
Input Artifacts: Interviews, domain observation notes, organizational issues, stakeholder complaints
Output Artifacts: Rich Picture diagram (informal conceptual cartoon/drawing of domain, actors, processes, and concerns)
Participants & Roles: BA, Business Owner, Sponsor, End User, SME, External Stakeholders
Prerequisites: Access to stakeholders and willingness to explore unstructured business contexts.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Observe and interview people in the business domain. 2. Draw an informal picture depicting actors, processes, inputs, outputs, external bodies, and physical assets. 3. Add symbols representing human emotions, conflict points, anxieties, and unwritten rules. 4. Use the picture in stakeholder workshops to discuss perspective differences. 5. Refine the drawing until a consensus on the real problem emerges.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is actually happening in this environment? Where are the friction points? Who feels threatened or concerned? What informal workarounds exist?
Minimal Realistic Example: A restaurant rich picture showing interactions between diners, waiters, cooks, suppliers, waste management, health inspectors (concerned about rats/insects), credit card processors, and tax authorities.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Validation through stakeholder walkthroughs; agreement that the drawing accurately captures the actual situation and core conflicts.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Making the diagram too formal or structured prematurely; omitting soft/social issues in favor of pure IT data flow.
When NOT to Use: When system boundaries, automated inputs/outputs, and operational events are already well-defined and uncontroversial.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Context Diagram, Mind Mapping, Use Case Diagram, Onion Model.
Supported Decisions: Problem definition, system boundary selection, scope of intervention.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic text processing synthesizes unstructured interview logs into descriptive scene descriptions, prompting multimodal AI models to generate candidate rich pictures for review by human business analysts.

Problem Solved: Eliminates scope creep by defining strict hard-system boundaries, external interfaces, and incoming/outgoing events.
Input Artifacts: Rich pictures, validated stakeholder list, domain boundary agreements
Output Artifacts: Context diagram, in/out scope list, incoming/outgoing event inventory, condition-action tables, 'when' requirements
Participants & Roles: BA, Architect, Developer, SME, Systems Engineer
Prerequisites: Agreed-upon soft system scope and identified external system neighbours.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Draw the proposed system/product as a single central box/circle. 2. Draw external entities (users, neighbouring hardware/software systems) outside the boundary. 3. Draw labeled data/signal/physical flow arrows crossing the boundary. 4. Compile an exhaustive event list for all incoming stimuli (external events and time triggers). 5. Define functional event-handling responses using 'When' statements or condition-action tables. 6. Explicitly document excluded items in an Out-of-Scope list.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What external systems connect to this product? What exact signals/data cross the boundary? What events wake the system up? What items are explicitly out of scope?
Minimal Realistic Example: An aircraft baggage system context diagram showing external entities (Air Traffic Control, Baggage Handling System, Refueling), boundary flows ('bags to load', 'fuel level'), and event-handling functions.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Exhaustive coverage of boundary flows; agreement with owners of external systems on interface specifications; event-handling logic verified against condition-action tables.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Drawing internal functional boxes inside the context circle; confusing use case actors with system boundary interfaces; omitting out-of-scope boundaries.
When NOT to Use: When organizational problem boundaries remain ill-defined, highly political, or fluid.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Use Case Diagrams, Rich Pictures, Enterprise Architecture Models, Data Flow Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: System architecture boundaries, project cost/effort estimation, interface contract definitions.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic parsing of interface documentation, API specs, and domain standards to generate precise Context Diagrams and Event-Handling tables, with automated verification of boundary completeness.

Problem Solved: Reduces ambiguity regarding operational requirements, usability failures, unhandled exceptions, and misalignment between developers and end users.
Input Artifacts: Goal models, event lists, user roles, domain definitions, business rules
Output Artifacts: User stories, storyboards, operational scenario step-lists, fully dressed use cases (including main/alternate/exception paths, preconditions, guarantees)
Participants & Roles: BA, SME, End User, Developer, Tester, UI/UX Designer
Prerequisites: Defined user roles and system boundary events.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify functional goals and primary roles (actors). 2. Draft the main success ('happy day') scenario as a numbered step-by-step sequence. 3. Brainstorm variation paths and exceptions for each step. 4. Write exception-handling scenarios (recovering or safe failure). 5. Define preconditions and success/minimal guarantees (postconditions). 6. Conduct walkthroughs, simulations, or prototypes to validate scenario flows.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is the first step? What does the operator do next? How does the system respond? What could go wrong at this step? What must be true before/after this scenario runs?
Minimal Realistic Example: Use Case 'Tune Radio' in a telematics system: Actor selects channel -> System tunes to frequency -> Audio plays. Exception: Signal lost -> System displays 'No Signal' and mutes audio output.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Scenario walkthroughs, user animation/simulation, 100% trace coverage of functional goals and acceptance test cases.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Writing use cases inside-out (making tiny UI button clicks separate use cases); omitting exception paths; overloading use cases with non-functional clutter.
When NOT to Use: When specifying pure algorithmic batch computations without user/system interaction.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Flowcharts, Activity Diagrams, User Stories, State Machine Diagrams, Sequence Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Software functional design, release planning, user acceptance test creation, user manual authoring.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic scenario expansion: AI agents generate exhaustive edge-case scenarios and exception flows from happy-day user stories, converting them into automated acceptance test scripts (BDD/Gherkin). Human review ensures domain relevance.

Problem Solved: Prevents late-stage product failures caused by poor performance, security breaches, safety hazards, unmaintainability, or regulatory non-compliance.
Input Artifacts: Stakeholder goals, regulatory standards, industry compliance guidelines, NFR checklists
Output Artifacts: Non-Functional Requirements (NFR) specification, quality goals model, compliance matrix
Participants & Roles: BA, Architect, Safety Engineer, Security Specialist, Compliance/Legal, SME
Prerequisites: Identified product context, operational environment, and applicable regulations.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Review goals, domain standards, and customized NFR checklists (performance, safety, security, usability, etc.). 2. Decompose vague quality goals ('easy to use', 'safe') into specific sub-goals. 3. Translate quality sub-goals into concrete functional requirements or measurable physical/design constraints. 4. Specify environmental, physical, and development process constraints. 5. Assign global vs. local scope (e.g., attaching NFRs to specific use cases). 6. Define testable criteria for each non-functional requirement.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How fast must this perform? What safety hazards exist? How secure must data be? What physical or environmental limits must the product withstand? What standards apply?
Minimal Realistic Example: Decomposing an outdoor leisure device's 'Dependable' quality goal into 'Waterproof to 3 atmospheres', 'Shockproof (survive 1m drop)', and 'Operational temperature -50C to +60C'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Verifiability (each NFR has an explicit measurement method and pass/fail criteria), consistency across global/local scopes, and architectural feasibility modeling.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Using unmeasurable buzzwords ('user-friendly', 'high-speed', '100% safe'); treating NFRs as an afterthought; imposing unrealistic/prohibitive constraints.
When NOT to Use: In lightweight internal utility scripts where operational qualities have minimal business impact.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: ISO/IEC 9126, IEEE 830 templates, Quality Function Deployment (QFD), Planguage (Gilb).
Supported Decisions: Architecture selection, hardware component picking, security model design, compliance sign-off.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agents cross-reference proposed specifications against legal/regulatory constraint databases (e.g., ISO, GDPR, FAA), automatically flagging missing compliance and environmental NFRs for human safety/legal expert approval.

Problem Solved: Eliminates unjustified or 'gold-plated' requirements, prevents loss of decision history during staff turnover, and protects key requirements from arbitrary deletion.
Input Artifacts: Vision statements, proposed requirements, change requests, risk logs, technical notes
Output Artifacts: Justification fields, assumption lists, rationale models (warrant/rebuttal graphs), Satisfaction Arguments, GSN/CAE safety cases
Participants & Roles: BA, Architect, Sponsor, Domain Specialist, Safety/Compliance Lead
Prerequisites: Draft requirements or proposed design choices requiring justification.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Analyze proposed features and ask 'Why is this needed?' or scan texts for giveaway words ('will', 'assumes'). 2. List explicit real-world assumptions underlying each requirement. 3. Model supporting arguments (warrants) and opposing arguments (rebuttals). 4. Invert identified risks into defensive functional/quality requirements. 5. Construct Satisfaction Arguments connecting requirements to parent goals. 6. Link requirements to their rationale via attributes or database traces.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Why do we need this requirement? What are we assuming about the operating environment? What happens if this assumption fails? What is the rebuttal to this argument?
Minimal Realistic Example: Justifying heating elements for a handheld device's CMOS processor: Assumption 1 ('Temperatures drop to -50C in mountains') + Assumption 2 ('CMOS fails below -20C') -> Requirement ('Provide internal processor heater'). Rebuttal ('Heater drains battery') -> Countermeasure ('Use insulated casing').
Quality Criteria & Verification: Completeness of rationale logic, validity of underlying assumptions, peer review of satisfaction arguments.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Circular justification ('Required because the client requested it'); documenting rationale for trivial self-evident items; duplicating rationale text across multiple items without tracing.
When NOT to Use: For standardized, self-explanatory, low-risk functional requirements.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Assumption-Based Planning (ABP), Goal Structuring Notation (GSN), QOC (Questions, Options, Criteria), Toulmin Argumentation.
Supported Decisions: Requirement prioritization, design option selection, risk mitigation, audit/compliance sign-offs.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLM agents monitor change requests and specifications to automatically extract implicit assumptions, construct Toulmin/GSN rationale graphs, and flag broken assumptions when project parameters change. Human approval validates argument logic.

Problem Solved: Prevents severe miscommunication, ambiguity, and software defects caused by synonyms, homonyms, domain jargon, and inconsistent data definitions.
Input Artifacts: Interview notes, domain documents, regulations, legacy database schemas, interface standards
Output Artifacts: Project dictionary (glossary designations, term definitions, acronym lists), Roles & Responsibilities matrix, UML Class Diagrams / ER Diagrams, data element catalog
Participants & Roles: BA, Data Modeller, Architect, SME, Developer
Prerequisites: Identified domain concepts, user roles, and system interfaces.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Capture unfamiliar terms, acronyms, and operational roles during elicitation. 2. Identify and resolve synonyms (different words for the same thing) and homonyms (same word with multiple meanings). 3. Create precise definitions (internal relationships) and designations (real-world pointers). 4. Define operational roles and map their functional responsibilities in a matrix. 5. Model business data entities, attributes, and relationships using UML Class or ER diagrams. 6. Express structural business rules directly as data model multiplicity and constraints. 7. Mark up terms in italicized text across specifications to link with the dictionary.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What exactly do you mean by this term? Are 'Customer' and 'Client' identical here? What attributes compose this data item? Who is authorized to execute this transaction?
Minimal Realistic Example: Resolving 'Equivalence' in a railway safety upgrade by defining 'Physical Equivalence' (identical hardware circuit board) vs. 'Functional Equivalence' (same decision-making logic in software).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Absence of unlinked/undefined italicized terms, absence of unresolved homonyms/synonyms, data model walkthroughs with SMEs.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Relying on generic corporate glossaries; creating redundant local definitions; allowing implicit unstated data constraints in models without explaining them to business stakeholders.
When NOT to Use: In brief exploratory spikes or small single-person scripts with no domain complexity.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Domain Driven Design (Ubiquitous Language), Entity-Relationship Modeling, UML Class Diagrams, CRUD Matrices.
Supported Decisions: Database schema design, user authorization design, software domain class design.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic glossary extraction: LLM agents scan all project artifacts to detect undefined acronyms, homonyms, and candidate data entities, populating a draft Project Dictionary and flagging naming conflicts for human BA resolution.

Problem Solved: Prevents delivery of unprovable, ambiguous, or unsatisfactory products and services by establishing objective, testable verification metrics up front.
Input Artifacts: Functional requirements, use cases, quality requirements, constraints, service level agreements (SLAs)
Output Artifacts: Acceptance criteria, postconditions/guarantees, Quality of Service (QoS) metrics, verification matrix (Test, Demo, Inspection, Analysis, Certificate)
Participants & Roles: BA, Tester/QA Lead, Architect, End User, Service Manager, Compliance Lead
Prerequisites: Draft functional, quality, and service requirements.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Review each requirement/use case and ask 'How will we test/prove this?'. 2. Define quantitative thresholds or specific postconditions (success and minimal guarantees). 3. For services, define continuous or sampling-based Quality of Service (QoS) metrics (repeatable, objective, representative). 4. Assign an explicit verification method (Test, Demonstration, Inspection, Analysis, Certificate) to each item. 5. Review criteria with QA/test engineers to ensure testability and affordability.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How will we know this requirement has been met? What specific output confirms success? How can we measure this service quality continuously? What is the pass/fail threshold?
Minimal Realistic Example: For a radio tuning function: Requirement = 'Tune to radio channel within 3 seconds'. Acceptance Criterion = 'Correct audio plays within 3.0 seconds from channel selection, verified by Audio Bench Test'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Verifiability (100% of requirements have explicit pass/fail acceptance criteria and assigned verification methods), test team walkthroughs.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Using unmeasurable words ('promptly', 'efficiently'); setting statistical targets that require cost-prohibitive sample sizes; using easily gamed QoS metrics.
When NOT to Use: During initial high-level goal brainstorming before technical feasibility and scope are understood.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Test-Driven Development (TDD/BDD acceptance tests), Fit Criteria (Gilb/Robertson), Service Level Agreements (SLAs).
Supported Decisions: Contractual sign-off, user acceptance, supplier payment authorization, service performance auditing.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic test synthesis: AI agents automatically convert functional requirements and acceptance criteria into executable Gherkin/Cucumber test scripts or automated unit/integration tests, flagged for QA engineer verification.

Problem Solved: Prevents project overruns and failure by making hard, realistic choices on what features to build, defer, or reject based on stakeholder value, technical cost, and risk.
Input Artifacts: Candidate goals/requirements, stakeholder preferences, cost/risk estimates from design options, dependency links
Output Artifacts: Input priority ratings (MoSCoW, 9-3-2-1, monetary allocation), Output priority ratings (release roadmap, Cherry Stones phase assignments, release matrices)
Participants & Roles: BA, Product Manager, Sponsor, Architect, Lead Developer, Customer Representative
Prerequisites: List of discovered candidate requirements, estimated costs/risks from candidate designs, and identified requirement dependencies.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Determine input priority (value to stakeholders) using techniques like voting, $100 allocation, or card sorting. 2. Perform Input Triage: reject or defer low-value goals. 3. Map requirement dependencies (scenario and infrastructural dependencies) to ensure dependent items share priority. 4. Evaluate cost, technical risk, and design feasibility (supply side). 5. Perform Output Triage (Optioneering): allocate high-value, feasible requirements into release phases (e.g., Phase 1, Phase 2, Future, Never). 6. Publish the baseline release roadmap.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How important is this to the stakeholder? What happens if we do not include this in Phase 1? What infrastructure does this feature depend on? Can this requirement be deferred safely?
Minimal Realistic Example: A software team uses MoSCoW to grade input priorities, groups features by infrastructural dependency (e.g., 'User Login' must precede 'Saved Preferences'), and assigns output priorities: 'Phase 1' (Now), 'Phase 2' (Later).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Consistency across dependent requirements, balanced distribution of priorities (avoiding '100% Mandatory'), stakeholder and dev team alignment.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Labeling all requirements as 'Mandatory/Must Have'; prioritizing individual features without accounting for infrastructure dependencies; ignoring dev cost/risk during prioritization.
When NOT to Use: When the project scope, budget, and implementation timeline are infinite or strictly fixed with a single monolithic release.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: MoSCoW, Cherry Stones method, Boston Matrix (Cost-Benefit Analysis), Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), QFD.
Supported Decisions: Release planning, budget allocation, baseline scope sign-off, supplier contract negotiations.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic dependency and roadmap optimization: AI algorithms analyze requirement dependency graphs, stakeholder weights, and cost/risk estimates to generate optimized release roadmaps, subject to human product manager approval.

Problem Solved: Elicits explicit stakeholder needs, personal perspectives, and detailed job knowledge directly from individual domain experts.
Input Artifacts: Interview plan, participant profiles, vision statement, Kipling's 6 questions prompt list, background documents
Output Artifacts: Interview transcripts/notes, raw goal lists, sketch models, validated interview summary reports
Participants & Roles: Lead Interviewer (BA), Scribe/Co-interviewer (BA/Tester), Interviewee (SME/Stakeholder)
Prerequisites: Identified stakeholder role, management permission, clear interview objectives, and background domain preparation.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define interview objectives and select target stakeholders. 2. Prepare interview guide using open-ended prompts (Kipling's Who, What, Why, When, Where, How). 3. Conduct interview in pairs (one primary interviewer, one scribe). 4. Use neutral, non-leading questions; play back understanding continuously. 5. Sketch real-time informal models (flowcharts, goal bubbles) during the session to confirm concepts. 6. Transcribe/clean notes immediately after the session. 7. Send summary report to interviewee for review, correction, and sign-off.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What do you do in your role? Why is that step necessary? Talk me through how you handle this task. What happens when an error occurs?
Minimal Realistic Example: An analyst interviews an accounts clerk about invoice processing, asking her to step through her daily routine and sketching a handwritten role/action list as she speaks.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Explicit sign-off and red-lining of notes by the interviewee, consistency with findings from other interviews, coverage of operational edge cases.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Asking leading questions; interviewing subordinates in the presence of their boss; trying to record complex UML diagrams on a laptop during the conversation instead of actively listening.
When NOT to Use: To discover multi-party business processes with complex cross-departmental conflicts (use workshops instead).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Observation/Apprenticeship, Workshops, Questionnaires/Surveys, Document Archaeology.
Supported Decisions: Individual user needs definition, initial goal discovery, workflow mapping.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic interview synthesis: Conversational AI agents conduct initial automated structured discovery interviews or transcribe human interview audio in real-time, extracting goals, entities, and requirements into draft models for BA validation.

Problem Solved: Uncovers tacit ('know-how') knowledge, unwritten real-world workarounds, and environmental constraints that users cannot easily explain in interviews.
Input Artifacts: Observation protocol, job descriptions, process manuals, safety clearances
Output Artifacts: Field notes, process flowcharts, video logs, paper prototypes of observed tasks, list of pain points and tacit requirements
Participants & Roles: Observer/Apprentice (BA), Master Craftsman/Practitioner (End User/Operator)
Prerequisites: Access to the operational environment, safety/confidentiality approvals, agreed observation format.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Choose observation style: Silent Observation, Talk-Through, or Apprenticeship (coached active participation). 2. Shadow the practitioner in their actual working environment. 3. Observe actual work sequences, tool usage, interruptions, and environmental factors. 4. In apprenticeship mode, perform simple tasks under practitioner coaching ('learning by doing'). 5. Record field notes, sketches, or video logs (with permission). 6. Debrief with the practitioner immediately after the session to clarify observed actions. 7. Document the observed workflow and validate with the user.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Can I try doing that step while you coach me? What are you looking at right now on that screen? Why did you perform that workaround just now?
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA shadows an air traffic controller or financial trader in a high-stress environment, observing rapid button presses, visual eye movements, and verbal shorthand that the operator could never describe in a sit-down interview.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Practitioner review of observed workflows, identification of tacit requirements missed in official rulebooks.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Assuming the official process rulebook reflects actual practice; interfering silently during critical operational tasks; generalizing a single user's unique habits as a universal requirement.
When NOT to Use: When the operational events are extremely rare (e.g., once-a-year audit tasks) or physically dangerous for an observer.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Contextual Inquiry, Interviews, Scenario Workshops, Video Analysis.
Supported Decisions: User interface design, operational workflow optimization, training program requirements.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Computer vision agents analyze video recordings of user workflows to automatically map task steps, screen interactions, and idle times, presenting candidate workflow diagrams to business analysts.

Problem Solved: Resolves cross-departmental conflicts, aligns disparate stakeholder viewpoints, and rapidly discovers comprehensive scenarios and goals in a high-energy collaborative setting.
Input Artifacts: Workshop agenda, mission statement, rich pictures, sticky notes, flipcharts, prototype models
Output Artifacts: Agreed goal clusters, swimlane charts, validated use cases, risk/threat lists, prioritized requirements list, workshop retrospective report
Participants & Roles: Facilitator, Scribe, Time-keeper, Rat-hole Watcher, Sponsor, Business SMEs, Technical Team (Architect/Dev/Test)
Prerequisites: Defined workshop purpose, selected cross-functional participants, pre-arranged room layout, and tested materials.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define workshop mission and invite a balanced cross-functional group. 2. Set up the room layout (U-shape/circle, ample wall space) and test tools. 3. Kick off with sponsor support and establish house ground rules and roles (Time-keeper, Rat-hole Watcher). 4. Execute planned collaborative activities (brainstorming, card sorting, role/action lists, acting scenes). 5. Document outputs continuously on walls/flipcharts or via digital photo capture. 6. Handle side-issues by placing them in a 'Parking Lot'. 7. Conduct a retrospective and distribute the summary report promptly for participant sign-off.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is the first step in this process? Does everyone agree with this definition? What could go wrong here? What is a higher priority for the business?
Minimal Realistic Example: A 1-day scenario workshop where retail staff, IT developers, and auditors use swimlanes on a wall to map an end-to-end checkout process, surfacing 12 exception scenarios and agreeing on priority fixes.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Active participation of all key roles, explicit sign-off on outputs by participants, post-workshop retrospective, resolution of parking lot items.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Turning the workshop into a passive lecture/presentation; inviting too many participants (>15-20); permitting dominant personalities to hijack discussion; lack of a dedicated scribe.
When NOT to Use: When stakeholders are extremely hostile and unwilling to communicate in a group setting, or for trivial single-user details.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Individual Interviews, Focus Groups, Delphi Technique, JAD (Joint Application Development).
Supported Decisions: Cross-functional scope baseline, use case approval, system trade-off consensus, release plan sign-off.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Multimodal AI assistants capture whiteboard photos, workshop audio, and sticky-note arrangements, automatically digitizing them into structured UML models, user stories, and action items in real time for facilitator review.

Problem Solved: Concretizes vague, abstract requirements, allows users to visualize proposed solutions, and uncovers missing functional/usability requirements early.
Input Artifacts: Draft scenarios, use cases, hand sketches, UI guidelines, paper/cardboard supplies, prototyping software
Output Artifacts: Throwaway paper/digital prototypes, storyboards, screen mockups, feedback log of newly discovered requirements
Participants & Roles: BA, UI/UX Designer, Prototyper ('Human CPU'), End User, SME
Prerequisites: Identified user goals and key operational scenarios to explore.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select throwaway prototyping medium (paper sketches, felt boards, presentation slides, or screens-only software). 2. Build quick, deliberately rough mockups corresponding to specific scenario steps. 3. Demonstrate the prototype to stakeholders by walking through a realistic story script. 4. Allow stakeholders to 'use' the prototype (e.g. pointing at paper buttons while a 'Human CPU' switches paper screens). 5. Observe reactions and capture immediate feedback on missing data or awkward flows. 6. Throw away or refine the prototype and update the requirement specifications.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Is this what you imagined? What information is missing from this screen? What button would you press next to achieve your goal?
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA draws a rough paper mockup of an electronic university enrollment screen on flipchart paper. Demonstrating it with an admissions clerk reveals that 'Prerequisite Course Verification' was missing from the initial requirements list.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Immediate user feedback capture, validation of task completion speed/accuracy, throwaway lifecycle sign-off.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Over-polishing prototypes so users think development is finished; spending excessive time coding backend logic for a throwaway mockup; falling into UI font/color debates instead of discovering functional needs.
When NOT to Use: When specifying backend batch algorithms, infrastructure protocols, or non-visual systems with no user interaction.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Storyboarding, Wireframing, Simulation, Evolutionary Prototyping, Acting Scenes.
Supported Decisions: User interface requirements baseline, workflow validation, functional scope selection.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Generative AI prototyping: Agents convert text user stories and sketches directly into interactive HTML/CSS UI prototypes in seconds, allowing users to test flows and provide instant feedback to refine specifications.

Problem Solved: Recovers lost or unwritten requirements from legacy systems, competitors' products, old manuals, and problem report databases during 'brown-field' development.
Input Artifacts: Legacy code, system user manuals, fault/defect databases, competitor products, old specification documents
Output Artifacts: Extracted business rules, functional requirement lists, bug-fix requirements, competitive feature matrix
Participants & Roles: BA, Systems Engineer, Maintenance Programmer, SME, Competitor Intelligence Analyst
Prerequisites: Access to legacy systems, codebases, user manuals, defect databases, or competitor samples.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Analyze legacy documentation ('archaeology') to extract original rationale, business rules, and error codes. 2. Systematically execute legacy software or simulators to map out existing operational capabilities. 3. Mine bug report databases and customer support logs to translate frequent user pain points into new requirements. 4. Analyze competitor products ('benchmarking') by testing user interfaces to identify innovative missing requirements. 5. Validate extracted requirements with current domain experts to weed out obsolete features.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What does the legacy system do when this error occurs? Why was this business rule originally implemented? What features do competitors offer that our users request?
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA mines 500 support tickets from an existing retail system, discovering that users frequently fail to complete returns due to an unstated authorization rule, which is then formally specified as a requirement for the upgrade.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Verification of extracted logic against legacy execution, SME validation of current business relevance.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Assuming legacy documentation is 100% accurate and up-to-date; blindly copying obsolete legacy bugs/limitations into new specifications; illegal/unethical code disassembly.
When NOT to Use: In pure 'green-field' domains where no legacy systems, analogous products, or competitors exist.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Competitor Benchmarking, Code Refactoring Analysis, Document Analysis, Change Management.
Supported Decisions: Legacy replacement scope, product upgrade roadmap, competitive feature parity.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic code and document archaeology: LLMs scan millions of lines of legacy code, system logs, and outdated PDFs to automatically extract business rules, decision tables, and data dictionaries for human BA review.

Problem Solved: Selects the optimal system design architecture among competing alternatives that best satisfies conflicting stakeholder requirements within cost, risk, and technical limits.
Input Artifacts: Input-prioritized stakeholder goals, proposed design options, engineering cost/risk estimates, evaluation criteria
Output Artifacts: Trade-off evaluation matrix, QOC diagrams, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) biplots, output-prioritized product specification, baseline design selection rationale
Participants & Roles: BA, Chief Architect, Systems Engineer, Product Manager, Sponsor, Domain Experts
Prerequisites: Validated stakeholder goals (criteria) and candidate technical design options.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Document input stakeholder goals (criteria). 2. Identify distinct technical design options (e.g., tram vs. subway vs. cablecar). 3. Convert goals into measurable evaluation criteria. 4. Score each design option against each criterion (quantitatively or via qualitative +/0/- scales). 5. Triage out options that fail mandatory constraints (e.g., safety limits). 6. Use qualitative decision frameworks (QOC, QFD) or statistical methods (PCA) to evaluate remaining options. 7. Select the winning design option through team/sponsor consensus. 8. Adjust requirements to match the capabilities of the winning design (setting output priorities).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Which design option best satisfies our top-priority goals? What are the cost, risk, and performance trade-offs of Option A versus Option B? Can we afford this design choice?
Minimal Realistic Example: An urban transport project uses PCA to evaluate four transit options across 11 criteria (cost, capacity, safety, traffic impact). While a subway scores highest on capacity, its prohibitive construction cost causes it to be triaged out in favor of an aerial cablecar.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Traceability of trade-off criteria to stakeholder goals, objective scoring validated by domain experts, mathematical validity of trade-off models (avoiding arbitrary naive weighting).
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Using arbitrary weighted scoring to add 'apples and oranges'; solutioneering (picking a favorite design before evaluating requirements); failing to triage out unsafe options.
When NOT to Use: When only one technical solution is feasible or pre-mandated by law/policy.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: QOC (Questions, Options, Criteria), QFD (Quality Function Deployment), PCA (Principal Component Analysis), Cost-Benefit Analysis, AHP.
Supported Decisions: System architecture selection, vendor selection, release scope baseline, output priority assignment.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic trade-off optimization: AI algorithms execute Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and multi-objective optimization across complex requirement/design option matrices, generating visual decision biplots and tradeoff summaries for executive review.

Problem Solved: Reduces uncertainty regarding system scope, unaligned stakeholder expectations, and undefined external system interfaces.
Input Artifacts: Vision Document, Business Process Reengineering (BPR) results, stakeholder analysis, existing project documentation.
Output Artifacts: Context Diagram, system boundary definition section.
Participants & Roles: Sponsor, BA/System Analyst, SME, Facilitator.
Prerequisites: High-level understanding of system goals and business problem.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Draw a large circle representing the system. 2. Identify external entities surrounding the circle. 3. Identify interactions/information flows between external entities and system. 4. Draw directed lines showing the direction and nature of interactions. 5. Review and validate boundaries with stakeholders.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Who or what interacts with the system from the outside? What information flows in and out? What hardware or external systems must we connect to?
Minimal Realistic Example: Loan Processing System interacts with Applicants (submits application), Credit Bureau (requests report), and Accounts Management System (retrieves history).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Stakeholder walkthrough; check if all external entities and high-level interaction flows are captured without detailing internal system logic.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Failing to define a clear boundary, leading to scope creep or forced inclusion of manual/external processes inside system scope.
When NOT to Use: When the system scope and boundaries are already fully known and agreed upon by all stakeholders.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Use Case Diagrams, Stakeholder Analysis.
Supported Decisions: Scope determination, preliminary architecture boundary decisions.

Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Fishbone (Ishikawa) Diagram, Root Cause Analysis, Problem Determination Game, Context-Free Questions.
Supported Decisions: Root cause confirmation, scope boundary decisions, solution feature prioritization.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic LLMs can iteratively prompt users with dynamic 'Why' questions based on textual analysis of previous answers, automatically tagging potential root causes in an issue-tracking system. Guardrails must prevent loop traps when user answers become circular.

Problem Solved: Resolves multi-stakeholder conflicts, reduces noisy symptom lists, eliminates out-of-scope/unowned requests, and isolates the single real business problem to solve.
Input Artifacts: Unfiltered list of stakeholder complaints, change requests, and candidate problem statements.
Output Artifacts: A single validated real problem statement, lists of out-of-scope issues, identified risks, and implied requirements.
Participants & Roles: Business Analysts (facilitators/analysts), Problem Owner, Key Stakeholders.
Prerequisites: Collection of multiple candidate problem statements from diverse business constituents.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Step 1: Gather all candidate problem statements from stakeholders and brainstormed lists. 2. Step 2: Filter out problem candidates that are out of scope (issues no one in the project can fix). 3. Step 3: Filter out candidates not owned by the target business unit paying for/authorizing the solution. 4. Step 4: Filter out non-relevant candidates (future 'if' scenarios or temporary conditions; move them to the risk list). 5. Step 5: Distinguish problems from requirements/constraints (eliminate items with only one possible solution). 6. Step 6: Distinguish problems from symptoms by systematically comparing remaining candidates to see if solving one completely eliminates others. 7. Conclude with a single real problem statement or present mutually exclusive alternatives to management.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: • Can anyone involved with the project do anything about this problem? • Is the problem owner within our target business organization? • Are you currently having this problem today? • Can anyone identify more than one solution to this issue? • When the problem identified in Statement A is solved, do Statements B, C, or D go away?
Minimal Realistic Example: Faced with 12 complaints (e.g., 'too much overtime', 'broken monitors', 'inaccurate payment calculations', 'high turnover'), the analyst filters out broken monitors (IT owned) and overtime budget (future risk), leaving 'inflexible vendor database terms' as the sole problem whose resolution clears all remaining symptom complaints.
Quality Criteria & Verification: The process must yield a single problem statement (or mutually exclusive set) stated in negative/constraining terms, stripped of pre-determined solutions, and verified to cause the listed secondary symptoms.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Selecting the problem definition based on executive hierarchy rather than systematic filtering; combining multiple unrelated problems using conjunctions ('and') instead of isolating the core problem.
When NOT to Use: When there is already a single, clear, uncontested, and fully validated problem statement established.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Five Whys, Root Cause Analysis, Pareto Analysis, Context-Free Questions.
Supported Decisions: Project initiation, problem prioritization, product scope definition, business case development.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: An agentic system can parse a repository of change requests, apply thematic clustering and dependency mapping to cross-reference items, and highlight potential root causes versus symptoms. Human analyst review is mandatory for final sign-off.
