Problem Solved: Defines explicit boundaries between project and product, mitigating scope creep and establishing clear decision criteria for project approval.
Input Artifacts: Confirmed real problem statement, product vision, stakeholder list, business case inputs, risk/constraint logs.
Output Artifacts: Product Scope Statement / Charter Section detailing problem, vision, acceptance criteria, functional goals, justifications, and constraints.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst (author), Problem Owner, Sponsor, Project Manager.
Prerequisites: Completed and confirmed real problem statement and product vision.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Draft the core statement using the structured formula template. 2. Insert the specific system/process solution scope. 3. Incorporate defined functional goals and desired vision. 4. Specify the acceptance criteria that prove problem resolution. 5. Attach the confirmed real problem statement. 6. Add optional parameters: target stakeholders, strategic justifications, business/product constraints, and business risks. 7. Review the formulated product scope with the problem owner and project manager.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: • What functional goals must be accomplished to achieve the vision? • What specific acceptance criteria will prove the problem is solved? • What business or regulatory constraints limit this product? • What strategic justification justifies this scope?
Minimal Realistic Example: Formula applied: 'This vendor management process will accomplish automated term calculations resulting in 100% correct vendor payments which will pass 0% payment discount forfeiture solving the inflexible vendor database problem on behalf of Accounts Payable to realize decreased costs within Sarbanes-Oxley constraints considering key staff turnover risks.'
Quality Criteria & Verification: The product scope must clearly distinguish product capabilities from project execution work, be directly traceable to corporate strategy, and contain measurable acceptance criteria.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confusing product scope (features/functions) with project scope (schedule, staffing, execution tasks); omitting business constraints.
When NOT to Use: In extremely minor operational defect fixes where scope boundaries are completely self-evident and localized.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Project Charter, Vision and Scope Document, Solution Scope (BABOK), User Story Mapping.
Supported Decisions: Project charter approval, budget allocation, release planning, scope change control.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can auto-generate structured scope draft statements by parsing conversation transcripts from discovery sessions against the scope formula template, highlighting missing constraints or unstated risks for the human analyst.

Problem Solved: Reduces the time and cost of interviewing large populations of process workers without risking loss of representative operational requirements or variance data.
Input Artifacts: Stakeholder list, organizational charts, process worker demographics, system usage logs.
Output Artifacts: Process Worker Classification Matrix, optimized Information-Gathering Plan (IGP).
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst (planner), Business Unit Managers, Process Workers.
Prerequisites: Identification of a large user/process worker population associated with the problem domain.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify key usage attributes/dimensions across the process worker population (e.g., work shift, job tenure, frequency of system usage). 2. Construct a multi-dimensional matrix combining these classification attributes. 3. Map the total worker population into the intersecting matrix cells (equivalence classes). 4. Select a small representative sample (e.g., 1-2 workers) from each populated class for interview/observation. 5. Conduct information-gathering sessions for each class, treating class responses as representative of that entire group.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: • How often do you use the system (dedicated, discretionary, casual)? • How long have you performed this specific operational process? • Which work shift or geographic location do you belong to?
Minimal Realistic Example: An analyst faced with 500 A/P clerks creates a matrix based on Shift (Day/Night), Tenure (<1 yr, 1-10 yrs, >10 yrs), and Usage (Dedicated/Casual). This defines 18 equivalence classes; interviewing 1 representative per class reduces required sessions from 500 to 18 while covering all user variances.
Quality Criteria & Verification: The resulting class sample must fully cover all operational edge cases, shifts, and tenure variations without omitting distinct operational sub-groups.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Assuming all process workers act identically without building a classification matrix; sampling only senior workers or manager-recommended 'favorite' employees.
When NOT to Use: When the user population is small enough to interview every individual directly, or when role activities are completely standardized with zero variance.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Surveys/Questionnaires, Persona Definition, User Role Modeling.
Supported Decisions: Elicitation planning, resource allocation for discovery, sample selection for UAT.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic analytics can cluster user telemetry and log data to automatically group system users into behavioral equivalence classes, suggesting an optimized sampling plan to the analyst.

Problem Solved: Prevents disorganized, haphazard elicitation, eliminates wasted stakeholder meetings, and ensures complete coverage of all required problem domain topics.
Input Artifacts: Confirmed real problem statement, initial product scope, stakeholder list.
Output Artifacts: Information-Gathering Plan (a dynamic matrix mapping required information, sources, methods, and logical sequence).
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst (author/investigator), SMEs, Process Workers, Business Managers.
Prerequisites: High-level understanding of the problem domain boundaries.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Column 1 (What Information): Brainstorm all questions and topics needed to understand the problem domain and solution. 2. Filter the topics by asking 'Why will this information help?' and 'What will I learn?'. 3. Column 2 (Source): Identify the specific hard-copy document, process worker role, or system for each topic. 4. Column 3 (Method): Select the appropriate elicitation technique (e.g., read, interview, observe, JAD, prototype). 5. Column 4 (Sequence): Establish a logical top-down sequence for acquiring the information. 6. Execute elicitation following the plan, crossing off topics as information is confirmed, and adding new questions as analysis reveals gaps.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: • What information do I need to understand this process? • Why will this specific information help solve the problem? • Where is this information located or who holds it? • What is the most effective method to capture this information? • In what order must these topics be investigated?
Minimal Realistic Example: An analyst builds a 4-column matrix on a whiteboard listing topics ('Layout of vendor tables', 'Voucher entry workflow'), maps sources ('Data dictionary', 'Clerk Charley'), selects methods ('Read', 'Observe'), and orders them 1 to 4. As topics are answered, they are struck through until the board is clear.
Quality Criteria & Verification: The plan is complete when all required domain topics are mapped to valid sources and methods, and is successfully executed when all plan items are crossed off through validated answers.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Scheduling interviews based on stakeholder calendar availability rather than logical information dependency sequence; gathering requirements without specifying the required information upfront.
When NOT to Use: Emergency bug fixes where the defect is already fully isolated and documented.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Elicitation Plan (BABOK), Communication Management Plan, Interview Guides.
Supported Decisions: Elicitation scheduling, discovery effort estimation, stakeholder engagement strategy.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: An AI agent can maintain a dynamic IGP knowledge graph, automatically identifying missing information nodes, suggesting optimal domain sources, and updating sequence priority as new text inputs are ingested.

Problem Solved: Provides a holistic, broad view of the current business process ('as-is' problem domain) to prevent point-solution failures, uncover hidden dependencies, and isolate root causes.
Input Artifacts: Elicited process information, operational documentation, interview notes, observation records.
Output Artifacts: Domain Diagram Model (visual map detailing Goal, Results, Requestor/Beneficiary, Trigger/Setup, Pre/Post-conditions, Supporting Resources/Information, and Internal Activities).
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst (modeler), Process Workers, SMEs, Business Unit Managers.
Prerequisites: Initial information gathered regarding the target operational business process.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Step 1: Define the overarching process goal (verb phrase) of the target process. 2. Step 2: Identify the tangible, persistent result(s) produced that satisfy the goal, and identify the beneficiary role. 3. Step 3: Identify the requestor role and the specific event trigger (plus setup conditions) that launches the process. 4. Step 4: Identify all preconditions (must be true before start) and post-conditions (environmental changes upon completion). 5. Step 5: Map supporting resources (human/system mechanisms) and supporting information consumed during execution. 6. Step 6: Step inside the process boundary to map internal process worker roles, activities, and event-driven transformations. 7. Review the model with process workers to confirm accuracy and identify process gaps/loopholes.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: • What is the main goal of this business process? • What tangible result proves the process was successful? • What exact event triggers this process to start? • What preconditions must be true before execution begins? • Who receives the final output (beneficiary)? • What information or human resources support this process during execution?
Minimal Realistic Example: A diagram is drawn for Accounts Payable: Goal = 'Pay invoices to receive maximum discount'; Trigger = 'Receipt of voucher batch'; Precondition = 'Purchasing authorization attached'; Result = 'Vendor check & A/P Journal'; Beneficiary = 'Vendor'. Mapping reveals missing terms in setup, causing late checks.
Quality Criteria & Verification: The domain model must clearly show complete inputs, triggers, outputs, and internal event-activity transformations, and be fully verified by operational process workers.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Designing deep technical system interactions before defining the broad business process; omitting preconditions or neighboring process interfaces.
When NOT to Use: When making an isolated, pure technical fix that has zero impact on business workflows or process worker roles.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Data Flow Diagrams (DFD), BPMN Process Maps, UML Activity Diagrams, Value Stream Mapping.
Supported Decisions: Business process re-engineering, gap analysis, solution scoping, impact assessment.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLMs can parse unstructured operational SOPs or interview transcripts and auto-generate structured Domain Diagram specifications (e.g., in Mermaid.js format) for analyst validation.

Problem Solved: Prevents passive, superficial document sign-offs where stakeholders approve solution specifications without truly reading or understanding them.
Input Artifacts: Draft solution document, use cases, screen wireframes, or business requirements specification.
Output Artifacts: Validated solution document, log of identified misunderstandings and corrections.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst (facilitator), Product Stakeholders, Process Workers, Solution Team Representatives.
Prerequisites: Completed draft of the solution document or functional specifications.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Distribute the solution document to participants prior to the review session. 2. Convene the review walkthrough session. 3. Instead of the analyst reading or paraphrasing the document, assign specific sections to individual stakeholder participants. 4. Have the participant paraphrase the section back to the group in their own words, explaining their understanding of how it works. 5. Evaluate the paraphrased explanation against the analyst's intent. 6. If the participant's understanding is correct and accepted, validate the section. 7. If the participant's understanding exposes a document ambiguity or incorrect logic, update the solution document immediately.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: • In your own words, how will this section of the system process your daily work? • What do you expect to happen when you click this option based on what is written here? • Does this written flow match how your department intends to operate?
Minimal Realistic Example: During a review of an A/P voucher requirement, instead of reading section 4.1, the analyst asks Clerk Charley to explain it. Charley says: 'This means I have to sign in twice.' The analyst realizes the written text was ambiguous regarding single sign-on and corrects the requirement on the spot.
Quality Criteria & Verification: 100% of reviewed sections are verbalized correctly by stakeholders in their own operational context, proving true mutual understanding prior to formal approval.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: The analyst reading the document aloud line-by-line while participants passively nod; accepting written sign-offs without conducting active comprehension checks.
When NOT to Use: For pure technical infrastructure specifications where business stakeholders have no operational interaction.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Structured Walkthroughs, Peer Reviews, Interactive Prototyping, Acceptance Test-Driven Reviews.
Supported Decisions: Formal baseline approval, sign-off on requirements, readiness for technical design.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: An AI assistant can generate simplified, role-specific summary prompts or interactive scenario quizzes from complex requirements documents to test stakeholder comprehension before formal sign-off.

Problem Solved: Prevents solution drift, technical gold-plating, and developer-introduced requirement changes from reaching production without business analyst and stakeholder awareness.
Input Artifacts: Baselined solution document/requirements, completed technical design specifications, system architecture models.
Output Artifacts: Updated baseline requirements document, verified technical design alignment log, business change requests (if needed).
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst (reviewer/owner of requirements), Technical Lead/System Analyst (presenter), Developers, Solution Architect.
Prerequisites: Completion of the detailed technical design by the development team prior to or during full code construction.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Schedule a formal Checkpoint Charley meeting once technical system design is complete. 2. The technical lead presents the technical design to the business analyst, explaining how it implements the solution. 3. The business analyst evaluates the design against the baselined solution document requirements. 4. Identify any design trade-offs, technical shortcuts, or added unrequested features ('gilding the lily'). 5. If technical changes alter business functionality, the analyst logs them and updates the requirements baseline. 6. If changes significantly impact business expectations or scope, the analyst takes the changes back to the problem owner for formal approval.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: • How does this technical design component specifically fulfill Requirement X? • Were any business rules or user workflows altered to accommodate system performance? • Are there any unrequested features added in this design? • Does this technical approach introduce any new operational constraints for the end user?
Minimal Realistic Example: The Tech Lead shows that to optimize database performance, voucher entry will require a batch job overnight instead of real-time display. The BA catches this at Checkpoint Charley, identifies that it violates the real-time UAT criteria, and negotiates a design compromise before coding starts.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Zero unaccounted variances exist between the technical system design and the baselined business requirements document.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Skipping technical design reviews and allowing developers to 'go dark' until UAT; allowing developers to change business workflows unilaterally without updating requirements.
When NOT to Use: In pure agile/Scrum environments where the BA/product owner sits collocated with developers daily and reviews working code every sprint.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Checkpoint Beta, Sprint Review, Architecture Review Board, Traceability Matrix Audit.
Supported Decisions: Authorization to proceed to coding/build, requirement baseline updates, scope change control.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: An AI agent can perform automated static analysis comparing technical design documentation or API schemas directly against natural-language requirement files, flagging discrepancies for the BA prior to the Checkpoint Charley meeting.

Problem Solved: Ensures the delivered solution actually solves the original business problem and satisfies business acceptance criteria rather than just passing technical unit/system specs.
Input Artifacts: Baselined solution document, vision statement, acceptance criteria, test scenarios/scripts, deployed candidate software.
Output Artifacts: Acceptance test execution logs, defect logs with classification, formal business acceptance sign-off.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst (test designer/lead), Process Workers / End Users (testers), Problem Owner, QA Team.
Prerequisites: Successful completion of system testing by the technical team and availability of acceptance criteria.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Step 1: Derive acceptance test scenarios and cases directly from the confirmed acceptance criteria, vision, and use cases. 2. Step 2: Establish the acceptable level of confidence and minimum passing threshold with the problem owner. 3. Step 3: Prepare the test environment and user test data representing real-world business scenarios. 4. Step 4: Guide end users/process workers through test scenario execution (or execute on their behalf as designated). 5. Step 5: Log all unexpected behaviors and evaluate each against requirements to categorize as a software bug, requirement defect, or test script error. 6. Step 6: Present defect impacts to the problem owner to decide fix priorities. 7. Step 7: Obtain formal business acceptance sign-off when all acceptance criteria pass.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: • How will you know the new system does what you want it to? • What is the first operational function you are going to try when the system is delivered? • What do you expect to happen when this end-to-end scenario executes? • Is this reported discrepancy a defect in code, an error in requirements, or a new feature request?
Minimal Realistic Example: The BA drafts 10 end-to-end test scenarios based on the A/P acceptance criteria ('Add vendor in <2 hours', '100% correct discount calculation'). The BA leads 3 clerks through testing, catches 2 calculation bugs, logs them for developer resolution, and re-tests until the problem owner signs off.
Quality Criteria & Verification: All acceptance criteria established at Checkpoint Alpha are 100% validated by passing test scenarios without critical unresolved business defects.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Abandoning end users to test without structured business scenarios; treating user-discovered scope changes as software bugs; testing only happy-path technical functions instead of business process goals.
When NOT to Use: For low-level technical unit or integration testing (which belongs strictly to developers/tech QA).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: User Acceptance Testing (UAT), Exploratory Testing, Beta Testing, Test-Driven Development (TDD).
Supported Decisions: Release to production decision, final product acceptance, defect remediation priority, warranty entry.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic test generators can convert natural-language use cases and acceptance criteria into automated UAT scripts or gherkin syntax (Given-When-Then), executing regression checks and surfacing business-logic anomalies to the analyst.

Method Name: Specification by Example (SBE) / Executable Specifications with Gherkin
Problem Solved: Reduces information asymmetry, misaligned business objectives, requirements ambiguity, domain concept misunderstandings, over-specification, hand-offs, under-documentation, speci-fiction (outdated specs), and test-inability.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Discovery, elicitation, analysis, specification, prioritisation, validation, change management
Input Artifacts: Business goals, stakeholder requests, interviews, existing documentation, user stories, domain models, acceptance criteria, customer feedback, incident/bug reports
Output Artifacts: Executable specifications (.feature files), living documentation, domain glossaries, Given-When-Then scenarios, scenario outlines with examples tables, context maps, user journey notes
Participants & Roles: Sponsor, business owner, domain expert/SME, end user/customer, BA/product manager, architect, developer, tester, compliance/legal
Prerequisites: High-level business goals/objectives, defined primary actors/personas, collaborative willingness across business and technical roles, access to domain knowledge
Step-by-Step Procedure: Understand business goals and derive scope from goals (e.g., using impact mapping or feature injection). 2. Specify collaboratively through workshops or Three Amigos meetings involving business and technical roles. 3. Illustrate requirements with concrete, realistic examples (happy path, counterexamples, exploratory outcomes). 4. Capture conversations using the Given-When-Then template into Gherkin scenarios or scenario outlines. 5. Refine scenarios to remove redundancy, maintain proper abstraction, and focus on outcomes over UI details. 6. Automate scenarios by connecting Gherkin steps to test code via step definitions. 7. Execute and validate tests frequently within continuous integration to keep documentation alive. 8. Evolve living documentation over time with lexical/illustrative definitions, warning/context notes, and glossaries. 9. Organize scenarios into domain-driven structures (Abilities, Business Needs, Bounded Contexts).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Why are we building this? Who are we building this for? What exactly are we going to build? How will we build it? Can you give a concrete example of this rule? What is the prerequisite needed before this happens? Is there a context that, for the same event, produces a different outcome? (Context questioning) Is there another outcome that also matters? (Outcome questioning) What happens on the angry/scary/embarrassing/delinquent/stressful/greedy/forgetful/desolate/indecisive path?
Minimal Realistic Example: Feature: Scheduling Scenario: Creating a meeting Given Mike, a member of our team When Mike chooses 2 p.m. as a start time for his meeting Then he should be able to save his meeting
Quality Criteria & Verification: Given-When-Then scenarios pass automated test execution (green); scenarios use ubiquitous domain language rather than UI buttons/fields; scenarios focus on single outcomes/user tasks; examples are realistic and representative; peer review/walkthrough in Three Amigos meetings; continuous integration verification.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Over-specification (up-front analysis paralysis); hand-offs without delivery team input; under-documentation; speci-fiction (unmaintained, false specifications); UI-focused scenarios; duplicate/redundant scenarios without scenario outlines; using classes of equivalence instead of boundary/Goldilocks examples; writing Gherkin steps that resemble raw SQL/database models; improper use of Backgrounds.
When NOT to Use: Small risk/trivial changes with zero business uncertainty; single-developer exploratory spikes; situations where stakeholders are completely inaccessible and domain knowledge cannot be verified; ultra-low-level unit logic better suited for standard xUnit tests.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Impact Mapping, Feature Injection, User Story Mapping, Domain-Driven Design (DDD), Traditional Acceptance Test-Driven Development (ATDD), Behavior-Driven Development (BDD), Screenplay Pattern, Goldilocks Principle, Pairwise Testing, Five Whys.
Supported Decisions: Scope definition, feature release approval, architecture/domain boundary design, release readiness, acceptance criteria sign-off, compliance and auditability.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: For agentic software engineering systems, Gherkin executable specs serve as unambiguous functional contracts and guardrails. LLM/Agent acts as developer/tester implementing step definitions and code to satisfy specs. Input: business goal prompt + structured Gherkin scenario. Human-in-the-loop: Product Owner/BA reviews and approves refined Gherkin specs before AI code generation. Guardrails: automated test runner (e.g., Cucumber) provides deterministic pass/fail execution output to the agent's feedback loop. Audit trail: git-versioned .feature files and test run results.

Problem Solved: Resolves goal uncontrollability when an agent expected to be in charge of a goal condition cannot physically control that condition.
Input Artifacts: Goal model, system objective specifications, agent responsibilities
Output Artifacts: Refined goal model (AND-refinement tree with controllable sub-goals and accuracy/expectation goals)
Participants & Roles: BA, Architect, System Actuators/Agents
Prerequisites: Identification of a goal condition that is unmonitored or uncontrollable by the assigned agent.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify a goal condition that an assigned agent cannot physically control. 2. Introduce a new intermediate condition that is directly controllable by the target agent. 3. Create an accuracy/expectation goal assigned to an actuator or environment agent to mirror the controllable condition into the physical condition. 4. Structure the decomposition as an AND-refinement tree in the goal model.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Can the assigned agent physically control this goal condition? If not, what intermediate condition can it control, and what actuator agent can ensure the physical condition matches?
Minimal Realistic Example: A train controller cannot physically close train doors directly (DoorsClosed condition). The uncontrollability-driven refinement pattern introduces a controllable condition 'DoorsStateClosed' assigned to the train controller, along with an expectation assigned to the doors actuator agent to keep doors state accurate.
Quality Criteria & Verification: The resulting refinement must be complete, minimal, and consistent with known domain properties. Verify that the assigned software agent controls its designated variable and the expectation on the environment agent is feasible.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Assigning goals to agents that lack physical controllability over the goal variables; assuming an over-ideal system where environment agents always execute perfectly without explicit expectations.
When NOT to Use: When the assigned agent already has direct control over all state variables involved in the goal formulation.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Unmonitorability-driven refinement pattern, Guard-introduction pattern, Milestone-driven pattern
Supported Decisions: Architecture decisions, system boundary definition, agent responsibility assignments
AI & Agentic Adaptation: For autonomous AI agents, apply this pattern when an LLM or agent system cannot directly alter an external environment state; introduce an agent-controllable action command combined with a specialized executor or tool agent to enforce accuracy.

Method Name: Goal Elicitation via Category-Specific Refinement Trees (Model Reuse)
Problem Solved: Reduces completeness uncertainty and missing requirements by reusing proven, standardized goal decomposition templates (e.g., satisfaction, safety, security).
Input Artifacts: Preliminary goal model, goal categories taxonomy (satisfaction, safety, security, etc.)
Output Artifacts: Instantiated category-specific goal refinement tree, identified missing sub-goals or alternative options
Participants & Roles: BA, Domain Expert, SME
Prerequisites: Preliminary goals categorized into specific taxonomic types (e.g., satisfaction, safety).
Step-by-Step Procedure: Introduce a preliminary goal into the system model and classify its goal category. 2. Browse reusable refinement trees corresponding to that goal category. 3. Instantiate the generic concepts and conditions in system-specific terms. 4. Adapt the tree as necessary to fit specific domain constraints, or reject non-applicable sub-goals. 5. Compare the instantiated tree against existing goal branches to identify missing sub-goals or alternative refinements.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What category does this goal belong to? Are there standard service request, guard, or alarm mechanisms for this goal category that we missed?
Minimal Realistic Example: For a meeting scheduling satisfaction goal ('RequestIssued'), reusing a generic satisfaction refinement tree highlights missing sub-goals related to scheduler appointment and issuing service responses.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Check for model completeness by verifying that instantiated sub-goals cover all essential phases (request, appointment, delivery, guard response) of the specific goal category.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Blinded reuse without adaptation to domain constraints; forcing irrelevant sub-goals into system specifications.
When NOT to Use: In novel, highly unstandardized domains where pre-existing category refinement patterns do not apply.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Keyword-based goal elicitation, Interviewing, Problem analysis of system-as-is
Supported Decisions: Scope determination, functional coverage, release planning
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic systems can automatically map identified high-level intents to domain-specific goal templates and pre-populate requirement trees for human-in-the-loop validation.

Method Name: Goal Model Elaboration (HOW / WHY Elicitation & Decomposition)
Problem Solved: Reduces scope ambiguity, goal conflicts, and missing functional/non-functional requirements by systematically exploring abstractions and decompositions.
Input Artifacts: Business goals, problem complaints about system-as-is, strategic objectives, interview transcripts
Output Artifacts: Goal Model (AND/OR graph, Goal Diagram) annotated with precise goal specifications, priorities, and assignments
Participants & Roles: BA, Business Owner, Sponsor, Architect, SME
Prerequisites: Access to strategic business goals, complaints about system-as-is, or preliminary interview transcripts.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify preliminary strategic and domain-specific objectives from documents and transcripts. 2. Ask 'HOW' questions to build refinement paths downwards into sub-goals until goals are assignable to single agents. 3. Ask 'WHY' questions to build abstraction paths upwards toward high-level goals. 4. Ask 'HOW ELSE' questions to uncover alternative refinements (OR-links). 5. Annotate each leaf goal with precise definitions, fit criteria, priority, and assign it to a single system or environment agent.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: HOW can this goal be satisfied? WHY is this sub-goal needed? HOW ELSE can we achieve this higher-level objective?
Minimal Realistic Example: Asking WHY 'Train stops at block signal' yields high-level safety goal 'Avoid collisions'; asking HOW yields sub-goals 'Driver reacts to stop signal' and 'Brake system functions'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Goal refinements must be complete, minimal, and consistent with valid domain properties. Leaf goals must be assignable to single agents.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confusing functional services/operations with intentional goals; stopping refinement before single-agent assignability is reached.
When NOT to Use: When system scope and technical requirements are completely fixed and deterministic with no alternative execution options or agent choices.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Use Case Modeling, Problem Frames, User Story Mapping
Supported Decisions: Scope boundary, system architecture, release scope, responsibility assignments
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can analyze transcript inputs to formulate candidate WHY/HOW trees and present alternative goal branches to analysts.

Problem Solved: Reduces requirements incompleteness, unhandled operational risks, and false confidence arising from over-idealized system assumptions.
Input Artifacts: Goal model (leaf goals and assumptions), domain properties, obstacle taxonomies
Output Artifacts: Obstacle Diagram (AND/OR risk trees), Countermeasure Goals integrated into Goal Model
Participants & Roles: BA, Risk Analyst, SME, Architect, Compliance/Legal
Prerequisites: A developed goal model with leaf goals and domain hypotheses explicitly specified.
Step-by-Step Procedure: SELECT: Pick critical leaf goals or domain hypotheses in the goal model. 2. IDENTIFY: Negate the selected assertion to form the root obstacle. Refine it via AND/OR links using tautologies, domain properties, or obstruction patterns until elementary obstacles are reached. 3. ASSESS: Estimate likelihood and criticality for each leaf obstacle. 4. CONTROL: Formulate alternative countermeasures (prevention, reduction, restoration, mitigation, goal weakening, agent substitution) and inject selected resolutions as new goals into the goal model.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What could go wrong to prevent this goal from being satisfied? What domain properties can fail? How likely and severe is this failure?
Minimal Realistic Example: Negating the goal 'Train stopped at stop signal' yields obstacle 'Driver unresponsive'. Assessing its criticality as catastrophic leads to injecting the countermeasure goal 'Send periodic responsiveness checks'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Domain completeness of OR-refinements; domain consistency and minimality of AND-refinements; feasibility of leaf obstacles verified by domain experts.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Analyzing high-level goals directly instead of leaf goals; assuming environment agents behave ideally without exception.
When NOT to Use: For non-critical features where obstacle occurrence carries minimal risk and cost-benefit analysis favors 'do nothing'.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Fault Tree Analysis (FTA), Threat Tree Modeling, Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA)
Supported Decisions: System robustness decisions, architecture selection, risk control strategies, release acceptance
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic systems can automatically negate temporal logic goal statements, query domain knowledge bases for potential pre-conditions of failure, and propose automated guardrails/countermeasures with Human-in-the-Loop review.

Problem Solved: Reduces terminology ambiguity, missing conceptual state variables, and irrelevant domain clutter by deriving object models strictly from intentional goals.
Input Artifacts: Goal specifications, domain properties, assertions, interview transcripts
Output Artifacts: Object Model (UML Class Diagram) with Entities, Associations, Attributes, Agents, Events, and Annotations (Def, DomInvar, Init)
Participants & Roles: BA, System Architect, Database Designer, SME
Prerequisites: Goal specifications and domain properties defined precisely or formally.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Extract all conceptual items referenced in goal and domain property specifications. 2. Identify linking expressions to define associations and participating roles. 3. Apply decision heuristics: classify items as attributes vs. objects, and objects as entities, associations, agents, or events. 4. Attach attributes to appropriate objects or associations. 5. Identify specialization/generalization hierarchies using discriminant factors. 6. Decorate associations with multiplicities and domain invariants. 7. Generate glossary of terms.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What conceptual items are referenced in this goal statement? Is this item a state function or a first-class object? What is the exact domain invariant governing this concept?
Minimal Realistic Example: Goal 'Maintain SpeedBelowBlockLimit' references 'Train', 'Block', 'Speed', and 'SpeedLimit'. This derives entities Train (attribute Speed) and Block (attribute SpeedLimit), and association 'On' linking Train and Block.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Pertinence and completeness relative to the goal model; verification of association multiplicities; absence of pointer attributes; correct semantic definitions (Def/DomInvar) agreed by stakeholders.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Including implementation pointers as attributes; mixing dynamic state machine behaviors or agent interface links into structural object models.
When NOT to Use: When building purely procedural or stateless scripts where structural state tracking is unnecessary.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Domain Driven Design (DDD) Modeling, ER Modeling, Classic UML Class Modeling
Supported Decisions: Database schema design, system vocabulary standardization, software architecture boundaries
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLM agents can parse natural language goal annotations, perform entity-relationship extraction, map entities to standardized schemas, and enforce anti-pattern guardrails automatically.

Problem Solved: Reduces unclear operational boundaries, unassigned goals, and system interface mismatches between software and environment agents.
Input Artifacts: Goal model, Object model (attributes/associations)
Output Artifacts: Agent Diagram, Context Diagram, Dependency Diagram (i* style), Capability & Responsibility Declarations
Participants & Roles: BA, System Architect, Software Engineer, Organizational SME
Prerequisites: Leaf goals in the goal model identified and mapped to candidate system or environment agents.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Map leaf goals to candidate agents based on monitoring and control capabilities. 2. Verify goal realizability for assigned agents (can the agent monitor evaluated variables and control constrained variables?). 3. Enforce the Unique Controller constraint (each variable controlled by at most one agent). 4. Specify instance responsibility and capability annotations. 5. Derive the Context Diagram by connecting agents whose controlled variables are monitored by other agents. 6. Conduct vulnerability analysis on agent dependency chains.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Which agent controls the variables constrained by this goal? Can this agent monitor all required input conditions? What happens to depender goals if this dependee agent fails?
Minimal Realistic Example: TrainController agent controls Command.Speed and monitors TrainInfo.Position. TrackSystem controls TrainInfo.Position. The derived context diagram shows a directed interface edge from TrackSystem to TrainController labelled Position.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Goal realizability verified for every assignment; Unique Controller constraint satisfied; context diagram data flows match goal inputs/outputs completely.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Assigning goals to agents lacking monitoring/control capabilities; assigning a single controlled variable to multiple concurrent agents; confusing process stakeholders with system agents.
When NOT to Use: Single-agent monolithic systems where no interface boundaries exist.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Use Case Actor Modeling, RACI Matrix, Interface Definition Languages (IDL)
Supported Decisions: Software/environment boundary definition, load distribution, architectural allocation, vulnerability mitigation
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic orchestrators can parse goal variable dependencies to generate agent capability graphs, verify monitoring/control bounds, and flag unrealizable agent goals in multi-agent workflows.

Problem Solved: Reduces the specification gap between declarative goals and executable functional services, ensuring operational specs correctly satisfy goals.
Input Artifacts: Leaf goals, Goal Model, Object Model, Agent Model
Output Artifacts: Operation Model (Operationalization Diagrams, Operation Specifications with DomPre/DomPost and ReqPre/ReqTrig/ReqPost), UML Use Case Diagrams
Participants & Roles: BA, Software Developer, System Architect, Tester
Prerequisites: Leaf goals assigned to single agents with defined monitoring/control capabilities.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Extract fluents (state conditions) from leaf goals and identify their initiating and terminating operations. 2. Specify domain pre-conditions (DomPre) and post-conditions (DomPost) for each operation. 3. Strengthen operations with required pre-conditions (ReqPre - permissions), trigger conditions (ReqTrig - obligations), and post-conditions (ReqPost - additional required effects) per goal. 4. Verify completeness and consistency of required conditions against underlying goals. 5. Generate UML Use Case Diagrams by grouping operations per performing agent.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What state transition initiates or terminates this goal condition? What permission (ReqPre) is necessary to avoid goal violation? What obligation (ReqTrig) forces this operation to run?
Minimal Realistic Example: Goal 'DoorsStateClosedIfNonZeroMeasuredSpeed' operationalized into OpenDoors operation with DomPre 'DoorsState=closed', DomPost 'DoorsState=open', and ReqPre 'Speed=0'; and StartTrain operation with ReqPre 'DoorsState=closed'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Operationalization completeness ({Spec(Op)} | = Goal); consistency between ReqTrig and ReqPre; frame axioms satisfied; single performer per operation.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Refining operations directly instead of refining declarative goals; missing trigger conditions leading to unfulfilled obligations; violating Unique Performer constraint.
When NOT to Use: When software functionality is entirely static or declarative without state transitions.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Use Case Specifications, Z/VDM Formal Specs, Contract-Driven Design (DbC)
Supported Decisions: Software functional specification, API design, system test case derivation, work unit estimation
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic systems can use operationalization patterns to translate temporal logic goal contracts into executable tool definitions (with preconditions, triggers, and postconditions) for autonomous AI agents.

Method Name: Behaviour Modeling via Scenarios & State Machines
Problem Solved: Reduces dynamic ambiguity, timing mismatches, and unhandled event sequences by making explicit the temporal state transitions of agents.
Input Artifacts: Operation specifications, Goal model, Object model, Sample interaction scenarios
Output Artifacts: Sequence Diagrams (MSCs), State Machine Diagrams (UML Statecharts / LTS)
Participants & Roles: BA, Software Architect, System Tester, Quality Engineer
Prerequisites: Defined agents, operations with pre/post conditions, and illustrative scenario traces.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Elaborate positive and negative interaction scenarios as UML Sequence Diagrams; decorate lifelines with state condition lists. 2. Generalize scenario paths into candidate State Machine paths for each controlled variable. 3. Merge state paths across scenarios into composite State Diagrams. 4. Alternatively, derive State Diagrams directly from operationalized goal specifications (mapping DomPre/DomPost to states, ReqPre/ReqTrig to transition guards). 5. Perform intra-diagram and inter-diagram checks (unreachable states, missing transitions, inter-diagram synchronization). 6. Verify state machines via model checking or animation.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What sequence of events leads to this state? What is the guard condition for this transition? Are all parallel state machines synchronized on shared variables?
Minimal Realistic Example: Decorating a train scenario timeline with Speed and DoorsState conditions, then mapping state transitions (DoorsClosed -> DoorsOpen) triggered by 'doorsOpening' event guarded by Speed=0 into a statechart.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Complete coverage of positive scenarios; exclusion of negative scenarios; absence of deadlock/unreachable states; synchronization on shared events.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Creating 'spaghetti' statecharts with unstructured inter-state jumps; failing to synchronize parallel state machines; over-generalizing scenarios into invalid state loops.
When NOT to Use: Simple batch processing or purely stateless query systems where temporal dynamics do not exist.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Petri Nets, Labelled Transition Systems (LTS), State Transition Tables
Supported Decisions: Component state management, concurrency design, automated test suite generation, system animation/validation
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can generate sequence diagrams from goal specifications, induce statecharts from scenario traces, and perform model-checking against temporal invariants with automated counterexample generation.

Problem Solved: Reduces uncertainty and lack of domain knowledge by acquiring background information, understanding organizational structures, terminology, and historical deficiencies from existing documentation.
Input Artifacts: Organizational charts, business plans, policy manuals, financial reports, minutes of meetings, job descriptions, business forms, domain books, surveys, regulations, reports on similar systems, defect/complaint reports, user manuals.
Output Artifacts: Initial sections of a preliminary draft proposal, glossary of terms.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst / Requirements Engineer (conducting the study).
Prerequisites: Availability of relevant organizational, domain, or system documentation.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Acquire meta-knowledge to identify what needs to be known and prune the documentation space. 2. Collect relevant documentation (organizational, domain, system-as-is, legacy software). 3. Read, analyze, and synthesize the documentation. 4. Extract key information, terminology, policies, and reported problems. 5. Establish a preliminary draft proposal and a baseline glossary of terms.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What do I need to know and what can I skip? What is the official terminology used? What business rules and regulations apply? What complaints or defects were recorded for the current system?
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA reads the existing library policy manual and legacy software manual before interviewing staff, extracting terms like 'patron' and 'borrowing limit' to populate the project glossary.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Source accuracy check, cross-referencing information across multiple documents, review meetings with stakeholders to validate synthesized knowledge.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Information overload (getting lost in a mass of irrelevant details); relying on outdated, inaccurate, or obsolete documentation.
When NOT to Use: When documentation is completely non-existent, radically inaccurate, or when time constraints make reading voluminous obsolete reports counterproductive.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Data Collection, Interviews, Observation. Alternative: Direct stakeholder interviews when no documents exist.
Supported Decisions: Scoping the elicitation process, defining target stakeholders to interview, establishing standard terminology.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can perform automated content analysis/RAG over large document repositories, extracting glossaries, business rules, and domain entities with Human-in-the-loop validation for accuracy.

Problem Solved: Reduces quantitative uncertainty regarding performance, usage patterns, costs, and marketing facts that are not explicitly documented.
Input Artifacts: System usage logs, operational databases, marketing reports, population samples.
Output Artifacts: Quantitative data sets, statistical summaries, baseline metrics for non-functional requirements.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Domain SME, System Administrator / Data Analyst.
Prerequisites: Access to operational data, logs, or user populations suitable for sampling.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify missing quantitative facts (e.g., peak load, transaction frequencies, operational costs). 2. Define target populations or data sources. 3. Select representative data sets using statistical sampling methods or conduct experimental data gathering. 4. Analyze and interpret collected data. 5. Translate data insights into non-functional requirements (performance, usability, cost targets).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What are the current transaction volumes during peak hours? What is the average cost per operation? How frequently is feature X utilized by users?
Minimal Realistic Example: Collecting server log data over a month to establish that the peak query volume for a library system is 500 requests per minute, used to set performance targets.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Statistical validity, representativeness of sampling, correct data interpretation and cross-verification with domain SMEs.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Drawing conclusions from unrepresentative or biased samples; misinterpreting statistical metrics.
When NOT to Use: When brand-new (greenfield) domains have no baseline data available or when quantitative precision is unnecessary at an early stage.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Background Study, Questionnaires. Alternative: Benchmarking, Prototyping simulation.
Supported Decisions: Defining performance requirements, cost-benefit trade-offs, capacity planning.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Autonomous data-mining agents can extract log analytics and synthesize baseline operational metrics with anomaly detection guardrails.

Problem Solved: Reduces subjective uncertainty and collects feedback or preferences quickly from a large, geographically distributed stakeholder population at low cost.
Input Artifacts: Target stakeholder list, predefined list of open/closed questions or weighting scales.
Output Artifacts: Completed questionnaire responses, statistical summary of user preferences/priorities.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst (designer), Target Stakeholders / End Users (respondents).
Prerequisites: Clear understanding of the objective of the survey; identified target respondent sample.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Determine the specific information or preference to be elicited. 2. Design questions (multiple-choice, weighting scales, or short answers) avoiding bias and ambiguity. 3. Pre-validate the questionnaire with a small sample group. 4. Distribute the questionnaire to the representative sample. 5. Collect, aggregate, and analyze responses to inform interviews or requirements prioritization.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Which feature is most critical to your daily work? On a scale of 1-5, how severe is problem X? Which option do you prefer: A or B?
Minimal Realistic Example: Sending a 5-question weighting survey to 200 university faculty members to rank the importance of online journal access vs. physical book reservations.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Statistical significance of responses, absence of leading/biased questions, non-ambiguity validation prior to distribution.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Biased sampling or low response rates leading to distorted conclusions; ambiguous wording leading to conflicting interpretations; relying solely on questionnaires without follow-up interviews.
When NOT to Use: When deep, qualitative exploration of complex, unstructured, or tacit knowledge is required.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Follow-up Structured Interviews. Alternative: Focus Groups, Brainstorming.
Supported Decisions: Feature prioritization, user preference selection, scope trade-offs.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can automatically generate unbiased survey questions based on identified gaps, analyze open-ended text responses using NLP, and summarize sentiment.

Problem Solved: Reduces ambiguity around domain concepts by helping stakeholders surface implicit categorization criteria, attributes, and mental models.
Input Artifacts: Elicited domain concepts, index cards (textual or graphical).
Output Artifacts: Concept-attribute matrix (repertory grid), categorized concept clusters, candidate domain properties and requirements.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst (facilitator), Domain SME / Stakeholder.
Prerequisites: A initial set of domain concepts previously identified during domain understanding.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Provide the stakeholder with cards representing domain concepts. 2. Ask the stakeholder to partition/group cards based on his/her own criteria. 3. Probe the stakeholder for the reason for grouping specific concepts together to reveal underlying attributes/properties. 4. Classify each revealed property as descriptive (domain property) or prescriptive (requirement). 5. (For Repertory Grids) Construct a matrix mapping concepts against attributes with value ranges. 6. Repeat iterations to discover additional implicit domain structures.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Why did you group these three items together? What feature distinguishes this concept from the others? Is this classification rule always true or a desirable policy?
Minimal Realistic Example: A stakeholder groups 'Meeting' and 'Participant' cards together, surfacing the prescriptive requirement that 'the scheduler must know participant constraints prior to date selection.'
Quality Criteria & Verification: Verification of derived properties with other SMEs, consistency checks across derived taxonomy trees.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Generating overly complex grids that are hard to manage; accepting subjective classifications as absolute domain facts without SME cross-verification.
When NOT to Use: When dealing with large, unmanageable sets of concepts without clear boundaries, or when concepts are strictly regulated and standardized.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Conceptual Laddering, Entity-Relationship Modeling. Alternative: Background Study of official taxonomies.
Supported Decisions: Domain conceptualization, data model structuring, entity/attribute definitions.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLM agents can perform automated clustering of domain terms and suggest potential taxonomy trees for SME review.

Problem Solved: Reduces miscommunication, tacit knowledge gaps, and abstraction errors by using concrete, narrative examples of interaction sequences to explore problem worlds and define expected system behavior.
Input Artifacts: Narrative outlines, user goals, UI sketches, mock screenshots, sequence traces.
Output Artifacts: Storyboards, positive/negative scenarios, normal/abnormal scenarios, UML sequence/event trace diagrams.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, End User, Domain SME, Developer.
Prerequisites: Identification of key system actors and high-level usage goals.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify the specific interaction context and participating actors. 2. Walk through a concrete step-by-step sequence of interaction events (normal course). 3. Ask probing questions ('What if...?', 'What could go wrong?') to discover abnormal/exceptional courses. 4. Document positive scenarios (desired behavior) and negative scenarios (unacceptable behavior/counter-examples). 5. Extract underlying implicit goals, requirements, and domain assumptions from the concrete narrative. 6. Generalize scenarios into behavioural models.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Who initiates this interaction? What happens next? What if the user submits invalid data? What should happen if the connection fails at step 3?
Minimal Realistic Example: Tracing a meeting scheduling scenario: Initiator requests meeting -> Scheduler requests constraints from invitees -> Invitees reply -> Scheduler calculates optimal date -> Scheduler sends notification.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Scenario walkthroughs with stakeholders, coverage of abnormal cases, checking scenario consistency against goal models.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Combinatorial explosion of scenario variations; premature overspecification (prescribing UI or exact ordering prematurely); keeping requirements implicit without abstracting them from scenarios.
When NOT to Use: As a sole specification method, because scenarios are inherently partial and capture single paths rather than complete system coverage.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Goal Modeling, Use Cases, State Machine Diagrams, Prototyping.
Supported Decisions: Defining operational workflows, error-handling requirements, interaction boundary determination.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can generate synthetic edge-case scenarios from user stories, analyze scenario coverage, and auto-translate natural language scenarios into UML sequence diagrams.

Problem Solved: Reduces uncertainty around user interaction and usability requirements; prevents stakeholder mismatch by providing early, concrete visual feedback.
Input Artifacts: Elicited functional requirements, UI layouts, high-level user goals.
Output Artifacts: Throwaway prototypes (mock-ups), evolutionary prototypes, validated UI interaction specs.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, UI/UX Designer, End User, Developer.
Prerequisites: Identified user roles and initial understanding of target functional features.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select unclear or high-risk requirements (e.g., complex UI dialogues or operational workflows). 2. Rapidly build a reduced functional or UI prototype/mock-up. 3. Demonstrate prototype execution to stakeholders in interactive sessions. 4. Collect feedback on usability, missing features, and misinterpretations. 5. Update requirements and refine or discard the prototype. 6. Repeat until stakeholder consensus is reached.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Does this screen lay out the required information logically? Is this dialogue sequence convenient for your daily work? What missing options do you need on this interface?
Minimal Realistic Example: Creating an interactive web form mock-up for meeting initiators to select participant constraints and visualizing how schedule results are displayed.
Quality Criteria & Verification: User acceptance testing on prototype dialogues, usability fit criteria evaluation.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Misleading stakeholders regarding backend readiness; using 'quick and dirty' throwaway prototype code in production; spending excessive time building evolutionary prototypes at the expense of early requirement discovery.
When NOT to Use: When requirements are purely backend, algorithmic, or heavily constrained by invisible non-functional requirements (e.g., hard real-time guarantees, batch processing).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Storyboards, Use Cases. Alternative: Formal Animation (for backend logic verification).
Supported Decisions: User interface layout, interaction dialogue design, functional workflow acceptance.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Generative AI tools can convert natural language descriptions or hand-drawn sketches directly into executable web mock-ups and gather synthetic user feedback.

Problem Solved: Reduces requirements elicitation effort and prevents errors by reusing domain-independent taxonomies, meta-models, or domain-specific abstractions (patterns) from past projects.
Input Artifacts: Requirements taxonomies, meta-models, abstract domain patterns (e.g., Resource Management, Asset Tracking).
Output Artifacts: Instantiated, domain-specific requirements, domain properties, and system models.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst / Requirements Engineer.
Prerequisites: Availability of structured reusable repositories, abstract domain patterns, or standardized taxonomies.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify the abstract domain(s) matching the target system (e.g., specializing 'Resource Management' for a Library System). 2. Retrieve relevant abstract knowledge fragments (concepts, tasks, goals, properties). 3. Transpose abstract fragments to the target domain through specialization, parameter instantiation, and renaming. 4. Validate transposed specifications with stakeholders for local adequacy. 5. Adapt and integrate the transposed fragments into the system model.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Is there a requirement in class X (e.g., Privacy, Availability) relevant to this system? How does this generic resource reservation pattern apply to our library book copy concept?
Minimal Realistic Example: Specializing the abstract concept 'Resource Unit' to 'Book Copy' and inheriting the abstract domain property 'A resource unit can be used by at most one user at a time' into 'A book copy can be borrowed by at most one patron at a time.'
Quality Criteria & Verification: Validation of inherited properties against local domain reality; consistency check of integrated fragments.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Forcing inappropriate generic patterns onto a unique domain; spending excessive effort adapting ill-fitting abstractions.
When NOT to Use: In highly novel, radical design projects with no existing conceptual precedents or domain analogies.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Goal Modeling, Problem Frames. Alternative: Greenfield interview-driven elicitation.
Supported Decisions: Selecting system architecture patterns, defining complete non-functional requirement sets.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: RAG-driven AI agents can automatically retrieve matching analysis patterns or IEEE templates from corporate knowledge bases and propose pre-populated requirements specifications.

Problem Solved: Reduces tacit knowledge gaps, uncovers personal complaints/expectations, and collects deep qualitative domain knowledge directly from stakeholders.
Input Artifacts: Stakeholder analysis matrix, interview guide (structured/unstructured questions), domain background notes.
Output Artifacts: Interview transcripts, summarized interview reports, newly identified goals/requirements.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst (interviewer), Selected Stakeholder / SME / User (interviewee).
Prerequisites: Stakeholder identification, background study to avoid asking basic/ignorant questions.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select the appropriate interviewee based on expertise and role. 2. Prepare a structured interview guide mix of closed and open-ended questions. 3. Establish rapport, state purpose, and get permission to record. 4. Conduct the interview, using structured questions first and following up on unexpected answers in unstructured mode. 5. Ask 'WHY' questions to uncover underlying goals and 'HOW' questions for operational details. 6. Document transcripts, synthesize findings, and submit the report to the interviewee for validation.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Why do you perform this task in this way? What are the biggest bottlenecks in your current workflow? What would happen if information X is missing?
Minimal Realistic Example: Interviewing a head librarian to discover that manual duplicate checking during book acquisition wastes 15 hours a week, yielding the goal 'Automate duplicate acquisition checks.'
Quality Criteria & Verification: Interviewee review and sign-off on transcript summaries; cross-interview triangulation across multiple stakeholders.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Asking opinionated, leading, or 'stupid' domain questions; failing to break the ice; interviewing wrong/unrepresentative stakeholders; failing to document transcripts immediately.
When NOT to Use: When trying to discover complex physical procedural nuances that the user cannot articulate (use Observation instead).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Questionnaires, Background Study, Observation. Alternative: Group Sessions / JAD.
Supported Decisions: Identifying high-level business goals, operational pain points, and user preferences.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can transcribe recorded audio interviews in real time, extract candidate goals/entities using NLP, and draft structured interview summaries.

Problem Solved: Reduces the problem of tacit knowledge, unarticulated routines, and social/cultural workplace nuances that stakeholders cannot verbally explain.
Input Artifacts: Observation protocol, video/audio recording equipment, field notes structure.
Output Artifacts: Observation records, task models, protocol analysis transcripts, identified tacit requirements.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst (observer), Operational Users / Workers (observed subjects).
Prerequisites: Access approval to the operational workplace; user trust and acceptance.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Gain access to the operational site and build trust with workers. 2. Observe tasks in passive mode (watching/recording) or active mode (participating/asking questions). 3. In protocol analysis, ask the subject to think out loud while performing the task. 4. In ethnographic studies, observe long-term social interactions, gestures, shortcuts, and environmental reactions. 5. Analyze field notes/recordings to extract implicit mental models and unstated operational needs. 6. Validate findings in debriefing sessions with workers.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Why did you perform that manual workaround just now? What information on that physical paper strip are you checking before pressing the button?
Minimal Realistic Example: Observing air traffic controllers using paper flight strips to realize they physically rearrange strips to organize mental traffic flows, yielding a requirement for flexible UI strip-reordering.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Debriefing and validation of field notes with observed subjects; cross-observation under varying workload conditions.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Hawthorne effect (subjects changing behavior because they are observed); observer misinterpreting actions without SME debriefing; excessive cost/time spent collecting irrelevant detail.
When NOT to Use: When defining future, non-existent software features where no existing physical/human process exists to be observed.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Interviews, Prototyping, Contextual Inquiry. Alternative: Storyboarding.
Supported Decisions: Designing human-computer interaction workflows, capturing tacit operational safeguards.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Computer vision and speech-recognition agents can process video logs of user tasks to map workflow sequences and identify process bottlenecks.

Problem Solved: Reduces conflict between stakeholder groups, bridges organizational silos, and fosters rapid consensus and creative problem-solving.
Input Artifacts: Session agenda, wall charts, preliminary proposal drafts, presentation slides.
Output Artifacts: Group-agreed high-level requirements, prioritized feature lists, workshop decision logs.
Participants & Roles: Session Leader/Facilitator, Scribe/Reporter, Business Analyst, Stakeholders, SMEs, System Developers.
Prerequisites: Clear workshop scope and objectives; commitment of key stakeholders to attend full workshops.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define session scope, participant roles, and agenda. 2. (Brainstorming - Stage 1) Spontaneously generate diverse ideas without censorship or criticism. 3. (Brainstorming - Stage 2) Jointly evaluate, prune, and group generated ideas against agreed criteria. 4. (Structured/JAD) Walk through structured document templates or feature architectures, resolving conflicting viewpoints in real time. 5. Record consensus decisions and unresolved action items. 6. Publish workshop report for participant sign-off.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What creative ways could solve this bottleneck? Do all departments agree with this proposed workflow? What is the relative priority of option A vs option B?
Minimal Realistic Example: A 2-day JAD workshop bringing together library staff, IT consultants, and student representatives to agree on the functional scope of an automated check-out kiosk.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Consensus sign-off by all participant roles; verification that generated requirements cover identified problems.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Dominance by vocal or senior individuals suppressing quieter experts; lack of strong facilitation leading to unstructured rambling; addressing low-level technical details prematurely.
When NOT to Use: When key stakeholders cannot commit dedicated time, or when participants have extreme interpersonal hostility requiring individual negotiation first.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Prototyping, Questionnaires. Alternative: Individual Structured Interviews.
Supported Decisions: Defining high-level system boundaries, trade-off decisions, and feature prioritization.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI facilitators can synthesize live chat/audio contributions during workshops, automatically group similar ideas into mind maps, and detect hidden policy conflicts.

Problem Solved: Reduces inconsistencies, divergence, and stakeholder disagreements between overlapping requirements or goals.
Input Artifacts: Overlapping/conflicting requirements, interaction matrix, boundary conditions for divergence.
Output Artifacts: Documented conflict logs, boundary conditions, agreed conflict resolutions (weakened/modified statements).
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Conflicting Stakeholders, Project Decision Maker / Sponsor.
Prerequisites: Identification and formal/informal detection of overlapping requirements or divergence.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify overlapping statements referencing common domain phenomena. 2. Detect conflicts or calculate boundary conditions that make statements logically inconsistent. 3. Document conflicts using an interaction matrix or requirements database links. 4. Generate alternative conflict resolutions using resolution tactics (Avoid boundary condition, Restore statements, Weaken statements, Drop lower-priority statement, Specialize source/target). 5. Evaluate alternative resolutions against non-functional quality goals. 6. Negotiate with stakeholders to select and approve the best compromise.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Under what specific conditions do these two requirements contradict each other? Can we weaken this requirement for lower-priority user groups? Can we restrict the scope of this rule to staff users only?
Minimal Realistic Example: Resolving a divergence between 'Borrowers return books in 2 weeks' and 'Borrowers keep books as long as needed' by applying the 'Avoid Boundary Condition' tactic—retaining reference-only copies on library shelves at all times.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Logical consistency verification of resolved statements; formal check that boundary condition can no longer hold; stakeholder sign-off on compromise.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Resolving conflicts too prematurely before exploring stakeholder perspectives; ignoring weak conflicts (divergence) that only manifest under rare edge conditions; jumping to a single resolution without exploring options.
When NOT to Use: When statements do not overlap or when apparent conflicts are merely terminology/designation clashes (which should be fixed via a glossary).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Goal Modeling, Win-Win Negotiation, Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP).
Supported Decisions: Scope determination, policy trade-offs, priority ranking.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Logic-based AI agents can detect formal divergences, compute boundary conditions, and automatically suggest tactical weakenings using pre-defined resolution patterns.

Method Name: Risk Analysis and Control (Fault Trees / DDP)
Problem Solved: Reduces product- and process-related risks, safety hazards, and security threats by identifying failure modes, evaluating exposures, and adding robust countermeasure requirements.
Input Artifacts: System objectives, goal models, risk checklists, component architecture, fault/threat trees.
Output Artifacts: Risk assessment tables, fault trees, cut sets, impact/effectiveness matrices (DDP), countermeasure requirements.
Participants & Roles: Requirements Engineer, Safety/Security SME, System Architect, Domain Expert.
Prerequisites: Initial system goals and proposed functional capabilities identified.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify potential product/process risks using risk checklists, component inspection, fault/threat trees, or scenario WHAT-IF analysis. 2. Construct risk trees linking top-level failures to root causes via AND/OR logical nodes. 3. Assess risk likelihood and consequence severity qualitatively or quantitatively (calculating Risk Exposure = Likelihood x Severity). 4. Explore alternative countermeasures using risk-reduction tactics (Reduce likelihood, Avoid risk, Mitigate consequence). 5. Evaluate countermeasures using Risk Reduction Leverage (RRL) or DDP effectiveness matrices. 6. Select cost-effective countermeasures and integrate them as new system goals/requirements.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What could go wrong if this component fails? What is the worst-case consequence of inaccurate speed data? How much does this countermeasure reduce our risk exposure?
Minimal Realistic Example: Analyzing the risk 'Train doors open while moving' using a fault tree to reveal the cause 'Emergency signal raised while moving', leading to a countermeasure requirement: 'Door actuator shall ignore manual emergency signals unless speed = 0.'
Quality Criteria & Verification: Completeness of cut sets; quantitative balance verification via DDP optimization; hazard/threat validation by domain SMEs.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Assuming over-ideal system behavior where nothing fails; treating qualitative risk scores as absolute mathematical facts; ignoring process risks like requirements volatility.
When NOT to Use: In trivial, non-critical greenfield administrative software where risk exposure is negligible and development costs dictate minimal ceremony.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Obstacle Analysis, Anti-Goal Modeling, FMEA. Alternative: Qualitative Risk Matrices.
Supported Decisions: Safety/security architecture decisions, countermeasure scope selection, release readiness.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic safety tools can automatically generate fault trees from structural goal models, run simulated annealing for optimal DDP countermeasure selection, and monitor risk thresholds.

Method Name: Option Evaluation (Qualitative NFR & Quantitative Weighted Matrices)
Problem Solved: Reduces decision uncertainty when choosing among alternative goal refinements, architectural options, risk countermeasures, or responsibility assignments.
Input Artifacts: Alternative system options, non-functional requirements (NFRs), criteria weights.
Output Artifacts: NFR contribution tables (+/++/-/-- labels), weighted decision matrices, selected 'best' system option.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, System Architect, Key Stakeholders / Decision Makers.
Prerequisites: Elicited non-functional quality goals to serve as evaluation criteria; identified mutually exclusive alternatives.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify the mutually exclusive alternative options to be evaluated. 2. Establish evaluation criteria based on elicitation of non-functional quality requirements. 3. Assign relative importance weights to each criterion. 4. (Qualitative) Map the positive or negative contribution (+, ++, -, --) of each option to each NFR criterion and propagate along goal graphs. 5. (Quantitative) Score each option's satisfaction percentage against each criterion and compute total weighted scores: TotalScore = Sum(Score_i * Weight_i). 6. Select the highest-scoring option and document the decision rationale.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How does option A impact our usability goal compared to option B? What weight should we give to response time vs operational cost? Which alternative offers the optimal trade-off?
Minimal Realistic Example: Evaluating 'Constraints via E-mail' vs 'Constraints via E-agenda'. E-agenda scores 100% on 'Minimal Inconvenience' but 30% on 'Reliable Accuracy', resulting in a lower weighted total score than the E-mail option.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Sensitivity analysis of weights/scores in spreadsheets; stakeholder consensus on assigned criteria weights.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Failing to make non-functional evaluation criteria explicit; manipulating scores artificially to justify a biased preference.
When NOT to Use: When one option is strictly mandatory due to absolute legal, regulatory, or hard technical constraints.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Goal Modeling (NFR framework), DDP. Alternative: Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP).
Supported Decisions: System boundary selection, architectural style choice, conflict resolution trade-offs.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI decision-support agents can run automated multi-criteria sensitivity analysis and generate natural language rationale summaries for trade-off options.

Problem Solved: Reduces project failure risks due to budget overruns or missed deadlines by ranking independent requirements into relative priority levels for phased release planning.
Input Artifacts: Candidate requirements list (at uniform granularity), value and cost criteria.
Output Artifacts: AHP pairwise comparison matrices, value/cost percentage allocations, value-cost scatter plot, prioritized release tiers.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Product Manager, Customer / User Representatives, Lead Developer / Architect.
Prerequisites: Comparable, independent requirements list; cost estimates from developers and value estimates from customers.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Verify that candidate requirements are at similar levels of abstraction and independent. 2. Apply AHP Step 1 (Value): Construct a pairwise comparison matrix (1-9 scale) estimating relative customer value between requirement pairs. 3. Apply AHP Step 2 (Value): Normalize matrix columns and average rows to derive the percentage value contribution of each requirement. 4. Apply AHP Steps 1 & 2 (Cost): Repeat the pairwise comparison process with developers estimating relative implementation cost to derive cost percentages. 5. Plot each requirement on a Value-Cost diagram (x=Cost %, y=Value %). 6. Partition the diagram into High, Medium, and Low priority tiers and negotiate final release increments with stakeholders.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Does requirement R1 contribute slightly, strongly, or extremely more to customer value than requirement R2? What is the relative implementation cost of R1 compared to R2?
Minimal Realistic Example: Applying AHP to 5 meeting scheduler features shows 'Produce Optimal Dates' yields 49% of total value for 20% of cost (High Priority), while 'Multilingual Support' yields 4% value for 22% cost (Low Priority).
Quality Criteria & Verification: AHP consistency ratio check (must be within acceptable mathematical thresholds); stakeholder agreement on release boundaries.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Comparing items at mismatched granularities (e.g., a whole subsystem vs a button tweak); treating non-independent requirements as separate; using overly granular quantitative scales (e.g., 100 priority levels).
