When NOT to Use: When all requirements are strictly mandatory for legal/safety reasons, or in micro-projects with very few simple features.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Goal Model Refinement. Alternative: Simple Qualitative Group Ranking (High/Medium/Low), MoSCoW.
Supported Decisions: Release planning, scope reduction, budget allocation, conflict resolution by dropping low-priority items.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can pre-calculate AHP matrices from raw stakeholder feedback logs, perform mathematical consistency ratio validation, and plot automated value-cost release charts.

Problem Solved: Reduces ambiguity, logical noise, and omissions in complex natural language conditional statements by structuring logic into tabular input-output combinations.
Input Artifacts: Complex if-then conditional statements, inputs/outputs lists.
Output Artifacts: Disjoint and exhaustive Decision Table, identified missing logic cases, cause-effect test cases.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Developer, Tester.
Prerequisites: Identification of atomic input conditions and output actions.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify all atomic input conditions and output actions. 2. Create a table with input conditions in top rows and output actions in bottom rows. 3. Populate top columns with all 2^N true/false combinations for N input conditions. 4. Specify corresponding output actions for each column. 5. Eliminate impossible columns based on known domain properties. 6. Merge redundant columns that yield identical outputs to simplify the table. 7. Check for missing columns (incompleteness) or extra columns (redundancy).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What are all the atomic conditions affecting this decision? What output must occur if condition 1 is True, condition 2 is False, and condition 3 is True?
Minimal Realistic Example: Structuring train braking rules into an 8-column table revealing a missing edge case: 'Train enters station block too fast AND preceding train is too close AND command is NOT outdated.'
Quality Criteria & Verification: Mathematical check for completeness (column count matches 2^N before simplification); cause-effect test case generation.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Including non-atomic or overlapping conditions; failing to document why an eliminated column is physically impossible.
When NOT to Use: When the logic is sequential, time-series dependent, or involves simple non-combinatorial rules.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Structured Natural Language, SCR Condition Tables. Alternative: Flowcharts, State Machine Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Verifying rule completeness, acceptance test case design.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLM agents can ingest complex unstructured prose requirements, auto-generate decision tables, and output formal notices of missing logical combinations.

Method Name: System Scope Diagrams (Context, Problem, and Frame Diagrams)
Problem Solved: Reduces boundary ambiguity by defining the problem world components, the machine solution, shared interface phenomena, and the domain properties/requirements constraining them.
Input Artifacts: Elicited system components, environmental phenomena, generic problem frames.
Output Artifacts: Context diagrams, Problem diagrams, instantiated Frame diagrams.
Participants & Roles: Requirements Engineer / Business Analyst, System Architect.
Prerequisites: Identified candidate system components (causal, biddable, lexical) and machine boundaries.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify domain components (people, devices, legacy software) and the machine to be built. 2. Identify shared interface phenomena (events, signals, data) between components. 3. Draw a Context Diagram connecting components via shared phenomena edges. 4. Expand into a Problem Diagram by highlighting the Machine (double stripe), environment components (single stripe), and adding dashed ovals for requirements. 5. Annotate links showing which phenomena are monitored, controlled, or constrained by requirements. 6. (Frame Diagrams) Match the problem against generic frames (e.g., Simple Workpieces, Information Display) and instantiate typed parameters.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Which component controls this event? Which environmental phenomena does the machine monitor? What requirement constrains this physical device?
Minimal Realistic Example: Drawing a problem diagram showing the 'Scheduler' machine controlling 'meetingNotification' events monitored by the 'Participant' biddable domain component, constrained by a 'Convenient Date' requirement.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Verification that all machine interface phenomena are monitored/controlled by valid domain components; view integration checks against sequence diagrams.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confusing machine-internal phenomena with problem-world phenomena; drawing unclear component boundaries without explicit phenomenon labels.
When NOT to Use: For internal software architectural design where problem-world domain components are irrelevant.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Agent Diagrams, Use Case Diagrams. Alternative: High-level System Architecture Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Defining the software-environment boundary, allocation of system vs software responsibilities.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic tools can parse problem text to identify causal/biddable entities and autogenerate problem frame diagrams in graphical formats.

Method Name: Conceptual Modeling with Entity-Relationship (ER) / Class Diagrams
Problem Solved: Reduces structural ambiguity and terminology clashes by defining domain concepts, their attributes, structural relationships, multiplicities, and specialization hierarchies.
Input Artifacts: Project glossary, goal specifications, interview transcripts, domain reports.
Output Artifacts: Entity-Relationship (ER) diagrams, UML Class diagrams, precise concept definitions.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst / Data Model Analyst, Domain SME, Database Architect.
Prerequisites: Elicited domain entities and terminology from domain understanding.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify key domain concepts (entities/classes) that have distinct identities and attributes. 2. Define intrinsic features (attributes) and value ranges for each entity. 3. Identify conceptual links (relationships/associations) between entities and assign role names. 4. Specify multiplicities (minimum/maximum bounds) for each relationship side. 5. Identify specialization hierarchies (superclasses/subclasses) for concept inheritance. 6. Annotate all entities and relationships with precise natural language definitions. 7. Derive/refine ER diagrams from system goal specifications.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Is concept X an entity, an attribute, or a relationship? Can a patron borrow multiple book copies simultaneously? Is this multiplicity a physical domain property or an enforced requirement?
Minimal Realistic Example: Modeling a 'Participant' entity with attributes Name/Email, linked via an 'Invitation' relationship (multiplicity 0.. ) to a 'Meeting' entity (multiplicity 1.. ).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Checking ER diagrams against goal references (concern links); verifying multiplicities against physical domain properties vs prescriptive requirements; SME walkthroughs.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confusing entities with attributes; failing to distinguish domain properties from prescriptive requirements in multiplicities; modeling implementation data structures prematurely.
When NOT to Use: When the domain is purely procedural or algorithmic with negligible persistent data or domain concepts.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Goal Modeling (concern links), Glossary. Alternative: Dataflow Diagrams (for functional-only view).
Supported Decisions: Data architecture design, domain vocabulary standardization, database schema generation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLM agents can extract entities, attributes, and relationships from natural language goal specs and automatically produce valid UML Class Diagram code (e.g., PlantUML).

Problem Solved: Reduces operational opacity by mapping information transformations, processing operations, data repositories, and functional data dependencies.
Input Artifacts: Elicited business processes, task descriptions, input/output data sets.
Output Artifacts: SADT Actigrams/Datagrams, Dataflow Diagrams (DFDs), process specs.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Business Process SME, Software Architect.
Prerequisites: Identified system operations and data stores.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify main system operations (data transformation processes/bubbles). 2. Identify external origin/destination components (boxes) and data repositories (double bars). 3. Connect operations via directed arrows representing input/output data flows. 4. (SADT) Specify Actigrams (inputs, outputs, controls, mechanisms) and dual Datagrams. 5. Hierarchically refine complex operations into child DFD diagrams. 6. Annotate leaf processes with concise operational specifications.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What data is required to perform this operation? Where does this dataflow originate? What store holds this information?
Minimal Realistic Example: Drawing a DFD bubble 'Schedule Meeting' receiving 'meetingRequest' from Initiator and 'individualConstraints' from 'Participant' store, outputting 'meetingNotification' to Participant.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Parent-child dataflow balance checks (input/output consistency across hierarchy levels); verifying that all data stores connect to processes; database query checks.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Infinite sinks/sources (data disappearing or created out of nowhere); control-flow branching confused with dataflow; overly complex non-decomposed diagrams.
When NOT to Use: When specifying object-oriented design encapsulation or strict reactive event timing where state machines are required.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: ER Diagrams, State Machine Diagrams. Alternative: UML Use Case Diagrams, Activity Diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Functional decomposition, data transformation interface design.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agents can analyze process specifications to construct functional DFD models and run automated balance checks across hierarchical levels.

Problem Solved: Reduces behavioral uncertainty in reactive systems by formalizing all admissible state transitions, event triggers, and guard conditions for controlled system components.
Input Artifacts: Controlled system variables, interaction scenarios, event definitions.
Output Artifacts: State Machine (SM) diagrams, Statecharts, transition matrices.
Participants & Roles: Requirements Engineer / Behavioral Analyst, Embedded Systems / Software Architect.
Prerequisites: Identified controlled state variables and external triggering events.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify the controlled variable and its discrete equivalence states (e.g., doorsClosed, doorsOpen). 2. Define the initial state and final states. 3. Identify external triggering events causing state changes. 4. Define guarded transitions: 'If in State S1 and Event EV occurs when Guard G holds, move to State S2.' 5. (Statecharts) Organize concurrent sub-states using parallel composition to avoid state explosion. 6. Verify determinism (no multiple outgoing transitions with identical triggers/guards).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What state is the component in initially? What event triggers a transition from state A to B? What guard condition prevents this transition?
Minimal Realistic Example: Modeling a train door state machine: From 'doorsClosed' state, receiving event 'opening' when speed = 0 transitions component to 'doorsOpen' state.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Determinism verification; deadlock/unreachable state detection; model checking against temporal safety goals; coverage of scenario traces.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Combinatorial state explosion due to monolithic design without parallel statecharts; non-deterministic transitions; confusing states (durations) with events (instantaneous).
When NOT to Use: For simple sequential data-processing batch applications where state transitions are irrelevant.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Event Trace Diagrams, Goal Models, SCR. Alternative: Decision Tables.
Supported Decisions: Reactive controller logic design, safety verification, state-based system testing.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Model-checking AI tools can verify statecharts for deadlocks, synthesize state machines directly from event trace scenarios, and output counterexamples.

Problem Solved: Eliminates ambiguity, noise, and incompleteness by providing a mathematically precise, machine-processable specification amenable to automated proof, model checking, and animation.
Input Artifacts: Agreed system goals, requirements, assumptions, domain properties, ER conceptual structures.
Output Artifacts: Formal specification schemas (Z), temporal logic assertions (LTL), tabular state machine functions (SCR), mathematical proof obligations.
Participants & Roles: Formal Methods Specialist / Requirements Engineer, System Architect, Safety/Security Verifier.
Prerequisites: Strong discrete mathematics background; well-defined domain concepts and boundaries.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define the mathematical domain of interpretation (given types, variables, state space). 2. (History-based / LTL) Formalize declarative goals using temporal operators (Always, Eventually, Until). 3. (State-based / Z) Define state variables and data schemas with invariants, then specify operations via pre- and post-conditions. 4. (Event-based / SCR) Define mode transition, event, and condition tables over monitored/controlled variables. 5. (Algebraic) Define signatures, generator operations, and equational composition laws. 6. Document precise designations mapping formal symbols to real-world domain phenomena.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What exact mathematical relation defines this operation's post-condition? Is this temporal requirement bounded by a specific time deadline? What is the explicit domain designation of symbol X?
Minimal Realistic Example: Specifying train door safety in LTL: 'Always (Moving(tr) -> tr.Doors = closed)' or in Z: 'Checkout' schema defining post-condition 'Available' = Available \ {be?} AND Onloan' = Onloan U {be?}'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Automated type checking; mathematical consistency proof; exhaustiveness/disjointness table checks; theorem proving; model checking.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Failing to document domain designations (making math meaningless); overspecifying implementation details prematurely; creating unreadable nested temporal logic assertions.
When NOT to Use: In low-risk, non-critical commercial projects where informal/semi-formal documentation suffices and formal verification costs are unjustified.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Semi-formal Diagrams, Model Animation, Inspections. Alternative: Structured Natural Language Templates.
Supported Decisions: Safety/security certification, formal verification of critical software logic, exact contractual specifications.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Neural-symbolic AI agents can translate structured natural language requirements into formal LTL/Z specs and invoke automated SAT solvers to verify consistency.

Problem Solved: Reduces defects, omissions, contradictions, ambiguities, and inaccuracies across all specification formats through structured human peer review.
Input Artifacts: Requirements Document (RD), review guidelines, inspection checklists (defect-based, quality-specific, domain-specific, language-based).
Output Artifacts: Inspection reports, defect logs, list of false positives, consolidated/revised Requirements Document.
Participants & Roles: Inspection Leader/Moderator, Author(s) of RD, Independent Reviewers (Domain SME, User, Developer, QA Specialist).
Prerequisites: Availability of a complete draft RD and structured inspection checklists.
Step-by-Step Procedure: (Planning) Select independent inspection team (min. 3), define scope, and distribute material. 2. (Individual Reviewing) Inspectors read RD individually in free, checklist-based, or process-based (role-based) mode, logging detected defects. 3. (Review Meeting) Inspectors meet (max. 2 hours) to evaluate logged defects, discard false positives, analyze root causes, and agree on recommendations. 4. (Documentation) Produce an official inspection report signed by all inspectors. 5. (Consolidation) Authors revise the RD to fix agreed defects.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Is this requirement measurable with a fit criterion? Does this assumption contradict domain property X? Are all failure/exception cases specified for this operation?
Minimal Realistic Example: A 3-person team (SME, Developer, QA) uses a safety checklist to inspect a train control RD, discovering that the exception handling for sensor signal loss was omitted.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Defect detection rate; verification that all logged inspection report defects are resolved in the consolidated RD.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Lack of independent reviewers (authors inspecting their own work); reviews degenerating into personal attacks; holding overly long, exhausting meetings (> 2 hours); skimming without checklists.
When NOT to Use: Never—inspections apply to all projects; however, formal heavy meetings can be streamlined to lightweight walkthroughs in small agile projects.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Automated Database Queries, Animation, Model Checking. Alternative: Informal Walkthroughs.
Supported Decisions: RD baseline approval, release sign-off, software readiness for development.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLM review agents can perform automated preliminary checklist inspections, highlighting potential ambiguities, passive voice, or missing exception clauses prior to human review meetings.

Problem Solved: Reduces structural inconsistencies, unlinked elements, and incomplete diagrammatic models through automated database query engines.
Input Artifacts: Semi-formal diagrams maintained in a structured Requirements Database (repository).
Output Artifacts: Query result sets, structural error logs, missing link reports.
Participants & Roles: Requirements Engineer / BA, Tool Quality Analyst.
Prerequisites: Specification stored in a tool with an underlying meta-model schema (e.g., MOF, ER meta-database).
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define structural consistency and completeness rules at the meta-model level (e.g., intra- and inter-view rules). 2. Formulate corresponding database queries (using SQL, graph query languages, or predefined tool rule sets). 3. Execute queries against the requirements database in press-button mode. 4. Review returned result sets representing rule violations (e.g., unreferenced entities, unbalanced DFD flows). 5. Correct the underlying diagrammatic models to resolve detected violations.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Is there any entity in the ER diagram that is not referenced by any goal or operation? Is there an output flow in a child DFD missing from the parent bubble?
Minimal Realistic Example: Running a pre-cooked query 'Unreferenced Entities' on a UML repository to automatically flag a 'PassengerLog' class that has no relationships or operational use cases.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Zero structural violations returned by standard verification query suites.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Relying on database queries for semantic adequacy checks (queries only check structural syntax, not whether the requirement is what the customer actually wants).
When NOT to Use: When documentation is maintained purely as unrestricted natural language prose without a structured database repository.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Inspections, Model Checking. Alternative: Manual Checklist Review.
Supported Decisions: Model well-formedness verification, static semantics sign-off.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Graph-database AI agents can continuously run background graph queries over requirement repositories to report broken traceability or orphan nodes in real time.

Problem Solved: Reduces requirement inadequacy and customer expectation mismatches by converting formal specifications into interactive, visual simulations.
Input Artifacts: Executable formal/semi-formal specification (state machine, Z, SCR, LTL-derived model).
Output Artifacts: Interactive simulation sessions, animation trace logs, domain scene visualizations, stakeholder validation feedback.
Participants & Roles: Requirements Engineer / Animator, Domain SME, End Users / Stakeholders.
Prerequisites: Formal/executable model of the system-to-be; animator tool with visualization interface.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Extract or generate an executable state machine or transition model from formal specifications. 2. Configure animation parameters and domain-specific visual control panels/scenes. 3. Instantiate test scenarios with representative component instances. 4. Execute the model by submitting simulated environment events via control panels. 5. Observe system reactions visually in real-time domain scenes. 6. Gather stakeholder feedback on whether visual reactions match expectations and record violating trace logs.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Is this visual behavior what you expect when the emergency button is pressed? Does the train doors visual open at the correct platform position?
Minimal Realistic Example: Executing an SCR train specification in an animator: clicking 'Start' on a control panel visually shows the train moving on a graphical track scene while its doors remain closed, validating safety expectations visually.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Stakeholder sign-off on visual scenario replays; runtime property monitor assertions evaluating to True during animation.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Animating unrepresentative, trivial scenarios that fail to exercise edge cases; confusing animation success with full mathematical proof.
When NOT to Use: When no executable formal specification exists, or for purely non-functional static requirements (e.g., development cost limits).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Model Checking, Inspections. Alternative: Throwaway Code Prototyping.
Supported Decisions: Validating behavioral adequacy, user acceptance of control logic, acceptance test data approval.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic animation tools can autonomously generate edge-case event sequences, run batch animations, and highlight visual state assertion violations to stakeholders.

Problem Solved: Reduces inconsistency, untraced impact, and maintenance costs during requirements evolution by documenting and navigating explicit links among requirements, goals, assumptions, and software lifecycle artifacts.
Input Artifacts: Requirements Document, traceability meta-model, link types (Dependency, Variant, Revision, Use, Derivation), software artifacts.
Output Artifacts: Traceability matrix/graph, traceability database, coverage reports, change impact logs.
Participants & Roles: Requirements Engineer, Change Control Board, Software Architect, Test Manager.
Prerequisites: Defined project traceability policy (determining link granularity and scope); uniquely identified artifacts.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define a project traceability policy establishing scope, link types, and granularity based on project risk. 2. Assign unique identifiers (RefName) to all traceable items. 3. Establish horizontal links (Use) and vertical links (Derivation) between goals, requirements, assumptions, architecture, code, and test cases. 4. Record links in a traceability matrix, database, or model repository. 5. (Exploitation) Perform forward/backward impact analysis, coverage analysis, and rationale tracking when changes are requested. 6. Maintain and update links whenever items are created, modified, or deleted.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What upward goals explain why this software module exists? What downward test cases must be re-run if requirement R1 changes? What requirements are impacted if assumption A1 is invalidated?
Minimal Realistic Example: Tracing goal 'G1: Safe Transportation' -> derived requirement 'R1: Doors closed when moving' -> derived architecture module 'DoorController' -> derived test case 'TC_Door_01'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: 100% downward coverage of high-priority requirements by test cases and architecture modules; absence of orphan requirements.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Traceability decay (failing to update links when requirements evolve); over-tracing trivial items causing unmanageable overhead ('traceability paralysis'); single-direction tracing.
When NOT to Use: Unselective fine-grained tracing on ultra-short, throwaway micro-projects where maintenance cost outweighs value.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Goal Modeling (Satisfaction Arguments), Configuration Management, Information Retrieval Link Mining.
Supported Decisions: Change impact assessment, release regression planning, compliance/certification auditing.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents using NLP/semantic similarity can automatically generate candidate traceability links across text specs, code, and tests, maintaining graph integrity continuously.

Problem Solved: Reduces scope creep, undocumented system decay, and architectural instability by enforcing a disciplined review procedure for all proposed requirement modifications.
Input Artifacts: Wishlist, motivated Change Request forms, impact analysis reports, traceability graph.
Output Artifacts: Change Evaluation log, approved/rejected/deferred change decisions, baselined RD revision/variant.
Participants & Roles: Change Control Board (CCB) - Decision Makers, BA, Architect, SME, Customer Representative.
Prerequisites: Traceable requirements baseline; established CCB review authority and policies.
Step-by-Step Procedure: (Initiation) Collect proposed changes into a motivated Change Request detailing rationale, urgency, and affected items. 2. (Evaluation) CCB reviews the request, uses traceability graphs to assess forward impact on architecture, costs, and schedules, and checks for conflicts with existing goals. 3. (Prioritization) Prioritize approved changes against project resources. 4. (Decision) CCB formally approves, rejects, or defers changes. 5. (Consolidation) Propagate approved changes through the RD, re-verify consistency, update traceability graphs, and baseline the new RD version.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is the business rationale for this change? What architectural components are affected? What is the cost of implementing this change vs the risk of not changing?
Minimal Realistic Example: Submitting a Change Request to add 'SMS Notification'. The CCB evaluates impact using traceability links, determines a $10k cost and 2-week schedule extension, approves it, and baselines RD Revision 2.1.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Formal CCB sign-off logs; zero undocumented requirement changes in production code; full propagation of approved changes across all dependent artifacts.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Bypassing CCB via informal developer-customer side agreements ('scope creep'); holding up critical bug fixes due to overly bureaucratic CCB procedures.
When NOT to Use: In early exploratory greenfield prototyping where requirements are still in raw discovery mode before the first baseline.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Traceability Management, Goal Modeling, Version Control Systems.
Supported Decisions: Scope baseline changes, budget/schedule adjustments, release versioning.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can automatically parse Change Requests, run automated impact analysis across code repositories using traceability graphs, and draft CCB cost-impact reports.

Method Name: Runtime Requirements Monitoring and Dynamic Adaptation
Problem Solved: Reduces system failures caused by changing or unexpected environmental assumptions at system runtime through continuous self-monitoring and dynamic reconfiguration.
Input Artifacts: Formal temporal logic goal assertions, unstable environment assumptions, alternative design courses of action, reconfiguration rules.
Output Artifacts: Software monitors, violation logs, runtime compensator, reconfigured software state.
Participants & Roles: Requirements Engineer (specifier), Software Architect, Runtime System Monitor / Compensator Engine.
Prerequisites: Formalized critical requirements/assumptions; identified alternative operational courses of action.
Step-by-Step Procedure: At RE time, identify mission-critical requirements or volatile assumptions subject to runtime violation. 2. Formalize assertions (e.g., in LTL) and compile them into automated software monitors (state machines or pattern matchers). 3. Design alternative courses of action and dynamic reconfiguration rules (e.g., threshold-based rules). 4. Deploy software together with concurrent monitors and compensator engine. 5. At runtime, monitors track system events; upon detecting assertion violations, the compensator executes reconfiguration rules to shift to alternative courses of action on the fly.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What assumption is volatile at runtime? What threshold of violation should trigger dynamic reconfiguration? What alternative workflow should execute if assumption A fails?
Minimal Realistic Example: Monitoring assumption 'Invited participant responds to email within 3 days'. If monitor detects 3 consecutive missed deadlines, compensator automatically switches workflow to query the participant's electronic agenda directly.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Real-time assertion detection correctness; mathematical proof that monitor compilation preserves original LTL property semantics.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Monitoring non-critical low-risk parameters causing high runtime CPU overhead; endless reconfiguration loops between unstable alternatives.
When NOT to Use: In static, fully predictable environments where operational assumptions never change, or in legacy systems without dynamic plug-in architectures.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Goal Modeling, LTL Formal Specification, Exception Handling. Alternative: Static Off-line Change Control.
Supported Decisions: Dynamic system reconfiguration, runtime fault tolerance, adaptive user customization.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Autonomous agentic architectures use ML monitors to detect assumption drifts in real time and dynamically synthesize new compensator workflows without human intervention.

Problem Solved: Reduces requirements incompleteness, irrelevance, lack of rationale, and stakeholder misalignment by systematically modeling system objectives, alternative refinements, conflicts, risks, and responsibility assignments.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Discovery / elicitation / analysis / specification / prioritisation / validation / change management
Input Artifacts: Elicited stakeholder wishes, domain background documents, interview transcripts, problem logs, scenarios.
Output Artifacts: Goal Model (AND/OR diagrams), Obstacle Model, Agent Model, Object Model, Operation Model, consolidated Requirements Document.
Participants & Roles: Requirements Engineer / BA, System Architect, Stakeholders, SMEs, System Agents.
Prerequisites: Identification of problem world boundaries and key stakeholder perspectives.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Elicit preliminary goals using keywords, problem analysis, or taxonomies. 2. Build goal refinement trees top-down (asking HOW) and bottom-up (asking WHY) using AND/OR nodes and reusable patterns (Milestone, Case-driven, Guard-introduction). 3. Refine goals until leaf nodes are reached that can be assigned as Requirements to single software agents or Expectations to single environment agents. 4. Identify and resolve goal conflicts (divergence) and obstacles. 5. Derive Object Models (class diagrams), Agent Models, and Operation Models (use cases) directly from leaf goals. 6. Generate the structured Requirements Document from the integrated goal model.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: WHY is this requirement needed (what higher goal does it serve)? HOW can this goal be satisfied? What sub-goals are missing for complete refinement? WHO (which agent) is responsible for this leaf goal?
Minimal Realistic Example: Refining 'AchieveBookRequestSatisfied' into AND-subgoals 'AchieveCopyBorrowedIfAvailable' and 'AchieveCopyDueSoonIfUnavailable', assigning the former requirement to the 'LibrarySoftware' agent.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Refinement completeness proof ({Subgoals, Dom} | = ParentGoal); 100% requirement pertinence; boundary completeness; formal verification.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confusing goals (declarative intents) with operations (single-state transition actions); confusing case-driven AND-refinements with alternative OR-refinements; creating unassignable multi-agent leaf goals.
When NOT to Use: Never—goal orientation applies universally across system engineering; however, formal temporal logic annotations can be skipped for non-critical, simple applications.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: UML Diagrams, Scenarios, Use Cases, Risk Analysis. Alternative: Flat unstructured requirements lists.
Supported Decisions: Defining system scope, selecting architectural options, assigning agent responsibilities, resolving conflicts, verifying completeness.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic RE frameworks can parse multi-stakeholder text to auto-generate KAOS AND/OR goal graphs, invoke SAT solvers to check refinement completeness, and auto-translate goals into executable B/Z specs.

Problem Solved: Reduces semantic uncertainty, misunderstandings, and miscommunication across business departments and IT by establishing a valid, clear, and intuitive understanding of core business concepts, definitions, and relationships.
BA Lifecycle Phase: Discovery, elicitation, analysis, specification, change management
Input Artifacts: Tacit knowledge from stakeholders, business models, strategy documents, spreadsheets, charts of accounts, standard database schemas, reports, administrative guidelines, and regulatory/standard vocabularies.
Output Artifacts: High-level, explorative, prototype, and solution-level Concept Maps; Business Vocabulary (written definitions document); Business Rules specification documents.
Participants & Roles: Executive Sponsor (e.g., CFO/Director of Sales), Business Project Anchor, Business Specialists/SME, Business Analyst/Synthesist (Facilitator), Scribe, IT Architect/Developer.
Prerequisites: Identification of a project business anchor, availability of knowledgeable domain experts, access to initial reference documents or existing operational spreadsheets, and setup of visual mapping tools (e.g., CmapTools with a data projector).
Step-by-Step Procedure: Prepare initial draft concept maps from existing business documents and passive sources. 2. Hold a top-down first workshop with business managers to draw an overall high-level scope map (e.g., overlaying concepts on the Business Model Canvas). 3. Conduct explorative workshops with business specialists to map the as-is concepts, terms, and relationships. 4. Conduct ideation workshops to identify holes, resolve contradictions, re-engineer terminology, and sketch prototype solution concept maps. 5. Apply generalization or specialization techniques if stalled by excessive complexity or lack of detail. 6. Conduct implementation workshops to refine final detailed solution designs and documentational concept maps. 7. Review and secure formal approval/sign-off of the concept maps and vocabulary definitions from business stakeholders.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What are we talking about when we use this term?", "What is the difference between Concept A and Concept B?", "What keeps management awake at night?", "Who does what with which objects?", "How is this calculated?", "What are the rules/exceptions for this relation?", "Is this general term or specific subtype necessary to run the business?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Mapping a kennel business: 'Puppy' (Business Object) --has for sale--> 'Kennel' (Business Object); 'Puppy' --can do--> 'Puppy Trick' (Business Object); 'Puppy' --has--> 'Puppy Name' (Property).
Quality Criteria & Verification: The concept map must be approved and validated by business stakeholders; diagrams must be readable in natural visual sentences (Subject-Predicate-Object propositions); definitions must be unambiguous, clear, and published on corporate platforms (e.g., Intranet).
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Including live/volatile data or intricate logical condition statements directly inside diagrams (over-complicating maps); treating concept mapping as technical IT data modeling; cramming more than 20 concepts onto a single diagram page; attempting to map processes/workflows inside concept maps.
When NOT to Use: Do not use when specifying low-level software execution logic without established business definitions, or in trivial small-risk projects where domain terminology is already fully standardized and unambiguous.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary/Preceding methods: Business Model Canvas, Brainstorming, Data Profiling. Alternatives/Succeeding methods: UML Class Diagrams, Entity-Relationship (ER) Modeling, Fact Modeling/SBVR, SKOS/OWL Semantic Web Models, Multidimensional (Dimensional) Modeling.
Supported Decisions: Decisions on project scope, business terminology standardization, business process/rule restructuring, data warehouse/BI architecture, master data management (MDM) hierarchy design, and software requirement acceptance.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Concept harvesting engines can use Natural Language Processing (NLP), text analytics, and machine learning to scan corporate documents, emails, and code to extract concept-relationship triples (triplets) automatically; Human-In-The-Loop (HITL) review by business analysts is required to filter, refine, and approve auto-generated graph triples to ensure semantic validity before integration.

Method Name: Understanding the Problem Before Converging on a Solution (Root Cause Analysis / Problem Statement)
Problem Solved: Prevents teams from building features or products that go unused or fail because they solve the wrong problem, address only symptoms, or jump prematurely to a suboptimal solution.
Input Artifacts: Initial project ideas, business cases, project charters, senior leadership or customer requests, stated problems, proposed solution descriptions.
Output Artifacts: Root Cause Analysis Diagram (Fishbone / Ishikawa Diagram), Problem Statement document/section.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst (facilitator/analyst), Executive Sponsor, Lead Customer, Product Visionary, Key Stakeholders, SMEs.
Prerequisites: A proposed initiative, business need, user complaint, or proposed solution provided by stakeholders.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Receive a stated problem or proposed solution request from a stakeholder. 2. Ask 'Why' repeatedly (e.g., using the 5 Whys technique) to trace backward from the symptoms or proposed solution to true underlying root causes. 3. Identify primary causes and contributing factors. 4. (Optional) Draw a Fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram placing the problem at the head and contributing causes along diagonal branches. 5. Evaluate all implications and determine whether the proposed solution actually addresses the root cause or if alternative/interim solutions are required. 6. Formulate a Problem Statement defining the Situation, Problem, Implication, Benefit, and Vision.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Why do we need to combine them / do this?", "Why is that a problem?", "Why are we not already achieving that goal today?", "If  is the answer, what was the question?", "Why do you think that's the right solution?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A stakeholder asks to combine four independent backend systems into one. Asking 'Why' reveals two root causes: customers are frustrated by logging in repeatedly across sites (losing 25% to competitors), and maintaining four separate programming languages is costly. The BA proposes single sign-on as a rapid interim fix for user churn while planning system consolidation.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Verify that every identified root cause is actionable; ensure the problem statement explicitly covers Situation, Problem, Implication, Benefit, and Vision; check that key stakeholders explicitly agree on the core problem statement.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Assuming a presented solution or initial problem description is automatically correct; solving symptoms instead of root causes; 'project success but product failure' (delivering what was asked for on time, but no one uses it).
When NOT to Use: When the problem domain and root causes are already fully understood, clear, and validated by data, or for trivial low-risk bug fixes.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Practice #2 Define Business Objectives, Practice #3 Define Solution Boundaries, Practice #13 Prioritize Requirements. Alternatives: Impact Mapping, 5 Whys standalone.
Supported Decisions: Scope definition, solution selection (e.g., build vs. buy, interim vs. long-term fix), project go/no-go.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: An AI agent can be prompted with initial user request texts to perform automated 5 Whys decomposition, generate fishbone structure in Markdown/JSON, draft structured Problem Statements, and flag potential mismatched assumptions between proposed solutions and stated goals. Human-in-the-loop validates root causes with domain SMEs.

Method Name: Defining Business Objectives (Vision and Scope / Business Objectives Model)
Problem Solved: Eliminates lack of alignment among stakeholders, prevents scope creep, and avoids building extraneous features that do not contribute to organizational value.
Input Artifacts: Problem Statement, executive directives, business case, project charter, market research.
Output Artifacts: Vision and Scope Document (or Project Charter), Business Objectives Model (RML diagram), Objective Chain, Vision Statement, Success Metrics list.
Participants & Roles: Executive Sponsor, Primary Customer, Product Visionary, Business Analyst, Product Owner/Manager, Key Decision Makers.
Prerequisites: Understanding of the core business problem or opportunity.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Facilitate a discussion with project sponsors and business leaders using targeted elicitation questions. 2. Extract explicit business opportunities, business objectives, and desired financial/nonfinancial outcomes. 3. Define quantitative, verifiable business objectives (stating absolute targets rather than vague relative changes). 4. Establish surrogate/interim success metrics (lagging and leading tracking indicators). 5. Draft a Product Vision Statement using the standard keyword template (For / Who / The / Is / That / Unlike / Our product). 6. (Optional) Construct a Business Objectives Model linking Business Problems to Business Objectives, Success Metrics, and Solution Concepts. 7. Document findings in a Vision and Scope document or Project Charter and obtain stakeholder alignment.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What business problem are you trying to solve or what business opportunity do you perceive?", "What's the motivation for solving this problem...?", "What are your business objectives?", "How would the proposed product provide value...?", "What would a highly successful solution do for you? Can you quantify its potential payoff?", "How could you judge the solution's success?", "What could the business impact be if you don't pursue this solution?"
Minimal Realistic Example: For a restaurant online ordering system: Problem '50% of phone requests drop off on hold' links to Objective 'Convert 95% of placement requests to submitted orders', measured by Success Metric 'Average order placement cost <= 5% of order value', mapping to Solution Concepts like 'Online menu' and 'Online order placement'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Objectives must be specific, realistic, absolute, and measurable (SMART). Success metrics must logically correlate with long-term business goals. Vision statement must be agreed upon by all key leaders.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Stating business objectives as features to build rather than business outcomes; specifying relative percentage goals without baseline references; writing vague non-verifiable targets.
When NOT to Use: When working on minor maintenance tasks, localized bug fixes, or minor refactoring where organizational strategy is unaffected.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Practice #1 Understand Problem, Practice #3 Define Boundaries, Practice #4 Identify Stakeholders, Practice #13 Prioritization.
Supported Decisions: Project chartering, funding/investment decisions, high-level scope inclusion/exclusion, feature prioritization alignment.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLMs can ingest unstructured interview transcripts or project proposals to extract business objectives, generate candidate Vision Statements using the keyword template, draft RML models, and highlight non-measurable or vague objectives for human review.

Method Name: Defining the Solution's Boundaries (Context Diagram & Ecosystem Map)
Problem Solved: Prevents scope ambiguity, unbudgeted integration effort, interface mismatches, and uncoordinated upstream/downstream system impact.
Input Artifacts: Business Objectives, Product Vision, Solution Concept, existing system catalogs, corporate architecture diagrams.
Output Artifacts: Context Diagram, Ecosystem Map, Release Objectives Table / Scope Statement.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Systems Architect, Product Owner, Owners of Connected Systems, Key Business Stakeholders.
Prerequisites: Agreed-upon business objectives and refined solution concept.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Refine the high-level solution concept by determining which business processes are automated versus manual. 2. Identify the central system of interest and draw a circle representing the system boundary. 3. Identify all direct external entities (user classes, external systems, hardware devices) interacting with the system and place them outside the boundary. 4. Draw and label high-level data flows (arrows) connecting external entities and the system to form a Context Diagram. 5. Expand to an Ecosystem Map by depicting all interconnected systems in the domain and their data flows (APIs, files, queues). 6. Analyze interfaces to identify scope boundaries, derived integration requirements, and multi-release implementation objectives.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Which business processes, functions, and events will be part of the solution? Which ones will remain outside it?", "Who will use or derive benefits from the solution? Who is excluded?", "Which software systems will be part of the solution? What will the interfaces look like?", "Where do each system's responsibilities begin and end?", "How do we fit our solution into the rest of our universe?"
Minimal Realistic Example: An Online Ordering Site is drawn at the center of a Context Diagram. Arrows show 'menu items' flowing from an existing Menu Repository, 'orders' flowing to Restaurant Order Placement, and 'payment info/confirmation' exchanged with an external Online Payment Processing system.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Context Diagram contains exactly one central circle (the system under design); all external interfaces and data flows are labeled; cross-check ecosystem map data flows against system architecture and database interfaces.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Drawing internal system components inside a context diagram (violating boundary abstraction); failing to consult owners of connected external systems; creeping scope due to missing interface boundaries.
When NOT to Use: When the project is a standalone application with zero external user classes, zero hardware interfaces, and zero external software integrations.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Practice #8 Assess Data Concepts, Practice #11 Create Requirements Models (DFD). Alternatives: Architecture block diagrams, Use Case diagrams.
Supported Decisions: Scope boundaries, release planning/roadmapping, system responsibility allocation, vendor interface constraints.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can analyze existing architecture specs or codebases to automatically draft Mermaid/PlantUML context diagrams and ecosystem maps, highlighting missing data flows or unmapped external systems for human verification.

Method Name: Identifying and Characterizing Stakeholders (Stakeholder Catalog & RACI)
Problem Solved: Eliminates overlooked user classes, unvoiced regulatory/compliance constraints, missing requirements, and late-stage stakeholder friction.
Input Artifacts: Vision and Scope document, Project Charter, organizational charts, historical stakeholder catalogs.
Output Artifacts: Stakeholder Catalog / Profiles (Section 3.1 of Vision & Scope), User Class list (identifying Favored User Classes), RACI Matrix, Product Champion designations.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Executive Sponsor, Product Owner, User Representatives / Product Champions, Subject Matter Experts.
Prerequisites: High-level understanding of project vision and business goals.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Brainstorm candidate stakeholders using standard categories (development team, inside organization, outside organization). 2. Review org charts, Vision Statement 'For' clauses, and historical stakeholder catalogs. 3. Segment direct and indirect users into distinct User Classes based on task frequency, privilege level, or experience. 4. Identify Favored User Classes whose needs align most closely with business objectives. 5. Characterize each stakeholder group using a profile template (Roles, Interests, Influence, Needs, Constraints). 6. Designate specific empowered individual representatives (e.g., Product Champions). 7. (Optional) Create a RACI Matrix specifying who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed for requirements activities.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Who has influence or control over the project's budget and schedule?", "Who will be using the product directly? Indirectly?", "Who is responsible for other systems or projects that yours will affect?", "Who could have legal, compliance, regulatory, or process influence?", "Whose business processes would the system affect?", "Who is expected to supply data?"
Minimal Realistic Example: For the Speak-Out.biz platform, stakeholders are categorized into Author (writes articles, high interest, low power), Reader, Publication Editor, and Administrator. Authors are designated as a primary user class needing an easy text editor and statistics.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Ensure every user class has designated, available human representatives or proxies; verify that favored user classes are explicitly identified; check for complete coverage across legal, operational, and technical roles.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Treating users as a monolithic group ('the user'); relying on non-empowered or unavailable surrogates; failing to involve compliance/legal early; overlooking indirect users or process workers.
When NOT to Use: Always applicable; every software project has stakeholders.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Practice #5 Identify Decision Makers, Practice #6 Usage-Centric Elicitation. Alternatives: Personas, Stakeholder Onion Diagram.
Supported Decisions: User representation selection, priority trade-offs (favoring certain user classes), governance and communication structures.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can analyze enterprise org charts and past project repos to suggest potential stakeholder roles, draft initial RACI matrices, and flag missing governance/compliance roles based on domain regulations.

Method Name: Identifying Empowered Decision Makers & Decision Rules
Problem Solved: Prevents decision paralysis, recurring rework, re-litigated requirements, unmanaged priority conflicts, and sluggish project governance.
Input Artifacts: Stakeholder Profiles/Catalog, Business Objectives, Vision & Scope document, RACI matrix.
Output Artifacts: Decision-Making Framework (Designated Decision Leaders, explicit Decision Rules per decision type, Decision Log/Record).
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Product Owner (Decision Leader), Executive Sponsors, Product Champions, Key Stakeholders.
Prerequisites: Identification and characterization of key stakeholder groups.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify recurring requirements-related decision types (e.g., scope changes, conflicting priorities, quality attribute trade-offs). 2. Determine appropriate decision-makers for each category based on alignment with business objectives and constraints. 3. Appoint a designated Decision Leader (e.g., Product Owner) for each decision domain to avoid ambiguity. 4. Explicitly select and agree upon a Decision Rule for each scenario (Unanimous Vote, Consensus, Plurality Vote, Decision Leader Decides, or Delegation). 5. Establish a protocol for documenting decisions, rationale, and trade-offs. 6. Communicate decision outcomes promptly to all affected stakeholders.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Who makes the final call when stakeholder needs conflict?", "How will the team reach conclusions (unanimous, consensus, leader decides)?", "What is the escalation path if a consensus cannot be reached?", "How will we justify and record decisions for stakeholders who challenge them later?"
Minimal Realistic Example: On a multi-user-class project, user representatives from four subgroups disagree on feature workflow. The designated Product Champion for the overall user class acts as the Decision Leader under the 'Decision Leader Decides' rule, resolving the issue quickly after consulting the group.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Decision rules and leaders are documented before major decisions arise; decisions are consistently logged with rationale; decision-makers are genuinely empowered without unannounced executive overrides.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Assuming team democracy without clear decision rules; endlessly seeking unanimity on minor points; delegating authority without real empowerment (overridden by hidden decision-makers); failing to document rationale.
When NOT to Use: Always applicable; clear governance is required on every project regardless of methodology.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Practice #4 Stakeholder Identification, Practice #13 Prioritization, Practice #20 Change Management. Alternatives: Rapid/DACI framework, Delegation Poker.
Supported Decisions: Scope trade-offs, priority ordering, release backlog acceptance, baseline change approvals.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can log key project decisions automatically from meeting transcripts, summarize rationale, track unresolved decision items, and analyze proposed options against stated business objectives to assist decision-makers.

Method Name: Understanding What Users Need to Do (Usage-Centric Elicitation: Use Cases & User Stories)
Problem Solved: Prevents feature-centric thinking that results in missing capabilities, gold-plating, unused functionality, and poor user experience.
Input Artifacts: Vision Statement, Business Objectives, Stakeholder Catalog / User Classes, Context Diagram.
Output Artifacts: User Requirements Document / Use Case Specifications, User Stories (with acceptance criteria), Epics, Feature Trees.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst (facilitator), User Representatives / Product Champions, End Users, Product Owner, Developers, Testers.
Prerequisites: Identified user classes and defined solution scope.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Conduct usage-centric elicitation sessions with representatives of specific user classes. 2. Ask users to describe the goals they need to accomplish and their typical interactive sessions with the solution. 3. Identify use cases, giving each a descriptive name starting with an action verb (e.g., 'Draft an Article'). 4. For each use case, elicit the Main Success Scenario (normal flow / happy path). 5. Probe for alternative flows (variations leading to success) and exceptions (error conditions). 6. Document use cases using a structured template (ID, Primary Actor, Pre/Postconditions, Flows) or break them into User Stories (As a... I want to... So that...). 7. Abstract or decompose usage descriptions across appropriate levels (Epics -> Features -> Use Cases / User Stories -> Functional Requirements).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What do you need to do with the solution?", "Please describe a session you might have with the product... What would you be trying to accomplish?", "How do you imagine your dialogue with the system would go?", "What could go wrong at this step, and how should the system assist you?"
Minimal Realistic Example: For Speak-Out.biz, the Author user class has the use case 'View Article Statistics'. Elicitation reveals a user story: 'As an author, I want to view page-view statistics for my published articles so that I can see which topics my readers enjoy most.'
Quality Criteria & Verification: Use case names start with an active verb; alternative flows and exceptions are explicitly defined; functional requirements and acceptance tests can be derived completely from scenarios.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Focusing elicitation on system features ('What do you want the system to do?') instead of user goals; omitting exception flows; writing user stories without underlying context or user class clarity.
When NOT to Use: For pure middleware, background batch jobs, real-time embedded sensor routines, or hardware drivers where direct user interaction is minimal or absent.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Practice #7 Events and Responses, Practice #11 Modeling (Process Flows), Practice #18 Testing Requirements. Alternatives: Story Mapping, Job-To-Be-Done (JTBD).
Supported Decisions: Functional scope, iteration backlog breakdown, UI/UX workflow design, test case creation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can analyze narrative user session transcripts to auto-generate Use Case drafts or User Stories in standard formats, extract potential exception paths, and generate candidate test cases for human review.

Problem Solved: Uncovers non-interactive system behaviors, background processing requirements, hardware/sensor interactions, and temporal logic often missed by usage-centric elicitation.
Input Artifacts: Context Diagram, Ecosystem Map, System Architecture descriptions, Domain/Hardware specifications.
Output Artifacts: Event List, Event-Response Table, State-Transition Diagram (STD), Acceptance Criteria (Given-When-Then).
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Systems/Software Architect, Hardware Engineers, Subject Matter Experts, Testers.
Prerequisites: High-level understanding of system boundaries and external integrations.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Brainstorm candidate external events across three categories: Business Events, Signal Events, and Temporal Events. 2. List each event along with its source and conditions. 3. Construct an Event-Response Table mapping each Event + System State to the expected System Response and Resultant State. 4. Analyze table gaps for unhandled state/event combinations. 5. (Optional) Draw a State-Transition Diagram (STD) to visually validate allowed states and trigger transitions. 6. Translate table entries into Given-When-Then acceptance criteria or functional requirements.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What changes in the environment must the system detect?", "What signals or messages arrive from external hardware/software?", "What time-triggered or duration-based actions must occur automatically?", "How should the system respond to this event if it is in State X vs. State Y?"
Minimal Realistic Example: For a home security system: Signal event 'Door sensor triggered' when system is 'Armed for Away' causes response 'Change state to Intrusion Detected, initiate countdown timer, control panel beeps'. If system is 'Disarmed', response is 'No response'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Every identified event has at least one defined system response for every valid state; state-transition model contains no orphaned states or unreachable transitions.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Forcing event-driven systems into usage/use-case formats; ignoring state dependencies (expecting identical responses regardless of state); incomplete event tables missing error conditions.
When NOT to Use: For straightforward CRUD administrative applications where processing is purely user-driven and synchronous without complex states or temporal triggers.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Practice #6 Usage-Centric Elicitation, Practice #11 Create Requirements Models (STD), Practice #18 Review & Test. Alternatives: State Tables, Rule-based decision tables.
Supported Decisions: Real-time behavior design, release scope allocation by event handling, automated test design.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can process system logs, hardware interface protocols, or API specifications to generate Event Lists and draft Event-Response tables, automatically detecting missing state/event logic combinations.

Method Name: Assessing Data Concepts and Relationships (Data Modeling & Data Dictionary)
Problem Solved: Eliminates data corruption, mismatched interface formats, missing CRUD operations, duplicate data, and non-compliance with data governance or privacy laws.
Input Artifacts: Context Diagram, Ecosystem Map, process descriptions, existing database schemas, regulatory policy documents.
Output Artifacts: Conceptual Data Model / Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD), Data Flow Diagram (DFD), Data Dictionary (field metadata), CRUD Matrix.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Data Analyst / Architect, Database Administrator, SME, Compliance/Legal Officers.
Prerequisites: Initial list of candidate domain terms and high-level business process understanding.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Extract data entities (nouns) from business problem descriptions, use cases, context diagrams, and reports. 2. Model logical relationships between entities and define cardinalities (e.g., 1-to-1, 1-to-many) using Crow's Foot ERD notation. 3. Perform CRUD (or CRUDCLUMT) analysis on each entity to ensure processes exist to Create, Read, Update, and Delete data. 4. Draw Data Flow Diagrams (DFDs) showing how data flows between external entities, processes, and data stores. 5. Build a Data Dictionary detailing field-level attributes (name, data type, length, required status, unique constraint, business rules). 6. Elicit data governance, security (PII), retention, archiving, and privacy requirements.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What data does each component require/produce?", "Which system or process 'owns' each data object as the single source of truth?", "Must an entity A always have at least one entity B?", "What policies apply regarding privacy, security, retention, and archiving?", "How should data type or length mismatches between systems be handled?"
Minimal Realistic Example: In a restaurant site, an ERD shows 'Customer Account' places zero or more 'Orders', and each 'Order' contains one or more 'Menu Items'. A Data Dictionary entry DD1 defines 'E-mail Address' as Alphanumeric, Required=Y, Unique=Y.
Quality Criteria & Verification: All data stores on DFDs match entities on the ERD; every entity has defined CRUD processes; field-level attributes match across interface boundaries without unhandled truncation.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Leaving data definitions entirely to developers without business analysis; failing to define data type/length transformations across integrations; missing data retention and regulatory rules.
When NOT to Use: Rarely skipped; applicable whenever software creates, reads, updates, or deletes persistent information.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Practice #3 Define Boundaries, Practice #11 Models (ERD/DFD), Practice #16 Business Rules, Practice #17 Glossary. Alternatives: Class Diagrams, Data Vault modeling.
Supported Decisions: Database architecture selection, interface integration design, data migration scope, compliance readiness.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can automatically parse requirements text to generate ERDs (in PlantUML/Mermaid), draft Data Dictionaries with inferred data types/lengths, and perform automated CRUD gap analysis across process flows.

Method Name: Eliciting and Evaluating Quality Attributes (Nonfunctional Requirements / Planguage)
Problem Solved: Prevents delivery of software that functions correctly in tests but fails in production due to slowness, poor usability, unreliability, insecurity, or unscalability.
Input Artifacts: Business Objectives, Stakeholder Profiles, Architecture diagrams, Corporate Security/Compliance Standards.
Output Artifacts: Nonfunctional Requirements Specifications (using Planguage or structured natural language), Acceptance Criteria / Fit Criteria, Quality Attribute Pairwise Matrix.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Software Architect, End Users (various classes), Maintenance/Operations Staff, Security/Compliance Officers.
Prerequisites: Understanding of business objectives and user task context.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify relevant quality attributes from standard catalogs (e.g., availability, performance, usability, security, maintainability). 2. Elicit specific stakeholder expectations using targeted probing questions rather than vague inquiries. 3. Analyze architectural and design implications of requested quality targets. 4. Analyze trade-offs among conflicting attributes and evaluate priorities (e.g., using Pairwise Comparison). 5. Specify nonfunctional requirements precisely using verifiable condition patterns like Planguage (Tag, Ambition, Scale, Meter, Goal, Stretch) or quantitative fit criteria. 6. Derive detailed functional requirements required to enable quality targets (e.g., password reset routines for security).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Is it more essential to have certain functions available than others?", "What time periods could be reserved for scheduled maintenance with minimal impact?", "What response time is required for 95% of user actions?", "What level of imperfection or downtime are stakeholders willing to tolerate given budget limits?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Planguage entry: Tag: Availability.MaintenanceDowntime; Ambition: Minimize downtime impact; Scale: Minutes system is offline per month; Meter: System clock logs; Goal: Avg <= 1 hour/week; Stretch: Avg <= 1.5 hours/month.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Requirements must be Precise, Necessary, Measurable, Verifiable (testable), and Realistic; trade-offs between conflicting attributes are explicitly resolved.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Writing vague statements like 'The system shall be fast and secure'; assuming 100% availability is attainable without assessing cost; treating nonfunctional requirements as isolated backlog items without architectural consideration.
When NOT to Use: When defining throwaway internal proofs-of-concept where production quality is explicitly out of scope.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Practice #5 Decision Makers, Practice #13 Prioritization (Pairwise Matrix), Practice #14 Consistent Writing. Alternatives: FURPS+, ISO/IEC 25010 SQuaRE framework.
Supported Decisions: System architecture design, infrastructure provisioning, technology stack selection, release readiness.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can evaluate logged nonfunctional requirements against quality checklists (checking for verifiability and metric presence), auto-format vague statements into Planguage structures, and suggest synthetic performance test suites.

Problem Solved: Identifies missing information, requirement conflicts, ambiguities, unfeasible features, unhandled exceptions, and bad assumptions before development starts.
Input Artifacts: Elicited draft requirements, User Stories, Use Cases, Business Rules, Quality Attributes, Models.
Output Artifacts: Refined/Decomposed Requirements, Feature Trees, Split User Stories/Epics, Acceptance Criteria, Analysis Checklists, Risk Analysis.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Developers, Testers, Systems Architect, User Representatives.
Prerequisites: Initial draft of requirements or backlog items gathered during elicitation.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Analyze individual requirements for quality properties: Completeness, Correctness, Feasibility, Necessity, Priority, Unambiguity, Verifiability (or INVEST for stories). 2. Decompose large requirements/epics into finer granularity (e.g., using Feature Trees or story splitting). 3. Trace each requirement back to its origin and rationale; verify underlying assumptions and constraints. 4. Proactively identify exception conditions and safety/business risks. 5. Analyze sets of requirements for gaps, inconsistencies, redundancies, and dependencies. 6. Represent requirements in alternative forms (models, tables) to surface hidden disconnects. 7. Refine requirements and define clear acceptance criteria.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Why is this requirement present?", "What assumptions are we making?", "What exceptions or error conditions could prevent success?", "Does Requirement A contradict Requirement B?", "Can this be verified/tested?"
Minimal Realistic Example: The BA examines an epic 'Order Placement' and uses a Feature Tree to decompose it into subfeatures (Order building, Order editing, Order cancellation). During analysis, an unhandled exception 'Attempting to order an out-of-stock item' is discovered and specified.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Individual statements meet all quality criteria (SMART/INVEST); the requirement set is modifiable, traceable, complete, and consistent.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Premature detailed analysis on volatile low-priority items; ignoring exception paths; accepting ambiguous words ('suitable', 'user-friendly'); duplicating text across multiple specification sections.
When NOT to Use: Always required; analysis is an essential bridge between elicitation and implementation.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Practice #11 Models, Practice #12 Prototypes, Practice #13 Prioritization, Practice #18 Reviews and Testing.
Supported Decisions: Estimation accuracy, sprint/iteration readiness (Definition of Ready), implementation scheduling, risk mitigation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can run automated ambiguity and quality scans on requirement documents, detect duplicated or conflicting statements across large backlogs, generate exception scenario candidates, and auto-populate INVEST checklists.

Problem Solved: Overcomes cognitive overload from dense text ('sea of details'), surfaces missing/conflicting logic, and bridges communication gaps with visual learners.
Input Artifacts: Draft text requirements, use case narratives, user stories, data dictionaries, process descriptions.
Output Artifacts: Visual Models (Process Flows/Flowcharts, DFDs, ERDs, Decision Tables/Trees, State-Transition Diagrams, Feature Trees, Requirements Mapping Matrix).
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, End Users / Stakeholders, Developers, Systems Architect, Testers.
Prerequisites: Unstructured or structured requirements text requiring validation or analysis.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select appropriate modeling notations based on the domain, problem complexity, and audience (e.g., Process Flow for workflows, STD for stateful objects). 2. Create initial draft ('strawman') models quickly using simple tools (whiteboards, sticky notes). 3. Walk through the models collaboratively with stakeholders to validate visual flows and spot errors or gaps. 4. Use strawman estimations (e.g., extreme values) to prompt stakeholders to provide accurate missing data. 5. Refine models and transfer them to formal diagramming tools (Visio, Lucidchart). 6. Cross-check multiple models against one another (e.g., compare DFD data stores to ERD entities, process steps to functional requirements) using a Requirements Mapping Matrix.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Can an invoice go directly from Prepared to Canceled?", "What causes the system to transition from State A to State B?", "Does every process step in this flowchart have corresponding functional requirements?", "Does this diagram accurately depict your daily work?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA draws a State-Transition Diagram for an Invoice object (Initiated -> Prepared -> Sent -> Partially Paid -> Paid). Reviewing the diagram with billing staff reveals a missing state 'Being Revised' when a customer requests job changes.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Models adhere to standard notation syntax; all model elements map to text requirements/data dictionary items; cross-model consistency checks pass without discrepancies.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Inventing custom, non-standard visual notations that confuse readers; treating modeling as a one-time documentation exercise rather than an iterative analysis tool; modeling parts of the system that are simple and well-understood.
When NOT to Use: When the logic, process, or data is extremely simple and can be unambiguously communicated in 1-2 plain text sentences.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Practice #8 Data Concepts, Practice #10 Requirement Analysis, Practice #12 Prototypes, Practice #18 Testing Models. Alternatives: Plain natural language text.
Supported Decisions: Workflow redesign, architectural component allocation, test scenario mapping, feature scoping.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can convert text specifications directly into code-based diagrams (Mermaid, PlantUML), analyze visual model scripts for unreachable states or dead-end process paths, and highlight discrepancies between models and user stories.

Problem Solved: Confronts 'I'll Know It When I See It' (IKIWISI), resolves user interface/workflow uncertainty, and validates technical feasibility early.
Input Artifacts: Initial user requirements, use cases, wireframe concepts, technology stack proposals.
Output Artifacts: Prototypes (Paper Sketches, Wireframes, Navigable Wireframes, Model Simulations, Executable Prototypes), Prototype Evaluation Scripts, Evaluation Feedback Logs.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, User Experience (UX) Designer, Developers, Target User Representatives (Evaluators).
Prerequisites: Uncertain user interface expectations, complex new workflows, or unproven technical approaches.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define explicit prototyping objectives and hypotheses to test (interaction design vs. technical feasibility). 2. Select the appropriate prototype fidelity class (e.g., low-fidelity paper sketch, mid-fidelity wireframe, or high-fidelity executable). 3. Construct the simplest possible prototype needed to answer the target questions. 4. Prepare task-based evaluation scripts with embedded diagnostic questions. 5. Observe target users executing tasks with the prototype without coaching them. 6. Capture usability feedback, missing requirements, exception flows, and false assumptions. 7. Decide the prototype's fate: discard throwaway prototypes or commit to planned evolutionary prototyping using production-quality code.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Does this layout allow you to complete your task efficiently?", "What would you expect to happen if you clicked here?", "Is any information missing from this screen?", "How natural did this task flow feel?"
Minimal Realistic Example: For Speak-Out.biz, a BA creates mid-fidelity mobile wireframes for the 'View Article Statistics' use case. User evaluation reveals that authors want an overview screen showing overall views before drilling into detailed social media share metrics.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Prototyping objectives are established prior to building; evaluators represent actual user classes; throwaway code is explicitly segregated from production repositories unless written to production standards.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Distracting users with premature visual cosmetics; over-building prototypes beyond what is needed to answer specific questions; succumbing to pressure to release a fragile, unarchitected executable prototype to production.
When NOT to Use: When requirements are well understood, UI patterns are standard/routine, and technical feasibility is proven.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Practice #6 Usage-Centric Elicitation, Practice #11 Models, Practice #18 Validation. Alternatives: Storyboards, UI mockups.
Supported Decisions: UI/UX design selection, technical architecture feasibility, build-vs-buy decisions, usability acceptance.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can generate functional frontend wireframe code (React/HTML) directly from text use cases, execute synthetic user journey simulations to identify navigation friction, and process recorded user session video/transcripts to compile UX feedback logs.

Method Name: Prioritizing Requirements (Relative Weighting, MoSCoW, Criteria Matrix)
Problem Solved: Resolves conflicting stakeholder demands, aligns development sequence with budget/time constraints, and ensures maximum business value delivery.
Input Artifacts: Product Backlog, Use Cases, User Stories, Quality Attributes, Business Objectives, Risk assessments, Cost/effort estimates.
Output Artifacts: Prioritized Backlog / Requirements List, Pairwise Quality Attribute Matrix, Relative Weighting / Criteria Matrix Spreadsheets, MVP definition.
Participants & Roles: Empowered Decision Makers / Product Owner, Business Analyst (facilitator), Key Stakeholders, Development Team (cost/risk estimators).
Prerequisites: Items at a consistent level of granularity with cost/benefit estimates.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify empowered decision-makers and agree on prioritization criteria (value, urgency, cost, risk, compliance). 2. Select a prioritization method suited to the item count (MoSCoW, Three-level scale, Stack ranking, Pairwise comparison, WSJF, or Criteria Matrix). 3. Evaluate candidate requirements against established criteria (rating value/penalty, cost, risk on numeric scales). 4. Calculate relative priority scores or rank order items. 5. Sequence requirements into releases or development iterations based on dependencies and capacity. 6. Communicate rationale and priorities to all stakeholders.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What would you do if that feature weren't present?", "Is there a manual or automated workaround?", "What would be the cost or risk to the business if this feature were delayed or omitted?", "Which quality attribute is more critical: Security or Usability?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Using a Criteria Matrix, 8 proposed features are rated across weighted criteria (Business Value 25%, Usage Frequency 20%, Cost 15%, Technical Risk 15%, Time Sensitivity 15%). Feature 1 scores highest (4.3) and is scheduled for Release 1, while Feature 5 scores lowest (1.2) and is deferred.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Only items at similar levels of granularity are compared; cost and technical difficulty are evaluated by technical staff; decision rationale is transparent and linked to business objectives.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Classifying everything as 'High Priority'; letting the loudest voice dictate priority; ignoring technical dependencies or cost when ranking value; prioritizing hundreds of fine-grained items simultaneously.
When NOT to Use: When there is only one requirement, or when capacity far exceeds total request volume.
