Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Practice #2 Business Objectives, Practice #5 Decision Makers, Practice #19 Baselines. Alternatives: Kano Model, WSJF, Buy-a-Feature.
Supported Decisions: Release scope allocation, iteration backlog order, MVP feature selection, trade-off choices during schedule pressure.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can run initial prioritization models (WSJF, Criteria Matrix) by ingesting historical velocity, cost estimates, and tag metadata, suggesting backlog orderings and highlighting potential dependency locks for human review.

Method Name: Writing Requirements in Consistent Ways (Patterns & Planguage)
Problem Solved: Eliminates ambiguity, misinterpretation, inconsistent granularity, unquantifiable targets, and confusion across diverse team audiences.
Input Artifacts: Elicited requirements knowledge, use cases, quality expectations, business rules.
Output Artifacts: Structured Requirement Statements (shall-statements, User Stories, Given-When-Then criteria, Planguage specifications), Requirement Attributes metadata.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst (author), Developers, Testers, Reviewers.
Prerequisites: Understood functional and nonfunctional needs requiring specification.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select standard writing patterns for functional requirements (e.g., 'The  shall be able to ' or 'When  the system shall '). 2. Consistently use a single keyword (e.g., 'shall') for mandatory requirements rather than mixing synonyms. 3. Write short, active-voice, declarative sentences with unique persistent identifiers. 4. Standardize User Stories using 'As a , I want to  so that '. 5. Specify quality attributes precisely using Planguage keywords (Tag, Ambition, Scale, Meter, Goal, Stretch, Wish). 6. Attach minimal required attributes (ID, Author, Origin, Rationale, Priority, Status, Acceptance Criteria) to each requirement.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Who is the specific user class performing this action?", "How can this requirement be tested or verified?", "What is the exact quantitative goal for this quality attribute?", "What is the rationale behind including this requirement?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Functional requirement: 'Security.Admin.1. The homeowner shall be able to change the security system's passcode.' Nonfunctional (Planguage): 'Tag: Availability.Downtime; Scale: Minutes offline/month; Meter: System clock; Goal: <= 60 mins/week.'
Quality Criteria & Verification: Requirement statements are concise, unambiguous, active-voice, uniquely tagged, and verifiable; consistent verb selection ('shall') is maintained throughout.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Mixing shall/should/might arbitrarily; combining multiple requirements into long narrative paragraphs using 'and/or'; writing vague non-testable goals ('system shall be user-friendly').
When NOT to Use: When non-textual representations (visual models, prototypes, decision tables) convey the specific rule or design more clearly and efficiently.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Practice #9 Quality Attributes, Practice #15 Organization, Practice #18 Review & Test. Alternatives: Executable specifications (BDD).
Supported Decisions: Contractual specification clarity, developer implementation scope, test plan design.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can parse natural language drafts and automatically rewrite them into standardized 'shall' or User Story formats, populate Planguage attribute tables, and flag ambiguous passive-voice statements for editing.

Method Name: Organizing Requirements in a Structured Fashion (Templates & RM Tools)
Problem Solved: Prevents unorganized 'piles of thoughts', lost requirements, missing topics, difficulty in finding information, and poor traceability.
Input Artifacts: All collected requirements objects, metadata, models, business rules, glossaries.
Output Artifacts: Software Requirements Specification (SRS), Vision & Scope Document, System Requirements Specification (SyRS), Requirements Management (RM) Tool Database.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Systems Engineer, Product Owner, Development & Testing Leads.
Prerequisites: Selected storage structure (document template vs. RM tool database).
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select appropriate requirement containers (Vision & Scope for business requirements, SRS for solution requirements, or RM database schema). 2. Adopt a structured template (e.g., standard SRS template with sections for System Features, Data Requirements, External Interfaces, Quality Attributes). 3. Apply a 'shrink-to-fit' philosophy to tailor template sections for project scale and type. 4. Group functional requirements logically (by feature, use case, user class, or functional area). 5. Assign persistent, unique identifiers to every requirement object. 6. Populate the container incrementally; explicitly mark empty sections as 'None identified' rather than leaving blank. 7. (Optional) Configure an RM Tool to manage attributes, versions, baselines, and traceability links.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Where would a developer expect to find nonfunctional performance limits?", "Have we explicitly addressed external system interface constraints?", "Is this section blank because it was overlooked or because it doesn't apply?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA populates an SRS template. Section 3 contains System Features ('Order Placement', 'Online Menu') with numbered functional requirements. Section 5 contains External Interface Requirements, and Section 6 holds Quality Attributes.
Quality Criteria & Verification: The repository is searchable, version-controlled, structured intuitively for readers, and uses persistent unique identifiers for every item.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Mixing business, user, functional, and nonfunctional requirements in a single unstructured list; using fragile hierarchical numbers that change when items are inserted; relying on static documents for massive complex systems without tool support.
When NOT to Use: For tiny, single-developer projects where informal backlogs or sticky notes provide sufficient persistent memory without administrative burden.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Practice #14 Consistent Writing, Practice #16 Business Rules, Practice #19 Baselines. Alternatives: Interactive wikis, digital backlog tools (Jira, Azure DevOps).
Supported Decisions: Baseline selection, impact analysis, regulatory audit compliance, artifact reuse.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can automatically categorize unstructured raw requirement notes into standard SRS template sections, generate structured RM tool export files (JSON/CSV), and detect missing mandatory sections in specification structures.

Method Name: Identifying and Documenting Business Rules (Decision Tables & Mapping Matrix)
Problem Solved: Prevents business policy violations in software, eliminates hardcoded volatile business logic, avoids duplicate rule specifications, and ensures regulatory compliance.
Input Artifacts: Corporate policies, laws, regulations, existing source code (reverse engineering), data models, interview transcripts.
Output Artifacts: Business Rules Catalog (Terms, Facts, Constraints, Action Enabler, Inferences, Computations), Decision Tables, Decision Trees, Requirements Mapping Matrix (tracing rules to functional requirements).
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Subject Matter Experts (SMEs), Legal/Compliance Officers, Developers, Database Architects.
Prerequisites: Access to business policies, domain experts, or compliance standards.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Active listen during elicitation for keywords indicating business logic ('only', 'must', 'may not', 'if/then'). 2. Extract rules from external regulations, policy manuals, and data cardinalities. 3. Classify rules into standard types (Facts, Constraints, Action Enablers, Inferences, Computations). 4. Assign unique persistent IDs (e.g., RET-1, DISC-1) and store rules in an enterprise asset catalog separate from project documents. 5. Write constraints clearly using ' must/may only ' and action enablers using 'If  then '. 6. Document complex multi-condition logic using Decision Tables or Decision Trees to ensure complete condition coverage. 7. Trace derived functional requirements back to source business rules using a Requirements Mapping Matrix.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What corporate policy or regulation dictates this behavior?", "What happens if a user attempts to violate this rule?", "Are there exceptions to this restriction?", "Does this computation or discount logic change frequently?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Discount business logic with multiple order totals and club membership conditions is represented in a Decision Table (DISC-1 through DISC-6) mapping conditions to outcomes (10% discount, 20% discount, free shipping), preventing missing boundary logic.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Decision tables cover all  $2^N$  condition combinations; rules avoid double negatives; every software-enforced rule traces to specific functional requirements or a business rules engine.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Confounding business rules with software requirements; embedding volatile rules directly into source code instead of databases/rule engines; duplicating rule text across multiple specifications.
When NOT to Use: When the application contains no business logic, policy restrictions, regulatory mandates, or complex decision calculations.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Practice #8 Data Concepts, Practice #10 Requirement Analysis, Practice #14 Writing Requirements. Alternatives: Business Rules Engines (BRE), Rule books.
Supported Decisions: Software design architecture (hardcoded vs. database/rule-engine driven), compliance verification, exception handling workflow design.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can analyze policy documents or legacy source code to discover implied business rules, automatically fill out complete decision tables from narrative text, and highlight boundary logic gaps for SME verification.

Problem Solved: Eliminates term ambiguities, conflicting jargon, multi-meaning acronyms, and miscommunication across stakeholders, developers, and vendors.
Input Artifacts: Elicited notes, data models, domain literature, legacy documentation, vendor contracts.
Output Artifacts: Project Glossary, Enterprise Glossary (reusable terms, acronyms, abbreviations, synonyms, domain definitions).
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Business SMEs, End Users, Developers, External Vendors, Technical Writers.
Prerequisites: Identification of domain-specific vocabulary and ambiguous terms.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify specialized domain jargon, acronyms, abbreviations, stakeholder role names, and terms with multiple meanings during elicitation. 2. Extract candidate terms from data model entity boxes and data dictionary definitions. 3. Resolve conflicting definitions and reconcile synonyms used by different departments. 4. Document precise, agreed-upon definitions for each term in a centralized tabular Glossary. 5. Publish the glossary to a shared, accessible repository (wiki, SRS section, RM tool). 6. Enforce consistent terminology across all project specifications, code comments, and user interfaces. 7. Harvest project terms into an Enterprise Glossary for future organizational reuse.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What is the exact difference between Term A and Term B?", "Do all departments define 'Customer' in the same way?", "What does this acronym stand for in your domain?", "Are these two terms synonyms for the same concept?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A project glossary defines 'Active Directory (AD) Group', 'CMS' (Customer Management System), 'COGS' (Cost of Goods Sold), and explicitly defines 'No Regrets Work' to prevent an external vendor from misinterpreting it as low-priority work.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Terms are defined unambiguously; synonyms are listed but a single canonical term is chosen for documentation; glossary is accessible to all team members.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Varying terms creatively in specifications to avoid repetition; assuming everyone shares the same definition for common words; creating project glossaries that are inaccessible or never updated.
When NOT to Use: Always applicable; every domain has specialized vocabulary or potential term ambiguities.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Practice #8 Data Dictionary, Practice #14 Consistent Writing, Practice #15 Organization. Alternatives: Domain Ontologies, Taxonomy catalogs.
Supported Decisions: Domain modeling, database naming conventions, contract agreement alignment.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can continuously scan project documentation and chat channels to detect undefined acronyms, highlight inconsistent term usages, auto-draft candidate glossary entries from context, and flag semantic mismatches across sub-teams.

Method Name: Reviewing and Testing Requirements (Peer Reviews, Fit Criteria, Acceptance Tests)
Problem Solved: Finds requirement defects, ambiguities, omissions, and un-testable logic early before code construction, avoiding expensive late-stage rework.
Input Artifacts: Draft Requirements Specifications, Use Cases, User Stories, Visual Models, Quality Attributes.
Output Artifacts: Inspection/Review Defect Logs, Acceptance Criteria / Acceptance Tests (Given-When-Then), Fit Criteria, Highlighted Model Test Traces.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst (author), Peer BAs, User Representatives / Product Champions, Developers, Software Testers.
Prerequisites: Documented draft requirements or analysis models ready for evaluation.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select review/validation technique based on risk (Peer Deskcheck, Passaround, Team Review, Inspection, or Test Generation). 2. Assemble a review team including information providers (users/SMEs) and information consumers (developers/testers). 3. Conduct structured reviews using defect checklists to identify ambiguities, gaps, and un-testable statements. 4. Write conceptual acceptance tests (e.g., Given-When-Then format) or quantitative Fit Criteria directly from requirements/use cases. 5. Compare derived tests against requirements text to reveal missing functionality or invalid assumptions. 6. 'Execute' tests on visual analysis models by tracing execution paths with highlighters to find missing paths or dead ends. 7. Log defects, revise requirements and models, and verify fixes.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "How will we judge whether this requirement is satisfied?", "What test scenario would demonstrate this use case works?", "Is there any ambiguous phrasing that could be interpreted in multiple ways?", "What happens if we execute Test X on Process Flow Y?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Given-When-Then test AT-1: 'Given I am logged in AND have published articles, When I request to view statistics, Then a graph of view stats from past 30 days is displayed AND a list of statistics is displayed in reverse chronological order.' Tracing a test on a process flow highlights a missing decision box for empty cart handling.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Reviewers include both users/SMEs and developers/testers; every requirement has associated testable acceptance criteria/fit criteria; all logged defects are resolved.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Treating executive 'sign-off' as a substitute for true validation; reviewing requirements without testers or end-user representatives; delaying test design until after code is written.
When NOT to Use: Always applicable; every requirement set must be validated prior to implementation commitment.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Practice #10 Analysis, Practice #11 Models, Practice #12 Prototypes. Alternatives: Formal Formal Specifications, Automated BDD frameworks (Cucumber).
Supported Decisions: Requirement baseline sign-off, iteration readiness, definition of done/ready, software acceptance.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can automatically generate Given-When-Then acceptance tests from draft use cases, run dry-run test execution paths on Mermaid process models, and perform automated defect checking against requirements review checklists.

Problem Solved: Prevents moving-target scope creep, uncontrolled schedule slippage, misaligned implementation expectations, and uncoordinated release commitments.
Input Artifacts: Prioritized Backlog, SRS / Use Cases, Sizing/Effort estimates, Release Roadmap, Feature Tree.
Output Artifacts: Requirements Baseline (iteration or release baseline snapshot), Baseline Approval Record, Scope-Annotated Feature Tree / Models.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Product Owner, Development Lead, QA Lead, Key Stakeholders / Approvers.
Prerequisites: Prioritized and analyzed set of requirements ready for commitment.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select a baselining strategy: Time-bound (allocating prioritized items to fit a fixed timebox) or Scope-bound (defining a logical feature set and estimating schedule). 2. Uniquely identify the specific subset of requirements included in the baseline (using RM tool attributes, document versions, or backlog iteration tags). 3. Communicate scope visually using annotated Feature Trees, Context Diagrams, or Roadmaps. 4. Conduct baseline review and obtain explicit agreement/sign-off from designated approvers. 5. Establish the approved baseline as a immutable snapshot in time. 6. Enforce change control for any subsequent additions, deletions, or modifications to the baselined items.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Which subset of requirements can the team commit to delivering in this timebox?", "What would it take for you to approve this baseline?", "Are these stretch goals clearly separated from committed baseline items?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A Feature Tree for a restaurant site is annotated with release tags (1, 2, 3). Release Baseline 1 is formally approved, encompassing core Order Building and User Account Creation, while Dynamic Menu Updates are assigned to Release Baseline 2.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Baseline contents are explicitly identified and unambiguous; designated approvers give documented agreement; changes to baselined items trigger formal change control.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Assuming baselining means 'freezing' requirements permanently without a change path; building unapproved baselines; forcing developers to commit to scope-bound baselines without sizing estimates.
When NOT to Use: For pure continuous delivery environments where individual micro-changes are deployed immediately upon completion without release batching, though iteration planning still utilizes micro-baselines.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Practice #13 Prioritization, Practice #15 Organization, Practice #20 Change Management. Alternatives: Kanban pull-system buffers.
Supported Decisions: Release delivery commitment, resource allocation, iteration scope lock, vendor contract milestones.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can calculate team capacity against story points to suggest optimal time-bound baseline scopes, auto-generate baseline release notes, and track drift between planned baseline items and actual implemented code.

Method Name: Managing Changes to Requirements Effectively (Change Control Process & Impact Analysis)
Problem Solved: Controls scope creep, prevents chaos from unvetted feature requests, evaluates cost/schedule ripple impacts, and maintains alignment across baseline updates.
Input Artifacts: Change Requests, Existing Baselines, Traceability Matrix, Architecture Models, Cost/Effort Estimation models.
Output Artifacts: Change Control Process Flow, Change Request Logs/Status, Impact Analysis Reports, Updated Baselines.
Participants & Roles: Change Control Board (CCB) / Product Owner, Business Analyst (impact analyst), Requestor, Development & QA Leads.
Prerequisites: An established, approved requirements baseline.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define and document a lightweight Change Control Process answering who submits, who analyzes, and who decides. 2. Receive formal change requests and log them with a unique ID and 'Submitted' status. 3. Perform Impact Analysis: BA analyzes scope, technical ripple effects, regulatory risks, cost/effort, and schedule trade-offs across ecosystem maps and traceability matrices. 4. Present impact assessment to the Change Control Board (CCB) or Product Owner. 5. CCB evaluates request against business objectives and capacity buffers, making a decision (Approve, Reject, Defer). 6. Log decision and rationale; communicate decision to submitter and affected team members. 7. If approved, update requirement text, models, and attributes, increment version numbers, and establish a new baseline snapshot.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Does this proposed change contribute to our stated business objectives?", "What other systems, interfaces, or requirements will be impacted if we make this change?", "What is the cost and schedule trade-off if we accept this request?", "Which baseline does this change apply to?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A request arrives to change a vendor integration URL to prevent timeouts. Impact analysis by the BA reveals it requires invasive code revisions across three separate systems. The CCB determines the risk is too high for the current release, rejects the request for now, and defines an operational workaround.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Every change request is logged and status-tracked; impact analysis precedes all approval decisions; approved changes are reflected in updated baseline documentation.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Allowing informal 'backdoor' changes directly to developers without impact analysis; implementing overly bureaucratic change processes that team members bypass; failing to update specification documentation after making changes.
When NOT to Use: Before initial requirements baseline approval (pre-baseline exploration is informal iteration, not change control).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Complementary: Practice #5 Decision Makers, Practice #10 Analysis, Practice #19 Baselines. Alternatives: Agile Backlog Refinement / Reprioritization.
Supported Decisions: Scope adjustment approvals, schedule buffer consumption, release trade-off choices, budget adjustments.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents can analyze change request text against codebase indices and dependency models to auto-generate impact analysis drafts, trace potential affected requirements, predict effort estimates, and keep change request status logs updated.

Problem Solved: Elicits precise and unbiased statements; uncovers subconscious requirements through clever questioning.
Input Artifacts: Stakeholders, existing knowledge/questions
Output Artifacts: Interview protocols, documented answers
Participants & Roles: Requirements Engineer (Interviewer), Stakeholder(s) (Interviewee)
Prerequisites: Predetermined questions prepared by the requirements engineer; interviewee willing to invest time.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Prepare predetermined questions. 2. Conduct conversation with one or more stakeholders. 3. Ask questions and record answers. 4. Control conversation flow and adapt to individual stakeholders. 5. Ask follow-up/clever questions to uncover subconscious requirements. 6. Discuss and clarify immediate questions or doubts.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Predetermined questions regarding requirements and immediate follow-up inquiries on specific domain aspects.
Minimal Realistic Example: A requirements engineer interviews a traffic domain expert about route calculation parameters, asking follow-up questions to uncover unstated rules about road avoidance.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Completeness of answers, clarity, and elimination of subconscious gaps verified through direct feedback during the conversation.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Overly time-consuming; surveyor-driven bias leading to forgotten or disregarded stakeholder concerns.
When NOT to Use: When time and resources are severely limited, or when surveying an extremely large target audience where questionnaires are more appropriate.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Questionnaires, Field Observation, Brainstorming
Supported Decisions: Elicitation of conscious/subconscious stakeholder needs to form basic system scope and detailed functional requirements.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic interviewers can dynamically ask follow-up questions based on real-time transcript analysis; human-in-the-loop validates complex context.

Problem Solved: Gathers a large magnitude of information from many stakeholders quickly at low cost.
Input Artifacts: Pre-existing conjectures or known requirements, domain knowledge, survey guidelines
Output Artifacts: Completed questionnaire forms, aggregated evaluation results
Participants & Roles: Requirements Engineer (Surveyor), Multiple Stakeholders (Respondents)
Prerequisites: Clear domain understanding; knowledge of psychological guidelines for creating questionnaires.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define known requirements or conjectures to be assessed. 2. Formulate open and/or closed (multiple-choice) questions. 3. Distribute questionnaire (e.g., via an online platform) to target stakeholders. 4. Stakeholders fill out and submit responses. 5. Aggregate and evaluate submitted data.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Open and closed/multiple-choice questions inquiring about stakeholder assessments and requirements.
Minimal Realistic Example: An online survey sent to 200 drivers asking them to rate the importance of dynamic traffic avoidance versus manual route selection on a scale of 1-5.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Statistical validity, non-ambiguous questions, high response rate.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Poorly formulated or forgotten questions; inability to receive immediate feedback or discover completely unknown requirements.
When NOT to Use: When trying to discover completely novel/unconscious delighter requirements or when immediate interactive feedback is required.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Interview, Workshops
Supported Decisions: Prioritisation and validation of existing requirement hypotheses across large user populations.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLM agents can automatically compile balanced questionnaires from existing domain documentation and analyze statistical distributions of responses.

Problem Solved: Collects a large volume of creative ideas quickly and fosters collaborative idea expansion across diverse stakeholder groups.
Input Artifacts: Initial problem statement or vision
Output Artifacts: Categorized and analyzed list of ideas
Participants & Roles: Moderator, Stakeholders (group of 5 to 10 people)
Prerequisites: Balanced group dynamics; willingness to withhold early criticism.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Assemble a group of 5 to 10 stakeholders. 2. State the objective or problem to be addressed. 3. Collect ideas within a specified time frame. 4. Moderator documents ideas without discussing, judging, or commenting. 5. Participants build upon and modify each other's ideas. 6. Analyze and structure the collected ideas post-session.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What features or capabilities could solve this problem?", "How can we expand on this suggested idea?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A 10-person cross-functional team meets to generate ideas on how a navigation system should react when GPS connectivity is completely lost.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Quantity of ideas generated, level of multi-stakeholder participation, unbiased initial collection.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Premature evaluation/judgment of ideas; muddled group dynamics dominated by loud or high-authority individuals.
When NOT to Use: When fine-grained system behavior is needed, or when dominant personalities prevent equal group participation.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Brainstorming Paradox, Method 6-3-5, Brainwriting, Mind Mapping
Supported Decisions: Scope definition, product feature selection, vision alignment.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI agents act as idea generators or moderators that categorize ideas in real-time without introducing cognitive bias.

Problem Solved: Identifies system risks early and establishes proactive countermeasures by focusing on unwanted events.
Input Artifacts: Problem domain context, high-level project goals
Output Artifacts: List of prohibited events/risks, list of protective countermeasures and requirements
Participants & Roles: Moderator, Stakeholders
Prerequisites: Understanding of project objectives and risk boundaries.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Assemble stakeholders and define the focus area. 2. Ask participants to generate events that must  never  occur. 3. Moderator records all negative events without judgment. 4. Group analyzes the list of negative events. 5. Develop system requirements and protective measures to prevent those events.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What is the absolute worst thing that could happen when using this system?", "What events must never occur under any circumstances?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Stakeholders brainstorm nightmare scenarios for an autonomous navigation system, such as "giving route directions onto oncoming traffic lanes," then define rules to prevent it.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Identification of critical edge cases and security/safety risks; actionable preventive requirements.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Focusing only on catastrophic risks while ignoring standard functional requirements.
When NOT to Use: When the team is trying to define routine user workflows or optimistic product vision features.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Classic Brainstorming, Mind Mapping
Supported Decisions: Risk mitigation, safety requirements definition, architecture constraints.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Agentic red-teaming to simulate worst-case failure modes and automatically draft defensive guardrail requirements.

Problem Solved: Reduces individual bias and overcome cognitive gridlock by forcing stakeholders to view a problem from six distinct standpoints.
Input Artifacts: Controversial or complex requirement/problem scenario
Output Artifacts: Multi-perspective requirement evaluations, balanced decision protocol
Participants & Roles: Moderator, Stakeholders (adopting assigned hat perspectives)
Prerequisites: Participants willing to temporarily adopt assigned emotional, critical, or creative perspectives.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Introduce the problem or proposed feature. 2. Assign or collectively systematically cycle through the Six Thinking Hats (White = Facts, Red = Emotions, Black = Risks, Yellow = Benefits, Green = Creativity, Blue = Process Control). 3. Require all participants to adopt the specific hat perspective during that phase. 4. Record insights gained under each perspective. 5. Consolidate perspective findings into rounded requirements.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Wearing the Black Hat, what could go wrong?", "Wearing the Yellow Hat, what are the best outcomes?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A team stuck on deciding whether to allow dynamic route recalculation cycles through all six hats to evaluate data facts, user anxieties, failure risks, and creative options.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Comprehensive coverage of emotional, factual, and risk aspects; consensus or empathy reached among biased stakeholders.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Attempting to apply it to fine-grained technical specifications, making it overly laborious.
When NOT to Use: When detailed, fine-grained technical requirements need to be specified.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Perspective-Based Reading, Role-Playing
Supported Decisions: Scope approval, feature feasibility trade-offs, conflict resolution.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Multi-agent systems where individual LLM agents represent different 'hats' to simulate balanced stakeholder debates.

Problem Solved: Recovers lost explicit domain/business logic and prevents missing legacy functionalities when building a replacement system.
Input Artifacts: Legacy system source code, legacy documentation, database schemas
Output Artifacts: Detailed functional requirements, extracted business rules catalog
Participants & Roles: Requirements Engineer (System Archaeologist)
Prerequisites: Access to legacy codebases, technical documentation, or executable legacy software.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Obtain legacy software artifacts (code, specs, database schemas). 2. Analyze code structure, business rules, and logic paths. 3. Extract implicit functional rules and algorithms. 4. Document extracted behaviors into natural language or model specifications. 5. Validate extracted rules with current domain experts.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What logic handles this edge condition in the current code?", "Are all legacy calculation formulas accounted for in the new specification?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA reads through legacy COBOL code of an old navigation server to extract the exact mathematical formulas used for traffic congestion estimation.
Quality Criteria & Verification: 100% functional equivalence coverage for critical business logic; elimination of obsolete technical workarounds.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Extremely laborious; blindly copying outdated technological decisions and suboptimal legacy processes into the new system.
When NOT to Use: When the new system intentionally radically changes operational paradigms and retains no legacy functionality.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Field Observation, Perspective-Based Reading
Supported Decisions: Migration scope, legacy deprecation, detailed algorithm design.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLM code-analysis agents parse legacy source code and automatically output modern natural-language requirements and decision tables.

Problem Solved: Elicits subconscious knowledge and dissatisfiers that users take for granted or cannot express verbally.
Input Artifacts: Operational workspace, active legacy process
Output Artifacts: Observation protocols, process flow diagrams, identified dissatisfiers/inefficiencies
Participants & Roles: Requirements Engineer (Observer), Specialist/End User (Observed)
Prerequisites: Physical visibility of operational procedures; access to end-user workplaces.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Obtain access to the operational workspace. 2. Observe users performing their routine work tasks. 3. Record process steps, pain points, workarounds, and user errors (optionally using audio/video). 4. Question observed processes to distinguish 'as-is' habits from true requirements. 5. Formulate target requirements that optimize inefficient steps.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Why do you perform that manual step?", "What error occurs most frequently during this routine?"
Minimal Realistic Example: An analyst watches a delivery driver interact with a vehicle terminal, noticing the driver manually re-keys addresses because screen transition is too slow.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Identification of tacit workflow steps; validation of observed findings with the user.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Documenting the 'as-is' suboptimal process instead of designing the improved 'to-be' process.
When NOT to Use: When developing entirely new processes with no physical or operational precursor, or when procedures cannot be observed physically.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Apprenticing, System Archaeology, Use Case Modeling
Supported Decisions: Usability requirements, workflow optimization, process automation scope.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Computer vision models analyze recorded user task videos to map workflow paths and highlight high-friction interaction points.

Problem Solved: Overcomes power dynamics and uncovers deeply ingrained, self-evident domain knowledge by immersing the analyst in the user role.
Input Artifacts: Active operational work environment
Output Artifacts: Detailed domain knowledge notes, unstated operational requirements
Participants & Roles: Requirements Engineer (Apprentice), Domain Specialist (Master)
Prerequisites: Willingness of the domain expert to act as instructor; time for active hands-on training.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Position the domain expert as the 'master' and the requirements engineer as the 'apprentice.' 2. The master instructs the analyst on how to perform the job tasks. 3. The analyst actively performs the work steps. 4. The analyst asks questions regarding complex or confusing tasks as they arise. 5. The analyst documents taken-for-granted rules and formulates requirements.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Could you teach me how to handle this case?", "Why is this step necessary before moving to the next?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA spends three days learning to dispatch service vehicles under the guidance of a senior dispatcher to understand implicit prioritization rules.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Accurate grasp of domain rules; explicit documentation of unstated operational needs.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Becoming bogged down in operational routine instead of abstracting requirements.
When NOT to Use: When domain experts lack time to train others or when safety/compliance prevents non-certified staff from performing tasks.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Field Observation, Interviews
Supported Decisions: User interface design, operational workflow scope.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Interactive simulation environments where AI agents evaluate user steps and highlight implicit logic gaps.

Problem Solved: Systematically detects requirements defects (ambiguities, contradictions, incompleteness) using a formal, multi-role review process.
Input Artifacts: Requirements specification/document, defect logging sheets, review guidelines
Output Artifacts: Consolidated error list, inspection protocol, approved requirements baseline
Participants & Roles: Organizer, Moderator, Author, Reader, Inspectors, Minute-taker
Prerequisites: Documented requirements available; formal review team assigned and prepared.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Planning: Define goals, inspect artifacts, and assign roles. 2. Overview: Author presents the requirements to ensure common baseline understanding. 3. Individual/Team Error Detection: Inspectors search the text/models for defects. 4. Error Collection & Consolidation: Convene a meeting to collect, filter, and document true defects into an error list. 5. Defect Correction: Author fixes logged issues.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Does this requirement satisfy all specified quality criteria?", "Is there any contradiction with existing system constraints?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A 5-person team (moderator, reader, author, tester, architect) conducts a formal 2-hour session to inspect a 30-page Software Requirements Specification, logging 14 defects.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Defect detection rate, strict adherence to roles/process, resolution of all logged defects.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Combining defect detection with defect correction during the review meeting; author acting as reader/moderator.
When NOT to Use: When requirements are extremely volatile/early concept stage where lightweight commenting suffices.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Walk-Through, Commenting, Perspective-Based Reading
Supported Decisions: Baseline approval, readiness for architectural design and implementation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Automated LLM inspectors perform pre-checks for ambiguity and rule violations before human inspection meetings.

Problem Solved: Establishes a common understanding of requirements and identifies quality flaws through an informal, author-guided group session.
Input Artifacts: Requirements document / specifications draft
Output Artifacts: Logged quality flaws, meeting minutes, shared understanding notes
Participants & Roles: Author, Reviewers/Inspectors, Minute-taker, (Optional) Moderator/Reader
Prerequisites: Requirements document distributed to participants in advance.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Hand out requirements documents to reviewers for initial reading. 2. Convene the walk-through session. 3. The author (or reader) guides participants step-by-step through the requirements. 4. Author provides background rationale, context, and alternatives considered. 5. Reviewers raise questions and point out flaws. 6. Minute-taker logs all identified quality issues.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What was the rationale behind this rule?", "Is this step clear to the development team?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A BA walks developers and testers through a new feature specification, explaining business rules and logging clarification points raised by developers.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Achieving team-wide shared understanding; logging of explicit defects and ambiguities.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Author defensiveness; lack of prior reading by reviewers leading to superficial feedback.
When NOT to Use: When formal compliance sign-off or contract-bound rigorous validation is mandatory (use formal Inspection).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Inspection, Commenting
Supported Decisions: Draft approval, clarification of implementation scope.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Virtual assistants present sections of specifications and auto-summarize developer queries and identified ambiguities.

Problem Solved: Improves defect detection rates by having reviewers inspect requirements through specific stakeholder viewpoints (e.g., tester, architect, user).
Input Artifacts: Requirements document, perspective-specific instructions/checklists
Output Artifacts: Perspective-specific defect logs, consolidated validation report
Participants & Roles: Auditors/Reviewers (assigned to specific perspectives: User, Architect, Tester)
Prerequisites: Defined reading perspectives and tailored instruction checklists for each perspective.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select relevant perspectives (e.g., User, Architect, Tester, Compliance). 2. Assign each auditor a specific perspective and provide corresponding directives/questions. 3. Auditors read and inspect requirements strictly through their assigned lens (e.g., tester builds test cases). 4. Collect responses to perspective questions and logged open issues. 5. Consolidate and analyze findings across all perspectives.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "From a tester's view: Is there sufficient detail to derive concrete test cases?", "From an architect's view: Are non-functional performance constraints fully specified?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A test lead reads a SRS purely to build acceptance test cases, discovering that edge-case error conditions are completely missing.
Quality Criteria & Verification: High defect yield per perspective; verification against specific domain/role checklists.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Reviewers drifting back into generic reading rather than maintaining strict focus on their assigned role perspective.
When NOT to Use: When reviewers lack domain knowledge of the assigned perspective.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Checklist Validation, Inspection, Prototypes
Supported Decisions: Testability verification, architectural feasibility approval.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Deploying specialized LLM agents persona-prompted as 'Tester', 'Architect', and 'End User' to scan documents concurrently.

Problem Solved: Exposes gaps, misunderstandings, and UI/UX issues by allowing stakeholders to directly experience and test interactive software mocks.
Input Artifacts: Selected critical requirements, prototype software/wireframes, user manual, scenario scripts
Output Artifacts: Auditor protocols, observation logs, consolidated change requests
Participants & Roles: Auditor/User, Observer/Requirements Engineer, Prototype Developer
Prerequisites: Implemented prototype (throw-away or evolutionary); prepared validation scenarios and checklists.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Select high-risk or critical requirements for prototyping. 2. Develop a throw-away or evolutionary prototype. 3. Prepare user instructions, test scenarios, and evaluation checklists. 4. Auditor independently executes scenarios on the prototype. 5. Observer documents user hesitation, errors, and feedback into an observation protocol. 6. Analyze results and formulate necessary requirement change requests.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "Does this screen layout match your expected workflow?", "What unexpected behavior did you observe during this step?"
Minimal Realistic Example: An end user attempts to input a destination into a GUI prototype; the observer notes hesitation because the 'Confirm' button is placed non-intuitively.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Successful execution of validation scenarios; subjective user satisfaction; identification of hidden requirements.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Misinterpreting missing functionality as a bug when it was intentionally omitted from the prototype scope.
When NOT to Use: When project budget/time constraints prohibit prototype creation or for simple, fully understood requirements.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Use Case Specification, Perspective-Based Reading
Supported Decisions: UI acceptance, usability approval, feature scope refinement.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: AI code generators instantly generate UI wireframes from specifications; AI user agents test interaction flows autonomously.

Problem Solved: Gathers all influencing factors surrounding a requirement conflict to prevent missing hidden drivers during negotiation.
Input Artifacts: Conflict description, stakeholder goals, domain constraints
Output Artifacts: Comprehensive list of prioritized conflict factors
Participants & Roles: Requirements Engineer / Conflict Manager, Disputing Stakeholders
Prerequisites: Identified requirement conflict between parties.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify the core conflict between stakeholders. 2. Brainstorm all possible factors influencing or affected by the conflict (costs, technical limits, user comfort, schedule). 3. Document all facts without immediate filtering. 4. Prioritize the importance of each factor. 5. Feed factors into decision techniques like PMI or Decision Matrix.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What underlying factors are influencing this disagreement?", "Which external or internal constraints impact this decision?"
Minimal Realistic Example: To resolve a conflict over automatic map updating frequency, the analyst lists data bandwidth costs, battery consumption, driver safety, and server capacity.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Thoroughness of identified factors; agreement by both conflicting parties that all relevant facts are listed.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Overlooking subtle organizational or political influences on the conflict.
When NOT to Use: When time constraints require an immediate executive decision (overruling).
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Plus-Minus-Interesting (PMI), Decision Matrix
Supported Decisions: Conflict analysis, trade-off evaluation.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Automated retrieval of domain constraints, compliance rules, and technical logs to present an objective fact sheet to disputing parties.

Problem Solved: Evaluates proposed solution alternatives objectively by categorizing positive, negative, and uncertain repercussions.
Input Artifacts: Solution alternatives (e.g., from CAF), decision criteria
Output Artifacts: PMI table, categorized impact report
Participants & Roles: Requirements Engineer / Moderator, Conflicting Stakeholders
Prerequisites: Defined solution alternatives to a requirement conflict.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Take a proposed requirement solution alternative. 2. List all positive consequences under the 'Plus' column. 3. List all negative consequences under the 'Minus' column. 4. List uncertain or neutral elements under the 'Interesting' column. 5. Investigate 'Interesting' items further to classify them as Plus or Minus. 6. Compare total scores/impacts across alternatives to select the best option.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What are the explicit advantages of this option?", "What negative side effects does this choice introduce?", "What consequences are still uncertain?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A team evaluates switching to open-source map data: Plus = lower cost; Minus = no vendor SLA; Interesting = potential community customization options.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Clear classification of consequences; thorough investigation of all 'Interesting' items.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Failing to convert 'Interesting' items into clear positives/negatives through research.
When NOT to Use: When quantitative decision criteria (e.g., monetary weights) are strictly required.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Decision Matrix, Consider-All-Facts
Supported Decisions: Alternative selection, conflict resolution.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: LLM agents quickly populate PMI tables by analyzing past project post-mortems and technical documentation.

Problem Solved: Provides a quantitative, objective scoring framework to select the best solution alternative among competing options.
Input Artifacts: Solution alternatives, weighted decision criteria (from CAF)
Output Artifacts: Completed decision matrix table with numerical scores and winning option
Participants & Roles: Requirements Engineer / Facilitator, Key Stakeholders / Decision Makers
Prerequisites: Clear set of solution alternatives and established evaluation criteria.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Create a matrix table with solution alternatives in columns and decision criteria in rows. 2. Assign weight/importance ratings to each criterion if applicable. 3. Evaluate each alternative against each criterion using a standardized point scale (e.g., 0 to 10). 4. Sum the total scores for each column. 5. Select the alternative with the highest total score.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "How does Alternative 1 rate against Criterion 2 on a scale of 0 to 10?", "Are all decision criteria included in the matrix?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Stakeholders evaluate 3 routing algorithm designs across 'Cost', 'Speed', and 'Accuracy'. Alternative 1 scores 18 total points, beating Alternative 2 (13) and 3 (17).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Objective, repeatable numerical evaluation; explicit justification for individual scores.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Manipulating score points to favor a personal preference regardless of objective criteria.
When NOT to Use: When decision criteria cannot be quantified or when stakeholders agree informally without complex math.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Plus-Minus-Interesting, AHP (Analytic Hierarchy Process)
Supported Decisions: Architecture selection, feature baseline inclusion, vendor choice.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Decision matrices auto-calculated by agentic evaluation models with rationale citations provided for every score assignment.

Problem Solved: Ranks requirements analytically by calculating priority scores derived from relative benefit, detriment, cost, and risk.
Input Artifacts: Set of requirements (same abstraction level), weight factors for benefit, detriment, cost, and risk
Output Artifacts: Wiegers prioritization matrix with calculated relative ranks
Participants & Roles: Requirements Engineer, Project Manager, Customer/Business Representatives, Developers
Prerequisites: Requirements selected at a uniform level of detail; weights defined for Benefit, Detriment, Cost, Risk.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Define relative weight factors (WeightBenefit, WeightDetriment, WeightCost, WeightRisk). 2. Estimate Relative Benefit and Relative Detriment (scale 1-9) for each requirement. 3. Calculate Value% for each requirement: Benefit x WeightBenefit + Detriment x WeightDetriment. 4. Estimate Relative Cost and Relative Risk (scale 1-9) and compute Cost% and Risk%. 5. Compute Priority score: Priority = Value% / (Cost% x WeightCost + Risk% x WeightRisk). 6. Rank requirements based on calculated Priority scores.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What is the business loss if this is omitted?", "What is the relative implementation risk score from 1 to 9?"
Minimal Realistic Example: Five core navigation requirements are scored in a spreadsheet; Requirement 1 achieves a priority score of 0.941, earning Rank 1 over Requirement 5 (score 0.489, Rank 5).
Quality Criteria & Verification: Math consistency in percentage distributions; reduction of subjective bias in ranking.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Mixing high-level goals with fine-grained technical requirements in the same matrix.
When NOT to Use: When rapid ad-hoc prioritization is needed and time/resources do not permit multi-factor estimation.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Kano Classification, Single-Criterion Classification, Ranking, Top-Ten
Supported Decisions: Release planning, budget allocation, backlog refinement.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Machine learning models estimate relative cost and risk inputs based on historical repository data to populate the matrix automatically.

Problem Solved: Channels, evaluates, and controls proposed modifications to requirements baselines to prevent scope creep.
Input Artifacts: Change Request document (ID, Title, Description, Justification, Priority, Applicant)
Output Artifacts: Impact analysis report, CCB decision log, updated requirements baseline, change assignment
Participants & Roles: Applicant, Change Manager, Change Control Board (CCB: Contractor, Architect, Developer, PM, QA, RE)
Prerequisites: Formally established requirements baseline; active Change Control Board.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Applicant submits a formal Change Request. 2. Change Manager/CCB pre-classifies request (Corrective, Adaptive, Exceptional). 3. Conduct Impact Analysis: estimate total effort across affected requirements and downstream artifacts. 4. CCB evaluates request: compare effort/cost vs. business benefit. 5. CCB decides (Approve / Reject). 6. If approved: prioritize change and assign to a specific release/project. 7. If rejected: communicate rationale to applicant.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: "What downstream artifacts are affected by this change?", "What is the total implementation effort across design, code, and test cases?"
Minimal Realistic Example: A customer requests adding real-time weather overlays; CCB performs impact analysis (40 hours effort), approves it as an adaptive change, and assigns it to Release 2.0.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Traceable documentation of all decisions; accurate impact analysis; zero unapproved scope changes.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Implementing changes informally without CCB approval; ignoring downstream artifact impacts during effort estimation.
When NOT to Use: In early discovery phases prior to creating an initial requirement baseline.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Traceability Matrix/Graph (used during Impact Analysis)
Supported Decisions: Scope changes, release content adjustments, budget/schedule re-baselining.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Automated impact analysis where AI traces requirement dependencies across the codebase and drafts effort estimates for CCB review.

Problem Solved: Prevents a backlog from becoming an unordered feature list; retains the end-to-end user journey and fosters shared understanding.
Input Artifacts: Stakeholder requests, user journeys, initial backlog ideas.
Output Artifacts: User story map, release slices.
Participants & Roles: Product Manager, Business Analyst, Stakeholders, Developers, Testers.
Prerequisites: High-level understanding of user goals and main workflow steps.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Frame the problem and user goals. 2. Map the big-picture user journey (activities and tasks) horizontally. 3. Slice features/stories vertically under each task by priority. 4. Define release boundaries.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What is the user trying to achieve from start to finish? What is the next logical step in the journey? What is the minimum viable slice for this release?
Minimal Realistic Example: A case analyst reviews a case submission starting from intake, evaluating evidence, viewing system recommendation, to final decision.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Story map clearly shows complete end-to-end user journey and actionable, prioritized release slices.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Treating user stories as self-sufficient specifications or replacing detailed requirements, rules, and quality criteria entirely.
When NOT to Use: When detailed functional behavior, multi-step system interactions, or complex decision logic must be precisely specified.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Use Cases (for detailed interaction), Atomic Requirements, Decision Tables.
Supported Decisions: Scope, priority, release planning.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Can be used to map multi-agent or human-in-the-loop workflows across distinct interaction steps.

Problem Solved: Resolves ambiguity in complex, multi-step interactions, permissions, recoveries, branching workflows, and exception paths across multiple systems.
Input Artifacts: User story map, stakeholder requests, process maps.
Output Artifacts: Fully dressed use case specification (actors, triggers, preconditions, main success scenario, extensions/alternatives, postconditions).
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Primary Actor (End User/SME), Architect, Developer, Tester.
Prerequisites: Identified primary actors and clear system boundary/scope.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify actors and their goal levels. 2. Define triggers and preconditions. 3. Write the main success scenario step-by-step. 4. Identify and write alternative flows and failure/exception recoveries. 5. Define postconditions.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What triggers this interaction? What can go wrong at this step? How does the actor recover from failure? What must be true before and after?
Minimal Realistic Example: Goal: Triage a submitted case. Trigger: Submission enters Ready for triage. Main flow: System extracts evidence and presents recommendation. Alternatives: Missing evidence, extraction failure.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Covers all exception paths; clear goal level; observable interactions between actor and system.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Writing internal design decisions instead of observable behavior; omitting failure branches; over-complicating simple CRUD interactions.
When NOT to Use: Simple, single-step operations or purely data-transformation logic without complex interaction.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: User Story Mapping (for high-level view), Atomic Textual Requirements, State Models.
Supported Decisions: Scope, functional design, test scenarios.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Define human-in-the-loop review flows as explicit alternative branches when AI confidence falls below a configured threshold.

Method Name: Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax (EARS) / Atomic Textual Requirements
Problem Solved: Reduces ambiguity, subjective phrasing, compound obligations, and unstructured natural language requirements.
Input Artifacts: Use cases, business rules, stakeholder requests.
Output Artifacts: Atomic functional requirements records with standardized structure.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Architect, Developer, Tester, Compliance.
Prerequisites: Glossary, clear domain concepts, defined system boundaries.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify specific system triggers, states, or conditions. 2. Select applicable EARS pattern (Ubiquitous, Event-driven, State-driven, Unwanted behaviour, Optional). 3. Draft requirement using pattern: Condition/trigger, the system shall observable response object qualifier. 4. Perform quality checks (singular, unambiguous, verifiable).
Analyst Questions & Prompts: When does this happen? While in what state? What exact response must the system produce? How will we test this?
Minimal Realistic Example: FR-TRI-02: If one or more mandatory evidence categories are absent, the Triage Service shall set the case status to More information required and identify every absent category.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Requirement characteristics (Necessary, Appropriate, Unambiguous, Complete, Singular, Feasible, Verifiable, Correct, Conforming).
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Using vague words ('user-friendly', 'fast', 'seamless', 'appropriate'), passive voice, design pre-determination, combining multiple triggers/obligations into one sentence.
When NOT to Use: High-level goal setting or open-ended exploratory product discovery.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Decision Tables (for rule combinations), State Models, Acceptance Examples.
Supported Decisions: Acceptance, architecture, compliance.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Add metadata fields for guardrails, audit logging requirements, and specific automated fallback behaviors.

Problem Solved: Eliminates ambiguity, missed combinations, and errors in rule-heavy domain logic, multi-condition workflows, and boundary conditions.
Input Artifacts: Business rules, policies, stakeholder interviews, regulatory documents.
Output Artifacts: Decision table matrix (conditions, combinations, and explicit required results).
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, SME, Business Owner, Developer, Tester.
Prerequisites: Identified condition inputs and possible system outcome actions.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify all condition variables and their possible values (e.g., Yes/No, ranges). 2. Calculate all potential condition combinations. 3. Determine the required system result for each combination. 4. Simplify/collapse redundant rules if logic permits.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: What happens if condition A is met but condition B fails? Are all possible logical combinations accounted for?
Minimal Realistic Example: Matrix evaluating 'Evidence complete', 'Confidence above threshold', and 'Policy conflict' to yield outcomes: Request missing information, Analyst review, Specialist review, or Automated path.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Completeness check (2^n rules represented or explicitly consolidated); no contradictory outputs for identical inputs.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Overlooking negative combinations, leaving missing conditions blank, embedding rules implicitly inside unstructured prose.
When NOT to Use: Simple linear processes with no conditional branching or simple single-rule scenarios.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Decision Trees, Atomic Functional Requirements, Executable Acceptance Examples.
Supported Decisions: Acceptance, business logic compliance, release verification.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Provides explicit guardrail evaluation matrix for routing agent outputs vs. requiring human escalation.

Method Name: Specification by Example (SBE) / Executable Acceptance Examples
Problem Solved: Bridging gaps between business, developers, and testers; eliminates ambiguity in business rules by providing testable, living documentation.
Input Artifacts: Use cases, decision tables, atomic functional requirements.
Output Artifacts: Concrete acceptance examples (e.g., Given/When/Then scenarios), living acceptance documentation.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Product Manager/Owner, Developer, Tester.
Prerequisites: Agreed functional requirement or rule scope.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Discuss requirements collaboratively using concrete realistic examples. 2. Formulate examples using standard structures (Given-When-Then). 3. Refine examples to expose edge cases and boundary conditions. 4. Link examples to automated test suites to form living documentation.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Can you give a specific realistic data example? What is an example where this rule would fail? What is the exact expected result for this input?
Minimal Realistic Example: Given a ready case missing proof of identity, when completeness is evaluated, then the status becomes More information required and proof of identity appears in the missing-category list.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Examples are concrete, realistic, objective, and can be validated automatically or manually as acceptance tests.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Creating abstract examples without real values, treating examples as complete replacements for core requirement definitions, failing to maintain examples as living docs.
When NOT to Use: Early exploratory research before domain concepts and rules are defined.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Quality-Attribute Scenarios, Decision Tables, Traceability Matrix.
Supported Decisions: Acceptance, release readiness.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Serves as validation datasets and prompt evaluation benchmarks (evals) for testing agent compliance.

Problem Solved: Converts vague quality claims (e.g., 'scalable', 'fast', 'secure') into precise, measurable, verifiable architecture-significant obligations.
Input Artifacts: Non-functional requirements, architectural risks, business constraints.
Output Artifacts: 6-part Quality-Attribute Scenario statements (Source, Stimulus, Environment, Artifact, Response, Response Measure).
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Architect, Developer, Tester, Security/Compliance.
Prerequisites: Understanding of solution context, operational environments, and critical quality attributes.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify quality attribute concern (e.g., performance, security, availability). 2. Specify Source of Stimulus and Stimulus. 3. Define Environment context and affected Artifact boundary. 4. Define system Response and precise numerical Response Measure.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Who or what triggers the event? Under what operational state? Which component responds? How fast/reliable must it be measured over what interval?
Minimal Realistic Example: During normal operation, when an analyst opens a evaluated case, the Case Review interface shall display recommendation within 2 seconds for at least 95% of requests over a rolling 15-minute interval.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Scenario contains all 6 elements; includes measurable, non-subjective acceptance threshold.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Using unmeasurable adjectives ('user-friendly', 'robust'); analyst inventing arbitrary targets without stakeholder or technical validation.
When NOT to Use: Low-risk, non-critical features where standard system baseline performance/security defaults suffice.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Fit Criteria (Volere), Non-Functional Requirements Catalog.
Supported Decisions: Architecture design, release criteria, SLA compliance.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Specifies thresholds for AI latency, confidence levels, hallucination tolerance, and security audit logging response times.

Problem Solved: Address stakeholder conflicts, missing rationale, unexpected obstacles, and misalignment between high-level business goals and software functions.
Input Artifacts: Business problem statement, stakeholder requests, high-level vision.
Output Artifacts: Goal model/tree, obstacle and mitigation set, conflict resolution protocol.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Sponsor, Business Owner, Domain SME, Architect.
Prerequisites: Defined business vision and access to key decision-makers.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify high-level business goals and refine them into sub-goals (AND/OR decomposition). 2. Assign goals to agents (human or system). 3. Analyze potential obstacles to goal satisfaction. 4. Define mitigations/resolutions for obstacles and stakeholder goal conflicts.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Why is this goal needed? What obstacles could prevent achieving this outcome? How do we resolve conflict between stakeholder goal A and goal B?
Minimal Realistic Example: Goal: Reduce manual triage. Obstacle: Unsupported automatic decisions due to low AI confidence. Mitigation: Route low confidence cases to manual review queue.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Goal tree is complete; all leaf goals are assigned to agents; all identified obstacles have explicit mitigations.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Focusing solely on functional features without understanding goals/rationale; ignoring stakeholder goal conflicts.
When NOT to Use: Small projects with trivial changes, well-known domain context, and no stakeholder disagreement.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Problem/Opportunity Statement, Context Diagrams, Use Case Modeling.
Supported Decisions: Scope determination, architectural direction, risk mitigation strategy.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Analyzes risks of agentic autonomy failures, defining guardrails and fallback mechanisms as explicit obstacle mitigations.

Problem Solved: Prevents superficial sign-offs and missing flaws by replacing single unfocused approvals with structured, multi-perspective reviews.
Input Artifacts: Draft specification artifacts (use cases, requirements set, decision tables, quality scenarios, examples).
Output Artifacts: Review defects log, quality gateway approval, updated requirement status.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Sponsor/Business Owner, Engineering/Architect, Tester/QA.
Prerequisites: Complete draft requirement specification set and review checklist.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Conduct Pass 1 (Business Validation): Verify problem fit and value. 2. Conduct Pass 2 (Requirements Quality Review): Check ambiguity, completeness, singularity. 3. Conduct Pass 3 (Engineering Review): Validate interface, dependency, and architecture feasibility. 4. Conduct Pass 4 (Testability Review): Verify testability and boundary coverage via walkthrough scenarios.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Does this behavior solve the intended business problem? Can this obligation be verified by a clear test method? Are negative cases covered?
Minimal Realistic Example: A team walks through realistic case intake scenarios to verify that manual triage exceptions are correctly routed before baseline sign-off.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Verification against ISO 29148 individual/set criteria and checklist sign-off across all 4 distinct review perspectives.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Asking stakeholders to sign off on massive unread documents without realistic scenario walkthroughs.
When NOT to Use: Extremely minor baseline changes or bug fixes where informal peer review is sufficient.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Peer Review, Prototype Walkthrough, Quality Gateway Checklist.
Supported Decisions: Baseline sign-off, release readiness, architectural acceptance.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Includes automated syntax check guardrails followed by Human-in-the-Loop review for logic and governance safety.

Method Name: Business Process Modeling (As-Is and To-Be Modeling)
Problem Solved: Reduces uncertainty and misalignment in business process automation by identifying current process bottlenecks, manual inefficiency, and gaps before building software.
Input Artifacts: Organization charts, current operational documentation, user interview notes, industry process standards.
Output Artifacts: As-is process flows, to-be process flows, swimlane diagrams, activity diagrams, flowcharts, use cases.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst (lead), SME / End User (process actors), Business Owner / Sponsor, Developer.
Prerequisites: Documented business objectives linked to business processes, identified affected organizations and user classes.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Understand business objectives and link each objective to specific processes. 2. Identify affected organizations and potential user classes via organization charts. 3. Identify all relevant business processes involving those user classes. 4. Document as-is business processes using flowcharts, activity diagrams, or swimlane diagrams. 5. Analyze as-is processes to identify bottlenecks and automation opportunities (optionally overlay metrics via KPIM). 6. Walk through as-is process flows with stakeholders to elicit software requirements for each step. 7. Trace software requirements to process flow steps to confirm scope. 8. Document to-be process flows and use cases to detail future interactions and transition requirements.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How do users currently perform these tasks? Where are the major delays or bottlenecks? Which process steps are manual versus automated? What transition gaps or manual steps need to be retired?
Minimal Realistic Example: Mapping a loan application process showing risk managers spending hours assembling spreadsheet data manually, then designing a to-be flow where data inputs are pulled automatically into the calculation tool.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Process models are walkable with stakeholders for validation; all in-scope process steps have requirements traced to them; end users confirm accuracy of steps and roles.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Over-modeling the as-is state down to irrelevant details; automating a broken manual process without redesigning it; assuming software alone will fix process shortcomings without process/culture change.
When NOT to Use: When process problems stem purely from lack of operational execution or missing roles rather than system gaps, or when minor low-risk changes do not justify formal flow modeling.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Data Flow Diagrams (DFDs), Key Performance Indicator Model (KPIM), Use Case Modeling, Value Stream Mapping.
Supported Decisions: Scope determination (which process steps to automate vs. keep manual), release phase planning, operational process change decisions.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Not in source

Problem Solved: Reduces misalignment and wrong prioritization by directly quantifying process efficiency gains and linking requirements to measurable business metrics.
Input Artifacts: As-is process flows (flowcharts, swimlane diagrams, activity diagrams), success metrics from vision and scope document.
Output Artifacts: KPIM diagrams (process models with KPI annotations overlaid on specific steps), prioritized requirement lists.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Business Owner / Sponsor, Subject Matter Expert.
Prerequisites: Established baseline values for current business performance metrics and process models.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Identify critical business performance metrics and KPIs (e.g., execution time, error rates). 2. Measure current baseline values for each KPI. 3. Overlay KPIs onto specific process steps in flowcharts or swimlane diagrams. 4. Prioritize process steps that show the highest impact on target KPIs. 5. Trace software requirements to process steps mapped to KPIs to establish implementation priority. 6. (Optional) Specify system functionality to periodically monitor KPIs post-implementation.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: How long does it take to execute individual process steps? What is the current baseline value for this metric? Which performance metrics are most critical to maintain or improve? What performance trade-offs are acceptable?
Minimal Realistic Example: Annotating a loan risk calculation flowchart with KPI-1: 'Reduce data aggregation time from 120 minutes to 2 minutes' and KPI-2: '100% error-free data inputs'.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Clear linkage between process steps, KPIs, and software requirements; baseline metrics documented and validated by business stakeholders.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Automating decisions or steps where custom logic development costs far exceed the operational value gained; degrading critical quality attributes in pursuit of a single metric.
When NOT to Use: When metrics data cannot be measured, or when process automation scope is trivial and metrics-driven trade-offs are unnecessary.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Goal modeling, Planguage metric specification, Quality Function Deployment (QFD).
Supported Decisions: Requirement prioritization decisions, release scope decisions, trade-off decisions between competing performance attributes.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Not in source

Problem Solved: Reduces uncertainty and feature creep in business intelligence and reporting projects by focusing on the specific decisions stakeholders need to make rather than just collecting lists of requested reports or fields.
Input Artifacts: Business objectives, stakeholder requests for reports/data, regulatory or policy constraints.
Output Artifacts: Decision statements, report specifications, dashboard designs, display-action-response models, data transformation requirements, formula specifications.
Participants & Roles: Business Analyst, Executive / Business Decision Maker, Data Specialist / Architect, System Analyst.
Prerequisites: Defined business objectives establishing the problem space.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Elicit and state the core business decisions stakeholders must make to achieve business objectives. 2. Prioritize business decisions based on their contribution to business objectives. 3. Decompose each decision into underlying diagnostic questions and precursor sub-questions. 4. Determine the information delivery mechanism (e.g., dashboard, portal, email), format, and required interactivity/flexibility (filters, drill-downs). 5. Specify data requirements (sources, volume, refresh rates, retention, security). 6. Define data transformation and computational logic (formulas, decision tables/trees) required to convert raw data into insights.
Analyst Questions & Prompts: Why do you think an analytics solution will help you achieve desired outcomes? What specific business decisions will you make using output from this system? Why do you need that information and how will you use that report? What time frame are you analyzing: past, present, or future? What formula or business rule defines this calculation?
Minimal Realistic Example: Defining a decision statement for a marketing VP needing quarterly regional budget allocation based on current sales, leading to specific dashboard requirements with regional and product-line drill-down filters.
Quality Criteria & Verification: Every analytics report/dashboard traces directly to an identified business decision; calculation formulas are fully specified with clear variables and sources; data latency and security constraints are defined.
Errors & Anti-Patterns: Focusing solely on specifying data fields without understanding usage; delivering static data when ad-hoc exploration is needed; overbuilding analytics capabilities beyond stakeholder readiness; assuming traditional use cases alone capture decision-making complexity.
When NOT to Use: When the system requires standard operational transactional capabilities with simple, static reporting needs.
Alternatives & Complementary Methods: Decision Tables / Decision Trees, Decision Models, Display-Action-Response (DAR) models, Report Tables.
Supported Decisions: Scope definition for analytics projects, decision automation vs. human-in-the-loop decisions, release iteration content.
AI & Agentic Adaptation: Not in source

Problem Solved: Reduces structural conflicts, integration failures, and cost overruns in complex embedded/real-time systems by systematically decomposing system-level requirements and allocating them across hardware, software, and human roles.
Input Artifacts: System Requirements Specification (SyRS), business rules, environmental constraints.
Output Artifacts: Software Requirements Specification (SRS), Hardware Requirements Specification, Manual Requirements, Architecture Diagrams, Requirements Traceability Matrix.
Participants & Roles: System Analyst / Requirements Engineer / System Architect (lead), System Engineer, Software Developer, Hardware Engineer, Subject Matter Expert.
Prerequisites: Completed or draft System Requirements Specification (SyRS) describing overall system inputs, outputs, performance, safety, and quality attributes.
Step-by-Step Procedure: Analyze system requirements and overall system architecture. 2. Partition the system into logical subsystems and components (hardware, software, manual operations). 3. Decompose high-level system requirements into derived software, hardware, and manual requirements. 4.
